name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Longtime homeless cleanup nonprofit shuts down, leaving 125 unemployed
text:
Advantage Services employees Anthony Tarchick, Max Loveridge, and Trevor Howell, left to right, clean out bins of abandoned property at the Transitional Storage Program  in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Despite efforts to save about 125 jobs, most of which were held by people experiencing homelessness and other challenges, the longtime Utah social enterprise nonprofit Advantage Services is shutting down amid financial struggles. 
“With heavy hearts, we announce that Advantage Services will be closing its doors and ceasing all services” effective Saturday, the nonprofit’s CEO Rob Ferris wrote in an email to customers and other community partners sent Thursday. 
He told Utah News Dispatch he and his team were in “shock” after receiving an email from the state Office of Homeless Services on Thursday that sank their last hope for a solution to save the social enterprise that’s existed for more than 34 years or the jobs it provides to vulnerable people. 
Rob Ferris, CEO of Advantage Services, Inc., poses for a photograph at their facility in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
“We didn’t think that we were too big to fail, but we thought we were too important to let go,” he said. “The services that we provide are vital to the unsheltered community, to our community partners.” 
Ferris said over the next 30 days he’ll be working on liquidating the company’s assets, which includes a fleet of vehicles, in hopes he can use the money to pay out employees’ unused vacation time as severance. 
He’s also encouraging any current customers or members of Utah’s homeless services network interested in hiring his former employees to reach out to him. 
Why is Advantage Services shutting down?
Utah News Dispatch reported in August that Advantage Services had been facing financial woes due to several issues: unexpected cost increases, higher insurance premiums, and scaled-back contracts from various customers. But one of the biggest reasons was its largest contract with Salt Lake City’s Urban Services Division was slashed in half from roughly $2 million to less than $1 million. 
Longtime Utah homeless cleanup nonprofit on brink of bankruptcy, issues ‘urgent’ call for help

Since then Ferris has been trying to expand Advantage Services’ contracts or merge with another nonprofit to preserve its jobs so that the people who rely on the nonprofit for work aren’t left unemployed. Earlier this month, he furloughed about 110 employees as a last-ditch effort to keep the company afloat after not being able to make payroll. 
Earlier this month Advantage Services’ situation caught the attention of the Utah Homeless Services Board, the powerful body that oversees the state’s homeless system and distributes state funding to homeless service providers. State Homeless Coordinator Tyler Clancy expressed a willingness to explore solutions, but none came before the clock ran out. 
In response to Ferris’ request for “emergency bridge funding” to keep Advantage Services afloat, an Office of Homeless Services staffer told Ferris in an email Thursday “OHS will not be able to provide funding for the requested purpose.”
Advantage Services employees Max Loveridge, Anthony Tarchick and Trevor Howell, left to right, drop off a trailer of garbage at the landfill in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
Ferris said the social enterprise nonprofit’s slide toward closure has been “devastating” to his employees. He also worries that the loss of Advantage Service will leave a “void” in Utah’s homeless services network — not just because of their now canceled clean-up contracts on city streets, state highways and more, plus transportation services to and from homeless resource centers, but also because of the people that relied on the work. 
“I have some of my homeless employees, or people who’ve just come off the streets and got apartments, now concerned that they’re going to be homeless again because nobody’s going to hire them because of their criminal record,” Ferris said. “Each person that is employed by Advantage Services has some sort of barrier to employment.” 
‘We need help’: Homeless cleanup nonprofit furloughs employees, faces full shutdown

Since it was formed in 1992, Advantage Services has employed people who are disadvantaged, whether they have disabilities, are currently or formerly homeless, leaving jail or prison, are refugees, or are living in poverty. 
The nonprofit doesn’t function like a typical employer, but rather provides “supportive employment,” offering job coaching, mentoring, and other resources to help meet employees’ needs so they can not only work, but “thrive.”
The work Advantage Services employees do isn’t glamorous. They pick up garbage, clean up homeless encampments, power wash streets of biohazards, shuttle people to and from homeless shelters, and more, depending on the contract. But the opportunity to work can be life-changing for people building their resumes and developing life skills. 
‘I feel betrayed’
Megan Belagam, who worked as Advantage Services’ office manager, was in tears after she learned that her employer would be shutting down and she’d be out of a job. 
“My heart stopped,” she said. 
Belagam said she’s worked in various roles for Advantage Services since 2013, when Ferris gave her a job during a time when she struggled to find employment. She said she was diagnosed with arthrogryposis multiplex congenita, which affects ligaments, tendons and muscles in her feet, arms and wrists, creating mobility challenges. 
Ferris gave her a chance, Belagam said, and the job gave her “independence,” enabling her to get off Supplemental Security Income, federal assistance that’s offered to people with disabilities and older adults with little or no income.

“The idea of possibly having to go back to that is paralyzing,” she said, choking back tears. “That’s what I’m looking at. Rob and his team saw past my hands and what I could do. They gave me a chance. And so having that taken away from me, I feel very robbed.” 
Belagam also grieved for her fellow employees, who she called “family.” 
“They don’t have anywhere else to go, either,” she said. But she said she’s urging her coworkers to “not give up hope, to keep moving forward. … I’m very scared right now and I know that I do not know what my future holds, but I’m going to keep trying.” 
Belagam said she’s devastated but also angry, especially because of the slashed Salt Lake City contract that in large part led to Advantage Services’ failure. 
“I feel betrayed,” she said, not just for herself but for the other employees. “I am damn mad that they took away their opportunity. I am damn mad at that.”
What angers her the most, Belagam said, is “this shutdown has dehumanized” Advantage Services’ workers, “and nobody cares.”
Advantage Services employees Anthony Tarchick and Max Loveridge, left to right, clean up abandoned property called in by a police officer in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)

title: A tale of two districts: Opportunities differ in Greenville and Western Line schools
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
GREENVILLE — Disheanna Brown is apartment hunting down the road from her home. The four-minute drive is the difference between two school districts, and from Brown’s perspective, whether her child has a positive academic experience.
She sees Greenville Public schools, her son’s current district, as holding him back. The nearby Western Line district provides the services and resources he would need for success, such as an updated learning plan and a full-time special education teacher.
Brown’s story isn’t unique. Mississippi Today spoke to two dozen real estate agents, parents, recent high school graduates from Western Line and Greenville, and Washington County community members who shared a similar sentiment: Parents want their families in the Western Line zone. School data makes it clear why.
A neighborhood that has students form different school districts is pictured in Greenville on Thursday, Sept. 17, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Western Line has achieved a rare feat in the Mississippi Delta: stable leadership, decent to good scores on the state accountability scale and a clean record with the state Department of Education as it relates to accreditation violations and investigations of wrongdoing.
Closer to the heart of the city, worse outcomes for students abound in the Greenville Public School District. The Greenville district gets more money than Western Line because it enrolls more students, but it struggled to balance its budget last year and posted some of the lowest test scores in the state the past decade. Administrative turnover is frequent, and the state Education Department has downgraded its accreditation to probation for the last three years.
The district did gain an additional 25 points on the state accountability scale for the past school year. The largest growth was at Coleman Middle School, which saw an 101 point increase, lifting the school from an F rating to a D rating.
The sheer number of school districts in Washington County has made the area a focus for consolidation. The county has four school districts, more than anywhere else in the state. 
But its county seat, Greenville, is the second-fastest shrinking city in the country, according to the U.S. Census Bureau. 
Whether combining the city school districts would expand opportunity for Greenville students or disrupt success in Western Line depends on whom you ask.
“I am scared. We need to be proactive instead of letting things happen to us,” Rep. John Hines, a Democrat from Greenville, said about the city’s waning population and other leadership problems. “We need a plan.”
Dysfunction in Greenville schools
Hines remembers when Greenville Public Schools was the highest-performing district in the Delta. A graduate himself, he sent all of his children to district schools. 
Lately, the district has been plagued with financial issues, high administrative turnover and underperforming schools. 
Brown, too, is a product of Greenville schools. She wanted her children to have the same experience: safe schools, engaging educators and activities available to students of all abilities. But it became clear in the past few years, the district had changed. 
Board members and school officials from Washington County’s four school districts assemble for a meeting on consolidation legislation at the Washington County Convention Center, in Greenville, Mississippi, on Sept. 24, 2026. Credit: Leonardo Bevilacqua/Mississippi Today
Last year, a school employee informed her that her son ingested bleach. She said she had to rush him to the hospital in her car. Later, she said, district officials told her they fired the special education teacher assigned to her son’s classroom.
She learned last month that the teacher wasn’t replaced. That means her son has been without a certified teacher since spring 2025, which is illegal under federal law. 
Jerron Parker said he waited nearly two years for Greenville school officials to test his daughter, who attends Stern Elementary, for special education services. He suspects that happened because of administrative turnover at the school. 
He worries his daughter will continue to fall behind.
“Because of where we stay, my kids don’t have another choice of going to another school in the district that I feel like will probably help with the issue that I have,” Parker said. 
Mississippi Today spoke to three other parents who faced the same obstacles in getting a quality education for their disabled children in Greenville. The state education department found the district was out of compliance with more than a third of special education standards. 
The agency has also downgraded the district’s accreditation status in March over financial issues. That same month, the district was operating $1.5 million over budget. 
Jerron Park is pictured with his daughters at Schelben Park in Greenville, Mississippi, on Sept. 16, 2026. Credit: Leonardo Bevilacqua/Mississippi Today
Some trace district dysfunction and poor oversight of Greenville schools to school board members and City Hall’s role in their appointment. School board members become too enmeshed in the politics of City Hall, some parents told Mississippi Today.
It wasn’t lost on lawmakers, either. While a 2025 bill to consolidate districts in Washington County did not include Greenville schools, it called for dissolving the Greenville school board and holding new elections for the positions.
“Part of the struggle of Greenville is appointed school board members over elected,” Hines said. “I’ve long wanted elected board members.”
Antoinette Williams, Greenville’s school board president, believes many of the challenges making headlines this year were the result of decisions made by inexperienced superintendents. She said Superintendent Ilean Richards, who was a state conservator in Leflore County School District from January 2016 to November 2017, will improve academic performance and clear remaining accreditation problems in her second full year on the job.
“There is going to be a lot of progress, but it’s a good portion that had to be cleaned up first,” Williams said. “We’re seeing a lot of light at the end of the tunnel.”
‘It starts at home’
But not all of the blame falls on Greenville school leadership, parents and alumni say. The roots of the district’s dysfunction run all the way down the very lines of the city. 
Some of the city’s highest poverty neighborhoods are in Greenville public schools zones. Some of the wealthiest areas are within the Western Line district.
Over half of students live below the poverty line in Greenville’s district. About 31% of students live below the poverty line in Western Line’s district.
Students from low-income families tend to have more responsibilities at home that they prioritize over school, Williams said. Sometimes school staff also have to ensure students have clean clothes and other necessities.
“If my child is hungry, they can’t learn. They focus on being hungry more than they focus on whatever the teacher is trying to say,” she said.
“It starts at home,” said Chris Williams, a parent teacher association member at T.L. Weston Middle School. Other parents and community members expressed similar feelings and said students’ poor outcomes aren’t the school district’s fault alone.
Bianca Miller, an alum and community member, said she doesn’t go to school events for fear of violence. 
Beatrice Mitchell, left, and Bianca Mitchell talk about school consolidation on Thursday, Sept. 17, 2026, in Greenville. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Greenville schools reported more incidents of violence than any other district in the state when adjusted for population. Antoinette Williams said the data reflects thorough reporting. She said Richards is addressing the problem by hiring more school resource officers and rotating administrators through different school buildings throughout the day. Another plan that was put into place is to have students transition between classes at different times to curb opportunities for fights, she said.
For Western Line parents, the district offers a quieter, more focused learning environment. Parents say they feel like partners in their students’ education.
The communities served are small, and so are the student populations. Western Line schools served 1,658 students in 2025-26, roughly half the Greenville schools enrollment. Parents describe it as a “family.”
A Western Line School District decal on a vehicle at Riverside Schools in Avon, Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
Western Line Superintendent Lawrence Hudson said the district has found success through strong partnerships with community stakeholders and parents, preparing children for achievements after school and focusing on financial health by aggressively applying for grants. 
“Things like that set us apart,” he said. “A lot of people believe in us.” 
Special education is another area where Western Line shines, as Greenville flounders. Students with disabilities are identified early in the district and given the best teachers. The success of their program leads to regular calls from parents, Hudson said, who want their child in his schools. 
‘Afraid of change’
State lawmakers have said it makes little financial sense for Washington County to have so many school districts. For parents like Deondria Watson, the setup can lead to better outcomes for all students, including those students who live deeper in Greenville.
Deondria Watson is pictured with her daughter at Schelben Park in Greenville, Mississippi, on Sept. 16, 2026. Credit: Leonardo Bevilacqua/Mississippi Today
“I don’t think that’s a bad thing,” Watson, a Western Line parent, said of consolidation in Washington County. “I think that if they all combine, whichever school is lacking, I think the ones that’s performing above standard, can get help to bring the others up.”
“I think people are afraid of change.”
But leaders in Hollandale, Leland and Western Line said they’re concerned a consolidation threatens their success. 
Lawmakers have only said that they’re interested in legislating a school district consolidation in Washington County. The plan they proposed in 2025 could hint at their plans. 
Last year, state leaders were considering legislating a consolidation for the Western Line, Leland and Hollandale school districts. Superintendents of those districts met with state leaders, including House Education Chairman Rob Roberson, a Republican from Starkville, and convinced him that a consolidation would only hurt their schools. The bill died in committee.
Hudson, the Western Line superintendent, said it wouldn’t make sense to merge the three small districts, all of which are C-rated or higher. He and the Rev. Jesse King, superintendent of Leland schools, pointed to Greenville’s struggles instead. 
“If Greenville is the trigger for this consolidation conversation, it does not make sense to us that they stay out of the conversation,” King said. 
But none of the three districts are volunteering to merge with Greenville and absorb its dysfunction and thousands of students, either.
Western Line School District Superintendent Lawrence Hudson chats with fourth graders during a visit at Riverside Elementary School, Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026, in Avon. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
“I’m just kind of confused,” Hudson said. “I have 1,700 students who look forward to school in their district. These students matter just as much as students in Greenville, Leland and Hollandale.”
Education researcher Marguerite Roza said consolidations can improve schools if they’re combined with a district that’s well run. 
“However, merging two underperforming districts isn’t going to get that done,” said Roza, a research professor at Georgetown University. 
Hudson was surprised that lawmakers are once again looking to merge districts in Washington County. 
“Nothing came up in the 2026 session, so we were under the impression that we may be off the table at least for a while,” he said. “We’ve never heard any mentions of any of the county schools being consolidated with Greenville city schools.” 
“That’s a whole different ball game.”
Delta towns fight to survive
Democrats who represent the area, such as Hines, Sen. Derrick Simmons and Rep. Willie Bailey, generally oppose consolidation in their county, citing equity concerns
They want their school districts to improve, but they said they worry about the impact on their small, struggling communities. 
“Everybody likes to pick on the Delta,” Hines said. “If it’s not poverty, it’s race. We’re always fighting for survival on every front.”
Democratic Rep. John W. Hines of Greenville speaks on the House floor at the Mississippi Capitol in Jackson on Wednesday, April 15, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
State lawmakers say they’re not focusing on a particular region, that they’re trying to curb administrative spending and improve student performance through consolidations. However, Washington County districts that serve majority-Black populations are often struggling because they have been historically under-resourced, said Carrie Hahnel of Bellwether, a nonprofit education organization that works to improve student outcomes.
Additionally, in rural communities, school districts can serve as economic engines and community hubs. Hines said he doesn’t want mergers to jeopardize the viability of Delta towns.
“Hollandale’s district is the largest employer there,” he said. “Leland is the same. We have to be mindful. These situations are not cookie cutter.”
Still, Roza said the facts don’t line up. Many small, underperforming districts in the state also spend the most money on students. 
“When you put those two pieces of information together, you can see why state leaders are thinking, ‘Why should we be subsidizing smallness?’” she said. “At what point do you keep putting state funds into the school district?”
Parker, a Greenville father, is skeptical about the benefits of consolidation. He said Greenville schools can only improve if more parents get involved, and take an active role in their children’s education. A consolidation, he said, could lead to worse outcomes for students.
“So you’re going to cut administrators, and overwork the ones that are there, and you’re expecting it to get better,” Parker said of lawmakers’ plans. “Everyone’s kids are walking past ours.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Shakopee man from Nicaragua deported to Central African Republic
text:
Kenis Lopez Gonzalez. Courtesy photo. Kenis Lopez Gonzalez fled political persecution in Nicaragua in 2022 and turned himself in to immigration authorities upon arriving in the U.S. Two years later, an immigration judge ruled that he could not be deported back to Nicaragua because he was at risk of being tortured there. 
He moved to Shakopee, Minnesota, started a construction company and paid taxes, he said. He has no criminal record.
After his arrest during Operation Metro Surge, Lopez was sent roughly 7,000 miles to the Central African Republic.
“I told them I was scared of going to that country,” Lopez said in Spanish during an interview from detention in the politically unstable, landlocked country, which has a population roughly equivalent to Minnesota but where the life expectancy is just 57. 
He is fighting for his return to the United States. 
In its quest to deport millions of immigrants, the Trump administration is sending people like Lopez, who have protections from deportation to their home countries, to nations that have agreed to accept deportees in exchange for cash or other concessions. Those countries are largely authoritarian. One of the most publicized examples is El Salvador, whose autocratic President Nayib Bukele accepted $6 million and more than 250 deportees, mostly Venezuelans, who were held in the country’s notorious Terrorism Confinement Center. Detainees have reported beatings by guards, sexual assault, psychological abuse, lack of medical treatment and poor living conditions. 
More recently, several countries in Africa have signed agreements with the Trump administration to hold deportees. The terms of the agreement between the U.S. and the Central African Republic have not been disclosed, but the African nation began accepting detainees following a payment of $85 million to the country’s International Organization for Migration, according to the U.S. Committee for Refugees and Immigrants, which is tracking third-country deportations. 
In Eswatini, an absolute monarchy, detainees have no pathway to freedom. In the Democratic Republic of the Congo, deportees from Latin America live among the millions of Congolese people whose homes and businesses were destroyed in war. 
The Central African Republic is a politically unstable country that has been mired in violence since rebels overthrew the government in 2013. Lopez, bound by the walls of the detention center, is isolated from daily life there. But his future is uncertain.
Immigration and Customs Enforcement did not immediately respond to the Reformer’s emailed questions for this story.
Ten months in detention and counting
Lopez was warming up his car in the driveway of his Shakopee home on the morning of Jan. 15 when eight immigration agents approached him and asked if he was a citizen, according to a court declaration. 
Lopez showed them the court order barring his deportation, along with his work permit and REAL ID. The agents took the papers, then handcuffed Lopez, placed him in a van and drove him to the Whipple Federal Building. 
For months, ICE transferred him from one detention center to another: El Paso; Alexandria, Louisiana; Jackson Parish, Louisiana; Dallas, and then Alvarado, Texas. In April, Lopez finally made contact with an attorney, who filed a habeas corpus petition — a lawsuit arguing that his detention was illegal. 
On Aug. 28, Lopez and dozens of other men, including several other Nicaraguans, were placed on a bus bound for a Texas airport. Lopez didn’t know where they were going, he said. He thought he was being transferred to another detention center in Mississippi. He and the other men were bound at the wrists, ankles and waist. 
It wasn’t until the bus pulled on to the tarmac that Lopez learned he was about to board a plane to the Central African Republic. 
“They didn’t give me any information,” Lopez said. “They tricked me into leaving.” 
The officers ordered the men off of the bus. Lopez and others refused. 
“In that moment I tried to explain to them that first, I had protection,” Lopez said in Spanish, speaking from his cell in a detention center in the Central African Republic. “Second, I had a habeas corpus pending. And third, they were violating my due process rights.”
Then, the officers shot the men inside the bus with pepper balls at close range, he said.
Lopez couldn’t breathe; he suffered wounds from the balls’ impact on his legs, chest and arms. The agents dragged the men out of the bus, and Lopez said he was placed in a “wrap” — a straitjacket-like restraint device — and carried onto the plane. Workers on the plane removed the wrap after what Lopez believes was about an hour, but he remained shackled at the hands, feet and waist for the entire trip to Central African Republic, which took about a day and a half. 
Bruises on Kenis Lopez Gonzalez’s arms after he was shot with pepper balls at close range for refusing to board a plane to the Central African Republic. (Photos submitted as exhibits in court documents.)
He was served food — a sandwich and water bottle — three times over that day and a half, Lopez said. 
Lopez was now among the more than 2,300 Minnesotans shipped out of the country since Operation Metro Surge began in Dec. 2025. 
Since his arrival in the Central African Republic, he’s been detained in what seems to be an apartment building converted to a detention center, he said. He has a phone, but cell service and electricity are spotty.
For the first two months, the food made him sick, he said. Now, he’s no longer ill, but finds the meals unappetizing. 
Every day, he wakes up and reads the Bible, then exercises in his room. He goes online and checks in with his family, then spends time with another Nicaraguan man he’s befriended. 
He identifies with the story of Job, a man faced with disaster after disaster, testing his faith in God. 
His parents both died in the past year. His wife ended their relationship after Lopez was detained, he said.
“It’s a difficult situation,” Lopez said. “Despite all of that, God’s plan is perfect. He knew all of this was going to happen.”
The Supreme Court is expected to rule on the legality of third country deportations in December. Lopez’s attorneys are asking a judge to order the U.S. government to return Lopez to Minnesota in the meantime. 
A hearing in Lopez’s case is scheduled for Friday at 1 p.m.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Caretakers maintain Alex Pretti memorial despite repeated vandalism
text:
A growing memorial stands Wednesday, Jan. 28, 2026 where Alex Pretti, 37, was shot and killed by Border Patrol agents days before at Nicollet Avenue and 26th Street. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)More than nine months after immigration agents disarmed, shot and killed Alex Pretti in the Whittier neighborhood of Minneapolis, the site of his death on Nicollet Avenue is marked with carefully arranged flowers, candles, art and other offerings brought by visitors from near and far. 
As the snow melted in the spring and the flowers accumulated over the winter began to decay, some neighbors took charge of cleaning and refreshing the memorial every day — replacing wilted flowers, clearing snow and dirt and neatly arranging the memorial’s items.
Lately, these caretakers have been facing another challenge: vandalism.
First, it was raw bacon left among the paintings and cards — a common tactic in Islamophobic hate crimes. On Sept. 11, motor oil coated the memorial, an unsuccessful attempt at burning the mementos. Then, raw tuna hidden throughout the flowers and greenery; the memorial’s signature banner cut from its cords and stolen; a bucket appearing to contain human feces.
On several occasions since September, the caretakers arrived at the memorial in the morning to find it had been covered in spray paint overnight. Another time, the vandal emptied a can of truck bed liner over the site, the sticky black substance presenting a new challenge for those who cleaned the items piece by piece. 
The incidents have shaken the community of people who have taken charge of the memorial — and insulted the memory of Pretti, whose killers have yet to be named by authorities or charged in the shooting. Pretti’s parents, speaking publicly for the first time Tuesday, said they’ve had no contact with the federal government since their son’s death. 
Volunteers clean up the Alex Pretti memorial after a vandal poured motor oil, which is not flammable, over the site Friday, Sept. 11, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)
“Whatever happens, we will be there to restore and repair and recover and clean,” said Jadah Green, one of the caretakers. “Now I think, ‘Okay, you’re coming with whatever violence you have in your life, and you’re inflicting that on the memorial, and the memorial is just going to generate more love.’”
The Minneapolis Police Department is investigating the vandalism. 
“The reported vandalism is troubling and we recognize the pain the repeated damage has caused the Pretti family and the community members who continue to maintain the memorial in his honor,” Brian Feintech, a spokesperson for the Minneapolis Police Department, said in a statement. “These incidents remain open and active investigations. In the meantime, we hope this site remains a place where people can come together to remember, mourn, and find comfort.”
The memorial has become a site for people to gather, grieve and process — not only Pretti’s death, but the entire impact of Operation Metro Surge and the actions of the Trump administration. 
Jeff Wendelberger, another caretaker, said he’s had hundreds of conversations with visitors to the memorial. Some are neighbors who experienced firsthand the chaos wrought by federal agents on the day of Pretti’s death. Others are international visitors, who view Pretti’s killing as an indication of the rise of fascism in America, Wendelberger said. 
Shortly after the immigration agents shot and killed Pretti, Wendelberger rushed to the scene, just a few blocks from his home, and joined in the protest. After the agents left in a cloud of tear gas, he vowed to stay near the scene, to tell visitors exactly what happened that day. 
The killing was “an absolute desecration, not only to our community and our neighbors — our neighborhood — but to humanity,” Wendelberger said. 
He also vowed to clean up the physical remnants of the agents’ presence there — the spent pepper balls and gas canisters, more and more appearing over time as the snow melted. That cleanup work naturally transitioned into caring for the memorial. 
Susan Pretti, the mother of Alex Pretti, said Tuesday that the memorial represents her family’s connection to Minneapolis and what the city experienced during Operation Metro Surge. (Susan and Michael Pretti, Alex’s father, live in Colorado.)
“It means a great deal to us that someone — many people — give their time and effort to take care of it,” Susan Pretti said. “What lovely people.”
Volunteers clean up the Alex Pretti memorial after a vandal poured motor oil, which is not flammable, over the site Friday, Sept. 11, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)

name: Washington State Standard
title: Two Dans, three Bobs: Alaska Senate controversy mirrors 2024 Washington fiasco
text:
Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson at his State of the State address on Jan. 13, 2026. Ferguson did not discuss the budget cuts he's proposing in his speech but they've stoked plenty of testimony in the first days of the 2026 legislative session. (Photo by Bill Lucia/Washington State Standard)The pivotal U.S. Senate race in Alaska is now embroiled in threats from the president and probes from the state’s governor over a candidate appearing on the ballot with the same name as the Republican incumbent. 
Washington state has been there before, though its drama fizzled out before reaching the level of the firestorm erupting in Alaska.
In Alaska, the campaign for Democratic candidate and former congresswoman Mary Peltola, along with the national Democratic Senate campaign arm, recruited candidates to act as spoilers against incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, according to The New York Times. Until the blockbuster reporting was published this week, Peltola had denied any involvement in the run by the second Dan Sullivan, a retired teacher living in remote Alaska. 
Alaska’s governor ordered an investigation into the issue. President Donald Trump called for Peltola to be prosecuted, and has threatened to sue to block the results if she wins a close election. The U.S. Department of Justice reportedly issued new subpoenas as part of a criminal investigation into the scandal Thursday.
This is one of the key campaigns that will decide control of the Senate.
In Washington, the same-name scenario played out in 2024 when three-term Attorney General Bob Ferguson entered as the odds-on favorite in the race for governor. 
It quickly got weird when Glen Morgan, a conservative Republican and founder of We the Governed, convinced two other Washingtonians named Bob Ferguson to join the race for governor, and paid their $2,000 filing fees. Neither had political experience — just disdain for the attorney general.
Ferguson cried foul. He argued the same names appearing alongside his on the primary ballot could mislead voters.

Ferguson’s campaign sent cease-and-desist letters to the other Bobs and threatened to have them criminally prosecuted if they did not withdraw. He vowed to see them charged under a longstanding state law that makes it a felony to run against someone of the same name and “whose political reputation is widely known, with intent to confuse and mislead the electors by capitalizing on the public reputation of the candidate who had previously filed.” 
That law resulted from confusion stirred up in the 1942 primary fight between Commissioner of Public Lands A.C. Martin and an unknown challenger named O.C. Martin. Democratic Rep. John O’Brien of Seattle introduced legislation in the ensuing 1943 session to deal with future situations when candidates with similar names squared off in the same contest.
More than 80 years later, Ferguson, with the help of attorneys from Pacifica Law Group, pushed Secretary of State Steve Hobbs, a fellow Democrat, to differentiate his name-sharers on the ballot with their middle initials and occupations. He also wanted the three to appear consecutively on the ballot.
Hobbs refused to change the candidates’ order, despite Ferguson’s wishes, which led to a “spirited conversation,” Hobbs said at the time.
Those hardball tactics led Mark Mullet, a Democratic state senator also running for governor, to accuse the attorney general of pressuring the secretary of state to break state law over the ballot order. Ferguson insinuated Hobbs wouldn’t change the order because Hobbs had endorsed Mullet, which the election official denied.
In the meantime, the other Bob Fergusons dropped out before the filing deadline, mooting the matter. At the time, one cited harassment and the potential legal action for his decision to exit. 
The episode resulted in various nicknames, including Three Bob Night and the Three Bob Problem. 
Hobbs said Thursday that he tries not to think about that brief issue “from the PTSD I suffered from it.” He added that he would’ve handled the situation the same way now.
“Just like Alaska, we would have clearly called out which Bob was who,” Hobbs said, but “let’s hope that doesn’t happen.”
Morgan said Thursday that he didn’t coordinate with a campaign for his ballot-stacking effort, a clear contrast from the allegations in Alaska.
“Obviously the Democrats think it is just fine in Alaska, but how dare anyone file for office with the same name in Washington state,” he said.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Judge rejects constitutional challenge to Missouri property tax caps tied to stadium bill
text:
Cole County Circuit Judge Christopher Limbaugh ruled that property tax caps included in a bill to support professional sports stadiums are constitutional(Anna Spoerre/Missouri Independent).A Cole County judge on Wednesday rejected a constitutional challenge to property tax caps lawmakers added to a bill aimed at keeping the Kansas City Chiefs in Missouri.
The caps, structured as credits against property tax bills, applied to 97 of Missouri’s 114 counties. The caps, voted on in April, will mean this year’s property tax bill cannot be higher than last year in up to 22 counties, and cannot increase more than 5% in 75 others.
Of the 97 counties listed in the legislation, 61 passed it, 14 designated for tax bill freezes and 47 with the 5% cap; 12 counties rejected it; and 23 counties did not hold elections.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The law was challenged by two individuals, six school districts and one fire district. Forty-three counties, as well as individual county commissioners, later joined the case.
In his decision, Cole County Circuit Judge Christopher Limbaugh ruled that none of the plaintiffs had the right to sue and that they were wrong on the legal issues they raised.
Individuals do not have a right to sue simply because they believe they are at a disadvantage to a person in another county because of a property tax law, Limbaugh wrote. And the taxing districts can’t sue because they haven’t lost any money, he ruled.
The counties didn’t have the right to sue either, he wrote. They can’t raise issues on behalf of the school districts and other agencies they collect money for, he ruled.
“Missouri case law does not recognize standing based on dissatisfaction that other jurisdictions may impose different local taxes or conduct assessments differently; rather, Missouri case law recognizes standing where the plaintiff can show a present, direct adverse effect,” Limbaugh wrote.
The lawsuit was filed in September 2025, challenging the right of the legislature to write a law that provided property tax freezes in some counties, caps in others and no limits on increases in individual bills in 17 other counties and the city of St. Louis. The lawsuit alleged lawmakers used population and other characteristics to single out individual counties, creating special or local laws prohibited by the Missouri Constitution.
It was the second case challenging the stadium bill passed in a June 2025 special session. On Sept. 1, the Missouri Supreme Court heard an appeal in a separate lawsuit filed by two lawmakers and a conservative activist.
The court must decide whether state Sen. Mike Moon, an Ash Grove Republican, state Rep. Bryant Wolfin, a Ste. Genevieve Republican, and conservative activist Ron Calzone have standing. In January, Limbaugh ruled they did not and dismissed their lawsuit.
If the court finds Moon, Wolfin and Calzone do have standing, their case returns to Limbaugh.
The Missouri Supreme Court will also be asked to reverse Limbaugh in the case decided Wednesday, attorney Jim Layton said. Layton represents one of the individual plaintiffs and several other districts.
“We are disappointed in the decision,” Layton said. “But we always recognized that the questions we presented are ultimately ones for the Supreme Court of Missouri to resolve, and this finally allows us to proceed to that court.”
In their challenge the districts also argued that the uneven application of the caps meant the tax burden could shift from county to county in districts that cross county lines.
The credits, which will be shown on each tax bill as the difference between the previous and current year, mean districts could lose revenue. The taxpayer will see an increase when levies to repay bond issues increase or new taxes are approved by voters. 
If the Legislature grants a tax exemption for homesteads, the districts argued, it must reimburse the districts for lost revenue.
The districts also argued that the division of counties among the three categories lacked a rational basis.
Limbaugh rejected those arguments, siding with the attorney general’s office. The officials in one county have no injury from tax elections and actions in another county, he ruled. 
The credits don’t divide property into subclasses — residential, commercial, agricultural, personal and state-assessed infrastructure — in ways the law prohibits, Limbaugh ruled.
“In sum, having different tax credits does not change the classification of the property as residential property,” he wrote. “A tax credit goes to the taxpayer, not the property.”
The individual counties were added to the bill during a lengthy, late-night debate as senators consulted local officials about whether their counties should be included in the caps..
In his ruling, Limbaugh found that chronic underassessment in counties across the state, and the spike in tax bills that can follow a catch-up assessment provided a rational basis for the law.
Limbaugh also cited the political pressures facing county assessors, pointing to an affidavit from Stacey Jacobs, administrative secretary of the State Tax Commission.
Assessors are reluctant to update property values, Jacobs said. 
“Many of these assessors have expressed concern to (the commission) that reassessment could subject their constituents to massive tax spikes and impact their re-election efforts,” Jacobs said.
The counties that joined the lawsuit are deciding whether to appeal, their attorney, Travis Elliott, said.
Natalie Hoernschemeyer, an attorney for individual plaintiffs and taxing districts who co-counseled the case with Layton, said Limbaugh’s ruling leaves no one with the ability to challenge an unconstitutional law.
“The Missouri Constitution prohibits special laws,” she said, “but that protection depends on someone being able to get through the courthouse door.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Shore, Solomon face off for NU Regents District 4 special election in Omaha
text:
Susanne Shore and Justin Solomon, both of Omaha, are facing off in a special election for an open seat on the NU Board of Regents. (Photos by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)OMAHA — A community volunteer and the chief operating officer of a company serving people with disabilities are facing off in a special election for the NU Board of Regents in Omaha. One is a former Nebraska first lady while the other is a former UNL student regent.
Susanne Shore and Justin Solomon, both of Omaha, are seeking the final four years of a six-year term for the University of Nebraska Board of Regents District 4 in Douglas County. Both are registered Democrats. Either would succeed appointed Regent Joel Makovicka, a Republican whom Gov. Jim Pillen appointed to the officially nonpartisan seat in February. 
The eastern Douglas County district includes the University of Nebraska Medical Center and University of Nebraska at Omaha.
The 2026 candidates for the University of Nebraska Board of Regents District 4 special election in Omaha: Susanne Shore, left, Justin Solomon. Appointed NU Regent Joel Makovicka declined to seek election after succeeding former NU Regent Elizabeth O’Connor of Omaha, who resigned in January. (Photos courtesy of the candidate/campaign | University of Nebraska Varner Hall photo by Aaron Sanderford/Nebraska Examiner)
Former NU Regent Elizabeth O’Connor was reelected to a second six-year term in 2024. She resigned in January as she faced a felony charge of driving drunk and causing serious bodily injury connected to a May 2025 crash. She pleaded guilty and was sentenced to one year in prison in August.
Five Democrats ran for the open seat in May, including Shore (who received 34.6% of the vote) and Solomon (who received 24.8% of the vote).
The candidates share many goals, including, as Shore and Solomon each put it, that the university must rebuild trust, focus on affordability and empower faculty, staff and students. Each also wants to take on a more active role as a regent in getting out to communities.
Both candidates sat down with the Nebraska Examiner in Omaha this month to discuss how they would approach NU’s budget, tuition, community outreach and more if elected.
Why they’re running
Shore, 62, said her experience working in the community and for universities, understanding healthcare as a former nurse and getting to know the state better as first lady of Nebraska (2015-23) has prepared her well.
“There’s not a lot that ties our state together the way the university system does, so if it’s not a strength, our whole state falls apart,” Shore said. “It is such a jewel and a value for the state. It needs to be treated like that.”
Omaha-area lines for the University of Nebraska Board of Regents in Douglas County. (Courtesy of Nebraska Legislative Research Office)
Solomon, 38, served as the student regent for the University of Nebraska-Lincoln in the 2010-11 academic year. He is COO for Integrated Life Choices. He said he is so “deeply ingrained” in his Omaha community, it’s who he is.
“I feel like now is really a moment where you need that type of leadership that understands that frugality is actually a differentiator, not a cross to bear, that has had to make really tough decisions that impact thousands of lives and has had to go make that case to people and still get them to feel respected,” Solomon said.
‘Breakdown in trust’
Solomon said part of the “breakdown in trust” he sees is an inability to justify academic cuts while spending hundreds of millions of dollars to renovate Memorial Stadium, for instance. While he understands the different pots of money, he said the optics come amid a general concern that in a changing economy, attending college might be out of reach for some.
He said some in federal and state politics are also “trying their best” to get people to distrust institutions like NU.
“It is our job — I feel a real pull, a real responsibility — to be the counterweight to those forces that want to get people to not trust the University of Nebraska, that want people to not trust public education as a way of improving their lives,” Solomon said.
Susanne Shore of Omaha, a 2026 candidate for University of Nebraska Board of Regents District 4, outside an Omaha coffee shop on Oct. 9, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Shore said up until about 2008, universities were often “automatically” seen as a place for opportunity. Today, she said, trust in universities and the quality and value they provide has declined while the choices for students after high school have increased.
A “universal goal,” Shore said, is that nobody stops in education after their senior year and that NU works with trade schools or community colleges to develop a pathway for students who might want more education after.
“It’s not just making sure they get in the door; it’s making sure they stay,” Shore said.
Balancing the budget
When the Nebraska Legislature convenes in January, lawmakers are set to face a budget deficit, as high as $847 million by mid-2029. Pillen, a former regent for 10 years, has slowed state support for NU after taking over as governor in 2023. He’s running for reelection this fall.
Solomon noted that NU enjoys a lot of state tax dollars already as an “outlier” among other universities in the Midwest or nationwide, which should be a point of pride. He said NU and its regents should focus on incentivizing employee retention, growing enrollment and leaning into affordability as a strength, not just a talking point.
“I don’t expect any giant swaths of new money to come and help the university,” Solomon said. “We’ve got to solve the problem from inside.”
Justin Solomon of Omaha, a 2026 candidate for University of Nebraska Board of Regents District 4, outside an Omaha coffee shop on Oct. 8, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Solomon said a solution could also be for NU to be “front and center” in helping schools address literacy issues statewide and improve teachers’ education, which could also improve teacher pay.
Shore said NU needs to show it’s looking at other options before cuts or tuition increases, which is also about trust. She said NU must work to set students up for success after college.
“For me, it’s also about value, because if a graduate can leave and get the kind of job that helps them pay back that student loan, then they’re ahead of the game,” Shore said. “That’s an investment, not a pit of debt.”
She criticized Solomon for supporting a tuition increase during his year on the board, which she said is an “easy solution, but it needs to be one of the last ones.” 
The Nebraska Constitution gives student regents a seat on the NU Board of Regents, but their votes are not counted with those of the eight elected regents.
If he’s elected this fall, Solomon has pledged to vote against efforts to raise tuition. He’s also noted on his Facebook campaign page that he successfully pushed to lower UNL student fees in 2011.
Race has divided progressives
Solomon has repeatedly sought to distinguish himself as a “homegrown” candidate to Shore, who he says is “handpicked.” He’s criticized Shore for not speaking out against her husband, U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb. Solomon said some regents have lost their way, seeing NU as a way to boost their status, and some he said have been installed politically by the Ricketts family.
“What’s unique in this time is that it seems to serve more the political and the donor class than the homegrown, working class that the university really needs to be focused on,” Solomon said.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates and the tools you need to cast your vote in Nebraska’s Nov. 3 general election, including NU Regents District 4.]
Shore said Solomon and his supporters have tried to portray her as “MAGA” or “conservative,” but she said her family and children know that’s not true. She’s a lifelong Democrat, and she said she sees every side and has experience building bridges.
She also has a long record of donating to Nebraska Democratic candidates, including more than $200,000 over the past four years.
“I can be who I am but still be somebody who can have conversations, difficult conversations, and find solutions, and that’s what I’m about,” Shore said.
She added that nobody has ever asked her husband if he can be independent of her.
“I never asked permission,” Shore continued. “I utilized every resource I could and got problems solved without asking anybody what they thought. I would be regent. In our family, in that household, I’m the expert on universities, and I own that.”
Community experience
As first lady, she celebrated her work working on foster care without regard to party, urban-rural divides or anything. She said that during the COVID-19 pandemic, she also personally drove out electronics for remote learning to four communities where students were in need.
“I’m proud that I was able to really try to make an impact,” Shore said.
Nebraska Examiner launches 2026 General Election Voter Guide

Solomon recalled his time as a student regent when he fought for students, he said, after UNL and law enforcement conducted “stings” to catch underage drinking as students tailgated in the North Bottoms near campus. He said he marched to demand answers the following Monday.
“I will always have the hugest heart for our students because they will largely lead me to the right direction,” Solomon said.
He also noted student-led work to secure domestic partner benefits for NU employees, which he said began his freshman year in 2008. Five years later, he said, NU approved employee-plus-one benefits.
Solomon said the “difference could not be more stark” in the regents race and that the choice is, “Do you trust more of the same?”
“I think if you compare them side by side, it’s a pretty easy choice,” Solomon said.
Shore said her record shows she can do the work and bring people together for NU’s benefit.
“We can’t take our regents and that university for granted,” Shore said. “It needs some TLC (tender loving care).”
The general election is Nov. 3. Early voting is underway.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming’s twin sacred cows — water and private property rights — clash on the ballot in Hyattville
text:
HYATTVILLE—At the end of Highway 31 in Big Horn County, this small, rural, agricultural community has been the definition of close-knit.
The sign at the edge of town boasts a population of 79, but locals say that’s only if you count the cats and dogs. Hyattville is tucked against the western slope of the Bighorn Mountains, an environment rich with wildlife and fields of corn, alfalfa, grass and other crops.
But Wyoming’s twin sacred cows — water and private property rights — are butting heads in these fecund fields. The conflict affects a landscape whipsawed by climate change and demographic shifts, changes seen across the West.
Wyoming could spend between $77 million and $113 million on the Alkali Creek dam and reservoir, which is proposed here to impound 8,000 acre feet of Big Horn mountain runoff, to save the water for late-season irrigation. That general idea won 79% of the vote when landowners formed the Nowood Watershed Improvement District in 2015.
“Everybody got along until this reservoir came along. Instead of a nice little community, you’ve got a war zone. It’s crazy.” Tom Shirran
“The state has spent upwards of $6 million to get us to this point,” Nowood Watershed Improvement District board member Martin Mercer said. Now a board of five area resident must finish the job, and that involves an unpopular action — the condemnation of private property.
That prospect has pitted neighbor against neighbor, sister against brother, maybe even cat against dog.
Condemnation and eminent domain, “them are cusswords,” said Tom Shirran, a self-described “lifelong Hyattville rancher,” one of three candidates challenging the sitting Nowood water district board members in Tuesday’s water district election. His slate seeks to win a board majority, potentially ending the condemnation threat.
“I just want the proposals to be balanced,” he said. “Make it fair to these people getting eminent domain on them.”
The coffee klatch at the Hyattville Community Center where the locals solve the world’s problems every morning. (Angus M. Thuermer Jr./WyoFile)
The first mention of condemnation a few years ago, “was enough to set people off,” Shirran said. “You don’t do that in this day and age, especially to your neighbors.
“Everybody got along until this reservoir came along,” he said. “Instead of a nice little community, you’ve got a war zone. It’s crazy.”
Once estimated at $34M
The ruckus began after state water developers estimated in 2017 the project would cost $32 million in state grants and $2.1 million in loans. Since then, estimates have increased to as much as $113 million and potential beneficiaries are not being asked to pay more.
Lawmakers and state officials appropriated enough to the Nowood water district to buy 260 acres of water board member Mercer’s land. The district paid him $1.6 million.
“To me it’s a big conflict of interest — terrible,” board candidate Shirran said. While not against the idea of water storage itself, Shirran said, “I’m against the way they’re doing it.”
Martin Mercer, owner of the Paint Rock Angus Ranch at Hyattville, who sold family ranch property for the site of the proposed Alkali Creek Dam. (Angus M. Thuermer Jr./WyoFile)
The state doled out funds and the reservoir land was sold and bought before the district obtained necessary easements to complete the project.
Now, the district has offered five landowners a total of $97,342 for right-of-way easements on 35 acres, to be adjusted according to appraisals, as described in documents WyoFile obtained through a records request. If the landowners don’t accept the “final offer” letters, the district “reluctantly will initiate eminent domain proceedings,” the correspondence reads.
If sacred cows are locking horns, the cart is also before the horse, Shirran said. “You don’t start a project without getting the easements first.”
Tom Shirran stands on his property next to the Anita Ditch, which could be enlarged to feed the proposed Alkali Reservoir. A water district said it will condemn an easement on his property to allow the troubled dam project to advance. (Angus M. Thuermer Jr./WyoFile)
The offers leverage water district power by offering a sweeter deal if landowners go along with it. If the landowners accept the deal, the district would spend extra money to bury the Anita Ditch — feeder to the reservoir — in a pipeline. If the district condemns the property, the ditch would be enlarged and left open, taking up more pasture and crop land.
The clock is ticking. The Legislature set a Jan. 1 deadline to use state money for condemnation. If the easements aren’t secured, with or without condemnation, by June 30, 2027, the $60 million allocated for the project will revert to other accounts.
“We’re running out of time,” water board Director Mitch Vigil said. Mediation with the affected landowners didn’t work.
Ticking clock
“I don’t know how you can make them say ‘yes,’” Vigil said. “We’re forced into eminent domain.”
Sitting directors reject criticism like that from board candidate Todd Jones who said the board didn’t listen to  the five landowners, give them options or treat them well. “There’s no way to talk to them most of the time,” Jones said of the board.
Mercer disagreed.
“The state and district made a welcoming process for anybody we needed an easement [from],” he said. “We could never get anything out of those folks.”
The dam would be large — an earth embankment 100 feet high and half a mile long. The resulting reservoir would be 312 acres when full, providing late-season irrigation in eight out of 10 years. It would always have at least a 132-acre pool for recreation. Backers say the project would benefit fisheries in the rivers and creeks.
The disgruntled ranchers targeted for condemnation, however, live upstream of the proposed dam’s outlet. Water doesn’t flow uphill, they observe.

Medicine Lodge Creek in Hyattville. (Angus M. Thuermer Jr./WyoFile)

But those in the condemnation crosshairs will benefit from a paper exchange of water rights, Nowood directors say. Extra water downstream would help keep upstream headgates open later into the fall.
“They would be huge beneficiaries,” Mercer said of the upstream irrigators who face condemnation. “We would not pull water out of their headgate. You cannot argue you’re not benefitting from that.”
Whether the paper transfer would work is uncertain.
“When it comes to fall, they’re not going to have enough water,” Shirran said of the exchange. “It don’t work if there’s no water in the crick.”




A diagram showing the approximate location of the proposed Alkali Creek Reservoir. (Geoff McGhee/The Water Desk)
Shirran didn’t agree with the $16,000 offer — a 2001 appraisal that would be updated — the district made for an easement on his land. Others on the eminent domain list had similar complaints. But the district can’t spend more, Mercer said. “You can only offer appraised value.”
Building the dam would be the best outcome, Mercer said, with far more benefits than drawbacks. The state calculates the project will create $122 million in benefits, including $10 million from recreation, at the lower $77 million price tag.
New face in town
About six years ago, when a couple of locals sauntered into the Paint Rock Inn, they espied something unusual. Sitting at his computer was an Idaho businessman from the posh ski town of Sun Valley, Idaho, clad in anything other than the area’s customary Wranglers or Carhartts. He wore salmon colored shorts — the locals called it pink — and a polo shirt.
Who changed the dress code, the locals asked.
Tim Gardiner had just bought 440 acres and named his new holding the Twisted Tippet Ranch. He ties his own files, casts them from Orvis reels and hunts upland birds with his stocky black lab, Ghillie.
Tim Gardiner at his home on Alkali Creek. (Angus M. Thuermer Jr./WyoFile)
Gardiner ran a multi-state commercial real estate company from Idaho that included apartment rentals. He built a house on the Twisted Tippet next to the bank of Alkali Creek. He’s a cast or two from the prized fishery in Nowood Creek. Just outside his house a cock pheasant, the proud patriarch of his brood, steals grain from the horse corral.
Gardiner treasures the history and art of the American West. In some ways, he contrasts sharply with some of that history and with Mercer, whose family’s area holdings go back generations.
Mercer is the great grandson of Asa Mercer, a newspaper publisher who railed against stockmen during the Johnson County Cattle Wars and published the seminal “The Banditti of the Plains.”
The elder Mercer stood against the entrenched forces of the Wyoming Stock Growers Association in Cheyenne and defended the little man, the settler. This generation of Mercers has Cheyenne on its side.
“Their intent was to turn this whole desert green.” Martin Mercer
Gardiner has slammed the state for unprofessional business practices — doling out good money before securing necessary easements. He wants insurance for his house and ranch that’s just below the proposed dam’s outlet.
The dam would be a high hazard structure and engineers face a challenge plugging an identified porous geologic formation, Gardiner said, drawing on state documents. Failure is more than an option, he believes.
“I’m in the line of fire,” Gardiner said on the bank of Alkali Creek. “I’m just trying to be indemnified for loss.”
Mercer said the opposite is true, that the dam “could be the only thing that saves [Gardiner’s] house” from a heavy rain on the hardpan covering the Alkali Creek drainage.
The project would subsidize as few as 33 irrigators at a cost of more than $3.4 million in taxpayer funds each, Gardiner said. His criticism ranges further. “The State should determine whether prior decisions require reconsideration by disinterested decision makers,” he states in 20 pages of criticism he’s assembled for those who would read or listen.
Board members reject conflict allegations. All board actions have been undertaken “the way the statutes read,” Mercer said.
Fellow board member Vigil said it is typical for rural water districts to have interested parties running the operation. “They all have the farmers, water users on their boards,” he said.
Cheap investment
Water storage is “an inexpensive investment” for the benefits it brings to sportsmen, families and others, Mercer said. The reservoir also would be an asset to firefighting.
Selling property for a reservoir was a family challenge, Mercer said.
“We spent a lot of hours deciding what is right,” he said. “I challenge anybody to sell 300 acres in the heart of their operation.”
Kris Robertson ushers Mocha into a milking barn as she begins the day at the Diamond S Ranch in Hyattville. (Angus M. Thuermer Jr./ WyoFile)
Wyoming historically has granted water rights to irrigators and others regardless of whether there was enough to go around, Mercer said. “Across Wyoming, water’s always been over adjudicated.”
The belief was that dams and reservoirs would resolve shortages. “Their intent was to get it all gathered up for the state,” he said of the water-storage vision. “Their intent was to turn this whole desert green.”
Conservation districts in Big Horn and Washakie counties have mailed a total of 453 ballots listing water board candidates to eligible voters, district managers told WyoFile. Each registered voter in the district gets one vote and the owner of each taxable parcel in the district gets one vote per parcel. A petition at Change.org claims 289 signatures against eminent domain.
Whoever wins the three open water board seats on Nov. 3 will assume office at the beginning of the year, Ashley Coenen, South Big Horn Conservation District manager, wrote in an email.
Kris Robertson, who sells raw milk and other products from her and husband Gene’s ranch at Hyattville, dislikes that the family’s Diamond S Ranch is a condemnation target.
Lois Shirran enjoys a quiet Hyattville Sunday watching football with Jackson and Dolly. (Angus M. Thuermer Jr./WyoFile)
“Property rights should mean something to all native Wyoming people,” she said. “We didn’t ever dream they would be fighting over water this way.”
If the project goes through, she said, “I guess we’ll suck it up.”
Vigil finds his family divided. “My sister’s on the other side,” he said.
That won’t stop him from Wyoming’s good Samaritan ethos. “If they called me today,” he said of his sister’s family, “I’d go help them.”
The election outcome may not satisfy the critics of eminent domain, even if their slate of three candidates wins. The sitting board would have almost two months to act before new members are seated.
If all three critics get voted in, “I don’t know how things are going to go,” Mercer said.
Vigil views the election as a blessing. “It’s going to come to an end,” he said of the conflict, “one way or another.” Then, “the healing can start.”
For Mercer, the dam would resolve the animosity. “The extra water will heal a lot of that,” he said. If it is not built, “there will be hard feelings for some time.”

name: WyoFile
title: Billionaire property owner to take over data center project in Natrona County
text:
A sprawling data center and energy complex proposal east of Casper is not dead, according to the property owner, despite Prometheus Hyperscale pulling out of the project earlier this week.
Falls Ranch, a limited partnership owned by Texas billionaire Russell Gordy, announced this week that “work will continue without delay.”
“The work by the community and local leaders has helped lay the foundation for a project with the potential to position Natrona County as a leader in the growing data center industry, building on Wyoming’s energy resources, skilled workforce and experience supporting major industrial development, and should not be wasted,” Falls Ranch stated in a press release following Prometheus’ announcement.
Though it was not involved in initial development plans, according to the company, the groundwork has been laid for it to see the project to fruition.
Residents who packed a Sept. 1, 2026, Natrona County Board of Commissioners meeting were asked to raise their hands if they support a proposal to build a data center. (Dustin Bleizeffer/WyoFile)
“We anticipate that with this change, the project should continue forward on a more efficient track, including community and business collaborations,” Falls Ranch representative Robert Hand said. “This has always been a Wyoming project, but today it represents something even greater: an opportunity for Natrona County to shape its own economic future.” 
More details will be revealed in the near future, Hand added.
Prometheus announced its departure from the project Wednesday. Originally, the $500 million, 1,250-megawatt complex was to be sited on Falls Ranch property spanning Natrona and Converse counties north of Interstate 25. In its latest configuration, it would sit entirely in Natrona County, south of the Interstate.
The move opened the door for developers to bypass a state-level Industrial Siting Council review and permitting process to instead empower Natrona County commissioners to vet the project. If green lit locally, however, the endeavor would still be subject to review from several state and federal agencies. That process had not advanced beyond initial discussions before Prometheus exited the project.
Prometheus is still pursuing a similar data center and energy complex in Uinta County, and the company indicated it is looking for more data center opportunities elsewhere in the state.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho County commissioners tell state officials they are seeking changes to public land management
text:
Members of the Idaho Legislature's Committee on Federalism meet Oct. 29 at the Super 8 motel in Grangeville. (Screenshot courtesy of Idaho in Session/Idaho Public Television)Idaho County commissioners are asking the state’s governor and other elected officials to change public land classifications within their county, Commissioner Skip Brandt told state legislators Thursday.
Idaho County Commissioner Skip Brandt (Photo courtesy of Idaho County)
Brandt detailed his proposal during the Idaho Legislature’s Committee on Federalism’s meeting Thursday, which took place at a Super 8 motel in Grangeville and was livestreamed online. 
During the meeting, Brandt told legislators serving on the committee that about 4.5 million acres of land in Idaho County is public land of some sort. That includes about 2.3 million acres of wilderness land and another 1.7 million acres of roadless areas classified under the Idaho Roadless Rule. 
The U.S. Forest Service describes Idaho’s Roadless Areas as “the core of the last intact forest ecosystem in the lower 48 states – where all of the native plants, fish and wildlife – from the smallest plant to the largest predator – can still be found.”
But Brandt says the problem with wilderness and Idaho Roadless Areas is restrictions on the land prevent logging, building roads and using motorized vehicles in those areas. Brandt also said restrictions make wildfire response more difficult and create a barrier to recreational access.
“And if you can’t afford to hire an outfitter to get you back there, or if you aren’t in shape enough to walk for five days with a big pack, you just don’t do it,” Brandt told the Committee on Federalism. “And so my contention is that the wilderness is land of no use as it stands. It’s just sitting there ready to cook.”
 Idaho County commissioner says he will petition Forest Service chief to change management rules of county’s public lands

Brandt told the Committee on Federalism he plans to petition Chief of the U.S. Forest Service Tom Schultz to change the management theme of Idaho Roadless Areas within Idaho County to the general forest, rangeland and grassland designation, which is the least restrictive management classification available. 
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Currently, Brandt said the vast majority of Idaho Roadless Areas within Idaho County are under more restrictive management classifications. 
Schultz, who formerly served as the director of the Idaho Department of Lands and a vice president with the Idaho Forest Group logging company, has strong ties in Idaho.
Changing to the least restrictive classification could allow for timber harvest and road construction on those lands. 
Brandt outlined part of his plans in a Sept. 29 letter he sent to Little and U.S. Sen. Jim Risch, R-Idaho.
USDA Forest Service Chief Tom Schultz meets with employees of the Kisatchie National Forest in Louisiana on April 2, 2025. (Photo by Preston Keres/USDA)
In the letter, which the Idaho Capital Sun obtained a copy of, Brandt and the other two Idaho County commissioners said they were notifying Little and Risch that Idaho County intends to request the modification of Idaho Roadless Area classifications in Idaho County.
“The lands would remain Idaho Roadless Areas; the requested modification would change their management classification to provide greater flexibility to properly manage them to meet Forest Service and county goals,” Brandt and fellow Commissioners Ted Lindsley and Brad Higgins wrote in the letter. 
Little and Risch wrote back to the Idaho County commissioners on Monday, telling the commissioners to work with the Idaho Roadless Rule Implementation Commission and provide it with specific examples of necessary projects that are blocked, wildfire risk information and other supporting materials. 
“We appreciate your request for the (Idaho Roadless Rule Implementation) Commission’s assistance, and we are committed to working with you on the country’s proposed modification once you have secured its support,” Little and Risch wrote. 
Returning to Thursday’s meeting of the Committee on Federalism, Brandt told state legislators he “needs to do a little more due diligence,” but hopes to move forward soon with filing official documents. 
“Hopefully within the next week or two weeks we are going to actually be able to step forward with a petition to formally request that all of our acres are moved into general forest and grassland,” Brandt said Thursday. 
The Committee on Federalism did not take any action on Brandt’s proposal Thursday.
