name: Michigan Advance
title: Trustees take legal action as controversy over changes to MSU Board Code of Ethics continues
text:
Michigan State University Trustees Mike Balow and Rema Vassar. June 3, 2026 | Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan AdvancePolicy changes intended to tamp down infighting within the Michigan State University Board of Trustees are now drawing legal scrutiny as two of its members have filed complaints in federal court seeking to halt the enforcement of the board’s updated Code of Ethics and Conduct. 
MSU Trustee Mike Balow on Wednesday filed a lawsuit against Board Chair Brianna Scott and Stefan Fletcher, the board’s secretary and chief of staff, arguing that revisions to the Board of Trustees code of conduct unlawfully restrict trustee speech. 
In May, the Board of Trustees voted 5-3 to add provisions barring trustees from divulging confidential information to unauthorized individuals before that information is made public and instructing them to “act ethically and not provide inaccurate, misleading, or false information concerning the university.”
The new provisions also bar trustees from representing their personal opinions as that of the university, and state that trustees will not undermine decisions made by the majority of the board.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
After the revisions were approved, trustees were required to sign a statement of acknowledgement, agreeing to follow the code of conduct’s terms. Trustees who did not sign were warned they could face sanctions including public censure, loss of privileges such as complimentary access to university sporting events and removal from any leadership position on the board.
Two trustees refused to sign: Balow and Trustee Rema Vassar. They were later censured as a result.
The Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, a civil liberties group focused on free speech issues, sent a letter to the university in May raising concerns about the revisions while offering itself as a resource to revise the Code of Ethics and ensure its compliance with the First Amendment. 
The group now represents Balow in his lawsuit against Scott and Fletcher.
“The people of Michigan elected Michael to be a watchdog, not a lapdog,” Greg Greubel, a senior attorney at FIRE said in a statement. “The freedom to voice opposition strengthens the university by encouraging ideas to be challenged and solutions to be worked out.”
According to the complaint filed in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Michigan, Scott and Fletcher have “cut Balow off from the ceremonial gatherings, conferences, sporting events, and other occasions at which trustees ordinarily interact with students, faculty, alumni, donors, and members of the public” due to his refusal to sign the statement agreeing to the revised code of ethics.
Michigan State University Trustees Rema Vassar and Mike Balow. June 3, 2026 | Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance
Balow’s attorneys argue that “Each day these restrictions remain in place, Balow loses opportunities to interact with the individuals he was elected to represent.”
“Asking hard questions and demanding honest answers is the only path to solid governance,” Balow said in a statement. “Healthy friction leads to accountability and transparency that boards often talk about, but don’t always deliver. It’s not easy, but it’s necessary.”
Last week, Vassar filed her own lawsuit against Scott, Fletcher, the Board of Trustees, MSU President Kevin Guskiewicz, Vice President for Legal Affairs and General Counsel Brian Quinn, and former trustees Dan Kelly and Dianne Byrum.
Vassar, who was previously investigated for misconduct alongside Trustee Dennis Denno, argued university officials had orchestrated a campaign of intentional discrimination and retaliation against her as the first Black woman to chair the board of trustees. 
Michigan State University Board of Trustees Chair Rema Vassar speaks to media after an MSU Board of Trustees meeting on Feb. 2, 2024. (Photo: Anna Liz Nichols)
As part of the suit, she has requested the board cease enforcing its requirements for trustees to sign a statement of acknowledgment regarding the Code of Ethics.
Amber McCann, a spokesperson for the university, told Michigan Advance the university would address Vassar’s suit through the appropriate legal channels. 
In a statement to Michigan Advance, Scott, who is seeking reelection for another 8-year term, called Balow’s lawsuit “petty and frivolous” and that she looked forward to seeking sanctions.
“The purpose of the Code of Ethics and Conduct is to help ensure the Board can effectively govern in service to students, faculty, staff, parents, research partners, taxpayers and the broader public,” Scott said. “The code does not limit speech or restrict members of governing boards from raising concerns, providing oversight or questioning decisions; instead, it establishes good and commonsense governance practices.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Commentary: Travel reports provide needed window of transparency but could be improved
text:
Reports covering July 1, 2025 to July 1, 2026, showed how often top state officials are traveling and how much they are spending. (Getty Images)For the second year, statewide elected officials and top agency leaders in Gov. Mike Braun’s administration filed reports detailing their travel in the past year.
We tallied up the days and cost of the trips and overall it was minor — about $132,000. Which is just as important as if it had been $1.3 million. It shows restraint and responsibility on their behalf.
Either way, the point is transparency and I applaud lawmakers for instituting these reports in 2025.
All the officials regularly travel in-state to various constituent events, meetings and conferences. So, we focused more directly on out-of-state travel. Here are some of the findings we reported:
A sample of Comptroller Elise Nieshalla’s travel report. (Screenshot)
– Braun hardly leaves the state. He had only one reported trip outside Indiana and it was paid by campaign dollars because he was attending a Republican Governors Association meeting in Washington, D.C.
– Attorney General Todd Rokita goes to the nation’s capital a lot. He listed seven trips to Washington, D.C. in a year’s time. Two visits listed no state expenses, while the other five totaled nearly $3,400.
– Energy and Natural Resources Secretary Suzanne Jaworowski was high on the list for spending at about $25,000. She accounted for about 62% of the $40,460 in expenses listed by Braun’s cabinet. Her largest expense was $8,283.97 for an April 20-May 1 visit to Seoul and Busan in South Korea.
– Education Secretary Katie Jenner reported substantially less spending — $5,815.78 — but listed more dated travel-related events than any other cabinet secretary. Her report contained 22 out-of-state activities. Those out-of-state entries covered 41 distinct calendar dates, including 39 weekdays.
I do think there is room for improvement in this process, though, starting with a uniform spreadsheet. Each individual approaches the report differently and there in no consistency in format or information.
Some simply list the city they went to with no accompanying information. I went through social media posts to try to create some context to the entries. That’s how we tied Lt. Gov. Micah Beckwith’s D.C. trip to a White House Christmas party and several of Rokita’s trips to events involving transgender topics.
A sample of Attorney General Todd Rokita’s travel report. (Screenshot)
I understand some discretion is needed in these, but a basic explanation is necessary. It could say the person spoke at a community’s Rotary meeting, attended a business opening, met with constituents etc.
Some officials also listed trips paid for by sponsoring organizations without disclosing those amounts or sometimes who paid. That information is very important given the quid-pro-quo possibilities in government.
Management and Budget Secretary Lisa Hershman listed 37 travel entries, including a Texas meeting, but supplied no numeric expenses. Business Affairs Secretary Mike Speedy likewise listed no numeric costs for 19 travel entries.
I’d like to give a shout out to Comptroller Elise Nieshalla for the best report. She provided a specific location, dates, purpose, expenses and fund for every single item. That included meeting with specific mayors, a tour of the CANDLES Holocaust museum, recording a podcast, attending an Association of Indiana Counties conference and stopping at the Seymour Tribune.
Everyone should be more like Elise.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana justices weigh whether golf course must stop balls from landing on neighbor’s property
text:
The Indiana Supreme Court is considering a dispute over Sandy Pines Golf Club's driving range, where golf balls have repeatedly crossed onto a neighboring property. (Photo courtesy of Sandy Pines Golf Club Facebook) A northern Indiana golf course could be forced to raise its protective netting or shut down its driving range if a homeowner prevails in a yearslong dispute over thousands of errant golf balls.
Indiana Supreme Court justices heard arguments Thursday in a case between Mitchell Schultz and Sandy Pines Golf Club in DeMotte, where an estimated 1,500 golf balls annually have landed on neighboring residential property since the club opened a driving range in 2018, according to court records.
A trial court previously found the golf course liable for trespass but assigned Schultz 95% of the fault because he acquired ownership of the property knowing golf balls were landing there. The Indiana Court of Appeals overturned that determination in December, finding that comparative fault cannot be used to reduce liability for an intentional tort.
But during Thursday’s arguments, Schultz’s attorney, Jacob Ahler, told the high court his client is not seeking financial compensation. Instead, he wants the golf balls to stop coming onto the property.



Quotation







It's going to affect everyone who plays the game of golf. From the super senior league to the people that are just doing it, to everyone in between.


– Donald Shelmon, attorney for Sandy Pines Golf Club


That prompted several justices to question whether Indiana’s Comparative Fault Act — the law at the center of the appeal — applies to the case at all.
“I think you may have significantly narrowed and simplified this case,” Justice Derek Molter told Ahler.
The court has not yet decided whether to accept jurisdiction over the appeal. Chief Justice Loretta Rush said Thursday that the justices must first determine whether to grant transfer, which would allow them to review the appellate ruling.
The court could then uphold the Court of Appeals decision or issue its own ruling on the legal questions raised by the dispute. If the justices deny transfer, the appellate ruling would stand.
Thousands of golf balls, years of complaints
The dispute dates to 2018, when S.P. Real Estate LLC, which operates Sandy Pines Golf Club, added a driving range next to property that had been in the Schultz family for more than five decades.
The golf course itself had operated for decades before the driving range was built. The club purchased the land for the new range from Schultz’s brother.
Schultz grew up on the neighboring property, moved away and returned around 2008 to care for his aging mother, according to court documents.
After the driving range opened, golf balls began regularly landing on the family’s property.
The appellate court described about 1,500 balls a year — some broke windows, fell into the swimming pool and caused other property damage.
Schultz said he began parking his vehicle at the far end of the driveway and sitting beneath a tent when using the backyard to avoid being struck.
He repeatedly complained to the golf course.
Sandy Pines responded by using lower-flight range balls, instructing golfers not to hit balls over the net separating the properties and discouraging use of tee boxes closest to the Schultz property.
But the changes did not stop the problem, according to court filings.
In 2020, Schultz’s mother transferred ownership of the property to him on an attorney’s advice so he would have standing to sue.
Schultz later filed claims alleging negligent design, nuisance and trespass.
The Jasper Circuit Court dismissed the negligence and nuisance claims before trial. The court applied the legal doctrine of “coming to the nuisance,” reasoning that Schultz had acquired the property knowing about the golf balls.
The trespass claim survived, however.
After a bench trial, the court found Sandy Pines liable for trespass. At a subsequent proceeding, though, the judge assigned Schultz 95% of the fault and the golf course just 5%, leaving Schultz unable to recover damages under the comparative fault analysis.
Sandy Pines Golf Club’s driving range in DeMotte, Indiana, is at the center of a legal dispute over golf balls landing on a neighboring homeowner’s property. (Photo courtesy of Sandy Pines Golf Club Facebook)
The Court of Appeals reversed that determination.
“Liability for an intentional tort turns on the tortfeasor’s deliberate choice to commit the act,” Judge Leanna Weissmann wrote for the unanimous three-judge panel. “That intent cannot be reduced to a percentage of fault.”
The appellate court concluded that Sandy Pines remained fully liable for the trespass once the trial court established that the intentional tort had occurred. It sent the case back for further proceedings concerning damages and whether Schultz had failed to mitigate them.
The appellate judges also dismissed Sandy Pines’ challenge to the underlying trespass finding because the golf course had not provided an adequate trial record for review.
Justices question who is responsible
Much of Thursday’s argument focused on whether Sandy Pines can be held responsible for golf balls struck by its customers, rather than by the business itself.
Donald Shelmon, an attorney for the golf course, argued that individual golfers are responsible for their shots and that Sandy Pines cannot control precisely where those balls land.
The course had obtained local zoning approval for the driving range and used a professional designer, Shelmon told the court. He also disputed the reported number of golf balls reaching the Schultz property.
The golf course maintains that the trial court wrongly attributed the actions of individual golfers to the business.
Justice Mark Massa challenged the golf course’s argument, noting that Sandy Pines charges customers to hit golf balls at its driving range.
“Well, that’s not really what’s going on here, counsel,” Massa said. “You’re suggesting that the patrons of the driving range are the tortfeasors, not the business that’s operating a driving range that invites people to come and strike golf balls for a fee. That’s the intentional trespass alleged, isn’t it?”
Indiana Supreme Court justices, from left: Geoffrey Slaughter, Mark Massa, Loretta Rush, Derek Molter, Christopher Goff. (Courtesy photo)
Shelmon maintained that the golfers, rather than the course, committed the underlying acts.
The justices also pressed him on whether a neighboring homeowner should bear responsibility simply for living beside a driving range.
“How is fault attributable to the homeowner being showered with errant golf balls?” Massa asked.
Molter additionally raised a hypothetical involving a shooting range.
“I mean, would the argument really be that, ‘Hey, if you don’t want stray bullets coming through your kitchen window, don’t live next to a gun range?'” he asked.
Shelmon said the estimated number was disputed at trial, but Rush pointed to evidence that Schultz had collected buckets of golf balls from the property.
Could the court order the driving range closed?
The justices also questioned whether the dispute could be resolved without deciding how Indiana’s comparative fault law applies to intentional wrongdoing.
Molter pointed to language in the Comparative Fault Act limiting its application to actions brought to recover damages.
If Schultz is seeking only an order stopping the trespass, Molter suggested, the court might not need to decide whether comparative fault applies to intentional torts.
Ahler agreed that his client wants the continuing trespass stopped, rather than a financial award.
He argued that money would do little to address the underlying problem.
The justices asked whether the trial court could order the golf course to make changes to its operations if the trespass finding stands.
Ahler said an injunction could require higher protective netting or the closure of the driving range.
Ahler told the justices that 15 five-gallon buckets of golf balls remain in the Jasper County Courthouse attic, arguing that the collection demonstrated the existing protections had not worked. 	


Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



Another question, too, was whether a request for an injunction would allow Sandy Pines to raise additional defenses on remand.
Molter noted that courts considering equitable relief must weigh competing interests and may consider legal doctrines that differ from those governing monetary damages.
Shelmon said that such defenses could potentially be available but maintained that the fundamental issue remained whether a golf course should be held responsible for balls hit by individual golfers.
He also disputed whether an injunction had been properly requested in the trial court, telling the justices that Thursday was the first time he had heard Schultz was seeking that remedy. Rush responded that Schultz’s brief identified an injunction as the relief sought.
He warned that allowing the trespass finding to stand could have consequences for golfers and golf course operators elsewhere in Indiana.
“It’s going to affect everyone who plays the game of golf,” Shelmon argued. “From the super senior league to the people that are just doing it, to everyone in between.”

name: National
title: Election officials brace for federal interference but expect to persevere
text:
Voters mark their ballots during the first day of early voting in Bismarck, North Dakota, on Oct. 22, 2026. Experts and voting rights advocates are bracing for the potential of federal influence over the results of next week’s midterm elections. (Photo by Jack Dura/North Dakota Monitor)As concerns rise about the potential for federal influence over the results of next week’s midterm elections, many voting experts and advocates remain confident that the nation’s highly localized systems of administering and counting votes will persevere.
Facing sinking approval ratings over high prices, the White House has amped up attacks on state-administered elections: In recent weeks, the federal government sued Alaska and California to intervene in their elections and demanded election officials in Washington state pull aside ballots of 400 alleged noncitizens — laying the groundwork for a high-stakes showdown at the U.S. Supreme Court. 
For months, state officials have been planning for federally induced electoral chaos in the form of federal law enforcement or immigration agents at polls, election investigations or attempts to overturn unfavorable results. 
But the nation’s vast network of state and local election offices is resilient by design, said Mai Ratakonda, program director of election protection at States United Democracy Center, a nonpartisan nonprofit dedicated to fair elections. Election officials are prepared for close races, recounts and potential interference, she said. And she noted courts have largely blocked President Donald Trump’s efforts to intervene. 
“There’s no one person or agency or office that controls our elections as a whole,” she said. “Instead, it’s thousands of nonpartisan election officials across the country that are administering these elections … Even if there are attempts by certain individuals to try to interfere with the election process, there are a lot of safeguards in place, and this isn’t the first time that state and local officials will have to deal with those kinds of issues, unfortunately.”
At stake is not only whether Republicans will maintain their grip on Congress, but also control of state governments across the country, which could provide a new check on Trump’s power.
Trump, who still has refused to acknowledge his 2020 election defeat, has sought to cast doubt and seize control of elections for years. His administration has aimed to nationalize elections, purge voter rolls, restrict mail-in voting and raise alarms without evidence about an epidemic of noncitizen voting.
No more ‘hypothetical situations’: States move to fortify elections against Trump

Since the chaos and insurrection that followed the 2020 presidential election, experts and advocates have worked to boost confidence in state and local election administrators, who operate a patchwork of highly decentralized — and scrutinized — voting systems. In recent weeks, Republicans and Democrats have pledged to operate fair and free elections regardless of how national politicians react.
“We all took an oath to uphold the Constitution of the United States and the Constitution and laws of the state we live in, and we take that oath very seriously,” Mary Hall, the auditor of Thurston County, Washington, told reporters during a briefing with other election administrators Wednesday. “And I would not break that oath for anyone.”
Hall, a Democrat, noted her Olympia-area district is home to a portion of one closely contested congressional district that could determine control of Congress. The Republican Party has invested deeply in that race as it looks to hold onto power in D.C.
“I don’t feel any pressure from them,” Hall said, “and if they want to try and insert pressure, I really don’t think I would respond to it in any way because we have a job to do.”
‘We can handle the pressure’
New Hampshire Secretary of State David Scanlan, a Republican, said the federal government’s actions have proven to be more of a distraction than an outright obstacle. He’s not expecting any major problems and said he’s ready to resist any outside pressure as the state is home to tightly contested races for both the U.S. Senate and U.S. House. 
“I am confident that the results that are going to come out of New Hampshire are going to be accurate,” he said. “And those are the results I’m going to stand by.”
Scanlan noted the Granite State is accustomed to heightened electoral attention because of its first-in-the-nation presidential primaries. 
“So, we can handle scrutiny, we can handle the pressure,” he said, “And I think New Hampshire is going to do what it does best, and just have a good, solid election that the voters here can have confidence in.”
Concerns are so serious that a group of U.S. national security officials has been discreetly advising state governments and congressional lawmakers how to prepare for potential interference from Trump, The Washington Post reported. That group includes about 10 current and former officials with experience in the Defense Department. 
Trump’s DOJ sends 1,000 election monitors to 50 states; locations not yet disclosed

But voters shouldn’t be dissuaded by the federal government’s rhetoric, said former Pennsylvania Secretary of State Kathy Boockvar. A Democrat who now consults on election security and administration issues, she said every state has laws designed to ensure safe and secure elections.
Boockvar expects that the federal government will attempt to sway unfavorable election results. But she doesn’t think those efforts will work. 
“Election officials at every level are all about the rule of law,” she said. “They know the law in their jurisdictions. They know the processes in their jurisdictions, and they have to follow them.”
She said election administrators come to work every day with a singular purpose: to ensure every eligible voter can cast their ballot. Even if certain officials wanted to change results, she said systems are designed with strict protections that don’t have “a lot of wiggle room.” And the courts would likely block any baseless efforts — as they did repeatedly during Trump’s 2020 election denial campaign. 
“I think the institutions will hold,” she said. 
In 2020, Georgia Republican Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger resisted pressure from Trump to alter the outcome of the presidential election there. 
This week, Raffensperger pledged that Georgia’s election process would prove open and transparent. The U.S. Department of Justice plans to send election monitors to six Georgia counties, all of which are considered Democratic strongholds. But Raffensperger said poll watchers from both parties and the nonpartisan Carter Center will be monitoring elections alongside federal officials. 
“It’s a transparent process, and we’re not concerned at all,” he told reporters on Monday.
Deep preparation
Like many local government workers, employees at Arizona’s Pinal County participated in tabletop exercises this year to see how they would react to all manner of Election Day chaos. Called “Ballotship,” the gamified exercise considered everything from power outages to disruptive protestors. 
This year’s preparations included the potential for federal involvement, said Dana Lewis, the Republican county recorder. 
“We know that there comes a certain amount of chaos, confusion, but that’s probably why we’re all heavily caffeinated, and we’re good at it,” she said, “because we’ve gone through several of them, and we work through it.”
Since 2020, Lewis said, election skepticism has increased in her central Arizona community. And the office has seen big turnover among election administrators and poll workers. But she’s worked to open up the voting process, showing how elections operate and underscoring the fundamental commitment to getting the results right — no matter the outcome or outside pressure.



Quotation







In no which way, shape or form will that kind of tomfoolery happen here.


– Dana Lewis, Republican county recorder of Arizona's Pinal County


“It’s an interesting time that we’re in, but no matter what, there is something to be said about putting your hands on a Bible and taking an oath to uphold the Constitution that I very much take seriously,” she said. “And my job in this role is to follow the law, and I will continue to do that and I will do it transparently. My staff also understands that, and in no which way, shape or form will that kind of tomfoolery happen here.”
The deep preparation for all manner of election complications in jurisdictions such as Pinal County have helped build more resilient systems that are able to respond quickly to a slew of Election Day hiccups, said Alex Gulotta, Arizona state director for All Voting is Local, a nonpartisan organization working to protect voting access at the local level.
But like other states, Arizona is home to politicians and election officials who still refuse to accept the results of the 2020 presidential election.
Among the most prominent is Justin Heap, the Republican recorder of Maricopa County, the state’s most populous county and home to Phoenix. All Voting is Local put Heap on its list of the nation’s “Top 10 Most Dangerous Election Deniers” because of his insistence that “inconsistencies and illegalities” occurred in previous Arizona elections.
Anxiety is growing Trump may try to disrupt the midterm elections. States are prepping.

Heap’s office did not respond to a Stateline request for comment. 
But Gulotta said even a powerful and controversial figure such as Heap does not have the ability to alter election outcomes because of Arizona’s bifurcated system. Arizona law divides election duties between county boards and recorders.
“Not everyone understands all the mechanics of how this system works and the level of checks and balances that are built into it,” he said. 
He does worry that close congressional races could lead the federal government to pressure certain counties not to certify election results.
“To me that’s the biggest risk,” he said, “and the biggest antidote to that is overwhelming turnout that reduces the likelihood that we have races that are that close.”
Stateline reporter Kevin Hardy can be reached at khardy@stateline.org.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: For injured bats and other wildlife, these volunteers are a lifeline
text:
An occasional look at Connecticut’s remarkable people, places and things

Maureen Heidtmann’s fourth call of the day was for a big brown bat stuck in a glue trap. She hoped to save its life, even if she had to amputate its wing.
She was able to coach her other callers through a variety of stuck-bat situations over the phone, but for this creature the size of a fig, she would need to use mineral oil and a tongue depressor to wiggle it free of the glue trap it arrived in.
Nelson — she names the bats that can’t be released — now snacks vigorously on mealworms, but it still carries signs of trauma after nearly starving in the trap.
Callers from across the state can deliver injured bats like Nelson to Heidtmann’s house for treatment, where she cares for up to 40 of them at a time. 
Heidtmann isn’t the only person with such a specialist’s toolkit in Connecticut. She is one of a small army of 57 volunteers licensed by the state Department of Energy and Environmental Protection to rehabilitate wildlife.

Bat Rehabilitator Maureen Heidtmann checks a bat cave at her home in East Hampton on Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026. Heidtmann is one of three licensed bat rehabilitators in the state of Connecticut. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

When a Connecticut resident reports an injured or distressed animal, DEEP refers them to rehabilitators who can nurse the animals back to health until they can be returned to the wild. Rehabbers also advise the public on how to stay safe around wild animals and run educational programming about the state’s species, many of which are endangered. 
And they do so without compensation, often spending their own money as well as countless hours in a labor of love. 
Heidtmann has been rehabilitating bats for 25 years, a passion that first took flight when one snuck into her family’s Brooklyn, N.Y., apartment, when she was 5 years old. 
“My mother went nuts,” Heidtmann said. “She was convinced this bat was going to get tangled in her hair, suck the blood of her children, just be an evil presence. So she slapped the newspaper on her head, picked up a broom and started to whale away.” 
Common belief at the time was that bats were blind, and echolocation was poorly understood, but Heidtmann watched as the bat expertly avoided her mother’s swinging broom. 
“I crept out from under the table, opened the window, the bat flew out, and I fell in love,” Heidtmann said. 
The path to becoming a bat-saver
For four decades after that first flight, Heidtmann kept the spark alive by scouring her local library for books about bats. She studied biology in college and became a librarian and a single mom.  

Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
Bat Rehabilitator Maureen Heidtmann checks on and feeds Nelson, a big brown bat, at her home in East Hampton on Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026. Heidtmann is one of three licensed wildlife rehabilitators who work with bats in Connecticut.
One day when she was working at the library some 25 years ago, a little boy found a young bat outside in a pool of water. He brought it inside, not knowing what to do, Heidtmann said.
When she saw the bat, “it was not even a week old. It didn’t even have fur.” She felt compelled to help. 
“I dried it off, got it home, warmed it up and fed it, just using my common sense,” Heidtmann said. “I did not have the specific formulas then that I now have when I’m raising baby bats, so I just bought a can of milk replacer for kittens.” It worked. 
For other rehabbers, the pipeline into the work is often similar. People come across injured wildlife, are referred by DEEP to a wildlife rehabber and realize the depth of the need. 
Aspiring rehabbers must pass a state exam and complete 40 hours of training over at least three years under an authorized rehabber to get their DEEP license. Those working with endangered animals must earn additional federal permits. 
“I actually found an injured turtle and didn’t know rehabbers existed,” said Angelina Carnevale, who has been rehabbing Connecticut’s native turtles in North Branford for the last eight years. 
“It wasn’t until years later, when I had some kind of disposable income, that I was like, oh, maybe I can do this. Because as soon as I looked into it the first time, it was very straight up front that they don’t pay you anything, and they don’t reimburse you for anything,” Carnevale said.
Even after donations from appreciative community members, Carnevale expects to spend $4,000 of her own money this year. Heidtmann’s personal share of the bill averages $2,000 each year she operates, she said.
This year, a lawmaker sought to change that. 
A labor of love and the law 
Sen. Paul Cicarella, R-North Haven, was on a walk with his family last year when they came across an injured turtle. 
DEEP’s wildlife program referred him to Carnevale, and he was impressed by the promptness of her response while still working her day job as a children’s librarian. Carnevale’s voicemail directs people to other resources if she doesn’t return their call within 10 minutes. 
“When no one else could help me, and the state refers me to a nonprofit and they’re not given anything, it seems like something that’s worth investing into,” said Cicarella. 
So last session, Cicarella proposed SB 456, a bill that would provide $500,000 in grants to DEEP-licensed wildlife rehabilitation nonprofits. Carnevale and other rehabbers testified in favor of the bill. 
The bill passed the environment committee unanimously but was not taken up by the full Senate. 

Art at Maureen Heidtmann’s home in East Hampton on Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026. Heidtmann is one of three licensed wildlife rehabilitators who work with bats in Connecticut. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

“I think it’s a great idea, and clearly my colleagues on both sides of the aisle thought it was as well,” Cicarella said. 
“If you follow the building, you’ll realize that bills have to be put forward multiple times before they pass. It’s part of the process. It’s unfortunate.” 
Cicarella said government leadership told him his legislation would be included in the final budget and implementer bill. He was surprised when he saw that it wasn’t there.
“Hopefully, we can get it done again,” Cicarella said. 
Carnevale says she hopes to see some of the language tweaked to make the carveout open to all DEEP-licensed rehabbers. 
“Most rehabbers are not 501(c)(3) nonprofits. It took me five years before I was able to get around to doing all of the paperwork to become one.”  
“And when you are rehabbing animals, that’s where all your time goes,” she said. 
Educating against the odds 
Rehabbers, especially of bats, are fighting a battle for education against misinformation. 
“Bats have been given a bad rap,” Heidtmann said. But if thoughts of vampires get the public interested in learning more about the science of bats, so be it, she said. 

A juvenile big brown bat hangs from their cave at Bat Rehabilitator Maureen Heidtmann’s home in East Hampton on Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026.  Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Connecticut is home to nine species of bats, and through their diet, they control the populations of pests including moths, ash borer beetles and spotted lanternflies, said Devaughn Fraser, a mammal biologist at DEEP. 
Bats are “the only really predominantly night flying insectivore that’s controlling night flying insects,” Fraser said. 
And all of Connecticut’s native bat species are in great conservational need. Five are endangered, with white nose syndrome decimating populations. 
Bats, like other mammals, can carry rabies, a disease that is nearly always fatal in humans once symptoms start. And that’s what many people’s fears hinge on, Heidtmann said. 
But those who study bats say that the disease’s prevalence is overstated. In her 25 years of rehabbing hundreds of bats, Heidtmann has only seen three rabies cases. And studies of bat fatalities at wind farms show less than 1% of wild bats to have the disease, Fraser said. 
If a bat is found indoors, the first step to get it out is opening a window, according to DEEP’s website. People can also use a cardboard box to safely remove a bat. 
While wearing thick leather gloves, move toward the bat slowly and place a container over it, then slide stiff paper under to form a lid and then release the bat outside, advises Heidtmann’s website.
People who are bitten or scratched by a bat should seek medical advice; effective post-exposure rabies vaccines are available. If a bat is found in the room of a child, someone sleeping, or a person otherwise cognitively impaired and unable to communicate about a bat encounter, rabies prevention care should be followed, and if possible, people should take the bat in for testing. 
About 4% of bats brought in for testing this year in Connecticut were positive for rabies, the same percentage as the last two years.
Healthy bats do not seek out interaction with humans, Fraser said. And if they are stuck inside, they most likely got lost and are trying to find a way out. 
Heidtmann’s busiest time of year is in June and July, when newborn bats may have become separated from their mothers. The next couple of months in Heidtmann’s care are about bringing them up to weight, encouraging flight and socializing them with other bats. 

Bat Rehabilitator Maureen Heidtmann opens the door to her flight cage at her home in East Hampton on Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026.  Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

In their first few weeks, Heidtmann feeds them species-specific formula every two to three hours throughout the night before gradually weaning them onto mealworms. She has had to improvise to find feeding applicators tiny enough. 
“I use whatever will work. Sometimes they will take to eye makeup applicators … they’re like little sponges.” 
If all goes well, she releases them into an outdoor flight cage on her property and, eventually, into the wild. The ones unable to hunt for themselves because of their injuries are kept inside for educational programs. 
But it takes newborn bats time to learn the skills of flight and navigation, and sealing up holes in a property at the wrong time of year can be a death sentence for pups nesting there with no way out. 
That’s why John Griffin, Senior Director for Urban Wildlife Programs at the Humane World for Animals, sees codifying humane exclusion standards as an important step in protecting bats and many of Connecticut’s wildlife species. 
“A stronger framework [for bats] could include prohibitions on exclusions (with certain exemptions) during pup season (June 1 through August 15), a ban on entombment, a requirement to use one-way devices, and meaningful enforcement for anyone performing exclusions for hire,” Griffin said. 
Animals are “adapting to our communities and flourishing because we’re providing habitat,” Griffin said. 
“Sometimes people think, ‘Oh, if I occupy my house, why would an animal want to live here?’ Well, they’re looking at your house with a different perspective. They’re thinking about, does it meet my denning or roosting needs, and is there an opening?”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Opinion: ‘Inauthentic accounts’ blur social media reality in Kansas Senate race, according to report
text:
An overseas firm has highlighted “coordinated activity” from inauthentic social media accounts in the U.S. Senate race for Kansas. (Illustration by Eric Thomas for Kansas Reflector)A swirling media storm.
That’s how I would describe the last few months in Kansas. The U.S. Senate race between Roger Marshall and Adam Hamilton has brought disinformation chaos to television advertising, journalism and social media.
Now this: A report this week from a cybersecurity firm based in Tel Aviv alleges that “coordinated activity” from inauthentic social media accounts has been routinely injected into the race.
The company, Cyabra, describes itself as an “artificial intelligence-powered narrative intelligence company.” Translation: They use emerging computing technology to find out what ideas are emerging online — and who is posting those narratives.
“That’s what we would call social listening,” said Keith Noble, Cyabra’s vice president for North America.
Cyabra, according to Noble, researches narratives that are shared online: “Are they authentic? And how are actors taking inauthentic narratives and trying to spread them?”
Cyabra monitored the Kansas Senate race along with five other tightly contested elections in other states. The company reported this week “with high confidence” that five of those races displayed “coordinated inauthentic accounts.” In other words, social media posts were generated and don’t represent human beings — let alone Kansas human beings.
Cyabra’s confidence in its analysis of the Kansas inauthentic accounts was 99%, according to the report.
In most of the races Cyabra monitored, including the Marshall vs. Hamilton contest, attacks targeted both Republican and Democratic candidates. Cyabra’s report reveals this relatively equitable social media attack in granular detail. 
“We did find a lot of this was a lot even-handedly,” Noble said. “It wasn’t always the same, but generally both sides got it.”
During September and October, Cyabra analyzed posts on X (or Twitter), TikTok and Facebook in the Kansas race. They found that inauthentic accounts published essentially the same number of posts targeting Marshall’s campaign as Hamilton’s. For instance, Cyabra reports that the TikTok social media conversations about both Marshall and Hamilton were made up of 22% inauthentic content. 
On Facebook, the results were also the same regardless of candidate: 4% inauthentic posts for both the Republican and the Democrat. The engagement from inauthentic accounts was similar on X.com as well: 16% for Marshall and 17% for Hamilton. 
Noble told me in an interview this week that the motivation for such attacks would be to sow distrust rather than give a particular candidate a partisan advantage in the election.
“Attacking both sides can really raise the temperature of a race and make the whole conversation look angrier and more divided than what it is,” Noble said. “Think of it like chaos theory. It can wear down the trust of both candidates rather than help either one of them in particular.”
If it strikes you as dystopian that, as Cyabra claims, inauthentic accounts posted one in every five social media posts related to the Senate race, hold onto your hat.
Cyabra also posits that “one operation, consistent with one coordinating actor, a person or a group” was likely running the accounts, “working mostly against Marshall while also attacking Hamilton’s church record.” The report suggests that this social media pattern is “possibly part of a larger network.”
I don’t bring this social media news to you without my own suspicions. What is Cyabra? How can they state these suspicions without revealing who is running the coordinated, even-handed social media distortion campaign during election season?
Our current social media reality gives us few choices other than to trust an internet security firm that was obscure to me. Social media platforms are difficult to monitor both for news organizations and for normal citizens. Who has the technical know-how or time to inspect, as Cyabra claims it did, “about 36,000 posts and comments” including about “6,000 off-topic items”?
During my interview with Noble, I explained how regular citizens feel: “We are marinating in social media, but we don’t know what we are marinating in.”
“One of the reasons why we did this study, why we released the press release, is we’re taking the same cutting-edge technology and analytic methodology to apply to public sector elections to really help the country and help the nation,” Noble said. 
That sounds helpful and altruistic. Yet the study Cyabra released doesn’t give us full access to what they know — what is inside their technological black box. 
For instance, the report mentions one coordinated actor in the Kansas campaign. Who is coordinating these inauthentic accounts? A foreign actor? 
“Who was doing it fell outside of our analysis,” Noble said.
Also still locked in the black box: what social media posts came from inauthentic accounts. For instance, three X posts are cited in Cyabra’s report, but I couldn’t find them even with the social media site’s advanced search feature. 
(Noble explained that X might be shielding those posts in search results because they come from insignificant or dubious accounts. He later provided the three posts via email, and they are still published on X.)
Even knowing the exact wording of a fake post doesn’t mean that I could find it. The black box of social media remained impervious, unless I had the direct help of an international online narrative monitoring company.
Despite how difficult social media can be to monitor comprehensively, these platforms — from Facebook to TikTok — steer public opinion and voting in Kansas and elsewhere. That reality makes reports like Cyabra’s both impossible to confirm from the outside, but also too consequential to ignore. 
As we barrel toward Election Day, Kansans should be forgiven for feeling off balance given the media tumult and social media fervor. Just in the past few weeks:

Marshall’s campaign filed campaign finance reports that showed essentially no money spent on campaign staff. They led to accusations that Marshall was using taxpayer-funded human resources to staff his campaign. 
Marshall’s campaign paid a long-overdue bakery bill after a Kansas small business owner revealed that she wasn’t paid for muffins and sugar cookies that she delivered to a Marshall campaign event.
Marshall’s campaign (you are noticing the theme here) defended the candidate’s pattern of tracking down former patients for small unpaid medical bills from his OB-GYN practice. 
Attack ads about Hamilton allege that he overlooked child sexual abuse at a summer camp link to the Church of the Resurrection, the megachurch he leads in Leawood. (Note: He baptized my son more than 15 years ago during a time when my family attended services more regularly.)

Add all of that to this report from Cyabra. 
At the University of Kansas, I’m lucky to teach the first class for students majoring or minoring in journalism and mass communications. (Don’t forget to study for Exam #2 on Tuesday!) In that class, one of my first lessons is this: Media messages are constructed, often by a sender invisible to us, the audience. 
“Yes, that was an ad for Gatorade,” I tell my students. “But it was an uncredited advertising agency that made it — not Gatorade and not the athlete.”
“Yes, that is a podcast about football,” I say. “But consider how it might be a media facade — elaborate sponsored content of an online gambling company.”  
I have never sensed this central tenet of media literacy operating as acutely as during this election season. The creator often disappears. Intentionally.
After all, I sit here, writing about elaborately hidden inauthentic social media accounts being investigated by a “narrative intelligence company” that I previously hadn’t heard about. 
The experience feels like looking through a kaleidoscope into another kaleidoscope, both of them spinning furiously in a digital heartland whirlwind of red, white and blue.   
With that, dear voter, my safety advice as you scroll social media before heading to the polls through prairie winds of media-induced vertigo: Brace yourself.
Eric Thomas teaches visual journalism and photojournalism at the William Allen White School of Journalism and Mass Communication at the University of Kansas in Lawrence. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Huge bipartisan majorities of Ohioans want a fix to Social Security, new poll shows
text:
Without congressional action, Social Security could be facing a a 22% reduction in benefits in 2032. (Photo illustration by Getty Images)With Social Security recipients facing automatic 22% cuts in six years, Ohioans could scarcely be more unified in their demand that it be fixed, according to a poll a nonpartisan foundation is calling attention to. 
Due to decades of congressional inaction, the Social Security Trust Fund is now expected to become insolvent in six years. The shortfall will trigger an average monthly cut in Ohio of $487, the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget reports.
AARP Ohio estimates that the program keeps more than 700,000 Ohio seniors out of poverty, so such a large reduction in benefits would plunge many seniors into poverty at a time in their lives when they can do little about it.
That’s emphatically not what Ohioans want, according to a poll commissioned by the Peter G. Peterson Foundation.
The August poll found that 85% of likely Ohio voters said it was important to fix Social Security. That includes 88% of Republicans, 81% of Democrats and 79% of independents.
The same poll found that many voters were unaware of Social Security’s pending insolvency.
“Over half of Ohio voters (53%) are unaware of automatic benefit cuts to Social Security set to take place in 2032,” it said. “However, once voters are informed of these automatic benefit cuts, nearly all Ohio voters say it is important for lawmakers to have a plan to reform Social Security to prevent automatic benefit cuts. This urgency for reform spans partisanship and generational divides as well.” 
It added that once they were told that the trust fund is running out of money, 75% said they’d be more likely to vote for a U.S. Senate candidate with a plan to stop automatic cuts to benefits.
The two major candidates in Ohio’s closely watched U.S. Senate race have expressed concerns about Social Security, but haven’t delved deeply into how they’d fix it. 
Former U.S. Sen. Sherrod Brown, a Democrat, earlier this month said that he’d raise the income level at which Social Security taxes are paid.
“To ensure that Social Security benefits are there for future generations, we need to ensure that billionaires are paying their fair share by raising the tax cap so we can extend the life of the program,” he said.
Wage earners pay a 6.2% Social Security tax only on their first $184,000 of income, and that tax is matched by employers. So applying the tax all the way up the income scale would raise a lot more money.
Ohio Republican incumbent U.S. Sen. Jon Husted has said that he believes Social Security is a “sacred” commitment that he wants to protect. But during a June appearance on the “Guy Benson Show,” Husted said he was against a proposal by Sens. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, and Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., to raise the Social Security cap as Brown advocates.
“We need to secure Social Security,” Husted said in the radio interview. “We need to protect it. We need to make it stronger. I also agree that it will require a bipartisan solution. But I’m not on board with the process they’ve outlined regarding the tax increase… the targeted tax increase they have.”
He added, “This rifle approach with a giant tax increase is not the way I’d go about it.”
The interview moved on to other subjects without Husted saying what he would do to fix Social Security. His office didn’t respond to questions for this story.
The proposal he rejected is popular. The poll for the Peterson Foundation found that 72% of Ohio voters support it.
However, undertaking that measure now wouldn’t be enough. Citizens for a Responsible Federal Budget estimates that it would only close 65% of the solvency gap — meaning that more needs to be done.
Sixty-eight percent of those polled said they would support capping benefits for higher income beneficiaries. Capping annual benefits for the wealthiest retirees at the normal retirement age (67 for people born in 1960) at $100,000 for couples and $50,000 for individuals would close another 20% of the solvency gap if the cap is indexed to inflation, Citizens for a Responsible Federal Budget estimates.
The group laid out another possibility that the Peterson Foundation didn’t ask about in its poll. It would be an employer compensation tax. 
It would replace employer Social Security and Medicare contributions with a flat tax on all compensation — including massive CEO pay and their gold-plated benefits. That measure is estimated to close 66% of the Social Security shortfall and half of a corresponding gap in Medicare.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: What early voting can – and can’t – tell us about how Georgia’s midterm election so far
text:
Georgia "I voted" stickers line a table at a Fulton County polling place on the first day of early voting. Maya Homan/Georgia RecorderFriday is the last day to vote early in Georgia ahead of Tuesday’s midterm election, and leaders from both parties have been poring over the record early voting numbers to try to figure out where their voters are turning out and where they need to marshal their resources.
Rick Jackson speaks at a campaign rally in Canton Oct. 24, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Some of Georgia’s top races are expected to be tight. The governor’s race between Republican Rick Jackson and Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms is polling within the margin of error, and Sabato’s Crystal Ball, which rates the competitiveness of contests, recently shifted Georgia’s attorney general and secretary of state races from lean Republican to toss-up.
The early voting numbers are in flux, and unlike some other states, Georgia voters do not indicate their party affiliation when registering to vote. That makes using early voting information an imprecise measure, says Trey Hood, director of the survey research center at the University of Georgia’s School of Public and International Affairs.
Democratic candidate for governor Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, speaks at a rally with former President Barack Obama and Sen. Jon Ossoff in south Atlanta on Oct. 28, 2026. Alander Rocha/Georgia Recorder
“We have to be cautious about inferring what’s going to happen for the election outcome as a whole just from early voting in Georgia, especially because we don’t have party registration figures,” Hood said.
“People just love to speculate using any kernel of information that may be out there, but it is speculation,” he added.
That being said, the partisan breakdown of the counties in which voters are casting ballots can be illustrative, especially in the context of what polling says about voter attitudes. Top Georgia Republicans have also been sounding the alarm about early voting turnout on the campaign trail.
Nearly 2.4 million ballots had been cast as of Thursday. In general, turnout has been higher in metro Atlanta and other areas where Democrats make up majorities and lower in more rural areas of the state where Republicans cast more votes. Data suggests that young and nonwhite voters are also turning out at a faster clip than in previous years, said University of Georgia political science professor Charles Bullock.
“Democratic areas are turning out well. Blacks are turning out well. Younger voters are turning out better,” he said Wednesday. “And for Democrats, the younger the voters, the better Democrats do. So yeah, it does look like the wind is blowing in Democrats’ direction right now in terms of this early voting.”
High Democratic enthusiasm jibes with what Georgia voters tell pollsters.
In a recent Atlanta Journal-Constitution poll, only 42% of respondents said they approved of Republican President Donald Trump’s performance, and only 33% of respondents said they feel the nation is headed in the right direction.
Voters report high levels of consternation over the economy as prices increase amid the continuing war in Iran and the White House’s tariff policies. The midterm election is widely seen as a referendum on Trump’s second term, with even the president pleading with his supporters to “pretend” he is on the ballot.
A tale of ‘Two elections’
One of the most important questions for Election Day will be whether Republicans can make up enough ground in one day to overcome the advantage Democrats build up in early voting.
Georgia Republican Party Chairman Josh McKoon. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Georgia GOP Chairman Josh McKoon said he’s hopeful they will.
“Historically, with the exception of the 2024 presidential election, Democrats have turned out in greater numbers during early voting in Georgia,” he said. “Essentially there are two elections — the early voting led by Democrats and Election Day voting led by Republicans. We will need Republicans, particularly in rural Georgia, to turn out on Election Day in order to win this election. This has been true for most election cycles since the advent of in person early voting.”
Bullock said that phenomenon might be less pronounced this year since President Donald Trump has stopped encouraging Republicans to wait until Election Day. And in a midterm election in which the president of the incumbent party has low poll numbers, Republicans could be hard pressed to outperform their baseline, he added.
“All the indications are the Republicans probably won’t,” Bullock said. “And if you go back and look at what happened in our primary, there were 150,000 more Democratic than Republican ballots cast there. That’s only the second time since 2010 where there’s been more Democratic than Republican participation in the primary, and the other time that happened was 2020, which was a good year for Democrats. So lots of evidence that the enthusiasm gap this year is favoring Democrats.”
At campaign events, Jackson has expressed concern about turnout in rural Georgia, indicating he believes that voters there could be taking the election for granted.
“If people in rural Georgia and other places think, ‘Oh, well, this is going to be easy,’ and they don’t show up, we’re going to lose,” Jackson told reporters at a stop in DeKalb County Tuesday. “This is a turnout race. When it’s this close, it’s a turnout race.”
Bottoms does not appear to be taking victory for granted, urging supporters to keep up their momentum from a Clayton County rally with former President Barack Obama Wednesday night.
“With just three days of voting remaining, we still have thousands of calls to make and doors to knock on,” she said. “Our turnout is looking great, but it ain’t over until it’s over. We’re starting to see an uptick in Republican votes, and we don’t want to be overtaken on Election Day.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Commentary: Brewers’ World Series win reminds us what Wisconsin can be
text:
The World Series game four watch party at American Family Field sold out, with fans packing into the stands along the first and third base sides. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)We don’t have a sports section at the Wisconsin Examiner. But when the Milwaukee Brewers went to the World Series for the first time in 44 years, we couldn’t ignore it. Fortunately, the one member of our staff with a sports reporting background, Henry Redman — the sports editor of his college newspaper at Loyola University Chicago— was willing to drive down to Milwaukee to claim a press box seat at American Family Field. Redman covered game four, watching the big screen with the sold-out crowd of Brewers fans who were ready to cheer a historic Series win as their team played in St. Petersburg. It turned out to be a long night, with the Brewers losing at the bottom of the 12th inning. The next night it fell to reporter Baylor Spears, who has plenty of experience covering late-night legislative hearings, to write up game five, and the Brewers’ first-ever World Series win. 
The World Series was a welcome break from the divisive politics of this edgy midterm election season. Every resident of our 50-50 purple state was united in rooting for the Brewers. (Well, almost everyone; Spears reports that the latest Marquette poll found 1% of state residents actively rooting against the home team.)  As Spears and Redman write, “The team, and its huge win, represents a point of unity.”  That feeling, of coming together as a community in a moment of shared civic pride, is a welcome reminder that toxic partisanship is not the only possible atmosphere we can live in. 
As Milwaukee resident from Brookfield Sarah Coleman told Redman while watching game four, “It says a lot that a small market team swept the highest paid team in Major League Baseball. It’s cool to talk about the underdog.” 
The Brewers beat the Los Angeles Dodgers in four games out of four in the National League Championship. The Dodgers’ payroll, the highest in Major League Baseball, is two and half times the size of the younger, scrappier Brewers’. 
Go Brewers!
“It’s nice to enjoy something so positive,” Chrystal Glynn-Skipini told Redman. 
That positivity had an effect on our state’s sour and fractious politics. It lightened voters’ mood and made them less angry, and gave everyone a breather in the heat of a contentious election. It made it harder for Republicans to run their usual play, bashing Milwaukee, the heavily Democratic city President Donald Trump has called “horrible” and generations of Republican lawmakers have portrayed in thinly veiled racist terms as a crime-ridden hell hole. Trump declared last week that “nobody cares” about a World Series featuring two small-market teams. But here in Wisconsin, Republican gubernatorial candidate Tom Tiffany was savvy enough to celebrate the Brewers’ win, separating it from the barrage of negative ads targeting his rival Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley.
There’s no doubt that the glow of the Brewers’ World Series victory is a boost for Crowley, who, with current Gov. Tony Evers, helped negotiate the stadium deal to keep the team in Milwaukee. But regardless of politics, the Brewers are for everyone. The players and their manager Pat Murphy acknowledged the outpouring of support from the fans after they won. “I think about the state of Wisconsin, they pushed us through for sure,” Murphy said. 
The last time the Brewers went to the World Series, in 1982, they suffered a heart-breaking game seven loss against the St. Louis Cardinals. Milwaukee had a massive parade to welcome them home anyway, to the players’ amazement. “This was true love, and it was mutual right down to the bitter end,” writes Brewers beat reporter Adam McCalvy. A despondent Robin Yount, the Brewers’ hall of fame shortstop and center fielder, was in no mood for a parade, McCalvy recounts. The players and owner Bud Selig were sure the turnout would be embarrassing. Selig even apologized to the players for agreeing to it. But the fans came out in such numbers they shut down the city, lining the roads while another 10,000 Wisconsinites packed the stadium. “It turned out to be a nice event, and I guess it helped take a little of the sting off. … It showed the class of the fans of Milwaukee,” Yount told McCalvy. 
This time, the Brewers are coming home as winners to bask in their city’s adulation at the championship parade on Friday. 
May all that good feeling carry us through next week and into a better era.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Pa. AG Dave Sunday launches effort to prevent cryptocurrency scams at Bitcoin ATMs
text:
A view of a Bitcoin ATM at Northgate Mall on February 05, 2026 in San Rafael, California. (Photo by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)Tens of thousands of Pennsylvanians lost millions to cryptocurrency scams last year. To help halt the flow of stolen funds, state Attorney General Dave Sunday is urging business owners with cryptocurrency kiosks to voluntarily place signage warning about popular tactics used to trick victims, especially the elderly.
Cryptocurrency may be an increasingly popular option for investments and banking, “but for many Pennsylvanians, particularly older adults unfamiliar with this technology, it can be very confusing,” Sunday said Thursday, speaking at a Monroe County senior center. 
“(Scammers) exploit the unfamiliarity through fraudulent investment opportunities, online romance scams and cryptocurrency kiosks, commonly known as Bitcoin ATMs,” continued Sunday. “These are calculated attempts to frighten, manipulate and deceive people into handing over their money with devastating consequences.”
One of the signs produced by the Attorney General’s Office to warn consumers who use cryptocurrency kiosks. (From the Attorney General’s Office)
The signs urge people to “stop and verify” if someone pressures them to send money through the machines, and to report suspected scams to the agency’s Bureau of Consumer Protection at 1-800-441-2555. 
“Stop before making a financial decisions because someone is threatening you or someone you love is promising you an opportunity that sounds too good to be true,” Sunday continued. “These signs are designed to reach people in that critical moment when they are standing in front of one of these machines, and they may be seconds away from putting their life savings into a transaction that they may never be able to reverse.”
It’s not clear how many cryptocurrency kiosks sit in the commonwealth’s gas stations, grocery stores or other retail locations, but one vendor reported upwards of 450 operating ATMs earlier this year. The machines convert cash into digital currency, which can be stored in a digital wallet. 
Lawmakers considered a proposal to regulate the kiosks earlier this year, requiring anti-fraud warnings and enhanced safeguards, but Senate Bill 1015 ultimately didn’t advance out of committee. 
 An ever-growing problem

Funds, once transferred to another person, are difficult to recover. 
Americans lost nearly $21 billion in cryptocurrency and artificial intelligence scams last year, according to the FBI, including $538 million in Pennsylvania. 
Sunday specifically warned about people who impersonate law enforcement or other government employees to pressure victims into turning over their assets. 
“They may claim you have an outstanding warrant, that you missed jury duty or that you owe money for a violation. Then comes the threat: pay immediately, or you will be arrested,” said Sunday. “Let me be absolutely clear: no legitimate law enforcement agency or court will direct you to a cryptocurrency kiosk to pay a fine, resolve a warrant or avoid arrest.”
Pa. senators weigh consumer protections from cryptocurrency scams

If someone makes that demand, he advised Pennsylvanians to hang up and call the agency independently. 
Other scammers may use romance or build trust over months before trying to collect money, he added. 
He noted that his office was working with the Pennsylvania Food Merchants Association to provide training and distribute flyers to their members, which includes convenience stores, supermarkets, grocers and more.
“Cryptocurrency is the latest front in the longstanding battle against consumer fraud,” said PFMA president and CEO in an agency press release. “PFMA remains committed to protecting our members from fraud and the public, our members’ customers, from abuse. We value our partnership with OAG and law enforcement across Pennsylvania to raise awareness about crypto fraud schemes and equip the retail community to fight back against this novel threat.”
Sunday reported 290 scam complaints involving cryptocurrency to his office last year, likely an undercount since many victims don’t report the crime to authorities. 
“Some (victims) are embarrassed, others believe nothing can be done and some do not realize that they even were targeted until it’s too late,” Sunday added. “Scammers rely on fear, secrecy and urgency. They want their victims to believe they have no choice, that no one can help them and that they must act immediately. Our goal with this effort is to break that cycle.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio voter registrations are down
text:
Getty Images file photo of a voter registration form.Ohio voter registrations are down as the state faces what may be one of the most consequential midterm elections in modern history. The decline follows four years of new laws passed by the Republican legislature making it harder to register and harder to vote.
Registrations as of Oct. 26 were down 52,562 from 2018, the last midterm election before the legislature began a series of election-law changes. The numbers come from the Ohio secretary of state’s voter registration dashboard and database of previous elections.
The decline in registrations is going the opposite direction from Ohio’s population.
The eligible citizen voting-age population in Ohio grew by at least 111,564 from 2018 to 2023, according to the latest estimates in the Federal Register. 
Combining the population growth and registration decline reveals a disappearance of more than 164,000 potential voters. In 2012, Barack Obama won Ohio by only 166,000 votes.
Even more startling is that in 2008 — a presidential election year and the economy was in a deep slide — Ohio hit its highest voter registration of 8.29 million. Today’s registrations are 737,178 lower. Kamala Harris lost to Trump in Ohio in 2024 by 641,000.
The U.S. Elections Project, a pro-voter rights organization, ranked Ohio 12th in the nation in 2008 for voter participation and in 2024 the state had fallen to 24th.
The declining voter participation raises questions as to whether it is purposeful.  Multiple requests for explanations, public records and an interview with the state’s chief elections officer, Secretary of State Frank LaRose, have been acknowledged but unanswered since Sept. 13. 
Public statements and available records show that as they enacted restrictions on voting, LaRose and the legislature echoed Donald Trump’s false claims of rigged elections and voter fraud. 
LaRose in the last five years has made claims of more than 1,200 instances of voter fraud in Ohio, though the Ohio attorney general’s own website shows only 16 felony convictions for illegal voting or registration in the last 10 years, out of about 35 million votes cast.
Public records obtained by pro-democracy groups over the last few years show that LaRose’s office met often with State Sen. Theresa Gavarone, R-Bowling Green, to discuss election-law changes. Among the legislative changes were:

In Gavarone’s Senate Elections Committee in December 2022, a seemingly innocuous bill was rewritten to require proof of citizenship to register to vote — proof that for many people was difficult to obtain. Ohioans also must prove citizenship again to vote by presenting photo identification. 
In February 2023 Gavarone introduced two bills that the Ohio Capital Journal identified as “priority voting measures” for LaRose. One created an election integrity unit within the Secretary of State’s office and the other required universal and more comprehensive voter-registration data among the 88 counties, a bill that LaRose said had been written with the help of the America First Policy Institute — a Trump-in-exile organization. 
In 2025, Gavarone introduced legislation that has the potential for aiding Trump’s attempts to interfere with mail-in ballots. It eliminated the grace period to accept mail-in ballots. Previously, ballots postmarked by election day had four days to arrive and be counted. She cited Trump’s 2025 executive order requiring that mail-in ballots must arrive no later than election night as a reason for the bill. Other states went to court to block Trump’s order — and won in the U.S. Supreme Court. If the law had been in effect in 2024, 20,896 ballots would have been incinerated rather than counted. 
The same bill required the secretary of state to conduct monthly comparisons of voter registrations against federal records rather than once-a-year registration audits. The law required the immediate purge of people suspected of being noncitizens, which the League of Women Voters and ACLU argue may violate federal voting rights law.

LaRose also actively opposed a national voter registration initiative that could have helped reverse Ohio’s decline. 
Immediately after taking office in 2021, President Joseph Biden issued an executive order to federal agencies to help states increase voter registration – if the states wanted the help. Agencies also were to review ways to encourage participation in democracy.
In the final months before the Harris-Trump 2024 election, LaRose joined with former Trump White House aide Stephen Miller’s America First Policy Institute to sue the administration claiming that Biden had exceeded his constitutional authority. Only one state was on the initial complaint, Ohio. The case was filed in Texas and three Texas lawmakers were included as plaintiffs. 
The America First news release about the lawsuit quoted LaRose as saying that Biden’s order “is a cynical attempt to turn government agencies into a Democratic turnout machine, and it’s wrong. That’s why I’m joining this lawsuit and working to hold the administration accountable.” 
To represent Ohio, LaRose hired a former Trump Department of Justice lawyer who in 2020-21 was instrumental in efforts to overturn the 2020 election.
The lawyer was Kenneth Klukowski, then in the D.C. law firm of Schaerr Jaffe and a former legal analyst for Breitbart. In December 2020, Klukowski was hired into the Trump Department of Justice to work for Jeffrey Clarke, who attempted to usurp leadership of the Department of Justice. 
Together, Klukowski and Clarke crafted letters telling state legislatures that they could replace Biden electors with Trump slates and overturn the election, according to Congressional testimony by Rep. Liz Cheney, R-Wyoming. 
The suit over the federal voter-registration initiative was dropped after Trump was elected and he rescinded the executive order.
In contrast, when Trump issued executive orders demanding that all states turn over their voter rolls so that his administration could control who votes by mail, LaRose complied. Thirty states refused, 26 have won in court and the others are still in litigation, according to the Brennan Center for Justice.
Polling shows Americans and Ohioans are growing impatient with corruption, the cost of living,  existential threats from artificial intelligence, war and the loss of healthcare benefits. Trump’s approval rating is the lowest for any president prior to a midterm election since 1946.
With billionaires and cryptocurrency backers spending at least $500 million on Ohio’s senate and gubernatorial races, the GOP super majority in the state legislature in question and the balance of Congress at stake, concerns are mounting about how Trump and Republicans might interfere if Ohioans are in a mood for change. 
Trump has already filed suit to block the Alaska U.S. Senate election, but only if his candidate loses, and his administration has dispatched federal agents to immigrant neighborhoods looking for potential voter fraud.
Pro-voting-rights groups have organized intervention teams for a variety of election-interference scenarios but also stress that individual ballots are secure and the local voting process has worked smoothly for decades.
 “One of the things here in Ohio is that we have the benefit of bipartisan local boards of elections. It’s a huge safeguard,” said Steve David, Ohio director of All Voting is Local, a pro-voter-rights organization. He said that Ohio’s boards of elections are generally high-functioning, collegial organizations of two Republicans and two Democrats. 
His group has spent years attending board meetings and building trust relationships, he said.
On occasion, there can be a tie vote at the local level and the tie is broken by the secretary of state. “The secretary of state can advance a false narrative to invalidate votes,” he warned. 
Asked about LaRose specifically, he said LaRose has aligned himself with a “harmful narrative” coming out of the current government. “One of the things I would point to is that he says Ohio runs good elections but there are problems elsewhere, which creates an atmosphere of doubt….. Because LaRose casts doubt, it hurts election workers in our own state.”
Doug Oplinger is a Pulitzer Prize winning journalist who worked at the Akron Beacon Journal. Oplinger can be contacted at oplingerdoug@gmail.com
