name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Race for Ohio attorney general pits longtime state leader against attorney hoping for change
text:
Voters mark their primary election ballots at Second Presbyterian Church in Little Rock, Arkansas, on March 3, 2026. This year’s statewide ballot measures are written, on average, at a graduate-school reading level, according to a new report. (Photo by John Sykes/Arkansas Advocate)Ohio voters will decide who the newest state attorney general will be in an open race to decide the state’s chief law enforcement officer and legal counsel.
The most recent elected attorney general, Dave Yost, resigned in June to take a position with a Christian non-profit law firm called Alliance Defending Freedom. Governor Mike DeWine appointed his public safety director, Andy Wilson, to fill in as interim attorney general until a new one is elected.
Vying for the job on the Republican ticket is current Auditor of State Keith Faber, and attorney John Kulewicz stands on the Democratic side.
Keith Faber. (Official Auditor’s Office photo.)
Faber has been in Ohio politics for decades, serving in both chambers of the legislature, and as Senate president before moving to the Ohio Auditor’s Office.
Kulewicz has had a four-decade career as a private attorney for Vorys, Sater, Seymour and Pease, LLP, and has sat on Upper Arlington’s city council.
As the campaign moves toward the Nov. 3 general election, Faber has touted his years of government experience, including criminal cases that were conducted by the auditor’s office to root out “waste, fraud, and abuse.”
Kulewicz has promoted his experience as a legal professional over the last 40 years as part of his campaign, but also pointed to a need for change after three decades of Republican leadership and the negative impacts he says it’s had on the state.
In an interview with the Capital Journal this week, Kulewicz said voters have made clear what they want to see from elected officials in Ohio like the attorney general.
“I literally see people who have woken up all over Ohio to the fact that 36 years of almost uninterrupted one-party rule has gotten us nowhere,” Kulewicz said. “We’re far behind, we are hurting economically, we are making less and less, and we are having to pay more and more for everything.”
Democratic candidate for Ohio Attorney General in the 2026 Election, John J. Kulewicz, a Columbus-area attorney. (Photo from campaign.)
Working his way across the state during the campaign, the Democrat said he’s run into tried-and-true Republicans who are now considering other options. Many people from all over the political spectrum, including a man at a football game in Middletown, have told him they are looking for a moment without chaos.
“The guy who nailed it, I thought, he told me ‘we’ve got to stop the insanity,’” Kulewicz told the Capital Journal. “People want to correct things.”
As attorney general, he said he wants to be in the courtroom as much as he is managing the office.
“I want to be an attorney general who actually goes to court, I want to have a caseload, I want to be in court,” he said.
Faber was unavailable for an interview with the Capital Journal for this article.
  The issues 
In a debate between Faber and Kulewicz hosted by the Youngstown Press Club, the state auditor pledged to bring “the experience, the skill, and the vision” to the office of attorney general.
During the debate, Faber said his priorities as attorney general would be on cybercrime, human trafficking, elder abuse, and “those companies that are taking advantage of Ohio.”
He and Kulewicz disagreed on most things, including Ohio being involved in multi-state lawsuits, where Kulewicz wants to hold back on those types of cases unless “they’re going to make a fundamental difference to the people of Ohio.”
In Faber’s view, there are times when it’s “a very important priority for Ohio to engage” in multi-state lawsuits.
“If you’ve got a case where the federal government is trying to encroach on Ohio’s sovereignty, it’s important to be able to push back on that,” Faber told the Youngstown audience.
Faber also promised to support federal immigration enforcement officials, push for the regulated use of Flock cameras, and litigate a resolution to the court case regarding Ohio House Bill 6’s energy company bailouts, and the leaders of FirstEnergy. The previous court case against FirstEnergy CEO Chuck Jones and VP Mike Dowling ended in a hung jury.
“We’re going to prosecute that case, that case will already be going on by the time I’m sworn in as your attorney general,” Faber said.
But he said it’s important for him as a prosecutor to get all the facts about the case when he comes into the office, rather than to comment on it before he’s the lead lawyer for the state.
Kulewicz pushed back on Faber’s comments, saying “we have all the evidence we need.”
“I have no hesitation in saying I have every intention in going forward with that trial,” Kulewicz said.
On the topic of immigration enforcement, Kulewicz and Faber both support doing what is required by law when it comes to federal enforcement, but past the letter of federal law, they differ.
Kulewicz called immigrants “the backbone of this nation” and said he was “100% for” lawful immigration.
“To the extent that the state of Ohio is required to cooperate in enforcement of immigration laws, of course we will do that,” he said during the Youngstown debate. “But to the extent that it is discretionary, I’d rather spend our resources on enforcement of our state and local laws.”
Faber said “it’s key” that local law enforcement cooperate with federal immigration officials.
“Where you have problems is when local communities decide they want to be a sanctuary community, and they don’t cooperate with federal law enforcement, that leads to all sorts of potential conflicts,” Faber said.
The two agree when it comes to capital punishment, in that state laws are in place for the use of the method, so the attorney general’s office has a role in litigating death penalty cases.
“It’s up to the legislature, the general assembly, to decide the state policy on capital punishment, but the reality is if we’re going to have it, it needs to be utilized, it needs to be carried out, and it needs to be administered in a fair and a transparent way,” Faber said in Youngstown.
Kulewicz said he had concerns about potential alternative chemicals that have been discussed nationally, but overall said Ohio’s laws are appropriate.
“I believe the people of Ohio and the Ohio General Assembly have appropriately observed capital punishment for only the most severe offenses, and they have done so wisely,” Kulewicz said.
Early in-person voting, along with military, overseas, and absentee voting are already underway in Ohio ahead of the Nov. 3 general election.
Absentee ballots must be received by local boards of elections by election day. The last day for early in-person voting is Nov. 1. Election-Day voting begins at 6:30 a.m. and ends at 7:30 p.m.

title: Catching Our Eye News Roundup, Oct. 30, 2026
text:
The Ohio burgee. (Getty images file photo.)Every morning in the Ohio Capital Journal’s free newsletter, The Eye-Opener, we round up the news and commentary from across Ohio and around the country and world that is catching our attention. We call this feature Catching Our Eye, republished here.

If you already subscribe, please share with your family and friends so they know about the Ohio Capital Journal too: https://ohiocapitaljournal.com/subscribe/

 Catching Our Eye

• Healthcare costs. Ideastream’s Ida Lieszkovszky reports, “’Out of control’ healthcare costs and too few solutions worry Northeast Ohio voters.”
Nationwide, healthcare coverage has been getting more expensive. Small group coverage rates are expected to rise by 14% for next year. Prices on the healthcare marketplace are anticipated to jump 15%, on top of steep premium hikes coupled with the loss of federal subsidies. Even private insurance is set to increase by more than 8% on average.
Then there’s Medicaid. New work requirements will kick in at the start of the year, which means some people may no longer qualify for coverage. One study estimates that as many as 356,000 Ohioans could drop off the Medicaid rolls in 2027. But some voters say what they’re hearing from the candidates does not reflect the increases they’re seeing on their healthcare bills.
• Caregiving costs. NPR reports, “What’s gone up even faster than gas or rent? The cost of caregiving.”
As prices have ticked up in recent years, the cost to caregivers has skyrocketed. A study, released Wednesday by AARP and shared first with NPR, finds that family caregivers — people helping out disabled, chronically ill or elderly adults — now spend an average $11,508 out of pocket each year. That’s roughly 60% more than just five years ago, and adds up to 31% of a caregiver’s income, on average.
The increase during those years is more than twice the overall rate of inflation of 24%, as measured by the federal Bureau of Labor Statistics’ Consumer Price Index. What’s driving the ramp-up? Food, housing and medical expenses are the biggest chunk, finds the study, which queried 2,538 family caregivers.
• Electricity costs. TIME reports, “Ohio’s Data-Center Revolt Is Upending the Midterms.”
The fervor against data centers is spreading across the state. Ohio has some 200 data centers, making it one of the biggest hubs in the country. In a former swing state that went red in the Trump era, Republicans admit the groundswell of political opposition to data centers has created a political opening for Ohio Democrats in the upcoming midterm elections…
A national Gallup poll published in May found that more than 70% of voters oppose building an AI data center in their area. In Ohio, where the average household’s electric bill climbed some 15% in the past year and more than 66% over the past decade, the sentiment is even more negative. A September survey by Bowling Green State University found that nearly 80% of Ohioans support a moratorium on data centers. More than 100 local governments in Ohio have reportedly enacted data-center moratoriums; in November, at least 10 will vote on adding a data-center ban to their charters, while two others will decide whether to recall mayors who cut data-center deals. In the eyes of opponents, the facilities—and the powerful AI industry that backs them—have come to represent an attack on their safety, jobs, pocketbooks, and quality of life.
• Data centers on the ballot. WLWT’s Giacomo Luca reports, “Ohioans will decide on most data center ballot issues in America.”
Ohio voters will decide on 21 local data center ballot issues this November, more than any other state in the nation. Buckeye voters are considering bans, regulations, and zoning changes related to data center infrastructure in 18 communities and 16 counties across the state.

name: California
title: Has the Trump administration doomed Newsom’s water plan?
text:
California water regulators have approved a new plan overhauling how farms and cities take water from the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta and rivers that feed it, setting up the next fight over Gov. Gavin Newsom’s plan to balance water supplies with the needs of a struggling ecosystem.
The plan gives water agencies a choice: agree to forgo some water and restore habitats, or fall under the regulatory backup — a set of mandatory rules for how much water must remain in rivers and streams to flow through the Delta. 
But the compromise the Newsom administration reached four years ago with the state’s most powerful water suppliers now faces opposition from unexpected quarters. 
Powerful water agencies that once backed it say Newsom’s voluntary agreements have become too restrictive. The Trump administration has threatened to withdraw support and several hundred million dollars in funding. And environmental advocates, tribes, and fishing groups warn that the deal and its regulatory backup gut protections for an ecosystem already in crisis.
Opening this week’s final hearings, E. Joaquin Esquivel, chair of the State Water Resources Control Board, said he was struck by the opposing criticism. He called water agencies’ narrative that the plan has strayed from Newsom’ original deal “convenient theater.” 
“Some agencies say we kept too much oversight,” Esquivel said. On the other hand, tribes and environmental groups say “we kept too little. They are pointing at the same provisions from opposite directions. That doesn’t make the plan perfect. It does tell me the plan sits where a regulator should.”
The question is how California’s water regulators will move forward without the buy-in of major water users these agreements had aimed to bring on board, and whether the regulatory backup will hold if they don’t. 
“That creates a world of confusion and dysfunction,” Gary Bobker, program director at Friends of the River, said at a briefing Tuesday. “And I think the board recognizes that they’re going to be handed an incredible morass.”
Supporters say the deal has changed
The Delta is the heart of California’s water delivery system, where state and federal pumps export Northern California river water to Central and Southern California. It’s also the center of California’s water wars, and in the throes of collapse. 
State officials have been warning for years that existing rules aren’t enough to stop the precipitous decline of native species like the state’s iconic salmon as they lose freshwater to cities and farms. Crashing populations forced the recent cancellation of salmon fishing for three unprecedented years in a row.
An aerial view of fall-run Chinook salmon migrating and spawning in the Feather River in Oroville on Oct. 28, 2024. Photo by Xavier Mascareñas, California Department of Water Resources
But the state last overhauled the Bay-Delta Water Quality Control Plan, a keystone document governing water quality and flows, in 1995. 
Late Thursday night, after two days of public comments raising concerns with the plan and several hours deliberating last minute changes, the State Water Resources Control Board approved an update centering Newsom’s voluntary agreements. 
Only one board member, civil engineer Nichole Morgan, voted against the update. Among the yes votes was Newsom’s former secretary for environmental protection Jared Blumenfeld, a signatory to the original deal. 
California Natural Resources Secretary Wade Crowfoot told a quiet room Thursday that he knew this path forward was uncomfortable for everyone. 
“We heard yesterday a lot of groups, including tribal governments, that continue to believe that this is not sufficient, and this is the wrong approach,” Crowfoot said. “We have water agencies that aren’t comfortable with the way that their proposal — our proposal — has materialized … That’s natural. This is a paradigm shift.”
Officially known as the Healthy Rivers and Landscapes Program and backed by $2.9 billion of mostly state as well as federal and water supplier money, the Newsom administration touted these agreements as a way to forestall legal fights while balancing competing demands on the Delta. 
But after years of regulatory processes, public comment and environmental review, the original signatories are balking. Water users, including Westlands Water District, a power player in the state’s $60 billion agricultural economy, say the current plan is not what they signed up for.  
“It’s unrecognizable,” said Jennifer Pierre, general manager for the State Water Contractors, which represents public water agencies serving 750,000 acres of farmland and 27 million people. 
Pierre called the latest version a “complete system of micromanagement” that centers too much decision-making with the state water board’s executive director, and retains too little flexibility. 
“I think everyone’s reviewing it to see, okay, we’ve all acknowledged this is not what we proposed, but is it workable?” she said. 
A second front opens up
In a major blow to the voluntary agreements, the federal government — which pumps Delta water to millions of acres of Central Valley farmland — is threatening to jump ship. If it does, it would take hundreds of millions of federal dollars with it. 
State water regulators clarify that no one has yet officially withdrawn from the deal. But the threat hits harder than those from other water users, said Barry Nelson, a senior policy analyst for the Golden State Salmon Association. 
“They’re the largest water project in the Central Valley. They have more storage than anyone else in the state of California. And they jointly operate the Delta with the state,” Nelson said at a briefing for reporters. 
Aubrey J.D. Bettencourt, principal deputy commissioner of the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation, which operates California’s federal water delivery system, wrote to the water board in September to express the Trump administration’s “serious concern” with the near-final draft. 
Bettencourt said it “reflects more of what has come to be expected from the State Board – executive and regulatory overreach, questionable legal authority, and continued downward pressure on water users throughout the state,” referring to reduced water supplies. 
These concerns include a new provision requiring that if state or federal managers make substantial changes to water deliveries that decrease flows through the Delta, they must submit a plan to make up for the loss. 
The addition comes after the Trump administration’s unilateral move last December to allow more federal exports from the Delta to Central Valley farms. California officials, who typically coordinate with federal water managers, warned at the time this risked leaving less for other water users and the environment. 
Bettencourt wrote that if the board fails to address the Trump administration’s concerns, federal water managers will pull out and stop funding a plan she said “threatens reliability of water supplies that support … the entire fabric of California’s agricultural economy, rural communities, urban centers, and natural vitality.”
War among the water users
State water regulators say the plan can still succeed without federal participation or money, which was originally anticipated to reach $740 million. 
“We’re still committed to making the (voluntary agreements) pathway work for the other participants. It does complicate things, and we’ll have to work through that,” said Eric Oppenheimer, the state water board’s executive director.  
The money is part of the voluntary agreements’ $2.9 billion price tag intended to pay for habitat restoration and water purchases. 
Oppenheimer said that if the Trump administration pulls out, federal water managers at the bureau instead would be bound by the backup plan. 
But he added  the board’s modeling shows it’s in the Trump administration’s best interest to stick with the voluntary agreements because it will allow them to export more water. 
“It has a reduced water supply impact for Reclamation and its contractors, and we also think that the voluntary agreement itself is a benefit for the ecosystem,” Oppenheimer said. “But we can’t make them volunteer.” 
Environmental advocates and the fishing industry are skeptical about many things, including that state regulators will truly hold the federal government to the regulatory backup. They point to increased federal releases from Lake Shasta to send water to Central Valley farms this past summer, despite state objections that this would sap cold water necessary for imperiled salmon. 
Those who fought voluntary agreements from the outset for failing to protect the Delta and all who depend on it say it’s ironic that water users are now fighting the deal, too. 
“There actually might be a war among water users,” Bobker said. “That’s kind of what you’re seeing here: people who think the (voluntary agreements) are a weak-enough gutting of the regulations, and those who think actually no, they don’t go far enough.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: Hayes takes over Finance as Ferguson announces early changes to leadership
text:
Sen. Antonio Hayes (D-Baltimore City) will take over as chair of the the Senate Finance Committee, becoming the first Black lawmaker to lead the committee. (File photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)Sen. Antonio Hayes, a two-term Democrat from Baltimore City, will become the first Black lawmaker to chair the Senate Finance Committee, one of a series of changes that will make Senate leadership younger and less Montgomery County-centric.
The changes announced by Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore) Thursday, days ahead of Election Day, recognize the growing diversity of the Democratic Caucus in the Senate.
“The Senate Finance Committee sits at the center of policies that Marylanders rely on to ease burdens and build prosperity,” Ferguson said in a statement. “Senator Hayes’ ability to collaborate, bring people to the table, and develop thoughtful solutions ensures the committee will be able to balance the needs of families and business across the state.”
After a contentious primary campaign, Ferguson is favored to win reelection in his heavily Democratic district and is expected to remain as president, a job he has held since 2019, when the General Assembly convenes in January. To do so, the Senate leader faced a number of challenges that required changes.
Senate President Bill Ferguson. (File photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)
Changes announced do not include the creation of new committees — at one time as many as two were talked about. Instead, there are a batch of subcommittees — complete with chairs — and an expanded, unique role for one legislative veteran.
Ferguson’s new leadership team includes new chairs in two of the four standing committees. Three committees get new vice chairs and five of the eight chairs and vice chairs announced Thursday are new to the positions.
Black senators currently hold 16 of the 34 members in the Democratic caucus, and they’re expected to be 50% of the caucus come January. Women senators comprise roughly one-third of the majority party membership.
Black lawmakers would step into half of the eight committee leadership roles under Ferguson’s plan.
Hayes, who turns 49 next month, succeeds Sen. Pamela Beidle (D-Anne Arundel), 72, who had been chair since 2023. The 20-year legislative veteran, who served two terms in the Senate, did not seek reelection this year.
Her decision sparked talk of replacements, and also raised concerns that women would be shut out of chairing any of the four standing committees.
In addition to Hayes, Sen. Cory McCray, 43, also a Baltimore City Democrat, will take over as vice chair of the Senate Budget and Taxation Committee. He will also chair its subcommittee on Education, Business and Administration.
Ferguson praised McCray’s knowledge of the budget process saying it “will be critical as we navigate fiscal pressures on existing state programs,” said Ferguson.
Those pressures include a $3 billion structural budget gap in the coming year. In addition to cuts, lawmakers may also consider tax increases, including possible changes to the state’s 6% sales tax.
Sen. Cory McCray (D) represents northeast Baltimore City in the Maryland Senate. (File photo by Danielle E. Gaines/Maryland Matters)
McCray fills a role held for six years by Sen. Jim Rosapepe (D-Prince George’s and Anne Arundel). Rosapepe, 75, will chair the newly created Revenue Subcommittee.
Sen. Ben Brooks (D-Baltimore County) becomes the new vice chair of the Senate Education, Energy and Environment Committee. At 76, Brooks, a 12-year veteran of the House and Senate, is the oldest member of the committee leadership team.
Brooks succeeds Sen. Cheryl C. Kagan (D-Montgomery), 65, who has held the position since 2023. Kagan, an active participant in the National Conference of State Legislatures — she is its representative on the U.S. Election Assistance Commission Board of Advisors — will be a liaison for national legislative affairs. She will also chair the EEE committee’s subcommittee on elections — a topic on which she is recognized within the General Assembly as a leader.
Brooks previously served as chair of the Senate Executive Nominations Committee — a panel not included in the four major standing committees. He will be replaced by Sen. Alonzo T. Washington (D-Prince George’s).
Other appointments include:

Sen. Malcolm Augustine (D-Prince George’s) will chair the Budget and Taxation subcommittee on Pensions and Procurement.
Sen. Kevin Harris (D-Prince George’s, Calvert and Charles) will be chair of the Energy Subcommittee of the Education, Energy and the Environment Committee.

New roles for Feldman
Ferguson’s announcement included a slew of new roles for Sen. Brian Feldman (D-Montgomery).
Feldman, 65 and a three-term senator, trades his three years leading the Education, Energy and The Environment Committee for a role akin to a legislative Swiss Army knife.
Senate Education, Energy, and the Environment Committee Chair Brian J. Feldman (D-Montgomery) moves to an expanded Senate majority leader role. (File photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)
Part of that role includes taking over as Senate Majority Leader, a position previously held by Sen. Nancy King (D-Montgomery). King, 77, leaves the Senate in January after losing her primary to challenger Amar Mukunda.
Feldman also assumes a newly created role of chief of policy. Ferguson said Feldman will focus on “solving problems using legislative solutions and oversight” in that role.
As such, Feldman will be the only senator other than Ferguson who is not assigned to any one standing committee. But unlike Ferguson, Feldman will be an ex officio member of all four standing committees. While most ex officio members lack the ability to vote, Feldman will have voting rights in any committee on any issue in the event of a tie vote on the committee.
Since committees typically are odd numbers, ties would likely result from members who are excused as absent, such as in the case of illness, or when a member abstains or declines to vote on a bill. It is not clear if Feldman’s new power would also include an ability to break ties in subcommittees.
Finally, Feldman will chair what Ferguson termed a “reconstituted” Senate Rules and Operations Committee, with Augustine as vice chair.
The newly named committee will have “expanded jurisdiction over late bills and original jurisdiction on select multi-jurisdictional issues and state government organization and procedures, including in the judicial branch.” Ferguson’s announcement did not provide further details.
Women at the helm
Ferguson’s announcement also answers questions about whether a woman would chair one of the four standing committees.
From 1987 to present, one of the four major committees has been led by a female senator, with the exception of a stretch from 1992 to 1995.
Beidle’s departure ended a nearly decade-long run of women serving as chair of the Senate Finance Committee. The panel has had four women leaders since 1991, the most since 1987.
Sen. Dawn Gile (D-Anne Arundel) will take over as the new chair of the Senate Education, Energy and the Environment Committee. (File photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)
The committee with the second-most number of women chairs during that time was the Education, Health and Environmental Affairs Committee with two. It was rebranded the Education, Energy and the Environment Committee in 2023 by Ferguson.
First-term Sen. Dawn Gile (D-Anne Arundel), 46, will take over as chair of EEE in January. She is the presumptive favorite in next week’s general election.
“Senator Gile has demonstrated the ability to navigate complex policy issues,” Ferguson said.
Additionally, Sen. Katie Fry Hester (D-Howard and Montgomery), who turns 52 next month, will take over as vice chair of the Finance Committee.
Other women appointed to roles in the Senate include:

Sen. Shelly Hettleman (D-Baltimore County) chair of the Budget and Taxation subcommittee on Public Safety, Transportation and the Environment.
Sen. Karen Lewis Young (D-Frederick), chair of the subcommittee on Health and Human Services within Budget and Taxation.
Sen. Mary Washington (D-Baltimore City), majority whip.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT will pay you to beat New York in court. Almost no one can collect.
text:
Last July, Connecticut passed a law that reads like a dare. 
Public Act 25-172 promises a Connecticut resident who pays New York income tax on days worked at home in Connecticut a credit equal to 60 percent of the extra Connecticut tax that results when the state recalculates the credit it gave for that New York tax. 
The act also waives penalties and interest on the late Connecticut tax. It reaches back to tax years beginning in 2020.
The target is New York’s convenience-of-the-employer rule. One sentence of New York regulation says a nonresident’s days worked outside New York count as New York days unless the work was done out of state “of necessity, as distinguished from convenience.” New York’s 2006 guidance confines the rule to employees whose primary office is in New York and excuses a home day only when the home is a “bona fide employer office.” A Connecticut resident with a Manhattan employer who works Fridays in Fairfield pays New York tax on Friday.
To collect Connecticut’s 60 percent, the resident must do four things, and the act joins them with “and.” Pay the New York tax. Apply to New York for a refund and be denied. Appeal that denial to a court or tribunal. Obtain a final decision ordering New York to refund the tax.
On July 2, the Appellate Division, Third Department, the court that hears appeals from New York’s Tax Appeals Tribunal, ruled against Edward Zelinsky, a Connecticut resident and law professor who has been fighting this rule since his first Tribunal decision in 2001. The Tribunal had ruled against him in May 2025. The court found “no constitutional or other infirmity” in the rule, said the debate over remote work “remain[s] the province of the Legislature,” and saw “no basis to disturb the Tribunal’s determination sustaining the taxation.” The one road the act requires a resident to travel, denial, appeal, and a final win, was just closed again by the court at the end of it. As far as I can find, nobody has yet qualified for the credit, and after July no one is likely to.
There is a second problem, and it is Connecticut’s own. 
Since tax years beginning in 2019, Connecticut has had the same rule. Section 12-711 of the General Statutes counts as Connecticut income the pay of a nonresident for “days worked outside this state for such person’s convenience if such person’s state of domicile uses a similar test.” The Department of Revenue Services says plainly that for a New York resident working from home for a Connecticut employer, “Connecticut will apply the New York ‘convenience of the employer’ test.” 
Connecticut taxes New Yorkers at home in New York exactly as New York taxes Connecticut residents at home in Connecticut. The act pays Connecticut residents to attack, in New York’s courts, a rule Connecticut keeps on its own books.
What actually protects a Connecticut commuter is older and duller than the bounty. Section 12-704 gives residents a credit for income tax paid to another state, claimed on Schedule 2 of the CT-1040. The instructions to that form define qualifying income to include compensation “for personal services performed from a home office in Connecticut for an employer in a qualifying jurisdiction that applies a convenience of the employer test.” 
In plain terms: Connecticut already credits the New York tax on those Fridays. The credit is capped at the share of Connecticut tax that the New York income represents, and it cannot push Connecticut tax below what would be due if the New York income were left out, so a resident still pays the difference where New York’s tax runs higher. But the resident is not taxed twice on the same wage. The commuter who files Schedule 2 correctly and attaches the New York return, as Connecticut requires, is made whole to the extent Connecticut law allows, with no lawsuit.
If the General Assembly believes the convenience rule is unjust, it has two honest options. It can repeal Connecticut’s mirror of the rule, which would cost the state revenue from New Yorkers and would at least match its words to its conduct. Or it can pursue what no two of New York, New Jersey and Connecticut have ever signed: a reciprocal agreement. New Jersey’s only such agreement, with Pennsylvania, covers wages and nothing else. A bounty for winning a case the courts have now rejected three times is neither.
In the meantime, Connecticut residents with New York offices should do three things this filing season. Keep a day log; New York audits these. Ask the employer, in writing, whether the home office meets New York’s bona fide employer office test. And claim the Schedule 2 credit, with the New York return attached. The remedy is already in the instructions.
Myung Keon Kim is a certified public accountant licensed in New York whose practice prepares New York, New Jersey and Connecticut returns for individuals and small businesses.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Pingree and Russell hold steady in first and only CD1 debate
text:
Incumbent U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, a Democrat, faced Republican challenger Ron Russell in the first and only 1st Congressional District debate, days before the election, on Oct. 29, 2026. (Screenshots courtesy of Maine Public)[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: How to register, key dates, who’s on the ballot and where the candidates stand on the top issues facing Maine.]Just days before the midterm elections, candidates for Maine’s 1st Congressional District met for their first and only televised debate.
Incumbent Democrat U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree faced off against Republican Ron Russell Thursday night, in a debate hosted jointly by Maine Public, the Portland Press Herald and NewsCenter Maine. 
Compared to the fiery clashes in Maine’s other federal debates, the 1st District event was relatively even-keeled — an accurate representation of how the race has been outshined by other, more competitive, contests. 
The CD1 race was not among those that party leaders were watching closely to determine the balance of power in the U.S. House of Representatives. The Cook Political Report had rated the district solidly Democratic in the lead-up to the election.
Pingree has represented the district since 2009, and is currently the ranking Democratic member on the subcommittee on Interior, Environment and Related Agencies under the Committee on Appropriations. She also served in the Maine Senate from 1992-2000, and was majority leader in her final four years in the state Legislature. 
She faced off against Russell in her last reelection campaign in 2024, and solidly defeated him. 
Russell, 72, grew up in Fort Fairfield, and is a retired Army colonel. He served for just over 30 years as an airborne ranger Green Beret, and was in combat in Panama, Somalia, Afghanistan and other crisis response operations. 
After retiring, he founded the North Carolina-based defense contractor Far Ridgeline Engagements, and returned to Maine in 2021. Russell said he knows he’s a repeat candidate for voters, but hopes it will work in his favor. 
Ultimately, neither candidate offered any surprising stances or statements Thursday, instead reiterating what they’ve said on the campaign trail this year and in 2024. 
Bipartisanship, Trump and Iran
Both candidates were quick to make clear their positions on President Donald Trump’s agenda — and it was no surprise that Pingree is staunchly opposed to the president’s actions while Russell is a strong supporter. 
“I don’t know that there’s anything that I disagree with,” Russell said. “I disagree with how he goes about conducting business, but I don’t disagree with the policies that he has implemented, and I think they are significant in terms of helping out the American people.”
Pingree attributed many of the current affordability issues to Trump’s agenda, and said she hopes Democrats reach a majority in Congress to undo funding cuts and policy changes. 
Pingree said many Republicans “have just been sitting on their hands and unwilling to fight back,” something she has seen up close from her position on the House Appropriations Committee. 
In Maine’s 1st District, Pingree and Russell square off again

“I have watched bill after bill go through our committee, where the Republicans refuse to fight the repurposing of money, the stealing of money from accounts from this administration,” Pingree said. “We can bring that back to a sensible level and restore the funding to a lot of areas where we really need it to make sure people are whole.”
In opposition, Russell said he hopes Republicans get a strong majority after the election to prevent things from going back to the way they were under the Biden administration, and raised further concerns about the Democratic Party priorities. 
“The Democrat socialists are rearing their ugly heads here and gaining a significant amount of traction in the Democrat Party, and I think that’s worrisome there to me,” Russell said. 
Both candidates agreed on the importance of working across the aisle.
“Any legislation passed in Washington, D.C. that is not a function of both parties working together is bad legislation, because if it’s a partisan piece of legislation, 50% of the nation is being ignored,” Russell said. 
Pingree noted that she broke with Democrats in September to vote in favor of a bill to shield lobstermen from new regulations to protect North Atlantic right whales until 2035.
Russell pointed to Maine’s U.S. Senate race, where Democrats have criticized incumbent Sen. Susan Collins for voting with Trump too often, and said Pingree votes with Democrats most of the time. 
But Pingree countered that in recent years, that’s only because Republican leadership will only bring a few bills to an actual vote, most of which are coming directly from Trump. 
“And as I said, I work with my Republican colleagues as much as I possibly can,” Pingree said. “We don’t vote on a lot in a very dysfunctional Congress, but I’m not taking responsibility for that. That’s the speaker of the House and President Trump, who refuses to work with Democrats.”
Pingree was also asked about impeaching Trump, and she said if the Democrats don’t have a majority in the Senate to successfully impeach him, then “it will be yet another exercise in just reminding the American public, who already knows all the things that he has done.” 
“But I do think that you know the question regarding impeaching Secretary (Pete) Hegseth was about to face the Congress,” Pingree continued. “It will face us when we get back, and I think he has not done a very good job.”
When given the chance to question Russell directly, Pingree asked what advice the veteran would give to Hegseth, and if Russell would vote to impeach the secretary. 
Russell said he would not vote to impeach Hegseth, and he feels Hegseth “hasn’t done anything wrong.”
“From my perspective, he should listen to war fighters if he’s interested in war fighting to get their advice about who to release and who to keep on board,” Russell continued.
Similarly, Russell said he supported the Iran War and felt there was an “imminent threat” that required the president to act.
“I don’t think it’s feasible to brief the American people or all of Congress because the cat’s going to get out of the bag when that happens,” Russell said. “And how many examples of that do we have in our past history there? So no, I don’t think that that’s a good idea.”
Pingree called the conflict “a war of choice” and reiterated her support for ending military action.
“It’s been all bad, by all accounts that any of us can read,” Pingree said. “Almost no one advised the president to move forward on this. He didn’t take a lot of advice. He certainly didn’t come to Congress. He didn’t even go to the American people to make his case for doing this.”
Social Security, healthcare and student loans 
The candidates were also asked about changes to Social Security, as the agency faces a looming budget crisis. 
Russell said he would increase the cap on Social Security contributions, but would also seek to make larger changes. 
“I also think we need to look at a different system other than Social Security to privatize that and get away from a government-run system,” Russell said. 
He compared it to retirement savings accounts for members of the military, and the youth savings accounts started by Trump. But Russell said any changes would have to be slowly rolled out, to not affect people already on Social Security.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“I would not impact the people who are relying on Social Security in any way, shape, or form here currently,” Russell said. “They have earned what it is that they are getting here now, and I don’t think we need to degrade that what it is that they are earning already.”
Pingree said she agreed that the cap on contributions should be increased or eliminated, and the problem needs to be addressed quickly.
“We need to give young people a sense of security that not just retirees now are going to be safe, but their money will be safe going into the future,” Pingree said. 
But she disagreed with Russell on privatizing the program, and said it would be too risky for too many people.
“I would be very worried about privatizing Social Security, and I’ve never seen anyone put forward a plan that didn’t raise a lot of concerns on the ideas of the risk that you would be taking with the American public’s money,” Pingree said. 
The two also disagreed on how to lower healthcare costs. Russell said he thinks increasing competition will help, and so will the “Make America Healthy Again” movement as people focus on preventative care. 
“I think, from a healthcare perspective, emphasizing primary care and relying on primary care is a decent way to go,” Russell said. “You need to be in touch with your primary care physician and get the regular checkups so you can detect problems before they become major problems.”
Pingree supports universal healthcare, and said rising insurance costs have left many people with no insurance and “nowhere to turn.”
“Whether you want to call this socialism or some other name, people want affordable health care,” Pingree said. “People want to go to a primary care physician, but so many of them don’t have any healthcare coverage. They can’t do it.”
Russell said he opposes Medicare for all, explaining that he evaluates the proposal like he would in the military, based on suitability, feasibility and acceptability.
“From a suitability perspective, healthcare for all is a wonderful idea, and from acceptability, it’s also a wonderful idea,” Russell said. “But from a feasibility perspective, it’s not feasible.”
Pingree and Russell did agree on the need for student loan relief, although they have different approaches to education more broadly.
Both said they would like to see federal student loans offered with no interest, to reduce how much borrowers pay back. 
Pingree said the student loan debt is often “crippling” for students, and that is “no way to run a healthy economy.”
“It’s not a place where we should be thinking about how to make money,” Pingree said. “It’s a place where we should be thinking about the excessive costs of going to college today.”
Russell said his approach would be to emphasize the trades for more young people. 
“We certainly need to get back to vocational education there and at a much higher level than where we are at here right now, because we know that we are hurting in terms of individuals with trades,” Russell said.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Bagged animal health IV fluids win 2026 ‘Coolest Thing Made in Nebraska’ contest
text:
Voters named Grand Island-based Nova-Tech’s animal health IV fluids as this year’s champ of the popular contest that highlights the state’s manufacturing industry. (Courtesy of Nebraska Chamber of Commerce and Industry)

La VISTA — Animal health IV fluids made in Grand Island took home this year’s title of “Coolest Thing Made in Nebraska.” 
After weeks of buildup and tens of thousands of votes, the winning product, by Nova-Tech Inc., was revealed Thursday during the final hours of the Nebraska Chamber of Commerce and Industry Manufacturing Summit in La Vista.
Animal health IV fluids produced by Grand Island-based Nova-Tech won this year’s  “Coolest Thing Made in Nebraska” contest organized by the Nebraska Chamber of Commerce and Industry. (Courtesy of Nova-Tech)
The annual bracket-style tourney began last month with 16 products narrowed down from a large pool of nominees that had been submitted by supporters and workers. The multiphase contest is aimed at highlighting the state’s manufacturing industry during Manufacturing Month.
All early contenders — including manufacturers of an airboat, popcorn and Nebraska license plates — were invited to showcase their products during the summit. 
This year’s champ of the annual contest that started in 2022 was kept a secret until the summit. Established in 1988, Nova-Tech uses sterile manufacturing processes. Its IV fluids offer a balance of electrolytes to support rehydration and fluid replacement for all animals.
Teresa Grabowski, president and co-owner, said the win highlights the work of employees. “We’re incredibly proud to operate Nova-Tech out of Grand Island, Nebraska, where it all started and be part of Nebraska’s incredible and thriving manufacturing industry,” she said.
The animal IV products join past winners: a Grand Island-produced combine series by Case IH (2025), Valley Irrigation’s center pivot irrigation machine (2024), Rocket Mobility’s all-terrain tracked wheelchair made in Columbus (2023) and Kawasaki’s subway car built in Lincoln to run on the rail tracks of New York City (2022). 
The summit featured a talk from Joseph Young, chamber president and chief executive, networking opportunities and workshop topics such as the datacenter ecosystem and an update on state manufacturing policies. 
Also at the summit, Royal Engineered Composites of Minden was recognized as the 2026 Nebraska Manufacturer of the Year. The award by the chamber recognizes a state manufacturer that implements innovative ways to conduct business urging  products, processes, technologies and other strategies.
Royal was founded in Minden, a town of about 3,000, more than 75 years ago. With a worldwide reach, the company specializes in the commercial and defense aerospace industry. Customers include Boeing, Northrop Grumman and Bell Helicopter. 
In April, Royal announced a $5 million investment in its Minden facility, including a 23,500-square-foot expansion and $2 million in advanced manufacturing equipment to enhance in-house production and inspection of large aerospace components.

name: California
title: For the record: Fresno man deported by ICE had previous illegal crossings
text:
In summary
Luis Arreguin had been deported five times before his recent immigration arrest in Fresno County, according to federal authorities.


A deported immigrant who was profiled in a CalMatters story earlier this week failed to disclose his criminal record and deportation history to the news organization. 
CalMatters learned of his background through a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement social media post attacking the news organization Thursday.
ICE’s X (Twitter) account said Luis Arreguin had been deported five times and had “a criminal history including aggravated assault with a weapon, firearms offenses, and DUI,” and said that CalMatters failed to include that context in its story published Wednesday. 
CalMatters editor in chief Kristen Go said the nonprofit news outlet’s reporter tried, twice, to reach ICE’s media team over a period of six days, with no response. The reporter also looked into Arreguin’s background in a court database and a public records database, neither of which turned up the records ICE described.
“We always want to believe what our sources tell us, but as journalists, we also take steps to verify that information,” Go said. “In this case, we did a background check and reached out to ICE two times. It wasn’t until after our story ran that ICE decided to provide the information we had requested.
“We believe in transparency from the people we cover and extend that standard to our reporting as well.”
Arreguin was arrested on an assault charge in Fresno County one year ago. The District Attorney’s Office declined to prosecute him and did not press charges, a spokesperson said.
The reporter, Wendy Fry, sent ICE’s media team seven questions about Arreguin’s immigration history on the evening of Oct. 21 seeking the legal basis for Arreguin’s deportation and the basic facts of his detention. 
“We did not find any recent criminal history for Mr. Arreguin, did ICE or the federal government consider him a threat to public safety. If so, why?” Fry asked in the email. 
The rest of the questions sought to confirm elements of Arreguin’s account of his detention and deportation flight. 
Fry sent a follow-up email to ICE the following Tuesday “Circling this back on top. Our story is publishing tomorrow.” 
Go said Fry received no response to those questions. 
In her story, Fry quoted Arreguin family members, who repeated his account. CalMatters has reached out to them, and to Arreguin, for comment but has received no response. 
Reached Thursday, Arreguin’s daughter said her father was focused on describing his ordeal in his interview with the reporter and did not intend to conceal his deportation and criminal history.
On Thursday, a day after Fry’s story published, a Fox News reporter wrote on social media that he was told by sources in the federal government that Arreguin has been deported five times. 
Exactly 30 minutes later, ICE quoted the Fox News reporter’s message in its own social media post. 
“We’d like to believe that government agencies operate in good faith — but there is a valid question as to why ICE waited until after publication and even so, (did) not contact the reporter directly,” Go said. 
ICE did not immediately respond to questions about its response from CalMatters, or whether the social media team has access to records that are unavailable to the media team responding to reporter requests. 
The agency has still not responded to Fry’s initial questions. 
Edward Wasserman, a journalism professor and former dean of UC Berkeley Graduate School of Journalism, said it’s impossible to know whether an agency as large as ICE “deliberately stonewalled.” 
“It’s dangerous to speculate whether they had a motive,” Wasserman said. 
From a “hard-nosed PR perspective,” Wasserman said, the strategy of releasing information after a story published doesn’t help an agency’s cause. 
“It doesn’t really serve their own purposes,” he said.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Gov. Mills said she voted for Jackson, despite lack of endorsement
text:
Gov. Janet Mills addresses senators before the chamber adjourns for the year on April 29, 2026. (Photo by Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)While never endorsing him, Gov. Janet Mills said she voted Thursday for Troy Jackson, the Democratic nominee in the U.S. Senate race, a nomination she initially sought. 
Mills, also a Democrat, wrote on social media that she cast her ballot in Farmington on the last day of early, in-person voting. She voted strictly down the party line, also backing Hannah Pingree for governor, Matt Dunlap for the 2nd Congressional District, Scott Landry for Maine House of Representatives District 75 and Bob Sullebarger for Maine Senate District 5.
“I encourage Maine people to vote for Democrats up and down the ballot who will stand up for our values and stand up to Trump,” wrote Mills.
Mills had launched her bid to challenge Republican incumbent U.S. Sen. Susan Collins last October but suspended her campaign in April, citing a lack of funds, though she’d also been trailing in polls. The governor did not endorse Graham Platner, who secured the Democratic nomination in the June primary but dropped out in July after an accusation of sexual assault, which he has denied. 
Since Jackson, former logger and Maine Senate president, replaced Platner later that month, Mills has remained silent about his candidacy.  
Mills and Jackson clashed during their time together in state government. During Jackson’s primary bid for governor, he frequently highlighted his disagreements with Mills and her vetoes of bills he sponsored.
Ahead of Mills sharing who she voted for on Thursday, Jackson told reporters at a press briefing in Westbrook that he wasn’t bothered by the lack of endorsement.  
“Look, this race is not about me and Janet or anything like that,” he told MS NOW. “This race is about people that don’t have health care, people that don’t know how to fill their oil tanks, people that don’t know how to get their prescription drugs.”
He said he doesn’t “take it personally” and pointed out that U.S. Sen. Angus King, Collins’ independent Senate colleague, also has not endorsed him.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Kamala Harris drops into Georgia to stump for Ossoff, down-ballot Democrats
text:
Former Vice President Kamala Harris and U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff fired up students from Atlanta’s historically Black colleges and universities at Clark Atlanta University on Thursday, asking young voters to make their way to the polls as early voting wraps up Friday.
About 800 students from Clark Atlanta, Morehouse College and Spelman College gathered to see Harris and Ossoff, who is up for reelection and is fighting off a challenge from Republican Congressman Mike Collins. 
Both Democrats framed the 2026 midterms as a necessary check on the Trump administration. Ossoff, who has a lead over Collins in the polls, said that despite “the foolishness, the corruption, the incompetence” from the current administration, young voters “have already shattered every turnout record for young voters in a midterm election in Georgia’s history.”
“I hope it will give you courage and a sense of the history that we all are living through and that we all are making right now,” Ossoff said. “Young people are voting and voting early because young people recognize the stakes of this election.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Harris, who graduated from Howard University, urged students to walk their frustrations to the polls.
“I’ve come here to remind you: don’t ever let anybody take your power from you. Don’t ever let anybody tell you who you are. You tell them who you are. You tell them you are active. You let them know you are paying attention. You let them know, not on my watch is this stuff going to happen without me stepping up and speaking out and acting,” Harris said.
Harris was a frequent visitor to battleground Georgia in 2024 when she was the Democratic nominee for president. She lost to President Donald Trump in Georgia by about 2 percentage points, or about 115,000 votes. She’s widely seen as a likely contender for the White House in 2028. 
This time, she was back in Georgia helping Ossoff hold onto his Senate seat and boosting other Democrats in their quest to loosen the GOP’s grip on state government.
And Harris is keeping her schedule busy while here. Earlier on Thursday, she joined Ossoff in Macon and joined NAACP president and CEO Derrick Johnson in the evening for a fireside chat. On Friday, Harris is headlining a Fulton County Democratic Party Committee fundraising dinner.
Nearly 2.4 million Georgians have cast a ballot as of Thursday, with just one more day to vote early. Election Day is Tuesday.
Harris also encouraged students to vote for Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, who would become the first Black woman governor in the country, and for Democrats “up and down the ticket,” saying that down-ballot races matter.
“Don’t overlook those races, because those are the folks who make decisions about your life every day,” Harris said.
The Republican Governor Association pounced at the opportunity to compare Harris and Bottoms, with deputy communications director Anna Marian Block saying that “not even Kirby Smart could coach them to a win,” if they are on the same team.
“Few people can match Kamala Harris’s failed record, but Keisha Lance Bottoms comes close,” Block said.
But Reagan Bligen, a 19-year-old junior at Clark Atlanta, said that she felt encouraged by the representation of Black women in leadership, saying that having Black women in these roles provides young women role models and is a reminder of what they can do.
“I couldn’t even get my phone out just because I was listening to what she was saying. She is very powerful. She’s very truthful. She’s very just motherly, and I just feel like right now that’s what we need,” Bligen said
Myles Billingsley, a sophomore at Clark Atlanta studying political science, said that seeing Harris and Ossoff on campus carried a lot of weight for students of color who can be overlooked by the political process.
“The fact that both Jon Ossoff and Kamala Harris actually took the time and came to our institution meant the world to us,” Billingsley said.
But while Billingsley said that students feel motivated to vote Republicans out, young voters want policy solutions from Democrats moving forward.
“I like this whole like de-Trump process. Get Trump out of office, get his policies, get his congressional people out of office. But at the same time, we want to see more from the Democratic Party than simply just ‘Trump bad.’ So if we can actually get some real policy from Democrats, a real direction on where y’all want to move in, except just anti-Trump, we would really love that,” he said.

name: California
title: DOJ subpoenas California election officials, despite judge’s order to stop threatening them
authors: Jeanne Kuang, Ryan Sabalow, and Sergio Olmos
text:
In summary
Federal officials delivered a subpoena to Orange County Registrar of Voters’s office on Thursday.


On Wednesday, a federal judge issued a blistering order warning federal prosecutors to stop threatening California election officials with crimes.
A day later, federal prosecutors kept going. 
At least four elections workers in California have received federal criminal grand jury subpoenas over the past week, with at least one delivered on Thursday after the court’s order.
In that subpoena, issued to the Orange County Registrar of Voters’s office, federal agents with the Department of Homeland Security are seeking unredacted voter records for 60 people, according to records obtained by CalMatters. 
The subpoenas signal an intensification of the federal government’s unprecedented targeting of California’s elections, setting up what could be a showdown over the fundamentals of American democracy around next Tuesday’s midterm elections. 
The prosecutors include those in the office of Los Angeles’ top federal prosecutor, Bill Essayli, a leading aide in President Donald Trump’s push to find evidence to support longstanding — and never proven — claims that California elections are rigged in Democrats’ favor due to noncitizen votes.
Bloomberg Law first reported Thursday that U.S. Justice Department leaders had directed top federal prosecutors to pursue criminal subpoenas of state and local officials in their efforts to find evidence that noncitizens were allowed to vote. The news outlet cited two unnamed sources familiar with the situation.
This month Essayli sued California and Los Angeles County, demanding they set aside the ballots of 20,000 registered voters he accused of not being U.S. citizens, and last week the Justice Department sent letters threatening local elections officials with criminal charges if they did not do the same with lists of voters in their own counties.
County election officials from across California have said spot checks found the government’s list of names to be inaccurate and have challenged the legality of the requests. Officials in only one county so far – San Luis Obispo – have announced they will investigate the voters from the Justice Department’s demand letters. 
What the subpoenas say 
In Los Angeles County, federal prosecutors last week subpoenaed three employees of the Registrar-Recorder’s Office, ordering them to testify before a grand jury in a criminal investigation on Nov. 4, the day after the election. 
Prosecutors demanded county employees bring records of how their department prevents non-citizens from voting and “records relating to or involving evidence collected by your agency which tends to indicate an alien has voted in a federal election.”
In a statement, Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder Dean Logan said prosecutors were taking a “confrontational, adversarial approach.” He said the federal judge’s warning to stop making threats directed at election officials “was well placed and appreciated.” 
“Threats and intimidation have no place in elections,” Logan said. “We will take whatever steps necessary to ensure the safety of our employees and to remain focused on serving the voters of Los Angeles County so they can exercise their voting franchise.”
In Orange County, federal agents obtained the new grand jury subpoena last week but elections officials received it Thursday. It is similar to previous information demands from federal prosecutors. Elections officials had in September produced records on 20 registered voters in response to subpoenas. On Thursday, Registrar of Voters Bob Page told CalMatters three of those names appeared again in the new subpoena.
The federal government downplayed the subpoenas and suggested elections officials weren’t the targets of its investigation.
“Receiving a subpoena doesn’t mean you are a target,” Justice Department spokesperson Kiersten Pels said in an emailed statement. “In fact, generally, the DOJ doesn’t subpoena targets.” 
Judge says ‘these threats must stop’
In his courtroom on Tuesday, U.S. District Judge David O. Carter made it clear that the federal government needed to stop threatening election workers with criminal charges if they didn’t comply with prosecutors’ demands. 
“This court believes it would be wise that any threats to state or county (election) employees cease immediately,” Carter told the courtroom. 
He made the warning formal in his written ruling issued Wednesday evening. 
“Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch,” Carter wrote. 
“The court reiterates what it said yesterday: these threats must stop,” he wrote.
The Justice Department has appealed Carter’s ruling to the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals. Pels said prosecutors are merely doing what Carter told them to do: prosecute illegal voting if it’s found.
In expressing skepticism about the Trump administration’s claims, Carter told Essayli in court on Tuesday that if noncitizens really are voting in as large of numbers as the Trump administration claims, there’s nothing stopping federal prosecutors from finding them and charging them without the risk of blocking legal voters from having their ballots counted. 
Last week, federal prosecutors across California charged 28 people with registering to vote despite not being citizens. Not all of those people had voted in past elections; those charged amount to 0.0001% of the state’s 23 million registered voters.
“If it’s this big, you’ve got a remedy for goodness sakes,” Carter told Essayli during the hearing. “Go out and indict.”
“To be clear, the district court judge explained that voting unlawfully results in criminal exposure,” Pels wrote in her statement. “Consistent with this, California also wrote in its filing that the remedy for unlawful voting is through criminal prosecution. Thus, while DOJ maintains that a civil remedy is still available, all agree that noncitizen voting is properly addressed through criminal law.” 
Justin Levitt, an elections law expert at Loyola Law School, said federal prosecutors can argue they’re carrying out a legitimate criminal investigation, but in that case, there shouldn’t be any rush to subpoena officials in the middle of the election. The statute of limitations on federal voting offenses, he noted, is five years.
“Because they have no role in affecting the election results, there is no reason whatsoever for them to demand this information now,” Levitt said. “It’s not directly against the judge’s order … but it’s certainly not going to make the judge happy.”
California Sen. Tom Umberg, a Democrat and former federal prosecutor representing the Santa Ana area, said he was appalled that his former employer was clearly attempting “to intimidate public officials in exercising their sworn duties.”“I’m embarrassed and outraged that they’re trying to interfere with the election,” he said.Essalyi didn’t return a text message seeking comment Thursday.Professor Michael Vitiello, an expert on criminal law at the University of Pacific’s McGeorge School of Law, agreed that the federal government is trying to make election officials “insecure and fearful.”
“Maybe technically they’re trying to avoid direct conflict with the judge’s order, but they’re sure signaling that … election officials should lose some money, lose some sleep and maybe even go consult with lawyers,” Vitiello said.

name: California
title: Did Trump invest more money in rural California health ahead of the election?
text:
The Trump administration announced a $233.6 million investment in California rural health just five days before the midterm election that could determine control of Congress. 
But state officials say the money isn’t new.
“Currently, California has not received additional funding from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services,” said Andrew DiLuccia, a spokesperson for the Department of Health Care Access and Information.
Instead, the $233.6 million is California’s share of a $50 billion national federal rural health investment approved in 2025. The state applied nearly a year ago, seeking $1 billion to improve primary, maternity and specialty care throughout the state, and received notice of the award in August.
The announcement highlighted parts of the state, including the north state, Central Valley and Orange County, where Republican incumbents have faced tough questions from constituents about dramatic federal healthcare cuts passed by Republicans last year. Voter-approved redistricting also thrust a handful of conservatives into competitive races with Democrats.
“Today’s investment was made possible through the Working Families Tax Cuts Act — passed by Republicans in Congress and unanimously opposed by Democrats — delivering a historic $50 billion investment to help states transform the way healthcare is delivered in America,” the news release said.
The Working Families Tax Cuts Act is the name Republicans now use for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the tax and spending law that President Donald Trump signed in 2025. The legislation will cut $900 billion from Medicaid over the next 10 years through stricter eligibility requirements and lower payments to states. 
California stands to lose $30 billion a year for its Medi-Cal program, which provides health insurance to low-income residents and people with disabilities. State officials and independent researchers estimate 2 million Californians will lose health coverage as a result, doubling the state’s uninsured rate.
The rural health fund grew out of a compromise with Republicans in rural states such as Maine and Missouri, who worried that Medicaid cuts would hurt rural hospitals hardest. Rural hospitals serve a higher share of low-income payers and rely more heavily on Medicaid payments than hospitals in wealthier or urban areas that have more privately insured patients.
California’s rural hospitals were already struggling. Madera Community Hospital abruptly closed in 2023 and declared bankruptcy before reopening in 2025 under new management. Last year Glenn Medical Center, Glenn County’s only hospital, closed after losing a special designation that increased federal funding. State lawmakers have also twice bailed out more than a dozen struggling hospitals in the past three years, including a $25 million investment earlier this year. A third $85.5 million hospital bailout is scheduled for later this year. 
CalMatters reporting also revealed that nearly 60 hospitals have stopped delivering babies since 2012 largely due to financial challenges and population decline in rural areas. 
Several Republicans seeking reelection have asserted that the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” did not cut Medicaid. 
Rep. Kevin Kiley, a former Republican turned Independent from Roseville, and Rep. David Valadao, a Republican from Hanford who represents the district with the highest percentage of Medicaid enrollees in the country, both argue that Medicaid spending still increases over time. That increase is due largely to the growing underlying cost of healthcare and the federal government’s mandate to pay for qualified enrollees’ care.
Democratic opponents argue eliminating people from Medicaid amounts to a cut.
One Republican, Rep. James Gallagher, who took over Rep. Doug LaMalfa’s seat after his death in January, told North State Public Radio in May he opposed the Medicaid cuts but also disagreed with California expanding coverage to immigrants without legal status.
Supported by the California Health Care Foundation (CHCF), which works to ensure that people have access to the care they need, when they need it, at a price they can afford. Visit www.chcf.org to learn more.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Question about your voter registration? Head to your elections office
text:
(Photo by Seth Tupper/South Dakota Searchlight)County election officials are stressing that Montanans need to show up in person to make changes to their voter registration after a postcard from the Montana Secretary of State’s Office caused some confusion. 
Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3, and Montanans who need to register to vote or change their registration should head to their local elections office.
Election administrators also are advising people to get answers about registering to vote straight from the source, their local elections staff.
“If electors have questions, have them contact their local elections office to get the answers — the right answers,” said Carbon County Clerk and Recorder Macque Bohleen. “Not hearsay, not the neighbor or the internet.”
The postcard caused frustration for some election workers, confused some voters, and caught the attention of an advocacy organization, Middle Fork Strategies, which described it as misleading at best, “voter suppression at worst.”


How to vote
If you still need to register to vote or change your registration, you must go to your local elections office in person.
Check your ballot status at myvoterpagemt.com.
Get information at votemt.gov. 


Austin James, with the Secretary of State’s Office, said the card was part of a national voter outreach study and “a good story to tell,” but he declined to answer questions about it this week.
James said the important information now is for voters to return ballots in person (it’s too late mail them), bring photo ID to the polls, and check votemt.gov for polling places and ballot status. 
Postcard causes confusion
On Sept. 28, the Secretary of State’s Office alerted local election offices of a mailer to voters expected to arrive that week, Wednesday, Sept. 30, or Thursday, Oct. 1.
An email from the Secretary of State’s Office obtained by the Daily Montanan in a records request described the postcard as part of a pilot with the EAC, the U.S. Election Assistance Commission.
The purpose of the card is to update voter registration, but that’s part of the problem: Changes starting Oct. 6, during “late registration,” need to be made in person for people who want to vote in the upcoming election. 
People who received the card could mark an option for themselves, such as “I have moved out of Montana; please cancel my Montana voter registration.”
Recipients also could mark an option for another person: “The person listed above does not reside at this address.”
The instructions advised people to sign the card, return it by mail, “no postage necessary,” with the Secretary of State’s Office as the business reply mail.
The card was sent right before late registration started, and it didn’t indicate voters need to go to their local elections office.
“It would have been helpful to voters if it had been done a couple of months earlier,” Bohleen said. “My frustration is the timing.”
Outcome of card
In Yellowstone County, election administrator Dayna Causby said Wednesday a couple of voters came to the office “very mad about the fact that they received them,” saying they’d lived in the same place for 20 years.
Causby said the number of postcards sent to voters in Yellowstone County wasn’t clear. The Secretary of State’s Office did not answer a question about the number of cards sent in the state.
Records show the Secretary of State’s Office is forwarding information it receives to local election offices for changes.
On Oct. 8, the Secretary of State’s Office declared the project was nearly complete, and it had helped prevent ballots being sent to undeliverable addresses.
“I am pleased to report that we have received thousands of mailers from voters confirming their information,” wrote Sadie Dallaserra, with the Secretary of State’s Office, in an email the Daily Montanan received in a records request. “While some of you received instructions from me to make updates, most of you did not need to take any action.
“We may still receive a few stragglers depending on when voters placed their mailers in the post, but the majority of this project is now complete, and it has been a success.”
Middle Fork Strategies, a progressive advocacy organization with a mission that includes holding leaders accountable, had a different perspective on the card.
It posted a picture of the mailer on its Facebook page with a red X across it and instructions for how people can update their registration — by going to their local elections office.
“It’s misleading at best and state-sponsored voter suppression at worst,” said Middle Fork interim executive director Nick Lockridge in an email. “Montana has come so far over the years with its rural-friendly absentee voting procedures. To act in this manner, at this stage, is just irresponsible.”
This week, voters were still asking questions about the card.
Working with voters
Bradley Seaman, elections administrator in Missoula County, said some voters showed up in person with the cards this week, and the Secretary of State’s Office had emailed scanned cards to his office.
He said a number of statutes discuss voter registration requirements, but he doesn’t have a legal opinion on how the card meets them at this point.
“There’s a lot of confusion going on,” Seaman said.
In the week before Election Day, Seaman said staff are focused on the needs of voters. He advised voters to check their registration online at myvoterpagemt.com.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: US Department of Justice to deploy federal elections monitors to Alaska, locations unknown
text:
A voter is seen in a voting booth at an early voting polling site at the Mendenhall Mall in Juneau on Aug. 17, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)The U.S. Justice Department announced this week that it plans to deploy 1,000 federal monitors across all 50 states. That includes Alaska polling places but there are few details on where monitoring will take place.
A DOJ spokesperson told States Newsroom this week that the full list of monitored locations won’t be disclosed until Election Day on Tuesday, Nov. 3.
The federal poll monitoring initiative is larger this year than previous years. In the 2022 midterm elections, the Biden Administration’s DOJ sent monitors to 64 jurisdictions in 24 states. 
Officials with the Alaska Division of Elections did not respond to a request for more information on federal monitoring or say if the DOJ is coordinating with the division on Thursday. 
Early voting in Alaska is already underway, with nearly 10% of voters or over 58,000 people having cast ballots as of Tuesday. The number already outpaces early voting in the 2022 midterms. Other states are seeing a similar wave of early voting — as of Thursday, 46.3 million voters nationwide had cast their ballots already, according to the University of Florida’s UF Elections Lab.[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Federal monitoring of operations at polling places is not new for Alaska, particularly in rural and Alaska Native-majority regions. Monitors watch for compliance with the Voting Rights Act, the Civil Rights Act, Americans with Disabilities Act, the Help America Vote Act and other federal laws to make sure there is equal access to the polls. 
In the 2024 general election, the DOJ announced plans to monitor several rural precincts for compliance with federal requirements for language assistance, including in the Bethel, Dillingham, Kusilvak, and Nome census areas and the North Slope and Northwest Arctic boroughs. 
In 2023, federal monitoring of local elections took place in the North Slope Borough, and the Dillingham and Kusilvak census areas as voters cast ballots in school board and local city and borough elections.
In 2022, federal monitors were sent to the Dillingham, Bethel and Kusilvak census areas, as well as Sitka. During the August primary, monitors observed polling places in the three Southwest Alaska regions as well as in Anchorage, Juneau and Fairbanks.  
A DOJ investigation of voting in 2022 and 2023 elections documented access violations for voters with disabilities and cited the Division of Elections. The findings included a lack of accessible machines at polling places and lack of accessible features on the division’s website. 
The DOJ’s Civil Rights Division has an online form for voters to report complaints of federal law violations. 
The Division also has a voter complaint form for violations of the Help America Vote Act on its website, and a complaint hotline at 1-888-465-5857. It also has resources for accessibility assistance, including language assistance, on its website or by phone at (907) 465-4611.
