name: California
title: “Mi vida entera quedó destruida”: un padre de Fresno, con 49 años en Estados Unidos, fue deportado repentinamente
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
MEXICALI, México — Mientras el olor a estiércol del Valle Imperial de California se extendía a través de la frontera hacia esta extensa ciudad industrial mexicana, Luis Arreguin levantó la vista hacia una catedral de color naranja quemado en la plaza del centro.
Era la primera vez que la veía desde que se marchó de México siendo niño, hace décadas.
 Arreguin, de 54 años, había vivido en una pequeña comunidad cerca de Fresno desde que tenía 5 años.
 Pero el 1 de octubre, agentes federales de inmigración lo detuvieron cuando se dirigía al trabajo. Fue uno de los primeros de aproximadamente 130 individuos que, según activistas, fueron detenidos durante los primeros días de la reciente ofensiva de control migratorio del gobierno de Trump en el Valle de San Joaquín.
 “Toda mi vida quedó destruida”, dijo Arreguin, quien está casado y tiene cuatro hijos.
La rápida deportación de este trabajador calificado a México demuestra la celeridad de la maquinaria de deportación de Trump, cuya eficiencia resulta casi vertiginosa. El Servicio de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas de EE. UU. deportó a más de 356,000 personas en los primeros nueve meses y medio del año fiscal 2026, que comenzó el 1 de octubre de 2025,según datos de la agencia . Esta cifra supera las aproximadamente 320,000 deportaciones realizadas durante todo el año fiscal 2025.
 La intensificación de las medidas de control que permitieron detener a Arreguin se extendió posteriormente al resto de California y se conoció como “Operación California Segura”.
 Arreguin pasó solo 15 días bajo custodia federal antes de que los agentes lo subieran a un vuelo de deportación repleto de pasajeros con destino a Tapachula, en el sur de Chiapas, cerca de la frontera sur de México con Guatemala. Desde allí, tomó autobuses de regreso a la frontera norte del país, donde su hija le alquiló una habitación de motel en Mexicali.
 “Tenía una casa de cinco habitaciones (en Fresno). Ahora no tengo nada”, dijo. 
 Luis Arreguin toca el muro fronterizo en Mexicali, Baja California, México, el 21 de octubre de 2026. Arreguin fue deportado de Estados Unidos el 15 de octubre de 2026. Foto de Daniel Resendiz para CalMatters.
 Mexicali, que en su día fue un punto de partida para quienes se dirigían al norte, es ahora una isla para marginados, lo más cerca que los deportados podrán estar jamás de sus familias, de los pagos del coche y de las hipotecas en Estados Unidos.
Ubicada justo al otro lado de la frontera de las granjas solares y los campos de alfalfa del condado de Imperial, Mexicali es conocida por su exquisita comida china y por ser la capital del estado de Baja California. Sin embargo, muchos de sus residentes también luchan contra la pobreza y la delincuencia.
 La gente se ducha con mangueras en el parque público. Un día de la semana pasada, unos delincuentes dejaron una narcomanta en un jardín de infancia público advirtiendo a las autoridades de Baja California que no cooperaran con “Los Rusos”, una facción del cártel de Sinaloa.
 Arreguin no sabe qué va a hacer. México es un país que desconoce. Entiende español, si se habla despacio, pero no lo habla.
 —Poquito —dice, disculpándose con la gente que pasa por la acera frente a la iglesia—. No quiero faltarle el respeto a nadie.
 La semana pasada, su esposa lo visitó desde Fresno, a siete horas y media en coche. Según él, en 31 años de matrimonio nunca habían pasado una noche separados hasta su arresto.
 “Ella dijo: ‘Voy a llorar durante todo el camino’. Yo le dije: ‘Bueno, yo también voy a llorar’, ¿sabes? Intentamos no pensar en ello. Simplemente intentamos aprovechar al máximo los días que pasamos juntos”, dijo Arreguin con la voz quebrada. 
 ‘Te he estado observando’
 Arreguin aún desconoce por qué fue el objetivo. El agente del ICE que lo detuvo camino al trabajo cerca de Fresno le dijo: “Te he estado vigilando”.
 Pero Arreguin no está seguro de creer que estuviera bajo vigilancia. Esa misma mañana, agentes allanaron el pequeño pueblo agrícola donde vivía la familia, dejando las calles desiertas.
 “Toda mi comunidad trabaja en el campo. Hicieron una limpieza en mi pequeño pueblo, y mi esposa me llamó y me dijo: «Está vacío, cariño. Está vacío», dijo.
 Afirmó no haber tenido ningún contacto reciente con las fuerzas del orden. Una búsqueda en los registros públicos no arrojó ningún antecedente penal reciente.
 “Soy padre. Me secuestraste esta mañana y me alejaste de mis hijos”, dijo.
 Tras su arresto, fue detenido en una oficina del ICE en Fresno y posteriormente trasladado a Bakersfield. Según relató, lo llevaron de un lado a otro mientras su presión arterial subía, hasta que finalmente pasó unas siete horas en la sala de urgencias de Bakersfield.
 “Me preguntaron: ‘¿Tienes miedo de volver a tu país?’ Y dije que sí, y pensé que eso lo iba a solucionar todo y al menos me daría una oportunidad en los tribunales”, dijo. 



Izquierda: Luis Arreguin sostiene su Biblia. Derecha: Luis Arreguin llora frente a la Catedral de Mexicali en Mexicali, Baja California, México, el 21 de octubre de 2026. Fotografías de Daniel Resendiz para CalMatters.
 Tras varios días, los agentes lo trasladaron al Campamento East Montana, en las afueras de El Paso.
 “No sabía adónde iba”, dijo.
 El centro ha sido objeto de demandas presentadas por organizaciones de derechos civiles y detenidos, quienes se han quejado de las duras condiciones, incluyendo la falta de alimentación y la atención médica deficiente. En septiembre de 2025, los propios organismos de control internos del ICE detectaron decenas de infracciones, según informó el Washington Post.
 Arreguin pasó cinco días allí antes de que, según cuenta, le cortaran la comunicación telefónica y lo subieran a un avión con destino al sur de México.
 “Al menos aquí estoy a salvo, y no estoy tras los muros de un centro de detención donde podría morir”, dijo. 
 Vuelo de deportación abarrotado
 Arreguin dijo que en su vuelo viajaban aproximadamente 300 deportados , todos esposados y encadenados de muñecas y tobillos. Contó 22 mujeres y un menor.
 “Encadenaron a un chico de 14 años”, dijo.
 Arreguin describió cómo los agentes restringieron el acceso de las personas al baño y al agua durante las 36 horas de viaje.
 Mientras tanto, los agentes lo provocaban: “¡Miren, es el famoso señor Arreguin!”, decían, mostrándole en sus teléfonos noticias sobre su arresto y videos de redes sociales que su hija había hecho para llamar la atención sobre su caso.
 Justo antes de desembarcar, contó, los agentes se apresuraron por los pasillos quitándoles los grilletes. Interpretó esto como un intento de impedir que los funcionarios mexicanos vieran cómo los habían transportado.
 “Mucha gente tiene miedo incluso de decir algo sobre cómo fueron tratados”, dijo.
 ICE no respondió a las preguntas de CalMatters sobre el vuelo ni sobre las condiciones que describió Arreguin.
 Otros pasajeros del vuelo que hablaron con CalMatters bajo condición de anonimato corroboraron los detalles que dio Luis. El ICE tiene una política operativa de larga data que exige que los pasajeros bajo custodia lleven esposas, cadenas en la cintura y grilletes en los tobillos durante los vuelos, incluso durante las escalas y las paradas para repostar combustible.
 Un detalle que el antiguo residente del Valle Central dijo que nunca olvidará: “Todos en ese avión llevaban puesta su ropa de trabajo. Absolutamente todos”. 
 Cambiar la estrategia de deportación de México
 Desde esta primavera, la administración ha dejado de enviar a ciudadanos mexicanos de regreso a través de la frontera terrestre. En cambio, los traslada por vía aérea a zonas más alejadas de México, donde las autoridades creen que los deportados que son dejados cerca de la frontera con Guatemala tienen menos probabilidades de intentar cruzar de regreso a Estados Unidos.
 En Tapachula, funcionarios mexicanos alimentaron a Arreguin y le dieron una tarjeta de débito con 2500 pesos, el equivalente a unos 130 dólares. «No tenían por qué dármela», dijo. Con eso pudo llegar hasta la Ciudad de México. Su hija adulta pagó el resto del viaje a Mexicali, donde, siendo adolescente, Luis pudo cruzar la frontera libremente con su grupo de la iglesia de Fresno.
La ciudad fronteriza recibe ahora menos deportados que en la última década. En 2024, las autoridades estadounidenses devolvieron a más de 43,000 mexicanos a través de los cruces fronterizos de Baja California en Tijuana y Mexicali, lo que representa aproximadamente una quinta parte de todas las repatriaciones a nivel nacional, según la Secretaría de Gobernación de México.
En los primeros siete meses de 2026, solo 1,567 personas cruzaron por el paso fronterizo de Mexicali , menos del 2% del total nacional. Las cifras disminuyeron cuando la administración Trump optó por trasladar a los mexicanos deportados más al sur, a Tapachula y Villahermosa, que en conjunto recibieron a 48,000 personas durante el mismo período, casi la mitad de todos los retornos.
 Esas cifras no incluyen a las personas que fueron trasladadas a Tapachula y luego emprendieron el camino de regreso al norte por sus propios medios, como Arreguin.
 “Sabes que no puedes simplemente separar a la gente de su familia”, dijo. 
 ¿Y ahora qué?
 “ No llores”, le dice Luis a su hija mayor, sosteniendo el teléfono extendido frente a él para hacer una videollamada con ella desde la Catedral de Mexicali en Baja California.
 En Fresno, la esposa de Luis está empacando sus cosas para mudarse. La familia no tiene dinero para quedarse sin que Luis pague el alquiler, ya que es el principal sostén económico del hogar. Sus dos hijos menores, de 6 y 10 años, tendrán que cambiar de escuela.
 “Estoy cansado de llorar”, dice. “Me agota mucho hablar de lo que tuve que pasar, de lo que estoy pasando y de cómo me trataron”, añadió. 
 Vista aérea de la frontera vehicular y peatonal entre Mexicali, México y Calexico, California, el 21 de octubre de 2026. Fotografía de Daniel Resendiz para CalMatters.
 Pero está buscando un abogado que le ayude a luchar contra su deportación y a regresar con su familia.
 “Tengo que luchar”, dijo.
 Hasta entonces, su hija está pagando el motel y la comida. Está agotando el límite de sus tarjetas de crédito. Busca un lugar en Mexicali lo suficientemente grande para que toda la familia pueda visitarlo en Acción de Gracias.
 Durante décadas, Arreguin trabajó para darles a sus hijos una vida mejor en Estados Unidos. Ahora, su hija Elaina intenta que se sienta cómodo en México.
 Me has apoyado durante años —le dijo—. Ahora puedo hacer lo mismo por ti.
 El fotoperiodista de CalMatters, Larry Valenzuela, contribuyó a este reportaje.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: State sued over Mass. rental assistance program’s paused third year
text:
AS DEMAND FOR the state’s emergency shelter beds ballooned in early 2025, along with the strain on its homelessness prevention programs, the Healey administration asked lawmakers to provide funding for its rental subsidy program HomeBASE. The funds would continue to cover two years for eligible families, with the possibility of a third year. 
The Legislature agreed. Then, a week before the governor signed the annual state budget into law, her housing office announced an indefinite pause on all approvals for the third year of assistance. 
Families who had been planning on the additional year got a fierce shock. And two single-mothers facing imminent eviction are now suing the Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities, which runs the program, to maintain the third year of coverage. 
“Without that HomeBASE stabilization,” lawyers for a woman referred to as Jane Doe wrote, “[she] and her young son are at risk of eviction every month.” 
HomeBASE, developed in 2011 to stabilize families in the state’s shelter system, provides case workers and financial assistance to low-income families in Massachusetts facing homelessness and determined to be emergency shelter eligible by the state. The program provides up to $30,000 in rental subsidies over two years, and lawmakers in 2023 added language to the budget line item stating that families that completed the two years and remained eligible could receive a third year of coverage of $15,000 or more. 
Suffolk County Superior Court Judge Catherine Hyo-Kyung Ham on Wednesday heard from lawyers representing HomeBASE recipients Doe and Kinisha James. The plaintiffs are seeking an injunction ordering the state to provide a third year of HomeBASE stabilization services, including the $15,000 in funding. 
“We’re really trying to keep these two single mothers in their homes so they’re not evicted by Thanksgiving,” said Elizabeth Alfred with Greater Boston Legal Services, which is representing Doe and James.
The state housing office asked the court to dismiss the suits. 
The decision to pause the third year, according to a spokesperson for the housing office, was part of a package of Right To Shelter reforms “so we can prioritize helping the greatest number of families with the resources available. HomeBASE remains a critical tool for helping families avoid or exit shelter and secure stable housing.”  
The attorney general’s office, which is representing the state, wrote that the program had a years-long funding deficiency and even with supplemental funding “is forced to prioritize how it utilizes the funds available for housing stabilization.” 
It simply cannot provide the third year at current budget levels, the state claims. The housing office estimates resuming third year coverage would mean that 1,098 families who would otherwise receive first-year benefits would not be able to access HomeBASE during this fiscal year.  
In filings, the state notes the HomeBASE line item specifically states that if there is a funding deficiency, there is no “enforceable right or entitlement to services” beyond the amount that the Legislature appropriated. 
The plaintiffs’ attorneys said the pause amounts to a unilateral decision not to fulfill the letter of the law, and these families are hanging in the balance. 
Doe and her infant son fled Doe’s abusive partner in 2021, according to court filings, experiencing homelessness for the next two years. Staying with family was largely off the table, as many of her relatives lived in subsidized housing with strict guest policies that could lead to eviction if violated. 
She says she was rejected from the state’s emergency shelter program in 2022, because the shelters were too full, and was finally found eligible for the HomeBASE program in 2023. 
According to the complaint, HomeBASE covers more than $1,600 of her rent, which has been raised twice and is now $2,049. When she met with a state caseworker in July 2025, Doe said she was shown paperwork that stated she was still eligible for almost $18,000 in rental assistance, but just weeks later was told that that was an error and she would have $3,000 that would expire in that coming January.  
Her take-home pay is about $2,700 a month and she is engaged in “active eviction proceedings for nonpayment of rent,” the complaint states. 
About one year after James and her then two-year-old, chronically ill daughter were forced to leave James’ mother’s house and became homeless, James applied for emergency assistance shelter and entered the HomeBASE diversion program. Her lease began in August 2024, with HomeBASE paying $1,800 of a $2,200 a month lease.  
The rent increased and the share covered by HomeBASE decreased over time, with James’ two years of funding exhausted in December 2025. Through a combination of family help and other state rental assistance, James has been able to cobble together about $1,200 a month toward rent since then.  James reached out to the housing office in May 2026 requesting an additional year, which she asserts was ignored until an email in August 2026 stating that the office had paused third year approvals for the program. 
Her landlord wants to keep her, but if James cannot come up with the rent by November, she will be evicted in December.  
Both women say they received no direct notice that the third year was off the table until they were in the process of seeking it. 
Information on the state’s website illustrates the messaging whiplash. The dedicated HomeBASE page refers only to a “2-year” period, as does the current administration plan for the program.  
But a monthly training presentation from May 2025 for administering HomeBASE, still on the state’s website, notes that “participants shall not access more than $30,000 within a 24-month period, and not more than $15,000.00 within an additional 3rd year.” The state’s housing needs assessment section on emergency housing supports states that there is “the possibility of a third year” for the funding assistance. 
The case, attorneys say, is in part about how the Legislature intended the program to be funded. The third-year expansion that went into effect in fiscal year 2024 was the result of years of advocacy from housing stabilization groups.  
“Many families in the Commonwealth need that third year to avoid entering homelessness,” said Laura Camara, an attorney with Greater Boston Legal Services representing James. The Legislature “made a decision, and yet it has essentially not been implemented,” said Alfred, who represents Doe.  
Healey’s proposed fiscal year 2026 budget asked for $57,322,001 for HomeBASE, with the budget item still including language that indicated the funds should cover a third year of assistance for some program participants. Lawmakers funded the item to the dollar, and Healey then signed the budget into law on July 4, 2025 — just days after her administration separately announced it was pausing third year coverage. 
The program has been far more expensive than the initial allocation. In filings, the state said HomeBASE expenditures that year exceeded $153 million. The gaps have been filled in recent years through supplemental budgets. 
“It is not that the agency has intentionally underfunded this program,” said Assistant Attorney General Matthew Burke. Rather, the third year was paused because of the surge in shelter demand, which has a trickle-down impact on the HomeBASE program. 
Between 2023 and 2025, the number of HomeBASE families surged more than fivefold to about 10,000 cases, he told the court. The housing office asked for additional funding in fiscal years 2025 and 2026, which the Legislature did not fully grant, but just under $100 million of supplemental funds were approved over the two years. 
The agency weighed the costs and benefits, Burke said, and understood the HomeBASE program to be a “short-term stabilization program and not a long-term financial assistance program.” The governor has to propose a balanced budget, and lawmakers were well aware of the funding shortfalls for HomeBASE, he said, adding that they could have offered up more funds if they wished. 
“This case paints a vivid picture of what’s not working with our programs to keep vulnerable families in their homes,” said state Sen. Julian Cyr, the Senate chair of the Joint Committee on Housing. The devastating housing crisis is keeping costs high all over the state, he noted, meaning even affordable unit costs are spiking — and with them the need for greater state subsidy. 
“Several colleagues and I worried about underfunding as it relates to [Emergency Assistance Family Shelter],” Cyr said, “but I’m all ears on what additional resources may be needed here for these programs. I’m also clear-eyed that these programs received tens of millions of dollars in funding, and we still may not be able to meet every bit of the need.”
The fiscal year 2027 budget signed this summer boosted the HomeBASE budget to about $82.3 million, but the housing office expects to spend almost $113 million on the program. Funding a third HomeBase year, according to the state’s filings, would cost as much as an additional $39.5 million. 
“They knowingly submitted a budget they knew was not going to fund the program,” Camara said. They cannot now “hide behind it,” she said. 
Judge Ham, who said during the hearing that she wasn’t sure how she could order the state to spend money it claims not to have, promised a decision as soon as possible. Winter is drawing nearer and the two women have exhausted their other options for family and state financial support, Camara said — “These families are scared.”

name: California
title: Un juez rechaza la solicitud del gobierno de Trump para anular 20,000 votos electorales de California
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
Tras afirmar que la administración Trump se había embarcado en “un patrón amplio y continuo de intentos de interferencia electoral”, un juez federal se negó el miércoles a ordenar a los funcionarios electorales de California que apartaran 20,000 papeletas alegando que esos votantes podrían no ser ciudadanos.
 “Nunca antes en la historia estadounidense el gobierno federal, en vísperas de unas elecciones, había intentado coaccionar a un gobierno estatal y local para que abandonara sus propios procedimientos electorales constitucionales y se doblegara ante la voluntad del Poder Ejecutivo”, escribió el juez de distrito estadounidense David O. Carter, nombrado por el presidente Bill Clinton.
“Esta solicitud viola principios constitucionales de larga data que exigen que los estados tengan control sobre sus elecciones”, escribió el juez , y agregó que si accedía a la solicitud de último minuto de la administración Trump, “cualquiera de las partes podría crear caos para sus propios fines políticos y perturbar el proceso electoral. Más de 20,000 californianos registrados podrían perder el derecho que generaciones de estadounidenses han luchado por preservar”.
 Este fallo supone la última derrota legal para la administración Trump, que ha intentado encontrar pruebas que validen las antiguas afirmaciones del presidente Donald Trump de que los demócratas ganan gracias a elecciones fraudulentas. Carter afirmó que se negaba a participar en un proceso que pudiera privar del derecho al voto a los ciudadanos.
 «La pérdida de confianza en nuestra democracia es irreparable», escribió. «Una vez que se manipula un voto, el daño es permanente. Si el poder ejecutivo puede desestimar votos y amenazar una elección en curso con acusaciones sin fundamento, entonces nuestra democracia está en peligro».
Carter también criticó duramente al gobierno federal por no proporcionar una explicación clara de su metodología para crear la lista de 20,000 posibles no ciudadanos, y afirmó que los fiscales dieron explicaciones vagas “y plantearon múltiples dudas sobre su fiabilidad”.
 Los funcionarios federales insisten en que su lista es mayormente precisa y proviene de investigadores que cotejaron archivos públicos de votantes, datos gubernamentales y bases de datos comerciales, pero los fiscales han reconocido que algunas de las personas en la lista probablemente sean ciudadanos.
 Funcionarios estatales y del condado, así como grupos de derechos civiles, han afirmado que la lista parece estar plagada de imprecisiones y que a menudo omite datos clave, como los números de la Seguridad Social y de las licencias de conducir, que permitirían a los funcionarios del condado confirmar la identidad de estas personas.
 En una rueda de prensa con periodistas el miércoles, antes del fallo de Carter, el fiscal general demócrata de California, Rob Bonta, dijo que el caso del gobierno federal no era más que una maniobra política de “aficionados” para validar la teoría conspirativa de Trump de que las elecciones están amañadas a favor de los demócratas. “Es una broma. Es vergonzoso, pero peligroso”, dijo Bonta. “Están intentando atacar el derecho fundamental al voto con datos basura”.
 En una entrevista con Fox News el miércoles, antes del fallo, Bill Essayli, el primer fiscal adjunto de Estados Unidos en Los Ángeles, dijo que la administración apelaría ante el Noveno Circuito de Apelaciones de Estados Unidos y posiblemente ante la Corte Suprema de Estados Unidos. “Estamos avanzando a toda velocidad porque, según el sistema electoral de California, todos ya tienen una papeleta”, dijo Essayli. “Ya se han recibido cientos de miles de papeletas y los condados ya han comenzado a procesarlas. Por eso necesitamos una orden ahora para separar y aislar estas papeletas, no para anular ningún voto, sino simplemente para aislarlas y poder resolver esto”. 
El tribunal superior se negó a intervenir
 Un panel del Noveno Circuito ya rechazó un intento de la oficina de Essayli para obtener una orden de emergencia. Un panel de tres jueces dictaminó el lunes, por 2 votos contra 1, rechazar una apelación urgente para evitar la sala del juez Carter. El gobierno federal alegó que el juez de distrito no programó la audiencia con la suficiente rapidez.
 Mientras tanto, el miércoles, un grupo de organizaciones de derechos civiles, incluidas las secciones de California de la Unión Estadounidense por las Libertades Civiles (ACLU), demandaron a la administración Trump e instaron a un tribunal federal a bloquear la “Iniciativa de Votantes Ilegales” de la administración.
 Los grupos afirman que la iniciativa ha estado atacando e intimidando a ciudadanos estadounidenses naturalizados, antiguos titulares de la tarjeta de residencia que han pasado por el proceso de ciudadanía. La iniciativa ordenó a los funcionarios de inmigración que elaboraran listas de posibles votantes no ciudadanos y que coordinaran con las oficinas locales del ICE para interrogar a las personas identificadas.
 Los grupos de derechos civiles sostienen que el gobierno federal está utilizando tácticas ilegales y datos erróneos para acosar a votantes legales inocentes.
 «Estas acusaciones ponen en riesgo el derecho al voto a votantes elegibles, incluidos ciudadanos estadounidenses naturalizados», declaró Theresa Lee, abogada del Proyecto de Derechos Electorales de la ACLU. «La administración no puede seguir creando maniobras políticas para sembrar desconfianza en nuestras elecciones y sentar las bases para cuestionar los resultados que no le gustan». Carter señaló en el fallo del miércoles que quienes corren mayor riesgo de ser privados de sus derechos son los ciudadanos naturalizados. “Personas que el gobierno federal identificó recientemente como no ciudadanas en los registros electorales de diferentes estados han resultado ser, en repetidas ocasiones, ciudadanos naturalizados”, escribió Carter. La demanda presentada por la ACLU y otros grupos se produjo una semana después de que un juez federal de California emitiera una orden que impedía al Departamento de Seguridad Nacional realizar interrogatorios presenciales a personas que los investigadores sospechan que podrían no ser ciudadanas estadounidenses.
 La jueza del caso, Araceli Martínez-Olguín, designada por el presidente Joe Biden, dictaminó que el gobierno federal se basaba en “fuentes de datos defectuosas que incluían a ciudadanos estadounidenses” y que probablemente estaba violando la Ley de Derechos Electorales, que prohíbe la intimidación a los votantes.
 La orden de Martínez-Olguín estará vigente hasta el día de las elecciones.

title: Homelessness declines, but still up over Newsom’s two terms
text:
Volunteers survey an unhoused person, who sits along a bike path near State Route 15, as they conduct the annual point-in-time count in San Diego on Jan. 29, 2026. Photo by Adriana Heldiz, CalMatters




We’ve got so much news in today’s WhatMatters: The latest homeless numbers, a brand new tool and the passing of an icon whose work transcended the California farmworker movement and became a worldwide symbol for human rights.
We also have some breaking news this morning. The head of California’s high-speed rail agency resigned late last night amid a scandal over travel expenses. Read more here by our Yue Stella Yu. 
Let’s get into it.
The number of people sleeping on California’s streets dropped in 2026 for the second year in a row, according to preliminary data from Gov. Gavin Newsom’s office. 
Unsheltered homelessness — people living in tents, vehicles, abandoned buildings or other places that aren’t official shelters — fell 6.5% in January 2026 compared to January 2025. Total homelessness dropped 3.4% to an estimated 175,836 people.
Since 2024, unsheltered homelessness is down nearly 13%, and overall homelessness is down 6%. 
Still, about 24,600 more Californians are believed to be homeless today than when Newsom took office in 2019. 
Newsom credits the recent progress to his investments in homelessness programs. Since he’s taken office, he created a new program to funnel homeless funds to cities and counties ($900 million in the current budget), launched grants to help cities clean up encampments and doled out money to turn hotels into homeless housing.

Newsom: “California is proving that homelessness is not inevitable.”

When interviewed by CalMatters earlier this year, officials in counties that were making progress on homelessness said it was because of those new state funds. 
But advocates also cautioned that those numbers may not be as rosy as they seem. Cities have ramped up enforcement against unhoused people in recent years, causing people to scatter from encampments and become harder to count. And recent federal cuts to Medi-Cal and social services will make it more challenging to fight homelessness. 
The data Newsom cited comes from the federally mandated point-in-time count that tallies the number of people sleeping outside and in shelters in each county. Some counties count every January, while some count every other January. 
The data is not exact. Counties use different methodologies and may change their methods between counts. Some counties also use estimates in their counts, and volunteers tasked with tallying unhoused residents are likely to miss people resulting in an undercount.

Our neighborhood-level voter guide


A Los Angeles County polling station clerk sanitizes a voting station at the Monsignor Ramon Garcia Recreation Center polling station in East Los Angeles on Nov. 8, 2022. Pablo Unzueta for CalMatters




By now you’re likely familiar with our voter guide. (If not, first off, how dare you; second, you can still check it out.) This election we rolled out a groundbreaking new feature called My Ballot, which includes nearly every race and measure in the state right down to your school board.
I spoke with CalMatters Director of Product Andrew Losowsky to learn more about the nifty tool and why he believes it’s “the most comprehensive statewide ballot lookup tool that exists.”
What were the goals you set for My Ballot before starting the project?
We knew that we wanted you to look up your address, get your ballot, then be able to make your choices. Then you could not only save it on your device, but also share it with others in a safe way. 
We don’t connect your address and your choices in any way that we can see. We believe the default should be privacy, and we want to make sure that your choices in the voting booth and your choices in this tool are private as well.
What was the biggest challenge you faced?
Figuring out all the multiple voting districts for more than 2,000 contests across the state. That required the data team to make calls to election offices in every county and to get the information about the districts and map all of those boundaries across the different races. It’s not just counties, it’s school districts, it’s Board of Equalization districts, it’s district courts. 



CA mourns labor legend


Dolores Huerta poses for a portrait during the Sundance Film Festival in Park City, Utah on Jan. 20, 2017. Photo by Taylor Jewell, AP Photo




California officials honored Dolores Huerta, an iconic leader of the state’s farmworkers rights movement, after a family spokesperson announced her passing Wednesday. She was 96.
As CalMatters’ Nigel Duara explains, Huerta coined the United Farmer Worker motto and rallying cry, “Si, Se Puede,” or “Yes, We Can.” She was instrumental in ending the 1960s Bracero program that granted Mexican farmworkers temporary status in the U.S. while deducting food and lodging from their meager pay while also exposing them to deadly chemicals.
Each year on April 10, California honors her contributions by declaring the day as Dolores Huerta Day. Newsom told reporters Wednesday that Huerta was a legend who became “a ubiquitous part of our lives.”

Newsom: “She had the kind of energy, she’s just jaw-dropping.  I felt like she was never going to pass. We just have to absorb her contributions, her energy, her passions and her contribution to this world.”

name: California
title: Dolores Huerta “se mantuvo en la lucha” durante siete décadas, inspirando a generaciones de californianos
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
En casi todas las etapas del movimiento de los trabajadores agrícolas, desde sus inicios organizándose en la huelga de la uva de Delano en 1965 hasta la ley de 1986 que concedió amnistía a casi 3 millones de inmigrantes indocumentados, Dolores Huerta estuvo presente.
 Huerta, de 96 años, falleció el miércoles en su casa en Bakersfield. Tan solo dos meses antes, había participado en una manifestación en las escalinatas del Capitolio estatal.
Los líderes políticos y sindicales de California la recuerdan como una incansable defensora de los derechos de los trabajadores agrícolas, quien acuñó el lema y grito de guerra de la Unión de Trabajadores Agrícolas: “Sí, se puede”. Cada año, el 10 de abril, California honra sus contribuciones declarando ese día como el Día de Dolores Huerta.
 “El liderazgo de Dolores en la lucha por un sindicato para los trabajadores agrícolas de California, la UFW, es solo una parte de su historia”, dijo Lorena González, presidenta de la Federación Laboral de California. “Dolores se mantuvo en la lucha por los trabajadores durante décadas”.
 Ella “demostró a generaciones de mujeres que tenían un lugar en este movimiento obrero”. 
 La líder de los Trabajadores Agrícolas Unidos (UFW), Dolores Huerta, en el centro, encabeza una manifestación junto a Howard Wallace, presidente de la sección de San Francisco de la UFW, a la izquierda, y María Elena Chávez, de 16 años, hija de César Chávez, a la derecha, en el distrito Mission de San Francisco, como parte de un boicot nacional en protesta por lo que la UFW describe como el uso peligroso de pesticidas en las uvas de mesa, el 19 de noviembre de 1988. Foto de Court Mast, AP.
 Su influencia aún se hace evidente en la forma en que California recuerda su propia historia: mientras el nombre de César Chávez se retira de los edificios universitarios y las calles de las ciudades de California tras las acusaciones surgidas a principios de este año de que Chávez agredió y violó a varias mujeres, incluida Huerta, activistas en Los Ángeles pidieron que el nombre de Huerta sustituyera al suyo.
 “No puedo imaginar por lo que ha pasado en los últimos meses”, dijo el gobernador Gavin Newsom a un grupo de periodistas el miércoles. “Las revelaciones sobre César y lo difícil que debe haber sido para ella en estos últimos cuatro meses… Simplemente tenemos que reconocer sus contribuciones, su energía, su pasión y su aporte a este mundo”.
 Incluso en sus últimos meses, Huerta siguió adelante.
 “En agosto, se unió al Centro de Políticas para Inmigrantes de California y a nuestros socios en las escalinatas del Capitolio estatal para luchar contra los recortes federales que privan de alimentos a familias, niños y jóvenes inmigrantes”, declaró Masih Fouladi, directora ejecutiva del Centro de Políticas para Inmigrantes de California. “Alzó la voz en defensa de los trabajadores agrícolas, quienes serían los más perjudicados, las mismas personas que alimentan a este estado”. 
 Dolores Huerta interviene en el evento de CalMatters titulado “Salud de los trabajadores agrícolas: ¿Cómo puede California proteger a sus trabajadores esenciales?”, celebrado en Bakersfield el 22 de febrero de 2024. Fotografía de Jules Hotz para CalMatters.
 Huerta desempeñó un papel fundamental en la finalización del programa Bracero en la década de 1960, que otorgaba a los trabajadores agrícolas mexicanos un estatus temporal en los Estados Unidos, descontándoles la comida y el alojamiento de su escaso salario y exponiéndolos además a productos químicos mortales.
 “Su labor de toda la vida fue empoderar a su comunidad para enfrentar y superar las injusticias, y ha dejado a los trabajadores agrícolas y a toda la comunidad latina más fuertes y organizados de lo que los encontró”, dijo la presidenta de la UFW, Teresa Romero. “El trabajo de Dolores sigue siendo tan importante ahora como siempre, y continúa con su ejemplo e inspiración. El mayor homenaje posible a su vida es que su labor de organización continúe”.
 La familia de Huerta dijo que seguirán adelante con los planes para reconocer y celebrar su increíble vida y legado.

title: In three-way Kansas secretary of state race, deep disagreements over election administration
text:
From left, secretary of state candidates Jennifer Day, Scott Morgan and Pat Proctor speak at a Sept. 24, 2026, candidate forum in Salina. (Photos by Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — In the race to become the state’s top elections officer, Kansas voters can pick from a Democrat who spent five months in the Legislature five years ago, a former Republican who is trying to establish an alternative party, and a Republican legislator whose campaign focuses on the fear of noncitizens voting.
The three are running to replace Secretary of State Scott Schwab, who pursued the GOP nomination for governor rather than seek a third term.
There’s Jennifer Day, a Johnson County Democrat, and Scott Morgan, director of the United Kansas party, who both said in interviews that Kansas elections are secure and that a constitutional amendment requiring voters be citizens is redundant because the requirement is already in the constitution.
And there’s Rep. Pat Proctor, a Leavenworth Republican who tilts against an imaginary and undefined “axis of ballot harvesting,” led the charge to put the constitutional amendment on the November ballot, and refuses to engage with Kansas Reflector reporters when questioned at campaign events or contacted by phone or email.
“There’s not a chance in hell I’m answering questions for your paper,” he said when approached at a September forum in Salina.
 
Jennifer Day, the Democratic nominee for Secretary of States, answers questions during an Oct. 22, 2026, interview. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)
Day’s background
Day said she came to Kansas to visit family, fell in love and decided to stay.
She has lived here for 30 years. She said she worked as an executive assistant before opening her own business in 2013 for real estate investment and interior design.
In 2020, she won election to the Kansa House by 62 votes. She then left the seat after her first legislative session when she moved out of the district.
She said she was motivated to run for secretary of state because of concerns about Proctor’s initiatives as chair of the House Elections Committee to restrict voting rights — some of which have landed the state in court. The Secretary of State’s Office should be “quiet and boring,” she said.
“The majority of Kansans really appreciate leaders that are not looking to make headlines and are really just wanting to do the job,” she said.
She said her “hands-on experience” of working elections will help her connect with county clerks across the state.
“I think it’s important that we elect someone to this position who has that disposition that is able to listen and connect well with legislators, voters, our elected officials across the state, and to collaborate in a way that is going to be impactful and not lead to litigation for the state in Kansas,” she said.
 
Scott Morgan, the executive director of United Kansas, the Free State Party, says the merger of two centrist political organizes will give voters an alternative to the Republican and Democratic parties in Kansas. (Photo by Tim Carpenter/Kansas Reflector)
Morgan’s background
Morgan is a fifth-generation Kansan who worked for U.S. Sens. Nancy Kassebaum and Bob Dole, and was Dole’s chief counsel when he ran for president in 1988. He also served as chief counsel for Gov. Mike Hayden.
In 1990, he was the GOP nominee for the 2nd District congressional seat, losing to Democratic U.S. Rep. Jim Slattery with 37% of the vote. He also challenged then-Secretary of State Kris Kobach in the 2014 GOP primary and received 35% of the vote. As his campaign website says: “Sure, he lost that one too. He is consistent.”
He managed to win two terms on the Lawrence school board along the way.
In recent years, Morgan said, he has been working to find a political home for those who aren’t being served by either of the major parties. He hopes to win enough of the vote to gain recognition for the fledgling United Kansas party.
“It’s just providing a choice is all it really is,” Morgan said. “We are an alternative. We’re trying to be the center-left and center-right, forming a coalition, instead of with the extremes.”
He said there is a “genuine hunger” among voters for “something different.”
As for the complaint typically lobbed at third-party candidates: “I’ve grown very wary of the whole ‘you’re a spoiler’ thing,” Morgan said. “I get that from hardcore Democrats a lot, and I think they really misunderstand the math in this thing. It’s not fair, because you’re not a spoiler. You’re a choice.”
He said a lot of the people who vote for him either would not have cast ballots for the office or picked the Republican, based on his background.
 
Kansas Rep. Pat Proctor prepares to speak ahead of President Donald Trump’s rally Oct. 19, 2026, at Heartland Credit Union Arena in Park City. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)
Constitutional amendment
Proctor said during a recent Statehouse news conference, to which Kansas Reflector was not invited, that when people vote, they exercise the “political power that used to be exercised by a gun.”
“We’re all endowed by our creator — not government, by our creator — with the inalienable rights to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness,” he said. “But we’re all so darn different, and that’s why it’s never worked before. That’s why no nation has ever been able to organize under principles.”
He continued: “Our founders found the secret sauce. They created the social contract that we still adhere to today that says, ‘Hey, every couple years we’re going to get together and we’re going to pick our leaders.’ Before 1776, the way people picked leaders is they picked up guns and they shot the other side until one side won and that person was in charge. The founders rediscovered the idea of the ballot box.”


The U.S. Constitution was written in 1787, and governments since at least ancient Greece have conducted elections.
“If we throw open the gates and let anybody exercise that political power, whether they have sworn to those principles or not, we’re not going to have a country anymore,” Proctor said. “We’re going to fly apart.”
Proctor said he started hearing concerns about noncitizen voting a couple of years ago and decided to look into the matter.
“You could have knocked me over when I found out that nowhere in our Kansas Constitution does it actually say you must be a citizen to vote,” Proctor said. “The way our constitution is written, it says ‘every citizen can vote,’ which is not ‘only citizens can vote.’ And so I thought, hey, that’s low-hanging fruit. We can fix that right now.”
Here’s what the state constitution currently says: “Every citizen of the United States who has attained the age of eighteen years and who resides in the voting area in which he or she seeks to vote shall be deemed a qualified elector.”
Here’s the proposed change on the November ballot: “No person shall be deemed a qualified elector unless such person: (1) Is a citizen of the United States; (2) has attained the age of eighteen years; and who (3) except as provided in subsection (b) or (c), resides in the voting area in which he or she such person seeks to vote.”
Amii Castle, who teaches constitutional law at the University of Kansas, wrote in a column for Kansas Reflector that the constitutional already requires voters to be citizens. She also warned that the proposed amendment could give Republicans a basis to reopen the legal fight over a state law that required people to produce a birth certificate or otherwise prove their citizenship before they could register to vote.
Federal courts determined the law was unconstitutional following a years-long legal battle. Kobach failed to prove his bogus claims about widespread voter fraud or show how the proof of citizenship requirement would solve a hypothetical problem. By requiring people to produce a birth certificate, the law blocked more than 35,000 eligible voters from registering.
Proctor pointed to the federal ruling as he complained about Castle’s column during his news conference.
“Nothing that we can do in the Kansas Constitution will, in any way, allow us to implement documentary proof of citizenship,” Proctor said.
He dismissed the argument that illegal voting is extraordinarily rare. He pointed to the conviction this year of the Republican mayor of Coldwater, who had a green card but wasn’t a citizen, as proof that immigrants sometimes vote. He said Kobach, now the attorney general, is prosecuting three additional noncitizens for voting.
“People will say, ‘Well, golly, it’s only four.’ I would just ask, ‘How many is too many?’ I would contend that one is too many because every time a noncitizen votes, they are canceling out the vote of a valid Kansas voter,” Proctor said.
Morgan said he was unimpressed with Proctor’s argument for the amendment.
“We know that thousands of actual citizens were denied the right to vote because they didn’t have the right paperwork, and all of that was to protect against a supposed threat of noncitizens voting, of which there are a minuscule amount,” Morgan said.
 
Rep. Pat Proctor, chair of the House Elections Committee, listen to testimony during a Jan. 27, 2026, hearing on legislation that adds restrictions to delivering advance ballots. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)
Election security
Morgan scoffed at Republicans who complain about election security, as many have since Donald Trump lost the 2020 presidential election fair and square.
In Kansas, Morgan pointed out, Republicans have won every election but one — in 1948, for a two-year term — for secretary of state since 1898.
He said the office needs to provide technical advice to county officials, especially smaller ones that don’t have the budget. He said the state could improve its election audits, and add risk assessment audits. The biggest vulnerability, he said, would be the list of registered voters, known as the “voter roll.”
“It’s just a gaping back door to the whole thing, and that is what really needs to be strengthened and can be strengthened,” Morgan said. “That is a solvable problem. It just requires will. But everybody’s worried about security, so I assume they’re willing to put a little bit of money toward that. Otherwise, you’re really just blowing hot wind.”
He said “ballot harvesting” — Proctor’s term for volunteers who deliver mail-in ballots — isn’t a real problem.
“It sounds scary,” he said, but it is really Kansans “just trying to help” their older friends and neighbors.
Day said she has heard concerns that people could somehow print ballots, randomly fill them out and turn them in.
“As I explained to my neighbor, you would have to know their driver’s license number. You would have to know how they sign their name,” she said.
“Harvesting — quote unquote — it just is not a thing,” she added.
Others have suggested, without evidence, that people who collect ballots on behalf of voters could throw them away instead of delivering them to the election office.
Proctor supported legislation that limited the number of ballots an individual could turn in to 10, and he proposed further restrictions earlier this year.
“There’s always these conspiracies, but I’ve just never seen them,” Morgan said. “Conspiracies are a lousy thing to make public policy on.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Question 7 is fair because it spreads the burden of building housing
text:
ON THE FIRST day of my undergraduate housing policy class, I show my students a headline from the satirical website McSweeney’s that encapsulates the problem at the heart of the Commonwealth’s affordability crisis. “Housing should be affordable,” it reads, “except when I sell my house for a million dollars.” 
Nobody wants denser housing built only near them, so no city or town wants to be the only one that builds. Spread McSweeney’s logic across all 351 cities and towns in Massachusetts, and you get a statewide housing shortage. The only way to break the zoning logjam is a statewide mandate, and Question 7 is a good first step. Anyone concerned about housing affordability should vote for it. 
Economists broadly agree that housing in “superstar cities” and regions like Greater Boston is unaffordable primarily because we have not built enough. Demand for living in thriving, dynamic, and innovative places like Massachusetts far outstrips supply. The shortage shows up as a gap between the cost of a house and the cost of building it, implying that house prices and rents are high because regulations have made buildable land artificially scarce. 
One such regulation is particularly notorious: minimum lot sizes. Localities have used large-lot requirements for over a century to limit density and keep the riffraff out. Among areas zoned for single-family homes, 66 percent nationwide have minimum lot requirements above 5,000 square feet and 7 percent require more than half an acre. These regulations are more common in affluent areas with fewer minorities. By limiting land supply, they drive up housing costs for everyone. 
Question 7 would require that single-family homes be allowed on any lot of at least 5,000 square feet with 50 feet of street frontage and access to public water and sewer. This would let market forces gradually densify cities and towns as developers subdivide large lots, pushing down housing costs. Both nationwide analyses and local policy studies provide strong evidence that rolling back minimum lot sizes reduces house prices and rents over time. Houston, for instance, cut minimums in 1998, leading to a boom in townhomes that added thousands of homes to supply. 
Opponents of Question 7, led by the Massachusetts Municipal Association, cry foul because it limits the autonomy of local governments, which they argue are best positioned to enact thoughtful zoning laws. They also claim that towns will voluntarily implement other, better policies. 
This is exactly the thinking that has led to our affordability crisis: We have failed to build because the balance has tipped too far toward local control. Cities and towns limit construction to free-ride on housing and density built elsewhere, so nobody builds enough housing.  
The resistance to the MBTA Communities Act shows that municipalities will not meaningfully relax zoning on their own, even with significant carrots and sticks. And when a law leaves wiggle room, towns exploit it: Marblehead complied with the law by rezoning a golf course that will never be redeveloped.  
The best way to overcome this is a simple bright-line policy that spreads the burden of density statewide through an across-the-board limit on lot sizes. This approach has gained momentum in recent years, with several states adopting similar limits. 
Question 7 is a modest step in this direction. It will not build a monstrous ziggurat next door. Instead, it will subtly change neighborhood character by allowing a few smaller single-family homes on land that would otherwise hold one large house.  
Some may argue that the 5,000-square-foot limit is too small and too one-size-fits-all. But any bright line is imperfect, and one that spares more towns would build far less of the housing we need and would not spread the burden. Furthermore, the water and sewer requirement means that Question 7 will not affect rural areas. Finally, the towns where Question 7 would have the greatest impact are precisely those that have used minimum lot sizes to avoid doing their share. They should not get a pass for their past resistance. 
Massachusetts needs more housing if we want to remain a place where smart, talented people want to move. Question 7 is a simple way to stop the zoning race to the bottom among cities and towns and force everyone to take on a bit more density for the Commonwealth’s greater good. Everyone worried about rising house prices and rents should support it. 
Adam Guren is an associate professor of economics at Boston University, where he teaches courses on housing policy.
