name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Louisiana Senate race enters home stretch tighter than expected
text:
Polling shows Democrat Jamie Davis, left, drawing closer to U.S. Rep. Julia Letlow, R-Baton Rouge in Louisiana's U.S. Senate race, but political analysts still expect Letlow to prevail in the Nov. 3 election. (Louisiana Illuminator photos)The U.S. Senate race in Louisiana is entering its final days much more competitive than many expected it to be even a few weeks ago.
Political experts from both parties said U.S. Rep. Julia Letlow, R-Baton Rouge, is still the strong favorite to win the election Nov. 3. But Democratic candidate Jamie Davis, a farmer and one-time Tensas Parish police juror, could finish closely behind her.
In Louisiana, where former Gov. John Bel Edwards is the only Democrat to win statewide office in the past decade, a competitive U.S. Senate race seemed improbable as recently as September. But a combination of strong Black turnout during early voting, better-than-expected fundraising for Davis and a national sentiment that favors Democrats has changed that outlook.
“Is it a stretch? Yeah, but less of a stretch than it was a week ago in people’s minds,” James Carville, the famous Cajun political consultant who helped Bill Clinton win the 1992 presidential election, said about Davis’ improving chances.
Letlow is still confident she will win the race.
“Louisianans know she has secured hundred of millions for our communities, fought for parents’ right in education, and worked to lower costs for working families, a record that stands in stark contrast to her opponent who would be nothing more than a rubber stamp for Chuck Schumer and the radical left,” Letlow’s campaign said in a written statement Wednesday.
Black voter turnout
Participation in Louisiana’s seven-day early voting period for the Nov. 3 election was the highest ever for a nonpresidential campaign cycle, according to John Couvillon, a Louisiana pollster who has traditionally worked with Republican candidates.
Almost 521,000 ballots were cast in-person and from absentee voters from Oct. 20-27, according to the Secretary of State’s office. By comparison, the early voting period for the 2022 U.S. Senate race, which Republican John Kennedy won over Democrats Gary Chambers and Luike Mixon, saw 363,000 ballots cast.
What’s likely encouraging for Davis and other Democrats is turnout among Black voters, who make up the backbone of the state party, was higher than usual at 34% for the November election’s early voting period.
In the two decades since Louisiana started early in-person voting, Black people have only made up a larger share of early voters in four previous election cycles, Couvillon said on social media. Those included presidential elections where either Barack Obama or Donald Trump was on the ticket and the May party primary elections for this year’s U.S. Senate race, he said.
Black voters have been more motivated to show up at the polls since April, when the U.S. Supreme Court issued a ruling that weakened protections for minority voting districts, U.S. Rep. Cleo Fields, D-Baton Rouge, said.
The decision led Gov. Jeff Landry and Republican state lawmakers to rework Louisiana’s congressional map to eliminate one of its two majority-Black U.S. House districts. The seat that was lost is held by Fields, who is Black and decided not to run again in 6th District now that it favors the GOP under its new lines.
“People feel that their votes are being disenfranchised, and people are motivated to go to the polls and vote,” Fields said.
Increased early turnout among Black voters doesn’t always translate into election victories for Democrats. For example, Trump still carried Louisiana with 58% of the state vote in 2020.
That’s why several political consultants continue to believe Letlow will win the race over Davis, despite encouraging early voting results for Democrats.
“I don’t think it is enough to win, but I do think he is going to do really much better than people thought,” said Roy Fletcher, a GOP political adviser who helped Gov. Mike Foster get elected in 1995.
Better-than-expected fundraising for Democrats
Letlow’s campaign has collected far more money than Davis’, with $7 million compared to his $5 million. That’s to be expected, political consultants said, given that Letlow is a member of Congress, and Davis has only held elected office at the local level.
Letlow had to spend more money to even make it to the general election. Unlike Davis, she had to beat an incumbent, U.S. Sen. Bill Cassidy of Baton Rouge, in a primary election to earn her party’s nomination. Cassidy had far more resources than any of the Democrats Davis faced in his primary.
The Davis campaign also had more cash available heading into the final two weeks of the election than Letlow did. As of Oct. 15, the Democrat had $1.2 million in his campaign account compared to Letlow’s $443,000, according to their most recent federal campaign finance reports.
The Letlow campaign made a $900,000 television advertising purchase right before the Oct. 15 Federal Election Commission reporting deadline, which could have depleted the campaign’s reserves.
Davis’ campaign touted its cash advantage as a sign he is gaining momentum.
“The fact that Jamie Davis … enters the final week of this race with more cash on hand than his opponent tells you everything you need to know about the enthusiasm on the ground in Louisiana,” Lawrence Mason, Davis’ communications director, said in a written statement Wednesday.
Is Mississippi more competitive?
Even as local political consultants characterize Louisiana’s Senate race as competitive, national party and political donors haven’t paid much attention to it.
Most major political groups spending money on competitive congressional races around the country have not spent money in Louisiana yet.
“I beat my head against the wall trying to get some national money in here. It’s almost impossible,” Carville said.
That could change over the coming days, however. Trump announced Wednesday night he intends to hold a “telerally,” typically an online event that wouldn’t require him to travel, for Letlow Monday, the eve of the election.

Still, Louisiana Democratic Party Chairman Randal Gaines said he has also made several requests to his national party and donors for help in Louisiana, without success so far.
“They do have the perspective that the Deep South is the future of the party,” Gaines said. “If they want that to be reality, they have to put some money in here.”
The situation is different next door in Mississippi, where Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith faces Democrat Scott Colom, a district attorney, in its U.S. Senate race. National Republicans and Democrats are both putting money into advertising for that race ahead of the Nov. 3 election.
Several high profile politicians — including Trump, former President Bill Clinton and former Vice President Kamala Harris — have made in-person appearances in Mississippi to rally voters.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Mixed reactions among disabled Granite Staters on the CFI lawsuit settlement
text:
Kathy Bates, Jim and Pat Piet and Dan Hebert, shown here in their respective homes, each receive services to help them perform the daily activities of life with their disability through New Hampshire's Choices for Independence program. A class action lawsuit over the program's inadequacies was settled earlier this month. (Photos by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)Kathy Bates was elated when she heard that her attorneys and the state of New Hampshire settled a yearslong lawsuit over the Medicaid program that she relies on for care.
Husband and wife duo Jim and Pat Piet are more skeptical and fear that this settlement alone won’t fix the lackluster program without harming other programs.
Dan Hebert, on the other hand, is cautiously optimistic. He sees the potential for big upside, but he also sees pitfalls.
 
Proposed Class Action Settlement For Fitzmorris v DHHS 

Bates, Piet and Hebert are all participants in New Hampshire’s Choices for Independence, a state-run Medicaid program that provides in-home care to people with disabilities and older adults. The goal of the program is to allow them to stay in their own home by hiring caregivers and other supports to avoid a nursing home, something that even the state acknowledges would cost roughly three times as much money.
After years of severe underinvestment in the program, a coalition of nonprofits focused on disability and elderly rights sued the state, arguing that by not properly funding the program the state was at risk of illegally institutionalizing people with disabilities. The case, which lasted almost six years and became a class action lawsuit, was set to go to trial next month before both sides came to an agreement to settle the case earlier this month.
The settlement still must be approved by federal Judge Paul Barbadoro, but class members like Bates, Piet and Hebert have all had a chance to review the settlement, which has major implications on their daily lives.
Elation
Bates is a named plaintiff in the suit. That means she’s been involved in the case since its earliest days and was a representative for the whole class.
“I’m really glad we got here,” she said, before joking, “I probably would’ve said no if I realized it would’ve taken this long.”
Bates, who lives in Somersworth, has cerebral palsy. In 2021, she and three other CFI participants represented by the AARP Foundation, the Disability Rights Center of New Hampshire, New Hampshire Legal Assistance and Nixon Peabody sued the state over the program. Soon after, the case became a class action and grew to encompass the thousands of New Hampshire residents in the CFI program. Bates said she’s relieved the case, which was time-consuming and draining, is over.
Kathy Bates poses for a photo in her Somersworth home on March 25, 2025. Bates said having aides help her with everyday tasks allows her to do fulfilling advocacy work. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
“It feels like it was a part-time job,” she said.  
Core to the plaintiffs’ arguments was that CFI participants weren’t getting the services the state had approved them for. Because of underfunding, CFI participants have long reported, wages were so low that hiring caregivers is near impossible. Vacancies mean shifts go unworked and CFI participants don’t get the help they need to do basic activities of living like getting out of bed, dressing themselves, showering, cooking meals and cleaning. This, their attorneys argued, was putting CFI participants at risk of being put in an institution, a violation of their rights under the 1990 Americans with Disabilities Act and the 1973 Rehabilitation Act. To settle the lawsuit and avert a trial, the state agreed to take a series of steps aimed at solving the issue:

The Department of Health and Human Services agreed to hire a third-party consultant to analyze the state’s network of caregivers to determine whether it meets the needs of the participants. Specifically, the consultant must identify the level of service the state approved for participants versus how much they actually received.
DHHS also agreed to ensure every participant has a contingency plan in place should they not receive their approved services and to execute that plan for any participants who received less than 50% of their approved services each month.
Reimbursement rates set by the state determine caregiver salaries. DHHS agreed to perform an analysis on its reimbursement rates.
DHHS also agreed to ask state lawmakers for biennial reimbursement rate increases to match inflation.
DHHS agreed to expand use of “specialized rates” given to participants who struggle to hire aides.
DHHS agreed to create an online portal and directory of caregivers.
Finally, DHHS agreed to expand its existing grievance system to allow complaints about missed services.
Twice a year, DHHS would be required to create a report outlining its compliance with the agreement.

Bates said the part she’s most excited for is the registry of caregivers. She’s long complained about how challenging it is to hire aides. Bate hires them herself and the caregivers are paid by a third party agency using state funds. She currently uses Craig’s List ads and staffing agencies to find caregivers but is excited to have a new tool she hopes will be more effective. Most of all she’s excited about what it means for the people that help her get out of bed in the morning, people she’s really grateful for.
She hopes “it’ll make the profession of caregiving and the people who do this work” more respected. She explained that lots of her caregivers are single mothers trying to support their own families in addition to supporting her.
“If they make more money in the profession, it becomes a real career option,” she said. “It’ll make life easier for them.”
The New Hampshire Department of Health and Human Services, photographed here on Oct. 19, 2026, operates Medicaid in New Hampshire, which encompasses several different programs aimed at supporting people with disabilities in addition to providing low-income Granite Staters with health coverage. The department has agreed to a series of changes to its Choices for Independence Program in exchange for settling a class action lawsuit and . (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
She knows, however, that change will take time.
“I guess I’ll just have to be patient,” she said.
Skepticism
When Pat Vincent-Piet first heard about the settlement, her first question was “like everything, who pays for this again?”
In a class action lawsuit where the plaintiffs’ attorneys represent thousands of people in one suit, complete agreement among class members is very rare.
Pat and Jim Piet live in Concord and both have cerebral palsy. However, cerebral palsy, like many disabilities, has a spectrum of symptoms. Pat does not need the same level of care as Jim, who uses a wheelchair and has caregivers help him perform many of the daily activities of life.
The couple is skeptical. The settlement doesn’t commit the state to spending more money on the program, which would be needed to raise caregiver salaries and ensure all services are provided. It merely instructs DHHS to ask lawmakers to increase funding to match inflation and create reports about the program. The plaintiffs’ attorneys hope the reports demonstrate the dire needs of this program and convince lawmakers to properly fund the program, but DHHS can’t force lawmakers to give it additional funding. And the reports mandated by the settlement do not have to be produced until after the Legislature commences its budget-making process early next year.
“The only way that works is if we take some money from someone else.” Pat said.
Pat is concerned that to fix one Medicaid program, DHHS will have to raid the coffers of another, such as the developmental disability waiver, another Medicaid program that supports people with intellectual and developmental disabilities rather than purely physical ones. She has little confidence the Legislature will give DHHS the funding needed to reform CFI. She pointed to recent cuts to the Medicaid program over the past two years.
Jim and Pat Piet pose for a photo in their Concord home. The couple said that hiring aides to help Jim with everyday tasks in light of his cerebral palsy is “damn near impossible.” (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Medicaid, which is run jointly by states and the federal government, encompasses several programs. In addition to the several that support people with various disabilities, traditional Medicaid offers health coverage to low-income Americans. In 2025, Congress passed a law that KFF estimated will cut $991 billion from Medicaid nationwide. That same year, New Hampshire lawmakers implemented multiple cost-saving measures on the state level. They are set to begin charging premiums to certain traditional Medicaid recipients soon and have decreased the amount of prescription costs the state will cover. Pat argues “all of those things are connected.”
Jim and Pat also questioned whether the state has the staff to create these reports and do the extra work this settlement requires. They said the Medicaid personnel they interact with to get reapproved for services every year and complete other bureaucratic tasks tell them they’re too understaffed to get the work they currently have on their plate done.
“There’s no one to implement these requirements,” Jim said.
Jim and Pat feel they’re luckier than most CFI participants. When they can’t find a caregiver to cover a shift, Pat steps in to help. Single participants don’t have that luxury. Still, Jim wants his wife to be his wife, not his aide. It’s also hindered Pat’s career and her ability to earn a living, pay taxes and contribute to the community.
Cautious optimism
Dan Hebert, who also lives in Concord, had dates set on his calendar for a potential trial and was surprised to learn about the settlement. His takeaway is cautious optimism.
What he likes about the settlement: “a greater push toward transparency” and “what’s hopefully going to be an increase in compensation for the caregivers.”
The class action lawsuit, entitled Fitzmorris v DHHS, was being litigated in the U.S. District Court of New Hampshire, photographed here on Aug. 27, 2025. The case narrowly averted a trial, planned for November, when the parties reached a settlement agreement in early October. (Photo by Ethan DeWitt/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Hebert agrees with the attorneys’ argument that demonstrating the lackluster nature of CFI could push lawmakers to better fund it.
“I counted no less than five reports that are mandated in this,” he said. “And while the department has had this information already, having it in five reports transparently and announced means that everyone sees it upfront and it’s readable. I think that’s important.”
He’s also planning to utilize the grievance system.
“I can’t tell you that it’s going to work,” he said. “I can’t tell you that it’s not going to work. I don’t know, but I do know that the monitoring is going to tell us the truth, and we’re all going to see it.”
Hebert is disappointed the reports won’t be ready before state lawmakers begin budget deliberations as this likely pushes back any real fiscal solution to the problems CFI faces until 2029, the following budget year. He wishes this could be solved sooner.
Dan Hebert, photographed here in his Concord home on Nov. 3, 2025, is one of the CFI participants involved in a lawsuit against the state. He’s hopeful the settlement will be enough to fix the lackluster program. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Overall, he said he’s happy the settlement was struck.
“I think that the attorneys that we have negotiated this settlement to try to do the best that they could,” he said. “And if this is what we’re gonna try, I’m optimistic.”
The Disability Rights Centers, one of the organizations litigating the case, is holding two webinars to inform CFI participants about the settlement on Nov. 17 at 10 a.m and Nov. 30 at 6 p.m. More details are available online at https://cfi.drcnh.org.
Any class member that objects to the settlement can have their voice heard in court on Jan. 21 at the U.S. District Court in Concord. They can also mail in their written complaints by Dec. 7 with the U.S. District Court at 55 Pleasant St. in Concord, NH (ZIP code 03301). Barbadoro, the judge, will decide whether to approve the settlement soon after.
Meanwhile, Hebert still relies on family and friends to help him out because he can’t find enough professional caregivers willing to work for the rates CFI offers.
“My world hasn’t changed today,” Hebert said. “But I’m hoping that it will.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: As feds cut key fee, Indiana Medicaid chief warns changes needed to avoid ‘catastrophic situation’
text:
Family and Social Services Administration Secretary Mitch Roob walks through slides about how a federally mandated phase-down in the hospital assessment fee might impact the Healthy Indiana Plan, or HIP, at FSSA's quarterly financial meeting on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)The leader of Indiana’s Medicaid program says the state must change up a widely used low-income health insurance program as the federal government slashes a key funding source over the next five years.
The phase-down is one way President Donald Trump’s administration is pushing health costs back onto states. Last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act also increases state shares for other aspects of Medicaid and for food aid.
“Changes in the hospital assessment fee will have a material, but not catastrophic, effect on the budget,” said Secretary Mitch Roob, whose Family and Social Services Administration administers Medicaid in Indiana. “And we need to recognize that … this budget cycle and begin planning for that, so we don’t end up in a catastrophic situation in 2032.”
At a quarterly financial meeting Tuesday, Roob revealed early projections produced with consultant Deloitte. They’ll be “refined” before an upcoming budget presentation to lawmakers.
“In December, we’ll have a complete Medicaid forecast, but I don’t want to catch you all off guard because these numbers are more dire than I would like them to be,” Roob said.
The hospital assessment fee, a tax levied by the state, is used to leverage a higher federal reimbursement rate for individual facilities.
Early state projections illustrate what a federally mandated phase-down in the hospital assessment fee might look like. The state’s purchasing power is expected to decline more steeply with inflation. (Screenshot of presentation)
Indiana keeps some of the fee to fund its share of expenses for the Healthy Indiana Plan, which serves an “expansion” population — hundreds of thousands of working-age adults who earn slightly too much for traditional Medicaid coverage — along with pregnant women, low-income caretakers and others.
Starting late next year, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act phases the 6% fee down annually to 3.5% in late 2031.
The state made more than $2 billion off the 6% fee and intergovernmental transfers over the last fiscal year, which ended in June. At 3.5%, the state would’ve lost roughly $900 million — or 40% of what was collected.
“That’s the purchasing power decline that we’re going to see by 2032,” Roob said.
He said officials must begin planning for the hit, “so we don’t end up in a situation where we have to reduce rates or reduce eligibility.” 
Roob doesn’t think the state can “cut (its) way to solvency.”
“We’ve got to find ways to deliver care less expensively, prospectively, than we are today,” he said. “We’ve got to find better care models. I don’t know what that is. But we have to develop that care model.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Hayes, Shea compete in CT 5th District as national attention shifts
text:
This is the fifth in a series of stories profiling candidates in each congressional district race.

Connecticut’s 5th Congressional District, a sprawling district reaching the northwest corner of the state, remains the most competitive congressional race in the state. But national attention has shifted away from the district as outside groups in both parties look to other U.S. House races in the battle for control of Congress.
After winning by a more comfortable margin two years ago, U.S. Rep. Jahana Hayes is seeking a fifth term against Republican Chris Shea. He’s a North Haven firefighter and retired Navy SEAL who lives in Cheshire. He also founded the nonprofit Hero to Hero, which encourages military veterans to consider a second career as first responders.
Shea, a first-time candidate, said he wants to bring change to a district that’s been elusive to Republicans for years. He secured his party’s endorsement at the nominating convention earlier this year and went on to win the GOP primary in August. 
“What I’m doing is trying to continue to serve,” Shea said, referencing his career in the military. “I’m trying to get into this because having a one-sided delegation does not really represent Connecticut. I don’t think that’s the right representation for Connecticut for a bunch of reasons.”
The race for this district has traditionally been at the center of Connecticut’s political universe when it comes to federal campaigns. This cycle, election analysts who rate competitive races moved the 5th District much closer to Democrats. That’s on top of a midterm year when the party in power historically faces political headwinds.
Hayes had a nail-biter reelection race in 2022 against Republican George Logan, a former state senator. She won by a larger margin in a 2024 rematch. While the general political environment bodes well for Democrats this year — as polls and early voting numbers indicate — she’s not taking this election for granted, though she notices some differences from previous campaigns.
“I’m gaining votes in different communities or holding steady, getting out there,” Hayes said. “So now I don’t have to introduce myself over again, every campaign.”
For his part, Shea said his career prepared him for the job because he worked a lot with Congress and “got a chance to see how things work — or not.” He worked in resourcing at the U.S. Department of Defense, where he said he got the nickname the “mayor of the Pentagon.”
“I got a lot of stuff done just by going around and addressing needs and talking to people face to face,” Shea said. “That’s the approach I would take in Congress.”
Hayes came to Congress after her first election in 2018 with no political experience. She’s a former high school government and history teacher in Waterbury who was awarded the National Teacher of the Year award in 2016.
Nearly a decade later, Hayes feels like there’s a confidence that comes from repeat victories and having a better understanding of how to navigate Congress both on policy and politics.
“I came to this space and I knew why I wanted to do this work and I was really passionate about helping people,” Hayes said. “I think over my last four terms, I’ve learned how to translate that help into action. I know how the Congress works.”

Chris Shea, Republican nominee for the 5th Congressional District, is joined by supporters as he campaigns at the intersection of Country Club Road and West Avon Road in Avon on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

As a first-time candidate, Shea said there’s a learning curve to running for office. Echoing a similar sentiment as Hayes, Shea said a lot of time is devoted to fundraising and feeling like “you’re always in beggar mode.”
During the past two cycles, Connecticut’s 5th District attracted outsized national attention and substantial outside money. That has largely dissipated, though both candidates got an 11th-hour boost from political action committees in the final weeks.
Pro-Choice Majority Action spent $250,000 against Shea in an ad that links Shea to President Donald Trump and “promised to do Trump’s bidding.” Seal the Deal PAC, meanwhile, invested almost $50,000 against Hayes in an ad that criticizes her campaign spending and accuses her of “using Congress to serve herself.”
In 2022, outside groups in both parties spent upwards of $12 million on the race. Two years later, those same groups still invested but not at the same magnitude. A few weeks out from the 2024 election, Republicans’ biggest super PAC cancelled some of its TV ad reservations to spend on other races.
The 5th District also drew a lot of star power in the past. Then-Vice President Kamala Harris discussed reproductive rights with Hayes in New Britain in 2022. And House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., visited the district to fundraise with Logan in 2024.
Republicans, who haven’t had a member of Congress from Connecticut since 2009, had heavily invested in trying to flip the 5th District, especially in the 2022 midterms. That year, Republicans went on to take back the House majority. The Republican National Committee opened multiple community centers to engage with Black and Hispanic voters around the country, including one in New Britain. But it didn’t reopen in 2024.
Shea said the National Republican Congressional Committee, the main committee working to defend the GOP’s majority in the House, helped pay for internal polling, which he noted “came out better than I think people would expect.” He quipped that he’s still waiting for a check from Elon Musk, who recently pumped hundreds of millions of dollars into the midterms to boost Republicans.
The NRCC “has been working closely with Chris Shea’s campaign, and we have been actively engaged in the race,” according to spokeswoman Maureen O’Toole.
One of the biggest contrasts between the candidates has been over H.R. 1, Republicans’ party-line tax legislation that passed last year and was dubbed by Trump as the “big beautiful bill.”

U.S. Rep. Jahana Hayes laughs as she talks with Gov. Ned Lamont following a press conference to discuss education priorities at the Meriden Board of Education on Friday, Oct. 23, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Hayes said she’d prioritize trying to rescind cuts to Medicaid and the federal nutrition program known as SNAP that the law will enact through changes like new work requirements. Nearly 63,000 residents in Connecticut have so far lost SNAP benefits since eligibility changed as a result of H.R. 1. Medicaid changes are coming in January.
Shea, on the other hand, said he wants to see the bill’s tax relief measures strengthened or made permanent. He noted his opponent’s opposition to the bill, which also included new federal deductions for overtime pay or tips, as well as an increase on the cap for state and local tax (SALT) deductions. (Hayes pointed out they’re temporary tax breaks that expire in 2028 at the end of Trump’s term.)
When asked specifically about SNAP and Medicaid cuts, Shea said he wants to make sure the programs don’t get abused.
“I’m concerned that the people who need it get it, and the people that don’t need it and are milking the system, so to speak, aren’t getting it,” Shea said.
Both candidates have talked about the importance of addressing cost-of-living issues that have become the common theme in the midterms.
Hayes said Democrats can’t be singularly focused on affordability, as important as it is. And with the limited leverage they might have even if her party takes the majority, she argues that Democrats need to show voters that they’re working to address their concerns.
“This is where the challenge is and where we have to manage expectations, because even if you can’t completely fix the problem, people need to know that you’re working on it,” Hayes said. “People want to know that you’re doing something about it or at least trying to, and that’s what they haven’t seen.”
Hayes identified some areas where she feels Democrats have previously fallen short. At a Connecticut AFL-CIO event around Labor Day weekend, she mused about how they should have done more for labor when they held all levels of power. And in a recent interview, she highlighted the need for conducting oversight, which she believes “Democrats failed to do when we took the majority.”
“There were some things that we could have addressed to make sure that the government was working in a way that the people needed it to, so that individuals couldn’t take advantage of the government or make money off the government, and we failed to do that,” Hayes said.
On top of seeking reelection, Hayes will also make a run for the top spot on the House Committee on Education and the Workforce. So far, Hayes and Oregon Rep. Suzanne Bonamici are challenging the current top Democrat, U.S. Rep. Bobby Scott of Virginia.
A top motivation for her to seek that leadership role is the Trump administration’s push to dismantle and relocate offices within the U.S. Department of Education. She said she’s also been calling for a hearing on addressing school shootings.
But as much as Democrats are planning for a possible return to power and what their roles might look like as committee chairs, Hayes said the future feels a bit unclear.
“We’re not even sure, if we were to take the majority, what we would be walking into, because they haven’t really responded to subpoenas. They haven’t turned over data or documents,” Hayes said. “We’d have to call people in and kind of see where we stand on all these things.”

Chris Shea, Republican nominee for the 5th Congressional District, is joined by supporters as he campaigns at the intersection of Country Club Road and West Avon Road in Avon on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Shea said he’d like to serve on a committee with jurisdiction over veterans or defense issues, which would be a “no-brainer” given his experience. But he would also want to broaden his interests, citing the House Agriculture Committee, which is one of Hayes’ current assignments.
When asked what he’d like to tackle if he’s elected to Congress, Shea said he didn’t want to overpromise, like candidates tend to do before they get to Washington. He didn’t have a general vision but went on to describe some work he’d like to get done for veterans and the military.
“There’s things about vets — I definitely would like to see the processes for folks to get their claims in, done and processed faster, better,” Shea said. “Anything we can do to get vets from sleeping on the street is a big concern of mine.”
“Having a military that’s properly funded to do the jobs that they are tasked with going forward and accomplishing,” he continued, “that’s a big priority of mine.”
Hayes and Shea squared off earlier this month in the one and only debate of the campaign. They shared contrasting views on Trump administration policies, immigration and the war in Iran.
Following the debate, Hayes argued in a post on social media that her opponent is “clearly not ready for this work.”
Shea pushed back on her characterization, arguing that the congresswoman sounded like she was playing “buzzword bingo” with government jargon at the debate.
“I have some insight that most civilians would not have, spending five-plus years in the Pentagon doing resourcing and working with Congress, at least on the Department of Defense side,” Shea said.
He knocked Hayes for repeatedly working into the debate that Trump isn’t a king.
“I think people are smarter than that,” Shea said. “And I think they can see substance and the genuine nature from where I approach this.”

U.S. Rep. Jahana Hayes speaks during a press conference to discuss education priorities at the Meriden Board of Education on Friday, Oct. 23, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Hayes argued that it’s more than understanding terms and memorizing bill numbers — those are all things that can easily be learned on the job and aren’t a requirement coming into Congress as a first-time candidate.
“He’s not prepared, and prepared doesn’t mean having a full understanding of policy. Prepared means understanding the people and the needs of this district,” Hayes said. “He has a very narrow vision of who needs help in this district.”
The two candidates also disagreed over the authority of the executive and the legislative branches in relation to the president’s tariff agenda and a war in Iran that has stretched into its eighth month.
Early voting is underway in Connecticut. In the first few days, Democrats outnumbered Republicans in the state. In-person early voting began Monday, Oct. 19 and runs through Sunday, Nov. 1. The last day to request an absentee ballot is Nov. 2.
Republicans are pushing their party to take advantage of all of their voting options, despite Trump seeking to rein in mail-in voting.
“Republicans are notorious for saying, ‘I’m just voting on Election Day, this is BS,'” Shea said. “It’s like, ‘Hey man, Election Day is just a little bit longer this year, so take advantage of it.'”
Hayes is on two ballot lines, cross-endorsed by the Working Families Party. Jonathan De Barros, who lost the Republican primary to Shea, is also running as a write-in candidate on Nov. 3.
When asked about her future goals and political life, Hayes told The Connecticut Mirror that serving in Congress is not a long-term ambition, though she doesn’t have an exact timeline. “No one will have to kick me out of this job,” she said, with a laugh.
Hayes was recently asked by WTNH whether she’d be interested in running for the Senate in 2028 if U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal decided to retire. She talked about her strong preference for the House, comparing it to public school, while saying the Senate’s more akin to private school. “I’m not title shopping,” she said.
WTNH political anchor Dennis House pointed out that Connecticut has never had a woman serve as a U.S. senator. Hayes said she’s “humbled” she made history as the first Black woman to represent the state in Congress. But she offered a quick aside, while laughing, that “I also think I’d be a great senator.”
She told CT Mirror that serving in Congress gave her a taste of what government can accomplish, whether that’s passing the PACT Act to expand veterans benefits or providing summer meals for students.
Because of the pandemic, Hayes said she feels like they lost time to make more progress, and she feels “fully invested” in getting more done on her committees. But she also relishes the thought of one day going back to the classroom to “have some very different discussions in a much less hypothetical way about the workings of Congress.”
“They try to push me out every two years,” she said, referring to her reelection races, “but it won’t be because I’ve overstayed my welcome.”

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Competing US Senate endorsements highlight tension between tribal sovereignty and investment
text:
Maliseet Tribal Chief Clarissa Sabattis and Mi'kmaq Nation Chief Sheila McCormack at the Wabanaki Alliance's annual celebration on Oct. 1, 2026, in Freeport. (Photo By Emma Davis Maine Morning Star)Citizens of Wabanaki Nations are divided in their pick for who should represent Maine in the U.S. Senate, highlighting the tension the tribes face between the need for investment and their ultimate goal of full sovereignty.
The tribal councils of the Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians and the Mi’kmaq Nation endorsed Democratic nominee Troy Jackson, citing his commitment to advocating for the Wabanaki Nations’ sovereignty. Meanwhile, the two chiefs of the two reservations of the Passamaquoddy Tribe endorsed incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, pointing to her ability to secure federal funding as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee. 
Neither the Passamaquoddy Tribe at Indian Township nor the Passamaquoddy Tribe at Sipayik have endorsed Collins. As a tribal citizen of the Passamaquoddy community at Sipayik emphasized in a recent op-ed, their chief is not authorized to endorse political candidates on the Tribe’s behalf.
But the individual endorsements still mark a departure from elections past, as the five-term senator had never before received such endorsements. They also illustrate the competing interests the candidates are appealing to as the Nov. 3 election nears. 
The reasoning behind Collins’ endorsements underscore the central component of her pitch to voters: her ability to secure federal funds for Maine. 
“Her ability to deliver has really made a difference in our community and we are so grateful,” Chief of the Passamaquoddy Tribe at Sipayik Amkuwiposohehs Bassett said in an Oct. 14 letter endorsing the senator. 
Bassett highlighted that the Tribe met with Collins last year when their wastewater treatment plant was at risk of failing due to extreme weather effects, and she got them $5 million for a new system. 
Hoping compromise is thing of past, Wabanaki Alliance eyes path to full sovereignty

Chief of the Passamaquoddy Tribe at Indian Township William Nicholas Sr. similarly highlighted federal funding he credits the senator with securing, including nearly $3 million to construct new affordable housing units during the 2026 fiscal year. 
“She has consistently advocated for and delivered crucial federal assistance for our community, including providing much-needed funds to upgrade tribal housing,” Nicholas said in a statement.  “She has been a loyal friend to us in Washington.”
The Wabanaki Nations have less sovereignty than other federally recognized tribes because of a 1980 land settlement agreement subjecting them to state laws in a manner more akin to municipalities. Remaining barriers to self-governance have left persistent disparities between tribal citizens and other Mainers, such as health inequalities and limited economic mobility.
Given the continued fight to restore full sovereignty, other tribes in the Wabanaki Nations see their champion in Jackson, citing his legislative record on the issue. That includes the Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians and the Mi’kmaq Nation. The Penobscot Nation has yet to endorse.  
“With his fervent support of the Mi’kmaq people, his consistent advocacy and his track record in the Legislature, there is no question that he will be a true partner to restore tribal sovereignty and improve outcomes for both the Mi’kmaq Nation and Maine people in the U.S. Senate,” Chief of the Mi’kmaq Nation Sheila McCormack said in a statement. 
In 2019, the Legislature convened a task force to review and reform that agreement. That work was initiated under the leadership of Jackson, then-president of the Maine Senate, and the speaker of the Maine House of Representatives at the time, Sara Gideon, who unsuccessfully ran against Collins in 2020. 
“As Senate President, Troy didn’t just talk about tribal sovereignty, he put it into action,” Chief of the Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians Clarissa Sabattis said in a statement. “From championing clean drinking water initiatives to his role in creating the commission to reexamine the 1980 Maine Indian Claims Settlement Act, Troy has consistently proven that he listens to indigenous voices and stands with the Wabanaki people.”
Jackson backed state legislation that gave the Wabanaki Nations more authority, as well as sweeping bills to overhaul the settlement act, though the latter were ultimately vetoed by Gov. Janet Mills. Because of his work, the Wabanaki Alliance, an advocacy coalition formed in 2020 to push for sovereignty, has long recognized Jackson as a champion of the Wabanaki Nations.
Gov. Mills, Wabanaki Nations shelve sovereignty overhaul in compromise measures

On the federal level, Collins has not championed sovereignty in the same way. 
The senator has supported specific extensions of tribal authority, including provisions in the Violence Against Women Act that allowed the Wabanaki Nations to exercise criminal jurisdiction over certain crimes and the Native American Child Protection Act to ensure tribes have tools to prevent and respond to child abuse. Collins did not actively support nor publicly share her stance on a federal proposal to provide the Wabanaki Nations access to future beneficial federal laws. 
“There are decisions around tribal sovereignty that are the responsibility of the Maine Legislature and the Governor on which they have yet to act,” Collins said in response to a question about whether she supports tribal sovereignty for Maine Morning Star’s voter guide. 
Jackson told Maine Morning Star decisions shouldn’t be made for tribal communities by politicians in Augusta or Washington.
“To me, this is pretty simple,” he said, “the Wabanaki Nations deserve the same respect, rights and opportunities as other federally recognized tribes across this country.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Opinion: Worried about election security in Kansas? Ask a poll worker — or become one yourself!
text:
An election worker prepares to hand out "I voted" stickers to Johnson County participants in the Aug. 4, 2026, primary election to consider a proposed constitutional amendment and determine nominations by the Democratic and Republican parties. (Photo by Tim Carpenter/Kansas Reflector)I just got home from my mandatory poll worker preelection training. It was 90-plus minutes long, and this was just a refresher class for experienced poll workers, not the longer new poll worker class. I got an updated 51-page election board manual to review at home.
My shift will be 14 hours long: Report before 6 a.m. and work until about 8 p.m. Flat-rate pay is $130 for a shift. I could sign a fee waiver sheet and work for free. But, nah, this year I think I want to use the big bucks for something I cannot otherwise afford — a massage or a steak. Fill up the tank without swearing. Have a feel-good moment. Or donate it to Just Food, which would also result in a feel-good moment.
I’ve been saying for years now that Donald Trump has never worked an election. If he had, how could he, with such blistering language, rant about how the system is rigged? He maintains that ballots can be stolen, boxes of them substituted or made to disappear, mail-in ballots forged, voting machines hacked. Ballots are how elections are rigged, he claims.
And that is just ridiculous.
Here is my pitch: Do what Trump has never dared to do. I encourage everyone who worries about rigged voting machines and stolen ballots, who believes that there is corruption lurking in every cardboard box, to take a deep dive into the alleged swamp of insidious fraud. 
Sign up to work the polls! Yes, it may be uncomfortable. You may feel suspicious. That’s OK. Ask lots of questions. Watch, from the inside, how the process unfolds. Respect the rules about not talking politics. It could be a relief to understand, from personal experience, how the system in place prevents voting fraud. 
It’s too late to sign up for the 2026 election. But you can at least get your name on a list to get a letter for the next election. 
I understand that some might not be eager to work the polls yet still worry about stolen ballots. So here are a few facts that might alleviate some of that worry.
 
Things voters might not be aware of

Most poll workers are 65-plus years old. Believing they would choose to collude to commit election fraud? Seriously? That’s way above our pay grade. We just want to contribute to making voting a validating experience instead of a duty. We know, from experience, that ballots are inviolate.
When serving, poll workers are apolitical. County election officials work to provide balance in each poll place, assigning workers of different political affiliations to work side-by-side. I’ve worked for years not knowing if fellow poll workers shared my party or positions. Discussing politics, or even world events, is verboten. We’re not there to persuade or convert. We don’t scroll our phones for reports of results.
In my county, every ballot is completed by hand. When you place your completed ballot into the tabulator, it registers, then drops into a locked metal box. Workers cannot reach in and grab a few ballots. Workers cannot substitute ballots. When the ballots are removed from the box at the end of the day, the tabulated total is compared with the total of written names taken down as voters arrived and showed ID. The results must match. Ballots are placed in a sealed bag, with witnesses to the process. No one is ever left alone with ballots.
Poll workers cannot leave their polling places on Election Day. No excuses. So, no hanky-panky with ballots. If you leave, you can’t return. No quickie runs to the nearest Subway or bakery. (Nothing like being in lockdown to make me lust for pastry.) When I show up at 5:50 a.m., I’ve packed a small cooler: breakfast yogurt, lunch, ample iced tea, snacks, a few extra sandwiches to share with anyone under-prepared. Plus a book to read if there is a break. 
Voting technology differs by county. In Douglas County, there is no internet connection between any tabulating machine and a central registry. There is no internet involved in the voting process, period. Hacking requires internet. However, counties that do use voting machines have their own rigorous security protocols. Plus, cross-counting ballot totals with signatures also takes place.  You, as a voter, can ask questions about the protocols and technology in your county.There are layers and layers of testing and trial runs before any new technology is allowed. Ask questions – don’t toss accusations — to learn the facts.

 
My takeaway
The serious threats to any fair election process are not inside individual polling places or machines.
The threats are much, much bigger. They come from laws that create blocks to registering to vote, laws that demand additional proof of individual legitimacy to vote. Are you really who you say you are? Prove your name change. Get an official copy of your birth certificate or marriage certificate. Show your passport. Doing all of this takes time and costs money.
Even more blocks are created not by laws but protocols. Polling places are less available. Advanced voting is shortened, along with fewer polls. Mail-in voting gets hyped as the big problem and the time limit allowed between ballots going out and being returned is shortened.
At the training, I heard frustration. Our county ballots, mailed to registered voters who had applied for mail-in ballots, were still “stuck” in Kansas City a week later. By the time voters receive their ballots, it may be too tight to mail them back. (Given that I recently had mail from Lawrence to Topeka take two weeks, I’m not confident.)
I do have a few suggestions to make voting less stressful.
First, walk into your election office and request a sample ballot in advance of however you choose to vote. Mine is bright green and says “sample” all over it, so there’s no chance of it being used for nefarious purposes. Having one gives me time to review the candidates and research any specific questions I may have. I can read, and reread, the often convoluted back-page constitutional amendments and county or city ballot questions.
Our polling sites provide privacy, but not an hour in an armchair with a cup of tea to reflect on important, individual choices. 
What I most appreciate about a sample ballot is being able to see all the judges up for retention. I used to feel ignorant, and it didn’t seem fair to vote if I didn’t know their records. Then I discovered a Kansas Bar Association website that provides data provided by attorneys who have tried cases, from both sides, with those judges.
It shares information about their biographies, prior employment, positions and experience. It’s reassuring to realize that so many of our appointed judges make thoughtful, deeply reasoned and judicious decisions on challenging issues. Kansas has a nonpartisan appointment process that works.
I hope this provides a slightly better understanding of what your poll workers bring to Election Day. Their commitment enables democracy. Wear your little “I Voted” sticker with pride. Your vote is critical to an enduring democracy.
If you haven’t considered being a poll worker yourself, think again. Your engagement, helping one voter at a time, can make a difference.
Susan Kraus has worked for decades as a therapist, university educator and court mediator. Through its opinion section, the Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Democrat David Crowley gains slight polling, fundraising advantage in last week of campaign
text:
Democratic candidate for governor David Crowley is heading into the final week of the campaign with an expanded polling advantage over Republican candidate Tom Tiffany. (Photos by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)Democratic candidate for governor David Crowley is heading into the final week of the campaign with an expanded polling advantage over Republican candidate Tom Tiffany. Crowley also had a slight fundraising advantage in the most recent reporting period, though Tiffany, who has raised more money overall, is still outspending the Democratic candidate.
The final Marquette Law School poll before Election Day found that Crowley maintained a 7-point lead over Tiffany among likely voters; 51% said they will vote for Crowley, while 44% said they’d vote for Tiffany. There were 4% who remained undecided. 
A month ago Crowley led the Marquette Law School poll 49% to 46% among likely voters.
“What’s happened in this month is Tiffany has gone down two points and Crowley gone up two points,” poll director Charles Franklin said.
Crowley was also ahead among registered voters; 49% said they would vote for Crowley, while 46% said they’d vote for Tiffany.
The poll was conducted from Oct. 14 through 22, with surveys ending just before the only debate in the race, so the poll did not capture voters’ response to the debate. It interviewed 818 Wisconsin registered voters about the election. The sample of likely voters was 668. 
Crowley has the support of 98% of Democrats, up from 96% in September, while Tiffany has the support of 92% of Republicans, down from 95% in September. 
Crowley has increased his support among independents to 56% from 44% in September, while Tiffany’s support grew from 18% to 26%. The percentage of undecided independent voters has decreased from 38% to 18%.
“Independents are coming in, they are making up their minds, and they’re going for Crowley pretty significantly,” Franklin said. 
Fundraising reports filed this week showed Crowley reported raising $15.5 million over the last four weeks, due in large part to transfers of $9 million from the Democratic Party of Wisconsin. The state party received $5.5 million from LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman during the pre-election period.
Tiffany reported raising a little over $10 million during the same time period, which included $9 million from the Republican Party of Wisconsin as well as $3.5 million in in-kind contributions. The state party reported receiving $13 million from Beloit billionaire Diane Hendricks, bringing her total donated to the party this year to $21 million. 
Tiffany reported spending $17 million over the time period and ended with $4.8 million in the bank, while Crowley spent $14.2 million and ended with $4.1 million in the bank.
In total over the year, Tiffany has raised $49.7 million and spent $46.6 million. Crowley has raised $26.7 million and spent $23 million.
Both candidates have been delivering their closing arguments to voters this week at campaign events and through ads.
Crowley has focused on addressing the cost of living by making healthcare affordable and funding education and tying Tiffany to the Trump administration. The Marquette poll found that Trump’s job approval fell one point in Wisconsin over the last month to another record low of 61% disapproval and 37% approval.
Tiffany has focused on addressing high costs by cutting taxes, limiting transgender students’ rights in schools and other cultural issues. Two ads released by the Tiffany campaign soon after the Marquette poll focused on Crowley’s previous support of placing tampons in all school bathrooms and criticized the use of racial equity policies in Milwaukee County while Crowley has served as the county executive. The ads call Crowley’s agenda “radical.” 
Crowley spokesperson Philip Shulman said in a statement that the campaign is “taking nothing for granted and running like we’re one point down in this final week.” 
“Wisconsinites are clearly fired up to elect David Crowley the next governor of Wisconsin as he continues bringing his vision of making life more affordable to every corner of the state,” Shulman said.
The Marqutte poll asked voters about which candidate would do more on specific issues. 
Among registered voters 39% said Crowley would do more on making healthcare affordable to Tiffany’s 23%; 44% said Crowley would do more to improve education to Tiffany’s 30% and 32% said Crowley would do more to handle data centers to Tiffany’s 25%. 
The only issue where Tiffany was ahead was reducing taxes — 42% said he would do more, while 17% said Crowley would. 
Voters across the state will also determine which party controls the state Legislature, which Republicans have held since 2011. Democrats are seeking to flip two seats in the state Senate and  five seats in the state Assembly to take majorities in both houses.
Among likely voters, the Marquette poll found 51% said they would vote for the Democratic candidate, while 44% said they would vote for the Republican candidate. 
Franklin said there is also a change in voters’ preference for unified government as opposed to divided government. The poll found that among registered voters, 60% prefer unified control and 38% favor divided government. 
“After a long period of divided government, people do seem to have a bit of a taste for unified control and the things that you can get done when you have one party in control,” Franklin said, adding that preferences for which party takes charge depends on voters’ partisan affiliations.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: There’s a big divide between Lt. Gov. candidates
text:
Wisconsin State Capitol (Wisconsin Examiner photo)When Wisconsin voters choose a governor on Tuesday, they’ll automatically choose that person’s second fiddle — the lieutenant governor who could end up stepping into the top job unexpectedly.
Republican Tom Tiffany’s running mate is David Varnam, a former small-town mayor and one-time staffer at a conservative Christian policy organization. Democrat David Crowley’s running mate, Sarah Godlewski, is a high-profile Democratic politician who has held two statewide offices, one elected and one appointed.
The two have little in common, but each has said they’re hearing from voters who are crossing party lines to back their ticket.
Neither was chosen by the candidate they’re running with. Wisconsin voters pick their political party’s lieutenant governor candidate in the August partisan primary.
Republican David Varnam: Conservative policy advocate
Republican candidate for lieutenant governor David Varnam, at an event in DeForest in August 2026. (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)
In August, David Varnam pulled an upset in the Republican primary for lieutenant governor, garnering 55% of the vote to defeat the party’s endorsed candidate, Will Martin, who received 45%. Martin had already been making campaign appearances with Tiffany.
The Tiffany campaign did not respond to requests this week for an interview with Varnam.
Varnam’s victory was powered by endorsements before the primary from U.S. Rep. Derrick Van Orden, Wisconsin Family Action and Pro-Life Wisconsin. Wisconsin Family Action campaigns against legislation that protects LGBTQ rights. Pro-Life Wisconsin has supported legislation that would define a fetus as “a person” — outlawing abortion for any reason and opposing exceptions for rape, incest or to protect the life of the mother.
Abortion is one of seven issues Varnam lists on his campaign website. He vows to “stand firm and support protections for unborn children,” citing his past work for Focus on the Family as well as his work as a congressional aide earlier in his career.
The website list also says he favors “protecting women sports” and vows to “keep men out of women’s sports and protect their locker rooms.” In the last several weeks Tiffany has promoted his own promise to prevent trans girls from playing on girls’ sports teams or using girls’ bathrooms and locker rooms.


What does the lieutenant governor do?
The job of lieutenant governor has mostly been defined by the people holding the office and the governors they’ve served. The primary responsibility in state law has been to succeed governors who leave office before their term is up. 
That prospect, although rare, makes the job potentially consequential.
That’s happened twice in the last 50 years. Democrat Martin Schreiber succeeded Gov. Pat Lucey in 1977 after Lucey was named ambassador to Mexico. Republican Scott McCallum succeeded Gov. Tommy Thompson in 2001 after Thompson was appointed U.S. Secretary of Health and Human Services.
Both lost when they ran for election to a full term as governor — Schreiber in 1978, McCallum in 2002.


On education, Varnam promotes school choice and declares that schools must “raise standards, test scores and expectations for our students.” He also supports the rights of gun owners, his website states.
Varnam served from 2012 to 2016 on the city council of Lancaster, Wisconsin, in Grant County, and as mayor from 2016 to 2022. He previously worked as a legislative analyst for Focus on the Family, a national conservative evangelical Christian organization that has opposed abortion rights and condemned civil rights measures covering LGBTQ+ people.
At the top of his issues list, Varnam calls for cutting taxes and highlights his veto of a 40% stormwater fee increase in Lancaster during his mayoral term. He also advocates “right-to-farm” laws that block nuisance lawsuits directed at farms and calls for improved rural broadband and rural road upkeep.
On immigration Varnam advocates working “with President Trump” and ensuring the cooperation of state and local law enforcement with federal agencies to carry out deportations of “criminal illegal aliens.”
Varnam says he supports more law enforcement funding and backs the use of “qualified immunity,” which puts a higher barrier to suing law enforcement officers for their actions. Critics contend the legal doctrine too easily shields police from accountability for violating people’s civil rights.
At an appearance with Tiffany in New Glarus this week, Varnam didn’t dwell on the campaign’s policy positions but instead leaned into a get-out-the-vote message.
He recounted the story of one voter he met last week who told him, “I usually vote Democratic,” but decided to vote for Tiffany and Varnam because they’re both “from rural areas.”
Varnam said he wants to see Christians “vote their values” — identifying them along with hunters and residents of western Wisconsin as “three major groups that don’t vote in a midterm election.”
“We need Christians to be the ones to deliver the victory on November 3,” Varnam said.
Democrat Sarah Godlewski: Political veteran
Democratic candidate for lieutenant governor Sarah Godlewski, with her son, announcing her campaign for lieutenant governor in August 2025. (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)
Sarah Godlewski, who is currently the Wisconsin secretary of state, was unchallenged in the August Democratic primary for lieutenant governor.
Elected state treasurer in 2018, Godlewski was one of several Democrats who sought the nomination to run for U.S. Senate in 2022, withdrawing before the primary that year.
In early 2023, Gov. Tony Evers appointed her secretary of state to replace Doug La Follette, who abruptly resigned just months after he had won his 12th consecutive four-year term.
After Evers announced in mid-2025 that he would not seek a third term, Godlewski decided to forgo running for a second term as secretary of state and chose to run for lieutenant governor instead.
“I wanted to be part of the team that was going to help get things done and stop this two-tier system that the Republicans have been working to create,” Godlewski said in an interview, “which is a system that works for billionaires and the wealthy 1%, and then a system that everybody else can barely survive in.”
Her nomination was a foregone conclusion. But the contest for top of the ticket was the opposite. After more than a half-dozen other Democrats entered the race and four dropped out — including Crowley briefly — the nomination battle culminated with Crowley’s primary victory by fewer than 4,000 votes.
Since then, Godlewski said, she and Crowley have been campaigning together and talking about what they want their work together to look like if they win.
They did a unity tour immediately after the primary that made 20 stops and covered 1,700 miles. In the week leading up to Tuesday’s election, they’re touring the state again, with twice as many stops and covering about 3,000 miles.
“What we are really hoping that Wisconsinites see is that this partnership — that collectively we are going to get things done here for Wisconsin, which I think is really important because when you look at the challenges that our state is facing,” Godlewski said.
“David understands that these challenges are — in order to tackle them and to truly deliver, you need a team, and I’ve made it very clear that I’m going to be a key partner,” she said.
The challenges Godlewski identifies include healthcare coverage, the cost of childcare and addressing public school funding.
On the statewide tour they’re reinforcing the Democrats’ core 2026 election message: that policies from Republicans in the state Capitol as well in Washington under the leadership of President Donald Trump are directly responsible. And they’re tying that same message to the Republican nominee Tiffany, a third-term member of Congress.
At the state level, Republicans “refused to pass legislation that would have funded our public schools,” Godlewski said. In Washington, Trump’s signature 2025 bill — the One Big Beautiful Bill Act — made cuts to food assistance and to Medicaid that will affect hundreds of thousands of Wisconsin residents, she added — “and Tom Tiffany supported that.”
Trump administration policies have also cut off clean energy investments in Wisconsin, which “took away thousands of good-paying union jobs,” Godlewski said.
While it’s been four years since the U.S. Supreme Court overturned a national right to abortion, Godlewski said Varnam’s opposition to abortion and LGBTQ rights have escalated the stakes in the election. “I do think this is still a salient issue,” she said of reproductive rights.
Crowley and Godlewski have proposed advocating with lawmakers to pass an amendment enshrining reproductive rights in the state constitution.
The bus tour is putting them in front of hundreds of voters across the state, but Godlewski believes that their message is reaching well beyond the ones that see them in person.
“Tom Tiffany and Donald Trump, their policies are hurting places where oftentimes maybe Democrats haven’t won before, which is why this tour is focused on going everywhere and delivering everywhere,” Godlewski said. “I am having people in these communities seek me out to tell me that they are registered Republicans and they are voting for David and I.”
 Godlewski compared the effort to her successful run for state treasurer in 2018 “as a political nobody from the Chippewa Valley” who got more votes than the other winning Democrats, Evers and Josh Kaul, who got elected attorney general.
“I believe part of the reason I was able to do that was because I showed up everywhere,” she said. “And David has that exact exact same philosophy that we need to go everywhere. We need to show up, meet voters where they are and listen.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: New report shows there were 2,529 oil and gas incidents in Ohio in a decade
text:
Anti-fracking advocates hung up signs before an Oil and Gas Land Management Commission meeting. (Photo by Megan Henry/Ohio Capital Journal)There were more than 2,500 oil and gas incidents reported in Ohio from 2015 through 2025, according to a new report. 
The number of incidents are generally increasing, going from 103 in 2015 to 268 in 2025, according to a new report published last week by FracTracker Alliance in partnership with Buckeye Environmental Network. 
FracTracker Alliance analyzed ODNR records from 2015 to 2025 for the report. 
“That’s much more (total incidents) than I would expect,” said Gwen Klenke, the report’s author. There were 2,529 incidents recorded in Ohio from 2015 to 2025.

“Obviously everyone’s human. Everyone makes mistakes, so there’s always going to be some amount of things going wrong, but 2,500 is a pretty massive number for 10 years. … It just feels like it’s more than it should be.”
The Ohio Department of Natural Resources did not respond to the Ohio Capital Journal’s questions by deadline.
The Ohio Oil and Gas Association said the report was not “an objective assessment of Ohio’s energy industry.”
“FracTracker’s conclusions should be viewed for what they are: advocacy, not a comprehensive assessment of the safety, environmental performance and regulatory oversight of Ohio’s oil and natural gas operations,” Ohio Oil and Gas Association Director of External Affairs Mike Chadsey said in an email.
“Ohio’s energy producers remain focused on responsible development, protecting our communities and delivering the reliable energy that powers our state.”
Bev Reed with Buckeye Environmental Network said the findings from this new report are alarming. 
“It’s incredibly important that ODNR and the legislature get their act together,” she said in an email.
“We also received documents showing that an injection well company in Washington County requested that ODNR not suspend its injection well near Marietta, despite the fact that the state had grounds to immediately suspend the well.”
The yearly total of oil and gas incidents in Ohio according to a report published from FracTracker Alliance in partnership with Buckeye Environmental Network. (Screenshot)
The report showed incident classifications are often unclear. 
“There’s this really pervasive lack of good data throughout the whole data set, which is concerning considering its incidents and spills, things that we would want good details about, and related to that was the characterization of the incidents,” said Klenke, FracTracker’s Midwest Program Coordinator. 
A 2016 incident in Columbiana County was categorized as a “minor” incident, but was described as “static electricity from overhead power lines caused a conventional well’s tank to explode,” according to the report. 
Another incident categorized as “minor” in Gallia County involved an unknown quantity of oil and gas wastewater was released from a well while it was being plugged. ODNR’s records reveal the well had been “flowing overnight with no well control in place.” 
“I pointed out major explosions being categorized as minor incidents, and that just doesn’t seem good for public understanding of these types of events,” Klenke said. 
ODNR has about 25 inspectors who are responsible for Ohio’s 96,000 wells, according to the report. This means one inspector is responsible for 1,500 wells in Harrison County while another inspector is responsible for about 24,000 wells in 26 counties, according to the report. 
“Really any increase, I think I’d be happy with,” Klenke said when asked how many inspectors she wishes ODNR had. 
“If they got 26 inspectors in Ohio, I’d be celebrating.”


More than 1,200 of the incidents were categorized as release/discharge. There 615 gas releases, 108 fires, 94 explosions or fires, and six injuries, according to the report. 
Of Ohio’s 88 counties, there were incidents in 73. Most of the incidents are in the eastern part of Ohio. 
Stark County had the most incidents with 133, followed by Noble County with 129, and Trumbull and Guernsey counties both had 114, according to the report. 
“Residents in those counties should be especially vigilant when they are doing things like going on hikes or walking more rural lanes,” Klenke said.  
“I would hope that residents in those counties would just really keep their eyes peeled for anything that doesn’t seem right. If they see something, they should definitely call emergency services to get them out there to at least check things out.”
Klenke said she hopes to see more oversight and accountability with Ohio’s oil and gas wells.
“It can happen with more inspectors,” she said. 
“It can also happen with just better tracking of the incidents, better follow through, just generally with well owners who may be concerned that something’s wrong with their well.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Domestic violence noted as ‘most prevalent violent crime in Ohio’ as state boosts funding
text:
A domestic violence awareness ribbon. (Stock photo from Getty Images.)With data showing domestic violence as the “most prevalent violent crime in Ohio,” state officials recently announced boosts to domestic violence programs, including survivor services and law enforcement training.
The Ohio Department of Public Safety’s Office of Criminal Justice Services found that more than half of all violent crime arrests in Ohio had a domestic violence charge as part of the case, with 70% of the arrests conducted on repeat offenders.
The researchers studied half a century of criminal history data in the state, including about 2 million violent crime arrests from 1974 to 2023, according to a release about the research.
The study also found that from 2014 to 2023, 54% of violent crime arrests involved domestic violence. That statistic went up to 56% in the last five years.
“Anecdotally, we suspected that domestic violence was among the most frequent violent crimes in the state, and this data confirms it,” Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine said in a statement.
“The data also reinforces the fact that Ohio must continue to be innovative in its work to protect both domestic violence survivors and the law enforcement officers who respond to calls for help.”
Ohio had its second highest amount of deaths from domestic violence-related incidents in 2025, according to data released this month from the Ohio Domestic Violence Network. The report showed 134 deaths in 101 cases.
The year before was the highest amount of deaths since the network began collecting fatality statistics 11 years ago. In 2024, Ohio had 157 deaths in 108 cases. Over the last two years of data, the network found that in 49% of cases, the victim was attempting to leave the situation.
“These homicides are not random,” said Maria York, the network’s director of policy and communications, when the report was announced. “They are the final act of control.”
As part of a recent announcement of funding set aside for “specific domestic-violence-related projects,” the governor’s office said an additional $1 million will be directed toward the state’s domestic violence shelters recognized by the Office of Criminal Justice Services.
The 55 shelters across the state will each receive a one-time grant of $18,000 for “immediate shelter and meeting the critical needs of family violence victims and their dependents,” according to the governor’s office.
The Office of Criminal Justice Services announced another $4 million in “federal emergency shelter and supportive services grants for domestic violence victims and their dependents,” in an Oct. 27 press release.
The funding is from the Family Violence Prevention and Services Act Formula Grant to States and Territories, administered through the U.S. Department of Health & Human Services.
The state office said 64 projects in 46 counties will be funded for one year, from July 2026 through June 2027.
The grant amounts ranged from $115,000 going to Stark County’s Domestic Violence Project, Inc., to $30,000 awards for Greene County’s Violence Free Futures, Geauga County’s Womensafe, and Summit County’s Asian Services in Action, Inc.
Law enforcement will also be receiving state funding meant for programs related to domestic violence, like one to provide training on “lethality assessments,” which are used to decide how much a survivor risks future domestic violence based on the situation to which law enforcement are responding.
The funding announced by the governor’s office is also set to help establish “co-responder partnership models.”
Those models would partner victim services advocates with law enforcement “to help ensure that trauma-informed support is immediately available on-scene for survivors after law enforcement responds to a domestic violence incident,” according to the governor’s office.
A separate grant is also set aside to fund “ballistic shields,” which would be used by law enforcement when responding to “high-risk calls like domestic violence incidents.”
In addition, DeWine tasked the Ohio Collaborative Community-Police Advisory Board to develop standards for responses to domestic violence, and investigations of it, using the Ohio Domestic Violence Network’s handbook for law enforcement working with domestic violence survivors.
The network praised the new grant funding and the work to set law enforcement standards.
“We are especially pleased to work with the Ohio Collaborative to provide law enforcement with more guidance about responding to domestic violence calls, which can be the most dangerous calls police get,” said ODVN’s senior director for survivor services, Alicia Williamson, in a statement.
The network worked with the Office of Criminal Justice Services on a training initiative to offer seven regional, in-person trainings, and seven virtual trainings for law enforcement in Ohio.
According to a press release from ODVN, topics in the trainings will include trauma-informed investigations, lethality assessments, strangulation and brain injuries, protection order enforcement, and victims’ rights.
The first of the trainings is scheduled for Nov. 18 in Columbus.
