name: Michigan Advance
title: Clerks must temporarily retain electronic pollbook after Nov. 3 election, Court of Claims rules
text:
A Voter Assist Terminal in the Lansing Elections Office is tested prior to the August primary. July 20, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. A Court of Claims ruling Tuesday granted a temporary restraining order instructing local clerks across Michigan to maintain the electronic pollbooks created in the Nov. 3 General Election until an underlying lawsuit brought by Bridgewater Township Clerk Michelle McQueer and the Michigan Republican Party can be resolved. 
The electronic pollbook, or EPB, is “used for processing voters, generating precinct reports, and recording voter history at in-person polling places,” according to a manual for election officials published in 2024 by the Michigan Department of State. 
Under current Michigan election rules, “electronic pollbook software and associated files must be deleted from all devices by the seventh day following the final canvass and certification of the election,” unless there is a pending recount or audit. 
McQueer’s lawsuit centers on that rule and what she sees as its potential conflict with federal law, which states that election officers for any federal election must retain “all records and papers which come into his possession relating to any application, registration, payment of poll tax, or other act requisite to voting in such election” for 22 months after any general, special or primary election. 
In late August, the Court of Claims issued a temporary restraining order directing McQueer to retain her electronic pollbook from Michigan’s August primary election and prevented the Michigan Department of State — the defendant in the lawsuit — from imposing penalties against her from doing so.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
On Oct. 5, a motion from the Michigan Republican Party and Republican National Convention to intervene in the suit was granted but a request for another temporary restraining order, this time requiring local election officials to retain their electronic pollbooks, was denied. 
Tuesday’s order, however, granted that statewide restraining order, citing that “The Court does not anticipate the full resolution of this matter before the General Election.”
“Defendants are directed to instruct all local election officials to retain the EPBs from the November 3 General Election,” the court order states. “The instructions must direct those officials to transfer the EPB from the precinct laptops onto the encrypted flash drives and then to securely store those flash drives until further order of this Court.”
Deputy Secretary of State Aghogho Edevbie explained at an August town hall in Ann Arbor how Michigan’s current policies align with federal law — through the use of a physical poll book that is retained for 22 months.
 “Those flash drives and the information on those flash drives are backed up by paper, by the poll book,” he said. “For 22 months, every step is memorized in some paper form. There is no step in the process that you cannot recreate in 22 months under federal law.”
Republicans called the court order a victory over Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, who is also the Democratic nominee for governor. However, the actual decision out of the Court of Claims on the legality of Michigan’s standing policy is still forthcoming, and that decision could be appealed.
“The Court of Claims did not rule on the merits or determine that the Bureau of Elections’ guidance conflicts with state or federal law. We are reviewing the ruling to determine our next steps,” Michigan Department of State Press Secretary Samantha May said in an emailed statement.
Macomb County Clerk Anthony Forlini, the Republican nominee for Secretary of State in the 2026 election, said in a news release following the ruling that Benson “has been consistent in her lack of transparency and avoidance of proper election law.”
“This one ruling will help restore confidence or expose what the Michigan Secretary of State office has been trying to hide,” Forlini wrote. “This order is temporary, and the underlying case remains unresolved. My position is straightforward: follow the court’s order, preserve the required records, protect sensitive information, and give our clerks the guidance they need to do their jobs properly.”

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Streamer Hasan Piker files $72.5 million defamation case against Kentuckian Scott Jennings
text:
GOP pundit Scott Jennings spoke live on CNN from the Fancy Farm political picnic on Aug. 5, 2023. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Austin Anthony)Progressive Twitch streamer Hasan Piker has filed a defamation lawsuit against Kentuckian and conservative political commentator Scott Jennings seeking $72.5 million in damages. 
In a complaint filed in federal court in Washington, D.C. Tuesday, attorneys for Piker argued Jennings “falsely told a nationwide podcast audience that Hasan Piker was ‘out there calling for Black voters to be lynched.’” The claims stem from an edited video Jennings shared on his show and on social media in August.
“All of Mr. Jennings’ accusations are false,” Piker’s complaint said. “Mr. Piker has never advocated the lynching of Black Americans, or anyone else. He has never called for a return to lynchings. And he has never proposed anything remotely resembling the supposed plan that Mr. Jennings falsely attributed to him.” 
Jennings didn’t immediately return a texted request for comment on Wednesday from the Kentucky Lantern. 
A Snopes review from August found that Piker was sarcastically mimicking others’ opinions and the clips were from hours-long streams and heavily edited without full context. 
In response to one of the clips Jennings’ shared, Piker said on X at the time: “ive never seen a more clear cut instance of defamation than this in my entire life. blatant disregard for the truth.”
Jennings, who now frequently appears on CNN to discuss Republican politics, is a former staffer of Kentucky U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell and a founding partner of RunSwitch PR, one of Kentucky’s largest public relations firms.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma tribal leadership fight puts Kalshi’s prediction markets at center of dispute
text:
The Alabama-Quassarte Tribal Town's flag flies Oct. 27, 2026 at the Indian Flag Plaza outside the state Capitol in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — A potentially high-paying deal between a major prediction market operator and a small, Oklahoma-based tribe may be in jeopardy amid a yearslong internal fight over who is the legitimate tribal chief.
The dispute over who is the Alabama-Quassarte Tribal Town chief has thrown the validity of an agreement with Kalshi – one of the nation’s best-known operators of prediction gaming markets – into question and raised the possibility of litigation over whether it is legal.

In October, the Alabama-Quassarte Tribal Town became one of the first Native American tribes in the country to enter into a highly touted agreement with Kalshi. 
The deal entered into by Wilson Yargee, who claims he is the tribe’s chief, allows the tribe to create PokkeTrades, an app that lets users tap into Kalshi’s prediction markets. Supporters say it will help the nearly 400-member tribe to profit from the fast-growing prediction market sector, which allows people to wager on pretty much anything from the outcome of sporting events to political races to the weather.
Election results were not publicly available, but Yargee’s administration provided a letter dated April 30, 2025, and addressed to the federal Bureau of Indian Affairs that claims he was elected. 
But Samuel Marshall Jr., who also claims he is chief of the Alabama-Quassarte Tribal Town, said Yargee did not have the authority to enter into the agreement. Marshall said Yargee was removed from office months after his election in 2021 and has been falsely presenting himself as chief since then, something his administration has also said in court records. 
Marshall said he was appointed by the tribe’s governing committee a month after Yargee’s removal. Marshall said he won election as chief in 2025. 
Prediction markets ‘undermine’ Oklahoma tribal gaming compacts, association says

“My main focus, still to this day, is to serve and provide our members what they need,” Marshall said. “With all this stuff going on, they’re not getting that help. So as far as that, you know, I’m just trying to keep my focus on our people and let our lawyers handle everything.” 
Marshall and his administration said they’ve never seen a contract or agreement with Kalshi. They said they first learned of the agreement after it was made public. They plan to file a suit to stop the agreement. They also do not know what will be done with the revenue PokkeTrades is supposed to generate for the tribe’s benefit.
Yargee, though, contends that his removal was not legitimate and that he was within his rights to forge an agreement with Kalshi. He also said he was reelected in 2025. 
While the Kalshi contract hasn’t yet resulted in revenue for the town, Yargee said, any money earned have to go through the tribe’s economic development authority. 
“So now we’re here, and we did our business with Kalshi and we made a deal with them,” Yargee said. “And it was a great, lucrative deal, too, for our little tribe at this time.”
Caught in the middle of this dispute, Kalshi said it stands by its agreement with Yargee and his administration. 
Jacki McGavick, a Kalshi spokesperson, said in a statement that there is a signed agreement in place that was approved by the tribal council of the Alabama-Quassarte Tribal Town, headquartered in Wetumka, about 90 miles southwest of Oklahoma City. 
Neither Kalshi nor Yargee’s administration were willing to provide a copy of their agreement to Oklahoma Voice. 
Litigation, federal agencies don’t clarify chief question
Court records show the dispute over who is the rightful chief has been going on for years. There have been at least three lawsuits concerning the town’s leadership. 
A case between the two factions in the Muscogee (Creek) Nation District Court was dismissed in 2022 because of a lack of jurisdiction. Only Marshall’s administration, not Yargee’s, had waived their right to sovereign immunity to allow the court to hear the case, according to court records. 
The Alabama Quassarte Tribal Town’s enrolled members hold dual citizenship at the Muscogee (Creek) Nation. The tribe was one of several, called tribal towns, that were part of what was previously known as the Muscogee Nation Confederacy. 
In the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Oklahoma, Judge Ronald White ruled in 2023 that the federal court also had no jurisdiction over the tribal dispute and dismissed the Marshall group’s lawsuit against Yargee and his administration. 
In a case filed to determine which faction should have access to the tribal town’s bank accounts, a judge in Okmulgee County in December ruled that Yargee’s administration was not the rightful custodian of the disputed bank account. Judge Pandee Ramirez wrote that the court was not deciding who the legitimate chief was. That was the role of the town’s solicitor, Ramirez wrote in the final order. 
Robert Gifford is pictured Oct. 22, 2026 at the Oklahoma County Courthouse. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)
Robert Gifford, an Oklahoma attorney who specializes in Native American law and has served as a tribal court judge, said leadership disputes like this are more common in small tribal towns. 
He said changes in power in smaller tribal governments often result in total turnover of tribal employees, which creates struggles with historical knowledge and continuity within the governments.
“Most of the tribes are pretty intimate within itself,” he said. “Everybody knows everybody. Everybody’s related to everybody.”
Gifford said while each tribal government is different, usually an agreement like the one with Kalshi would need to be approved by the tribe’s legislative body.  
“The only way that it can be resolved, unless it’s resolved at the lowest level or someone just gives up, is you have to litigate it,” Gifford said. 
Litigation must start in tribal courts, he said. 
The Bureau of Indian Affairs, or BIA, prefers to see disputes like this resolved internally, Gifford said. 
“The BIA will not and does not want to get involved with tribal politics,” he said. “So BIA overall does not try to get in and decide who the elected leader is, and they are very resistant to it and they rarely want to voice an opinion on it.”

Gifford said the same goes for the Muscogee (Creek) Nation which usually does not want to “be the one that decides these internal fights.”
The Bureau of Indian Affairs lists both Yargee and Marshall as chief in their tribal leaders directory with the caveat that the town’s leadership is subject to dispute.
A spokesperson for the federal agency said the Department of the Interior, which houses the Bureau of Indian Affairs, honors tribal sovereignty and supports tribal self-determination, which limits its legal authority to intervene in disputes like this one. 
Kalshi deal exposes tension with state gaming compacts
The Oklahoma Indian Gaming Association also got involved, backing Marshall’s position against the prediction markets. 
The association, a nonprofit that represents Oklahoma tribes that operate gambling enterprises, had previously said that prediction markets infringed on the tribes’ exclusive gaming rights. Matthew Morgan, who chairs the group, did not return messages seeking comment for this story.
A Kalshi prediction market is pictured that allowed people to wager on what Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt would mention during his 2026 State of the State speech. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)
The association includes 25 member tribes. Tribal gambling generates more than $7 billion annually, a portion of which is paid to the state for the exclusive right to offer casino-style gambling through approved compacts. 
But Michael Stopp, who said he worked on the Kalshi agreement with Yargee, said the Bureau of Indian Affairs did involve itself in the dispute. Stopp is a citizen of the Cherokee Nation who serves as Yargee’s vice president of economic development. 
Stopp said the Bureau of Indian Affairs involved itself by acknowledging a leadership dispute when he said the actions of Marshall’s group were not legitimate under tribal law. 
He said PokkeTrades, which is being developed by a business under the tribal town’s jurisdiction, will essentially connect people to the Kalshi platform. This allows smaller tribes like Alabama-Quassarte to access a new revenue stream, Stopp said. 
The decision of what this revenue will fund is up to the town’s leadership, like Yargee and the governing committee, and will be made later, he said. 
“What the prediction markets do, because of the internet, allows smaller tribes who don’t have access to gaming markets access to the global market through prediction markets,” he said. “And quite frankly, it is not gaming, it is a financial service.”
Prediction markets are currently regulated by the federal Commodity Futures Trading Commission, but many states and the gambling industry dispute that authority. Many industry leaders do not consider prediction markets gambling. 
Stopp said while he recognizes why the Oklahoma Indian Gaming Association has concerns about prediction markets, tribes like the Alabama-Quassarte still have a voice. 
“What is wrong with them continuing to explore other economic opportunities like prediction markets?” he said.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: FCC set to vote on cellphone jamming in prisons after yearslong push from SC
text:
Around 1,500 cellphones sit on a table outside Broad River Correctional Institution in Columbia on Tuesday, Oct. 22, 2024. (Skylar Laird/SC Daily Gazette)A decision allowing state prisons to jam cellphone signals is potentially weeks away, federal officials announced Wednesday in Little Rock, Arkansas.
The Federal Communications Commission is scheduled to vote Nov. 19 on the change, which would establish cellphones inside prisons as unauthorized and allow local officials to get permission to block their signals.
The proposal comes after more than a decade of advocacy from South Carolina’s top prison officials, whose quest for more tools to make contraband phones useless included multiple trips to the nation’s capital to testify.
FCC votes to move forward with cellphone jamming, a longtime priority for SC prisons

Federal prisons can use jamming technology, but a policy prohibiting the interference with authorized cell signals bars state prisons and local jails from doing the same. Inmates in state-level prisons who get their hands on cellphones can — and often do — use them to orchestrate crimes with people outside of prison, officials have said.
“This has been a huge issue, the issue of prisoners holding communications technology in prison and using it, using this technology, these cellphones, to commit more and more crimes,” Arkansas Attorney General Tim Griffin said in a news conference livestreamed from his office. “Not just crimes, but violent crimes.”
In South Carolina, inmates have used contraband cellphones to run extortion schemes, operate major drug rings, and order hits on people outside of prison, including corrections officers responsible for confiscating illicit items from inmates.
The policy change has been in the works for more than a year. In September 2025, the three-member FCC opened the potential change up to public comment. The vote next month will determine whether that proposal is finalized.
If approved, state prison officials will be able to apply to the FCC for permission to use jamming technology, said Brendan Carr, head of the commission.
Joel Anderson, who leads South Carolina’s prison system, has already said he plans to seek permission to install jamming devices in the state’s 21 prisons. He was among officials at the announcement in Arkansas’ capital.
SC officials hopeful FCC will allow cellphone blocking in prison: ‘Jamming is the answer’

The technology is extremely precise, allowing prisons to block only signals coming from within certain buildings without interfering with nearby communications, Carr said.
“This isn’t going to be a silver bullet at the end of the day, but it’s a tool that’s been denied law enforcement and correction officials for too long,” he said.
South Carolina’s Department of Corrections is ready to act as soon as that permission is granted.
Legislators spent $18.5 million over two years on technology that tracks cell signals within prisons, which South Carolina was the first in the nation to adopt.
But that’s a tedious process that involves reporting the numbers of individual phones to carriers to turn off those specific phones.
That same technology can block cellphone signals completely, former corrections director Bryan Stirling said previously.
All the state needs is the federal commission’s OK.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana parole board urges governor to reject death row inmate’s bid to avoid execution
text:
The five-member Indiana Parole Board listens to public testimony during death row inmate Jeffrey Weisheit's clemency proceedings on Oct. 19, 2026, in Indianapolis.  (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)The Indiana Parole Board on Wednesday recommended that Gov. Mike Braun deny clemency to death row inmate Jeffrey Weisheit following competing appeals from the parents of the two children he killed in a 2010 house fire.
The unanimous recommendation came just eight days ahead of Weisheit’s scheduled Nov. 5 execution and followed hours of testimony about his mental health, claims of remorse and ability to safely serve a life sentence.
In a letter to Braun signed by board Chair Gwendolyn M. Horth, the panel rejected assertions that Weisheit simply “snapped,” pointing to preparations before the killings that included emptying bank accounts, quitting his job and attempting to return Lisa Lynch’s engagement ring.
“Whether or not this particular violent act is what he was preparing for in the weeks leading up to the fire, we cannot know,” the board wrote. “However, we do believe the evidence shows that there was a plan to do harm in place and we cannot accept the assertions made by those close to Weisheit that he simply ‘snapped’ and was completely outside of his own character.”
The board said it considered testimony and evidence about Weisheit’s mental illness and neurological deficiencies but concluded that the jury had sufficient information to impose the death penalty.
Story continues below.
Weisheit-Recommendation
 
The board’s recommendation is nonbinding, leaving the governor to decide whether to commute Weisheit’s sentence.
Weisheit was sentenced to death in 2013 for murdering 8-year-old Alyssa Lynch and her 5-year-old brother, Caleb, in a fire near Evansville while their mother, Lisa Lynch, worked an overnight shift. His execution is scheduled before sunrise Nov. 5 at Indiana State Prison in Michigan City.
The five-member board interviewed Weisheit at the prison Oct. 16 and heard public testimony Oct. 19 in Indianapolis. His attorneys and relatives sought a sentence of life without parole, citing mental illness, head injuries and his religious conversion. Prosecutors and investigators argued that the death sentence should stand.
During his prison interview, Weisheit acknowledged setting the fire but repeatedly struggled to explain why anger toward Lisa Lynch led him to kill her children.
“There is no excuse or explanation for what I did,” Weisheit said.
Board members pressed him to explain inconsistencies in his account of the killings and how he would manage anger and conflict outside death row. They also asked why he had not sought mental health treatment while incarcerated.
Weisheit described placing a phone book on an electric stove burner and leaving the children inside the house. He acknowledged binding and gagging Caleb but denied placing road flares near the boy. He speculated, without evidence, that police or emergency responders could have put them there. His attorneys later said they did not endorse that explanation.
Jeffrey Weisheit answers questions during his Oct. 16, 2026, clemency hearing at Indiana State Prison in Michigan City. Board members questioned him about the murders of Alyssa and Caleb Lynch and whether he could safely serve a life sentence. (Screenshot from livestream)
Weisheit told the board he wanted to continue helping other prisoners.
“I want to live now,” he said.
The parole board’s letter cited 13 prison conduct reports, including battery on incarcerated individuals, disruptive behavior and animal cruelty. His most recent conduct report was in May 2025, the panel said.
But the board also acknowledged his participation in spiritual services and his spiritual adviser’s account that he had been making progress toward becoming a more positive member of the prison community.
The children’s parents differed on whether Weisheit should be put to death.
In a sworn statement supporting clemency, Steven Lynch asked that Weisheit receive life without parole and said an execution would subject another family to the loss he had experienced.
“What good does it do the memory of my children to put this man to death?” he wrote.
He closed with a message to Weisheit: “Jeffrey, I forgive you.”
Lisa Lynch, who spoke remotely at the public hearing, urged state officials to uphold Weisheit’s death sentence. She described surviving domestic violence and emotional abuse and said efforts to blame her for his actions had continued into the clemency proceedings.
Lynch recalled Alyssa’s love of drawing and Caleb’s affection for helping her in the kitchen, saying their deaths robbed them of futures and her of watching them grow up.
“They will always be my children,” she said. “They will always matter, and I will never stop speaking for them.”
‘Every single day without them is a struggle’: Mother urges Indiana to uphold death sentence

The board’s recommendation also follows an unsuccessful effort by Weisheit’s attorneys to delay his execution for additional brain testing.
The Indiana Supreme Court unanimously denied that request Oct. 22. His lawyers had sought to move the execution to Nov. 19 so experts could assess injuries they contend affected his behavior before the murders.
The justices said the executive branch could arrange transportation for testing without a court order if the board or governor considered the evidence relevant.
Still, the parole board said the evidence of Weisheit’s mental illness and neurological impairments did not justify clemency.
“The information we were presented with does not greatly distinguish his situation from a vast majority of incarcerated individuals,” the board wrote. “We must consider whether the fact finders in this case were given sufficient information to come to the decision they reached, to impose the death penalty, and we believe they did have sufficient information.”
Braun denied clemency to Benjamin Ritchie and Roy Lee Ward before their executions last year. If carried out, Weisheit’s execution would be Indiana’s fourth since the state resumed executions in December 2024 after a 15-year pause.
This story will be updated.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama sells $190 million worth of bonds to Regions division to finance Escambia prison
text:
A prison cell in Holman Correctional Facility in Atmore, Alabama, as seen on Oct. 22, 2019. The state of Alabama sold $190 million of bonds to a division of Regions Bank this month to finance the construction of a 4,000-bed men's prison in Escambia County. (File)Alabama sold more than $190 million worth of bonds earlier this month to Regions Capital Advantage, a division of Regions Bank, to finance the construction of a new men’s prison in Escambia County.
A document of the bond sale on the Electronic Municipal Market Access indicated the bonds were issued by the Alabama Corrections Institution Finance Authority in August and were sold in a private transaction on Oct. 6. The identity of the buyer was initially redacted from the documents. The Alabama Department of Finance identified Regions as the buyer in a statement Wednesday.
“To align the additional indebtedness with the optional redemption date of its Series 2022 A Bonds, the Authority elected to pursue a direct loan through an invitation for bids,” the statement said. “This approach was intended to secure more favorable rates and lower issuance costs than might otherwise have been achieved through a traditional public bond sale.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
A message seeking comment was left with Regions on Wednesday.
According to the terms, the bonds will mature in 2046 and carry an annual interest rate of 4.86%. Interest payments will be due in January and July beginning next year. Alabama has the option to call the bonds in July 2032.
Sen. Greg Albritton, R-Atmore, the outgoing chair of the Senate Finance and Taxation General Fund Committee, which oversees the Department of Corrections’ budget, said Tuesday he knew the bonds had been sold but not the identity of the lender.
“I think because they got a better deal,” Albritton said. “The amount that was borrowed and things such as that, it seemed to be the appropriate way to move.”
ACIFA in August authorized the state to borrow $200 million to pay for the Escambia County prison.
Alabama prisons have been plagued for decades by overcrowding and violence. State lawmakers in 2021 authorized $1.3 billion to build two 4,000-bed facilities in Elmore and Escambia counties, hoping the facilities would require less staffing, be safer than existing prisons and allow the Department of Corrections to close aging facilities.
But the cost of building the facilities in Elmore and Escambia counties has soared.  The prison in Elmore County, named the Gov. Kay Ivey Correction Complex, has cost $1.25 billion. The company in charge of construction missed a completion deadline earlier this month. The Escambia facility is expected to cost between $700 to $900 million, according to Albritton.
Alabama used a different process to sell the bonds for the Escambia prison than the one in Elmore. The state chose to go through a “direct placement” and sell the bonds to a lender instead of selling them through the traditional public process.
The bonds for Elmore were underwritten by investment banks Frazier Lanier and Stephens, with Wells Fargo and Raymond James also participating in the process. The institutions purchased the bonds and then sold them to their clients who then collected the interest payments.
Albritton said selling bonds through direct placement could allow the sale to move forward “without fanfare and without difficulty.”
“Last time we tried to sell bonds, but it was a matter that it went to a point that we had riots in England, in San Francisco, in Birmingham, because Alabama was trying to sell bonds to build prisons.”
The state in 2022 attempted to sell $725 million in bonds for the Elmore prison, but only raised $509 million in the initial offering. Bill Poole, then the Alabama State Finance Director, blamed a “lack of interest in long-term maturities” in the market.
Activist investors had encouraged investors not to purchase the bonds, citing the ongoing violence in Alabama prisons and questions about the new facilities’ ability to address the crisis, though Poole said at the time the activists’ efforts were not a “significant factor” in the bond sales.
“Going public isn’t always the best thing to do,” Albritton said. “Not only did that affect the public market, but it also affected people even willing to loan. It may have been that the public market would not have made the purchase.”

name: Delaware
title: First State Educate webinar focuses on school board leadership in improving literacy
text:
Image courtesy of First State Educate
Tonight’s Board Matters discussion will examine the Science of Reading, student data and how school boards can turn research into action
WILMINGTON, Del. — Improving Delaware students’ reading skills will require more than changes inside individual classrooms, according to First State Educate, which is putting a spotlight Wednesday night on the role school boards can play in strengthening literacy outcomes.
First State Educate will host its October Board Matters webinar at 6 p.m. Wednesday, Oct. 28, bringing together state and local education leaders for a discussion about literacy, evidence-based reading instruction and the governance decisions that can influence student achievement.
The online event will feature Kathy Kelly, associate secretary of academic excellence at the Delaware Department of Education, and Dr. Amy Trauth, a member of the Christina School District Board of Education.
The discussion comes as Delaware schools continue working to improve reading proficiency and expand the use of instructional approaches grounded in the Science of Reading.
School boards have an important role in that effort because they approve budgets, establish district priorities, monitor academic performance and help determine how resources are directed toward classroom instruction.
From research to boardroom decisions
First State Educate said the webinar will focus on how board members can better understand literacy challenges and use student data and academic research when evaluating district programs and investments.
Topics are expected to include the Science of Reading, evidence-based instructional practices and ways boards can hold school systems accountable for improving student outcomes.
The Science of Reading generally refers to a large body of research examining how children learn to read and which instructional practices are most effective. Delaware has increasingly emphasized evidence-based reading instruction as part of broader efforts to improve literacy performance.
For school boards, that can translate into decisions about curriculum, professional development, staffing, intervention programs and how districts measure whether students are making progress.
Building stronger education governance
The webinar is part of First State Educate’s Board Matters series, which is designed to give Delaware school board members access to information, research and experts that can help them make more informed governance decisions.
The organization has increasingly focused on strengthening school board leadership as one component of improving Delaware’s public education system.
First State Educate also is developing a broader statewide literacy initiative focused on expanding evidence-based reading instruction and helping school leaders translate research into classroom practice.
The organization argues that improving literacy requires cooperation among educators, administrators, school boards, families and community leaders — with governing boards playing an important role in establishing priorities and tracking results.
Wednesday’s discussion is open not only to school board members but also to educators, parents and community members interested in Delaware’s literacy efforts.

Topics: Science of Reading, evidence-based literacy instruction, student performance data and the role of school boards in improving academic outcomes

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Lack of major property tax relief in Kansas prompts fingerpointing in governor’s race
text:
Democrat Cindy Holscher and Republican Ty Masterson appear at the Sept. 12, 2026, debate at the Kansas State Fair. The two rivals for governor agree on the need to reduce property taxes for homeowners but clash on the details. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Kansas Senate President Ty Masterson shared with television viewers Jan. 12, 2021, a vision for how Republicans could deal with runaway property taxes.
In the GOP reply to Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly’s State of the State speech, Masterson promised GOP lawmakers would address the burden of $5.4 billion in property taxes collected statewide at that time. It wasn’t an unimaginable political feat given Masterson’s authority over the GOP supermajority in the Senate and House Speaker Dan Hawkins’ control of the two-thirds Republican majority in the House.
It was a politically astute pledge, because polling consistently affirmed property tax applied to homeowners was the most hated, relative to sales and income taxes.
“We must work to enact meaningful property tax reform to allow seniors and families to stay in their homes,” Masterson vowed.
Senate President Ty Masterson, the 2026 Republican nominee for governor, promises in a 2021 video message to make property tax reform a top legislative priority. (Kansas Reflector screen capture of Kansas Legislature video)
The Legislature spent the next five years nibbling on the edge of reform, but annual statewide revenue from property taxes ballooned to $6.6 billion by 2025. Legislators continued to hear from folks outraged by double-digit escalation of property valuations that triggered tax increases even when mill levies remained flat.
Sen. Cindy Holscher, the Democratic Party’s nominee for governor, said Masterson and Hawkins failed to leverage their Republican supermajorities to grapple with property taxes in the manner they did to slash state income taxes and trim the state’s sales tax on groceries. In the 2026 legislative session, the House and Senate ran into gridlock as they took turns voting down competing GOP property tax bills.
“Ty Masterson has had years as Senate president, with a Republican supermajority behind him, and time and again he has repeatedly failed to deliver the property tax relief Kansans need,” Holscher said. “He said, ‘We can do whatever we want because we’re in charge.’ He either doesn’t want to do this or doesn’t know how.”
Masterson, the Republican gubernatorial nominee, joined the outcry. He said he was disappointed obstinate Democrats and “phony Republicans” stood in the way of efforts to limit the ability of school, city and county officials to pile up property tax revenue.
“The truth of why your taxes are so high … people like Cindy have not met one of your tax dollars she didn’t want to spend two of. You have to put constraints on the local government,” Masterson said. “I want to make your life more affordable and property taxes is a big part of that.”
In 1997, residential property owners in Kansas accounted for 38% of property tax revenue, while commercial property owners picked up 62%. The accumulation of tax exemptions for businesses reversed the math. By 2024, residential owners paid 57% of the property tax bill in Kansas and commercial property owners in the state covered 43%.
 
The track record
The Legislature during the past five years considered dozens of ideas for modifying the property tax landscape, but momentum for reform was tempered by the reality that local government received the majority of its funding from property tax. Cities and counties objected to the Legislature wading into their funding stream.
In 2021, the Legislature approved a “truth in taxation” law preventing cities, counties or townships from raising property tax revenue above the previous year’s inflation-adjusted total without mailing advance notice to taxpayers and conducting public hearings before voting on property tax changes.
State lawmakers in 2022 agreed to provide property tax reimbursements to retail business owners subjected to shutdown orders during the COVID-19 pandemic. Attempts by the Legislature to implement vehicle property tax relief prompted vetoes by Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly. Legislators did raise the residential exemption on property taxes to fund K-12 public schools from $20,000 to $40,000. That saved the average homeowner about $46 per year. Meanwhile, the Legislature approved property tax exemptions for telecommunications equipment.
In 2023, lawmakers debated, but failed to pass, an amendment to the Kansas Constitution to cap growth in property valuations that were the cause of higher tax bills for many homeowners.
In 2024, Kelly signed a measure raising the residential property tax exemption to $75,000 when calculating the 20-mill levy for aid to K-12 public schools. The Legislature’s focus that year was on cutting state income taxes. During a special session, the Legislature and governor agreed to a $1.2 billion, three-year reduction.
The Legislature voted in 2025 to eliminate 1.5 mills of state property tax levies relied on to finance state building construction projects. But that $80 million annual reduction in state property tax collections did nothing to change the reality that local governments continued to depend on property taxes for the vast majority of operating revenue. Kansas did adopt a property tax exemption in 2025 for off-road vehicles, boats and trailers.
In 2026, the House and Senate clashed for months without finding consensus on a sweeping property tax fix.
With Masterson’s blessing, the Senate tried to bulldoze through the legislative process an amendment to the Kansas Constitution limiting increases in annual assessment of property values to 3%. The House declined to endorse that approach. Instead, the House sought to prevent local units of government from increasing revenue from property taxes by more than 3% annually. Amid that debate, proposals calling for phasing out the property tax and replacing that revenue with a higher sales tax floundered.
Kelly vetoed a bill in the 2026 session that would have capped city and county spending increases at 3% or the rate of inflation and would have authorized Kansans to file signature petitions to block local property tax increases above that threshold. The governor dismissed the measure as evidence of the legislative leadership’s “false promise” of meaningful property tax reform.
Instead, she encouraged the Legislature to double to $150,000 the portion of a home’s value not subject to property taxes for schools. She recommended creation of a $60 million state fund to reward cities or counties that held budget increases to less than 3%.
 
Sen. Cindy Holscher says many of the Republicans’ ideas for property tax cuts amount to “gimmicks.” (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector)
Plans for change
Masterson, who has said during the governor’s race that property tax reform was a top priority, offered voters a “Homeowners Bill of Rights” that would guide the Republican if he were elected governor Nov. 3.
The blueprint would be anchored by a constitutional amendment to cap at 3% annual growth in the valuation of taxable property. In the alternative, the amendment would enable the Legislature to impose a limit on property tax rates. Constitutional amendments require consent from two-thirds of the House and Senate before placed on a statewide ballot.
“I have a neighbor. He’s spending more than double the property tax alone than he had been for his entire mortgage, interest, insurance taxes combined,” Masterson said. “At the same time, that’s putting such a load on our young people to afford housing, and homeownership is the underpinning of the middle class of any country. Our first-time average homeowner is now close to 40, and that’s just not acceptable.”
Masterson, who has represented Andover in the Legislature for 20 years, said he wanted local taxing jurisdictions to secure direct voter consent for “unreasonable” budget increases linked to property tax revenue. He would freeze or reduce property taxes for senior citizens and work toward inhibiting Kansans from being “taxed out” of a home, farm or business.
Holscher, an Overland Park resident elected to the Legislature in 2016, said much of the GOP’s strategy for property tax reform amount to “gimmicks” or concepts designed to financially starve local governments responsible for delivering essential public services.
“They squeeze the balloon, they shuffle the responsibility somewhere else, and it makes it harder for our local levels to raise the revenue they need for their critical services,” she said.
Holscher recommended the Legislature provide funding to fully meet its obligation to finance special education programs in K-12 public schools. When the state avoided its responsibility to students, she said, local school boards were forced to dip deeper into property tax revenue to cover program costs.
“Special education hasn’t been fully funded since 2011,” she said. “We’re federally mandated to fund it. When we don’t do that, that burden gets shifted to the local level.”
The Democratic senator said Kansas ought to lower the taxed percentage of home values from 11.5% to 9%, which would deliver property tax relief to homeowners across all income levels. In addition, Holscher recommended restraining the issuance of tax breaks to wealthy business owners. She also support specific property tax exemptions for seniors and disabled veterans.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho to receive another $186 million in federal grant to improve rural health access
text:
Weiser paramedic Ashley Lynn beside an ambulance in this file photo. Idaho awarded federal rural health grants to projects statewide, including some to try and improve rural emergency medical services. (Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun)Idaho is slated to receive another approximately $186 million grant in the second year of the five-year federal Rural Health Transformation Program. 
The state awarded all of its first $186 million to organizations statewide for projects meant to improve access and services for rural and tribal healthcare systems, according to a press release from Idaho Gov. Brad Little. States had an Oct. 30 deadline to distribute the funds or the federal government could claw it back. 
The U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid announced Wednesday that Idaho was awarded the same amount for the second year, which was not guaranteed under the program and was based on performance of the first year. 
Idaho Republican Gov. Brad Little gives his State of the State Address from the House chambers on Jan. 12, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
“For many Idaho families – especially in rural areas – affordable, accessible health care is a real concern,” Little said in the press release. “This investment recognizes those challenges and puts resources where they’re needed most. It helps strengthen local health care and ensures Idahoans can get the affordable care they need, no matter where they live.” 
Idaho officials awarded nearly 115 subgrants to organizations across the state for programs including for healthcare workforce development, chronic disease prevention and cancer screening, infrastructure improvements for rural hospitals, substance use disorder prevention programs, maternal and child health initiatives, and 911 emergency communications improvements.  
The federal money came from the $50 billion that will be allocated nationwide as part of the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” approved by Congress in July 2025.
Here are some of the projects awarded in Idaho: 

The City of Riggins Ambulance received $507,000 to improve emergency medical services in the area. 






The Riggins Ambulance & Salmon River Ambulance District posted on Facebook that its award would go toward a paramedic command vehicle to allow a paramedic to travel to patients before the ambulance arrives, as well as to transport patients with mental health needs to larger facilities without taking an ambulance out of service. It will also go toward new or updated equipment for the district. 
“This is a HUGE win for our small community and will allow us to make some incredible upgrades to our emergency medical services!” The district posted. “Major win.” 






Benewah Community Hospital was awarded over $6.6 million to modernize rural healthcare infrastructure in the region. 






The hospital announced in a press release that it would prioritize the funding for new MRI and digital X-ray capabilities, IT improvements, cybersecurity, facility renovations, laboratory equipment and hemodialysis systems. The money was awarded conditionally, the press release said, and final projects and allocations are subject to state review and approval. 
“This conditional selection is a meaningful step toward bringing modern diagnostic equipment and stronger infrastructure to the rural patients we serve,” Hospital Chief Executive Officer Burt Keltner said in the release.






Idaho Educational Services for the Deaf and the Blind received $897,788 for a statewide pediatric mobile hearing clinic. 






The mobile audiology clinic will be designed to bring specialized hearing testing for infants and young children in rural and frontier communities, according to the governor’s press release.   






St. Mary’s in Cottonwood was awarded more than $4.8 million for infrastructure improvements. 






The money is expected to go toward multiple projects in northern Idaho, according to the governor’s press release, including the purchase of an MRI and replacement of aging X-ray equipment. 






Shine Dental Co. received $1.54 million for a mobile dental clinic in North Idaho. 






The mobile clinic will serve Kootenai, Bonner and Benewah counties. 






Mountain View Hospital was awarded $2.26 million for a mobile clinic to serve eastern Idaho. 






The Idaho Falls-based hospital plans to serve Jefferson, Bingham, Fremont, Clark and Madison counties. The mobile clinic would offer preventative care, immunizations, health screenings, pediatric care, preventive care, immunizations, health screenings, pediatric care, chronic disease management, behavioral health services, mammograms, diagnostic imaging, and laboratory services. 






St. Luke’s Health System received $1.59 million for a mobile screening program. 




The healthcare system would offer mobile CT screening in Twin Falls and Canyon counties as its initial service area. The mobile unit would provide low-dose lung cancer screening, coronary artery calcium screening, smoking cessation services, and cardiovascular risk assessment.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Children’s Mercy insurance loss calls attention to struggling Kansas hospital system
text:
Children's Mercy's logo and locations are found throughout the Kansas City area, including greeting people arriving at the Kansas City International Airport. The hospital made news recently when it announced that it wouldn't accept any Affordable Care Act plans beginning in January after the one company it contracted with pulled their plans from two Kansas counties and six Missouri counties. A Kansas expert says many factors play into why this situation occurs. (Photo by Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — When Children’s Mercy announced patients won’t be covered by Affordable Care Act insurance beginning Jan. 1, stressed parents vented online and some politicians blamed the refusal to expand Medicaid in Kansas.
Children’s Mercy, which has locations in Kansas and Missouri, has just one insurance plan on the ACA marketplace this year, Medica, which covers about 400 current patients, hospital leaders said in a statement. The Medica ACA plan decided to exit the market in Johnson and Wyandotte counties in Kansas, and in Clay, Jackson, Johnson, Lafayette, Platte and Ray counties in Missouri. 
“The other ACA plans servicing the KC Metro were previously out of network with Children’s Mercy and have elected not to contract with Children’s Mercy in 2027,” the hospital statement said.
A Medica spokesman did not answer questions about why the company is exiting the market, saying in a statement only that the company recognizes the impact such a decision has on patients.
Although the Children’s Mercy statement said staff will work with parents to ensure continuity of care, worried parents took to Facebook to point out the problems the change will cause. 
“What makes this situation so alarming is that Children’s Mercy is the only comprehensive pediatric health system in our region — there is simply no backup local hospital equipped for this level of specialized care,” wrote Destiny Zelsnack, a Kansas City, Kansas, parent, on her personal Facebook page. “If a child loses network access, parents aren’t just switching to another clinic down the street; they are being forced to look three to four hours away to cities like St. Louis, Omaha, or Wichita just to find in-network pediatric specialists.”
Sen. Cindy Holscher, the Democratic nominee for governor, said decisions made by Kansas Republicans not to expand Medicaid are a significant factor contributing to situations like that at Children’s Mercy. Her GOP opponent in the governor’s race, Senate President Ty Masterson, has always opposed Medicaid expansion.
Kansas is one of 10 states that hasn’t expanded Medicaid.
“Medicaid expansion would be the single biggest factor to strengthen our healthcare system overall,” Holscher said in an interview. “Expansion would cover approximately 150,000 working Kansans and people working in childcare, construction, retail, agriculture, and some of those are families who rely on the marketplace plans today.”
 
Multiple factors
In Kansas, 58 of its 100 rural hospitals are at risk of closure, with 21 at risk of immediate closure, according to a June report from the Center for Healthcare Quality and Payment Reform. 
“Hospitals in rural areas are six times more likely to shut their doors without Medicaid expansion, and we know when a rural area loses its hospital, not only are they losing access to care, they’re losing good jobs,” Holscher said.
Masterson didn’t respond to Kansas Reflector questions about whether Medicaid expansion affects issues like Children’s Mercy losing ACA coverage and what he would do as governor to strengthen rural hospitals.
Kansas hospitals and organizations have supported Medicaid expansion, saying it would stabilize hospitals and offer insurance to Kansans who are uninsured or under-insured. However, Missouri has expanded Medicaid and Medica also chose to leave Missouri counties. 
Insurance companies leave markets when they determine they can’t be profitable there, which can happen for several reasons, said Cindy Samuelson, spokeswoman for the Kansas Hospital Association. 
Hospitals consider several elements when deciding whether to accept insurance from a specific plan, including whether payments for services actually cover the cost of providing the service and whether the plan has good customer service, Samuelson said. 
For instance, hospitals look at how long a plan takes to authorize or deny care, which can cause delays in the patients receiving care, she said. 
 
Hospital revenue
Samuelson said the complexity of insurance and hospital operations makes it difficult to summarize how decisions are made. Revenues are affected by everything from the amount of charity care and uncompensated care hospitals have in their communities to prescription drug programs and percentage of Medicare and Medicaid patients hospitals are serving. 
Kansas hospital operating revenue, which is solely from treating patients and not from investments or other income, comes from private and public payers. 
Public payers are government programs like Medicare and Medicaid, while private payers are employer insurance plans, people who self-pay and ACA marketplace plans, according to a brief from the Kansas Hospital Association.
“In 2024, Medicare payments to Kansas Hospitals covered only 87% of the total cost of caring for Medicare beneficiaries,” the brief said. “In the same year, Medicaid payments covered just 70% of the total cost of treating Medicaid patients at Kansas hospitals.”
The difference is made up by charging private plans more to cover the gap created by public payers. 
“In order to maintain a viable financial status, hospitals attempt to negotiate payment rates from private insurance groups,” KHA information said. “The margins on these payments subsidize hospital losses from public payer underpayment, bad debt and charity care. This is known as cost-shifting, and can result in higher premiums for privately insured individuals.”
To illustrate what happens, KHA said that in 2024, Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries received nearly 54% of the clinical services from Kansas hospitals, but public payer revenue was just 43% of the hospitals’ total revenue. 
“In comparison, private payers received 30% of the care provided by Kansas hospitals and represented 49% of its total net revenue,” KHA said.
Samuelson said 21% of Kansas hospital uncompensated care comes from insured patients who can’t pay their out-of-pocket costs. 
 
Changing environment
Although Holscher has said throughout her campaign that she will expand Medicaid, that is likely to be a tough battle in a Republican state that missed out on hundreds of millions of dollars in incentives from the federal government to expand before now. 
“I come from a very collaborative approach,” Holscher said. “I’m the most successful Democrat in the Senate in terms of getting bills passed, and actually more successful than 90% of the Republicans.”
Holscher said she co-founded the Women’s Bipartisan Caucus and as a House member in 2017 helped to pass Medicaid expansion, which was vetoed by then-Gov. Sam Brownback. 
But she sees a changing environment in Kansas, including the fact that House Speaker Dan Hawkins won’t be returning to his seat. Hawkins, who served as Speaker of the House, and Masterson, who is Senate president, led efforts to stop Medicaid expansion. Hawkins is running for state insurance commissioner.
“We’re working to flip some of those seats, and now it feels like there are more citizens that are speaking up because we have this affordability crisis,” she said. “People are absolutely struggling and hurting in terms of access to affordable healthcare, childcare and housing.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: 30-person search committee convened to find next UNL chancellor
text:
University of Nebraska-Lincoln campus. (Aaron Sanderford/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — The University of Nebraska has convened a 30-member advisory committee to search for the next permanent chancellor of the University of Nebraska-Lincoln.
NU Executive Vice President and Provost David Jackson, NU’s chief academic officer, announced the formation of the committee in an email to the UNL community on Wednesday. Jackson will chair the committee, and he said 29 others will join him.
Jackson said the committee members offer a “broad range of perspectives and experiences,” including faculty, staff, students and leaders at NU, the three other NU chancellors for campuses in Omaha and Kearney and community members across Nebraska.
“I am grateful to these individuals for their willingness to serve and for the time and expertise they will contribute to this important process,” Jackson wrote.
University of Nebraska-Lincoln Chancellor Rodney Bennett speaks at University of Nebraska President Jeffrey Gold’s investiture ceremony. Sept. 5, 2024. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Previous UNL Chancellor Rodney Bennett took over as chancellor in July 2023 after UNL Chancellor Ronnie Green retired. The UNL Faculty Senate voted to express “no confidence” in Bennett as he led the flagship campus through significant budget cuts last year, including the elimination of four departments that the NU Board of Regents approved. 
Bennett abruptly resigned in January, about six months before his three-year contract expired. NU paid Bennett $1.1 million as part of a separation agreement.
NU President Jeffrey Gold tapped former UNL College of Architecture Dean Kathy Ankerson as interim chancellor. She is the second woman to lead UNL, both times in an interim capacity. She has expressed an interest in pursuing the permanent position.
The search firm WittKieffer will help guide the search and seek to identify potential candidates.
UNL students, faculty and staff and those in the broader community can participate in listening sessions Nov. 12-13 to help create a position description for the next UNL chancellor. Jackson said the committee plans to release the description in late December or early January. Zoom information and further details on the sessions will be provided in the coming weeks here.
University of Nebraska President Jeffrey Gold, left, and interim University of Nebraska-Lincoln Chancellor Kathy Ankerson host a listening session after Ankerson assumed the top UNL administrative role Jan. 12, 2026, and after UNL finalized $27.5 million in cuts under former UNL Chancellor Rodney Bennett in December 2025. Jan. 15, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Commentary: ‘The degree is not the finish line.’ Question 1 bond would prepare RIC students for what comes next
text:
Question 1 on the November ballot seeks a total of $275 million for projects at Rhode Island's three public higher education institutions, including $50 million to renovate the Adams Library at Rhode Island College and expand career readiness programs there. (Photos courtesy of Rhode Island College and by Rhode Island Current staff)I am a Rhode Island College (RIC) alumnus, adjunct professor in the School of Business, and chair of the Rhode Island College Alumni and Foundation Board. I have experienced RIC as a student, an educator, and a leader. And each perspective has reinforced my belief that a college education should do more than prepare students to graduate. It should prepare them to succeed in life. 
That is why I support Question 1 on the Nov. 3 ballot, the higher education bond, which includes $50 million for the modernization of Adams Library by creating a new Student Success and Career Readiness Center at RIC. 
For me, this is about much more than renovating a building. It is about what we make possible for the students who will walk through its doors. 
As a business professor, I want my students to leave the classroom with more than a degree. They need to apply what they have learned, communicate their value to employers, build professional relationships and navigate the transition into their careers. Academic preparation is essential, but graduates are being asked to display much more than comprehension of their subject matter. Secondly, higher education has an obligation to also connect their education to opportunity – prepare them with these skills and connect them to employers and a network.
About 70% of RIC graduates stay right here in Rhode Island to build their lives and careers. That retention rate is a massive asset for our state. It means the talent we cultivate today directly strengthens our local communities tomorrow. But to keep that momentum going, we have to bridge the gap between graduation day and the local workforce. A dedicated Student Success and Career Readiness Center would bring together vital student services like career guidance and resume and interview training, while also giving students access to professional networks and employer connections. Because so many of our students have jobs or families, we should make it as easy as possible for them to access the services they need to pass their courses, graduate on time, be prepared for the workforce and secure internships and jobs. 
Our graduates become the nurses who care for us when we are sick, the social workers who support individuals and families in need, the educators who prepare our children for the future, and the business leaders and entrepreneurs who create jobs and drive our economy. 



Quotation







For me, this is about much more than renovating a building. It is about what we make possible for the students who will walk through its doors.


I’ve witnessed firsthand how Rhode Island College can change a student’s life. 
I’ll never forget watching one of my students, who was a mother and a student-athlete, work her way through college while her husband lived overseas. College is challenging enough on its own without such family obligations. I’ll never understand how she made it all work. When someone works that hard to accomplish a goal, we have to do our part to support them and give them every chance to succeed.
I’ve seen first-generation students and working parents navigate incredible challenges to earn a college degree. But the degree is not the finish line. The Student Success and Career Readiness Center would give these remarkable high-achievers the resources and support to turn their degree into a career that will benefit their community and the entire Rhode Island economy. 
No building can guarantee success. That takes dedicated faculty and staff, hardworking students, and support from families, employers, alumni, and the broader community. But the right spaces and resources can connect these efforts and give students the support they need and the best possible chance to succeed. 
Question 1 is an investment in the people who will serve our neighbors, support our families, lead our organizations and help shape Rhode Island’s future. Investing in RIC students means investing in the people who will keep our state moving for years to come.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska is on pace to match 2024’s record-high early voting numbers
text:
A voter casts their ballot on the first day of early in person voting in Juneau on Oct. 19, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)One week before Election Day, turnout in Alaska’s general election is nearing 10%. 
As of 4:43 p.m. Tuesday afternoon, according to figures published by the Alaska Division of Elections, 58,168 people had cast early or absentee ballots for the Nov. 3 election.
The number of early votes cast through Tuesday afternoon already exceeds the number of early votes cast before the last midterm election, in 2022. 
Other states across the country are seeing a similar surge in early voting.
According to a daily report published by the Alaska Division of Elections, 34,738 people had voted at the state’s 10 in-person early voting stations between Oct. 19 and the end of the day Monday, Oct. 26. 
That tally includes significantly more registered Republicans, which are currently 26.7% of early voters, than registered Democrats, at 18.4%. 
Figures for votes cast on Tuesday are expected to be published Wednesday.
Of Alaska’s 604,771 registered voters, 11.6% are Democrats and 23.5% are Republicans, indicating that while Republican turnout is higher, Democratic turnout is disproportionately high.
Early votes cast through Thursday will be included in the totals published on Election Day, but votes cast from Friday onward will not be included because elections officials will need to check those against the Election Day voter register to prevent double voting. 
There is no set schedule for counting absentee ballots, which must be reviewed by elections officials before being counted.
Absentee ballot review boards — groups of paid, multipartisan temporary workers — were scheduled to begin reviewing absentee ballots on Tuesday and will continue working until the last absentee ballots arrive at various regional headquarters on Nov. 18.
State law allows late-arriving absentee ballots to be counted as long as they are postmarked on or before Election Day. Ballots mailed from within the United States can be counted as long as they arrive by Nov. 13, while ballots mailed internationally must arrive by Nov. 18.
All results until Nov. 18 will only show voters’ first-choice preferences.
Alaska uses ranked choice voting in general elections. If a candidate in a race gets more than 50% of the first-choice votes, they win.
If no candidate does, the candidate with the fewest first-choice votes is eliminated and votes for them go to their voters’ second preference. The process continues until only two candidates are left, and the person with the most votes is the winner.
Alaska performs that ranked choice tabulation on Nov. 18, after the last international absentee ballots are received.
The Division of Elections aims to certify the election results by Nov. 25.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Longtime treasurer, career financial examiner vie to be SC’s chief banker amid federal investigation
text:
Democrat Vincent Coe, left, is taking on incumbent Treasurer Curtis Loftis in the race to be the South Carolina's top banker. (Photo by Jessica Holdman and courtesy of Coe campaign)COLUMBIA — South Carolina voters are weighing their choices for state treasurer as the state remains under a federal securities investigation. The question is which candidate will best calm the waters and work to further prevent errors that led to the inquiry in the first place.

For more on our 2026 election coverage and information on voting in South Carolina, check out our Voter Guide.

The choice lies between the 16-year incumbent — a businessman with no banking experience before taking office — or a career banker with no political pedigree.
What happened
The investigation stems from fallout over a series of multibillion-dollar accounting errors, which sat on the state’s ledger for nearly a decade.
Forensic accountants hired by the state have said the errors were a paperwork problem and involved almost no actual money. Still, the issue raised eyebrows at the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, which has been looking into the matter since at least 2024.
SC under federal investigation as auditors determine mystery $1.8B didn’t actually exist

Two of the state’s three top financial officials at the time, including longtime Comptroller General Richard Eckstrom, have resigned since the problems with the state’s books first came to light publicly in early 2023.
But one — Treasurer Curtis Loftis — has clung to office, despite efforts to oust him and an earlier statement that he would not seek re-election.
The accounting mistakes happened amid a decade-long changeover from the state’s legacy accounting system to a new bookkeeping program. During that process, electronic ledger entries made it appear the state had $1.8 billion sitting untouched in a fund with no record of its origins.
Loftis has maintained that the error did not occur within his office and none of the cash in the bank that the Treasurer’s Office manages was misspent or lost.
The error, Loftis told the SC Daily Gazette, was with the comptroller general’s records. Those records have since been corrected and that office has been the focus of the federal securities investigation.
But a Senate-led investigation into the matter and subsequent impeachment proceedings against Loftis were less about which office controlled the records and more that Loftis’ office knew and did not alert the General Assembly, instead leaving it to linger.
It was the bipartisan push to oust him, led by members of his own party, that ultimately led Loftis to change course and enter the race.
“There is important work that remains unfinished, and I believe my experience and leadership continue to be valuable to our state,” Loftis told the Daily Gazette.
SC treasurer avoids being ousted this year over $1.8B accounting error

His Democratic challenger, Vincent Coe, agrees the fault does not lie with Loftis alone but said the long-time treasurer did shirk his reporting responsibility. And when it comes to finances, perceptions matter.
“When you have things like this, you have to do a shift or change in leadership to get back on track,” Coe said. “Because if you don’t, you’re going to have a continuation and that breeds into mistrust.”
Candidates’ experience
Despite the issues that have dogged Loftis, Coe faces an uphill battle. He doesn’t have Loftis’ political following and he’s running as a Democrat in a state that has not elected a member of that party to statewide office in two decades.
Coe said he thinks the Treasurer’s Office should be nonpartisan. And he contends that what he lacks in political know-how, he makes up for in professional expertise.
He studied finance, risk management and insurance at the University of South Carolina before going to work as a bank examiner with the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, the U.S. agency that regulates the industry.
He took a break in his FDIC service to attend law school at Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland, where he studied constitutional law and financial institutions regulations.
He left the FDIC and moved back to his home state of South Carolina at the end of 2015, helping his mother start a rural health clinic.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Florence native then worked as a consultant for financial giant PricewaterhouseCoopers for a couple years before taking a job with the Federal Reserve Bank in Atlanta.
He came back to South Carolina in 2020, amid the COVID-19 pandemic, and started his own bank consulting business — Balcony Advisor — and spent time at United Community Bank in Greenville, advising them on investments.
Loftis ran and grew his family’s pest control company and worked in real estate until running for treasurer in 2010.
He beat out former state Rep. Converse Chellis, R-Summerville, who was seeking his first public election to the office. The Legislature elected Chellis, a certified public account, to the role following Thomas Ravenel‘s resignation in July 2007 — just six months after being sworn in — amid a federal indictment on cocaine distribution. (He pleaded guilty to possession two months later and spent 10 months in prison.)
Loftis billed himself as a GOP outsider who would combat waste and corruption amid the state’s ranking politicians.
Voters elected and continued to re-elect him for four terms. Now he’s seeking a fifth.
Campaign promises
If elected, both Loftis and Coe vow open access to the state’s bank records and to work alongside the comptroller general.
“My priorities are straightforward: even greater transparency and accountability, protecting taxpayers’ money, preserving South Carolina’s excellent credit ratings, and enhancing programs that directly benefit our citizens,” Lotis said.
‘Mismanagement’ by SC treasurer could have added millions to voting machines’ cost, report finds

“South Carolina needs accurate financial reporting, greater transparency, and better cooperation among its financial agencies,” he added.
But some of the criticism lobbed at Loftis by senators is that he was behind on making reports and his ongoing rift with the state’s current top accountant, Brian Gaines. Gov. Henry McMaster appointed Gaines, his budget director, to replace Eckstrom in May 2023 when the legislative session ended without the Legislature filling the vacancy.
Most recently Gaines and Loftis sniped at each other over an $11 million records discrepancy related to the state’s Capital Reserve Fund, which is used to finance major infrastructure projects. Gaines accused Loftis of holding up bank statements and delaying issuance of the state’s annual report to Wall Street investors. That report has since been released.
“If I’m elected, I’ll make sure that the books are open every single month so that the taxpayers can see where the money is,” Coe told the Daily Gazette. “Just about any and all money that flows through South Carolina, in some way, shape, or form flows through the office, and so we have to have good management, good practices, so that people understand that their money is being managed well.”
Coe pointed to his Democratic colleague, Tiffany Boozer, who is running for comptroller general. Boozer has been working in the office as an internal auditor. Coe said he wants to make a similar hire within the Treasurer’s Office.
And he said achieving a clean audit should be the first step to satisfying federal investigators.
Other issues
More South Carolinians with disabilities qualify for a savings program providing a ‘Better Life’

Beyond the treasurer’s record-keeping duties, the office also runs the state’s unclaimed property program, meant to return money turned over to the state by companies that cannot locate the owner.
Loftis has touted returning more than $470 million since his election.
But the state still has $1 billion available to claim.
Coe said, if elected, he wants to send out checks automatically to get more of that back to South Carolinians.
Loftis has automated some of the office’s claims.
“However, not every claim can or should be automated,” he said. “As technology advances, we’ll continue expanding automation where it is accurate, secure, and affordable. Our goal is to return every dollar possible while protecting citizens and taxpayers.”
Coe also wants to see more of the state’s money invested with smaller community banks, so long as it aligns with state  and federal law and continues to generate good returns.
Coe said 90 cents of every dollar that the Treasurer’s Office currently invests is in national banks.
Loftis said this earned $1.8 billion in investment income last year for the state and local governments.
But Coe said smaller banks, which he called “the lifeblood of communities,” would benefit from holding some of the state funds. The towns they serve would, too, because the banks would have more funds to lend out to local businesses.
