name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico environment secretary urges lawmakers to advance outgoing governor’s climate agenda
text:
New Mexico Environment Department Secretary James Kenney spoke before lawmakers on the interim Water and Natural Resources Committee on Oct. 26, 2026, about his priorities for the 2027 legislative session. (Joshua Bowling/Source NM)As Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham’s final term nears its end, her environment secretary this week asked state lawmakers to spend the upcoming legislative session continuing to advance her administration’s climate goals, particularly those relating to water and air quality.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Lujan Grisham will leave office at the end of the year, after first winning election to the state’s highest office in 2018, and New Mexicans will elect a new governor on Nov. 3. Kenney said he and his staff have already begun preparing environmental legislation for the next administration to consider.
Kenney told lawmakers on the interim Water and Natural Resources Committee during their Monday meeting that he wants to explore creating a fund to finance actions related to the state’s 50-year water action plan; codifying the state’s emission reduction goals in state law; passing a “circular economy” bill to reduce consumer waste; and bolstering the state law to require manufacturers to label consumer products that contain “forever chemicals” known as PFAS.
50-year water action plan
Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham in 2024 unveiled the state’s 50-year water action plan, which outlines strategies such as conservation and watershed protection to address the state’s water woes.
Kenney credited the plan with NMED’s Leak Tracer program, which uses satellite imagery to identify potential water leaks in small communities across the state. He said he’d like to see the Legislature create a fund that could continue to pay for projects like this and enshrine in law a mechanism to appropriate money into that fund.
“We are putting together some legislation to hand off to those who want to sponsor it, as well as the incoming administration,” he said. “We’re not just wishing this will happen. We are drafting for that outcome.”
Codifying emission reduction goals
A proposal to codify Lujan Grisham’s statewide emission reduction goals into state law failed in this year’s legislative session. Kenney said he’d like to see the effort taken up again, particularly as it would give his department greater power to regulate the growing data center industry.
New Mexico off track for 2030 greenhouse gas goal, environment official says

Senate Bill 18, known as the Clear Horizons Act, would have etched the requirements of a 2019 Lujan Grisham executive order into state law. The executive order called on the state to curb its greenhouse gas emissions by 45% relative to 2005 levels by 2030.
Environmental officials this week told state lawmakers that New Mexico is off track to meet that goal.
Kenney said he thinks the failed bill is still a good starting point for such legislation.
He pointed to Project Jupiter, the controversial hyperscale data center under construction in Doña Ana County, and said such a law would give his employees greater authority to regulate such developments.
“For things like Project Jupiter where they’re planning to emit somewhere between 5 and 8 million tons of carbon dioxide…we don’t have any way at the Environment Department to regulate the CO2 emissions that come from data centers,” he said. “That’s painful, to have been a champion with the governor, and to be an administration that’s championed climate goals and to consider that they could be eliminated with the data centers prospectively looking at New Mexico.”
Officials in Kenney’s department are set to preside over a Dec. 7 public hearing over whether to give Project Jupiter’s developer an air quality permit for its proposed natural gas fuel-cell system.
Reducing consumer waste
Kenney said he wants to see the Legislature adopt measures to create a “circular economy,” in which goods are manufactured to be reused or repaired rather than discarded. 
He said it would be a “next step” for lawmakers to build on House Bill 291, a 2025 law that amended the Recycling and Illegal Dumping Act to promote reuse over one-time consumption.
PFAS labeling
Lujan Grisham in 2025 signed the Per- and Poly-fluoroalkyl Protection Act into law, which required manufacturers to clearly label products containing the “forever chemicals.” 
The chemicals, which are present in everything from carpeting to firefighting foams, have been linked to certain cancers, decreases in fertility and fetal developmental delays.
Last month, a federal judge issued a preliminary injunction that said New Mexico’s labeling requirement infringed on commercially protected speech after a number of manufacturing organizations sued the New Mexico Environment Department over the rules.
“We thought an icon would be a great way to merely inform the consumer that there is PFAS associated with that product,” Kenney told lawmakers Monday. “I think it goes back to the Legislature now.”

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Maine students back Pingree for governor, Jackson for US Senate in mock election
text:
Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows holds up a ballot given to students in statewide mock elections held Oct. 29, 2024, a week before Election Day. (Photo by Eesha Pendharkar/ Maine Morning Star)Maine students, if able to vote, would send Democrat Hannah Pingree to the Blaine House, and would elect Troy Jackson, Chellie Pingree and Paul LePage to Congress, according to results from the mock election organized by the Secretary of State’s Office. 
More than 12,000 students cast ballots Tuesday for governor, U.S senator and members of the U.S. House of Representatives. Each of the candidates created campaign-style videos that were provided to 115 participating schools across the state. 
Hannah Pingree won the gubernatorial race with 41.8%, compared with 30.4% for Republican Bobby Charles and 24.4% for independent Rick Bennett. Incumbent U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, also a Democrat, won the 1st Congressional District with 57.5% over Republican Ron Russell; while the former governor, LePage, took the 2nd District with 52% of the votes over Democratic challenger Matt Dunlap. 
Jackson, a Democrat, eked out a win in the Senate race against incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins with 50.8% of the student vote. More than 4% of students, however, wrote in another candidate in that race.
In a statement announcing the totals, Secretary of State Shenna Bellows hailed the mock election as “an engaging way for students across the state to learn about elections and have their voices heard even before they can cast a real ballot.”
Bellows, who travelled to Maranacook Community High School in Readfield to kick off Tuesday’s voting, noted that practicing voting before students turn 18 can help them feel prepared. In Maine, 16- and 17-year-olds can preregister to vote and those who will be 18 by Election Day may cast a ballot. New voters who are not yet registered can do so at the polls on Nov. 3.
More information about the candidates and how to register and vote can be found at Maine Morning Star’s 2026 Voter Guide.

title: atTAcK addiction honors Delaware leaders in fight against addiction
text:
atTAcK addiction presented atTAcK addiction’s highest honor, the Medal of Honor, to Joanna Champney, director of the Delaware Division of Substance Abuse and Mental Health, at the organization’s Oct. 22 Be a Hero Gala.  Image created on 10/28 and was edited with AI.
Joanna Champney receives organization’s highest award as Delaware records sharp decline in overdose deaths
NEWARK, Del. — Delaware’s progress in reducing fatal drug overdoses — and the people working on the front lines of addiction treatment, recovery and prevention — took center stage as atTAcK addiction honored community leaders at its 11th annual Be a Hero Gala.
About 240 people attended the Oct. 22 event at the Executive Banquet Center near Newark, where Joanna Champney, director of the Delaware Division of Substance Abuse and Mental Health, received the organization’s Medal of Honor, its highest recognition.
Champney was recognized for her work expanding access to addiction treatment and recovery services, increasing the availability of naloxone and helping lead Delaware’s response to the opioid epidemic.
The recognition comes as Delaware has recorded a significant reduction in overdose deaths. State figures show accidental drug intoxication deaths declined from 527 in 2023 to 314 in 2025, a decrease of more than 40%.
“Recovery doesn’t end when treatment ends,” Champney said while accepting the award on behalf of her DSAMH colleagues and the Delawareans they serve.
Champney has led DSAMH since 2021, overseeing the state-supported system of substance use disorder treatment, services for people with serious mental health needs and the Delaware Psychiatric Center. The division also manages federal funding, including a $38 million State Opioid Response grant.
She also co-chairs Delaware’s Overdose System of Care, which brings hospitals, emergency medical services, treatment providers and state agencies together to coordinate care for people experiencing overdoses or opioid use disorder.
Champney was appointed by Gov. Matt Meyer in 2025 to co-chair the Delaware Prescription Opioid Settlement Distribution Commission with Attorney General Kathy Jennings. The commission recommends and awards funding for treatment, prevention, recovery and other programs addressing the opioid crisis.
The gala also recognized Delawareans whose work ranges from direct outreach and recovery support to theater, volunteerism and efforts to reduce the stigma surrounding substance use disorder.
Corey Ryan, senior outreach coordinator with Oxford House Delaware, received the Medal of Valor for his work serving people in recovery, building collaborations and advocating for policy changes while maintaining his own recovery.
New Light Theatre received the Persistence Award for its production of “The White Chip,” a biographical play about one man’s experience with alcohol use disorder and recovery. The company staged nine performances in Wilmington in March with atTAcK addiction as its community partner and plans free performances in New Castle, Dover, Georgetown and Lewes in November.
Dana Timmons of Springboard Delaware received the Blue Heart Award for work with atTAcK addiction’s Sussex County Chapter connecting people in Kent and Sussex counties with treatment and recovery services.
Michael Clemons and Jesse Valeri, both affiliated with Impact Life, received Courage Awards. Clemons, a former intern at atTAcK addiction’s Glasgow Resource Center and a person in long-term recovery, was recognized for turning his recovery experience into service. Valeri, a treatment engagement specialist, was honored for leadership in helping people affected by substance use disorder.
Shayla Beaulieu of Oxford House Delaware received the Unsung Hero Award, while longtime atTAcK addiction volunteer Karen Godfrey received the Distinguished Service Award.
Timothy’s of Newark received special recognition for its annual We Are Stronger Together fundraiser, which supports atTAcK addiction while raising awareness and working to reduce stigma associated with substance use disorder.
Alyssa Hayes and Carolyn Thompson received Outstanding Volunteer Awards for their work at the organization’s Resource Center and community activities.
Scholarships were presented to Jennifer Calton, Chase Garrison, Samantha Jenkins, Brian Lawson, Lindsey Ogden and Francine Muti.
“So many people across our state are giving their all to help individuals access treatment and recovery services for substance use disorder and to fight the stigma associated with the disease of addiction,” said Dawn Hess-Fischer, president of atTAcK addiction. “We are proud to honor this group of leaders who are making a difference.”
The Be a Hero Gala is one of several annual events atTAcK addiction uses to recognize people working in addiction prevention and recovery and to raise awareness about substance use disorder. The organization also operates community programs and a Resource Center and provides naloxone, drug-testing supplies and connections to treatment and recovery resources.
Previous recipients of the Medal of Honor include former Gov. Jack Markell and former first lady Carla Markell, former Lt. Gov. Bethany Hall-Long, Jennings, former Attorney General Matt Denn, state Sen. Stephanie Hansen, former state health officials Rita Landgraf and Dr. Karyl Rattay, and former ChristianaCare President and CEO Dr. Janice Nevin.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Día de Muertos springs to life at the Wadsworth
text:
Not far from the heavy front doors of the Wadsworth Athenaeum, artist Helena Martinez was ready to welcome in the spirit world.  
Amidst the glow of electric tea lights, beeswax skulls and a tiny, black-and-white skeletal dog, she pointed out the people she carries with her. There was her older sister, Charlie Gonzalez, frozen in time as a high school senior; her Titi Mary Ann Rosa, who inspired her to become a community-based artist and organizer; and her niece, Celestia Summer Gonzalez, who died at just two months old in 2016. 
In front of Celestia’s portrait, encased in a heart-shaped frame, two tiny, lacquered wooden animals flanked a toy car, its red paint glittering in the gallery’s low light.  
The ofrenda, or memorial altar, is part of “Todavía Aqui,” a multi-part, stunningly bright installation from Martinez and members of the greater Hartford community that translates to “Still Here,” and is on display for Día de Muertos, or Day of the Dead, in the Wadsworth’s post-war and contemporary art galleries through Nov. 8. 
This coming Sunday, on Día de Muertos itself, it will be the centerpiece of the museum’s free community celebration of the holiday, during a collaboration between the Wadsworth, Martinez’s cultural organization Helena’s Casita, and the City of Hartford’s “Mayor’s Day Out” program. For Martinez, who launched the celebration as a small, out-of-pocket event four years ago on Hartford’s Pratt Street, it is as much a reminder of life, including its miraculousness and fragility, as it is a moment of reflection. 
“For me, Día de Muertos is not just a chance to honor our loved ones [who have passed], it’s also a chance to celebrate the joys in life,” Martinez said last Thursday afternoon, framed by soft electric flames and skeletons that seemed to scale the sides of an 11-foot arch covered in giant, delicate paper marigolds.
This year, the hours–long celebration includes live mariachi from the group Mariachi Tercera Generacion, as well as free Mexican hot chocolate from Evelyn Ruiz’ Hartford-based coffee truck Hasta Luego Friend, and sweet, fragrant pan de muerto from Guadalupana Bakery in Brooklyn, for the first 100 attendees. For years now, Martinez has also worked with the Brooklyn-based shop Mexico In My Pocket, which is owned by her friend Luisa Navarro, for some of the celebration’s furnishings, like hand-painted skeletons and clay skulls from Mexico. 

A ceramic skull from Mexico In My Pocket, a store that Martinez’s friend Luisa Navarro runs from Brooklyn.  Credit: Lucy Gellman / CT Mirror

Día de Muertos itself, celebrated in Mexican households across the globe each year, dips back into thousands of years of history. Long before the Catholicism that accompanied Spanish colonization in the sixteenth century, the Aztecs dedicated two rituals, Miccailhuitontli and Hueymiccailhuitl, to the memory of children and adults who had died. The words, like the festivals themselves, come from the name of the deity Mictēcacihuātl, thought to rule the underworld.
It was during these rituals that the custom of using cempasúchil, or marigolds that glow a fiery, almost otherworldly orange, became common (other common flowers include chrysanthemums, baby’s breath, and cockscomb among others, Martinez said). At the time, just as in the present, families believed that the flower helped guide the spirits of the dead temporarily back into the world of the living. Their vibrancy, along with the scent of copal, has remained an enduring part of the day even as it became a fusion of Indigenous and Catholic traditions. 
As Día de Muertos evolved, shifting with both the influence and force of colonialism, it took on many of the contours that are still familiar to it today, including a shift to celebrating it later in the year, closer to All Saints’ Day. In addition to putting up an ofrenda that includes photographs of those who have died, including especially the very young and the very old, families often set out sweet, eggy pan de muerto, libations like beer, water, whiskey, tequila and soda that the departed loved in life, bowls of fruit or food, and flowers, sometimes laid so thickly they resemble a carpet. 
For Martinez, a speech language pathologist, serial crafter and artist raised between New Jersey and Connecticut, it’s a chance to both deeply grieve those she has lost, and celebrate life with a creative community she has come to love, and to which she is fiercely committed. Four years ago, she launched the celebration as a grassroots gathering on Hartford’s Pratt Street, as she and fellow artists were still coming out of a pandemic that had turned the arts, and the ability to gather, on its head.

Portraits of Helena Martinez’s ofrenda, or memorial altar, include Martinez’s niece Celestia Summer Gonzalez, who died at just two months old in 2016.  Credit: Lucy Gellman / CT Mirror

That year, dozens of people came out, including Alexisjacqueline “AJ” Martinez, a childhood friend who had recently taken a position as community engagement and access coordinator at the Wadsworth Athenaeum Museum of Art. When the two reconnected, they began talking about opportunities for collaboration, which led to a location change to the Wadsworth in 2025 (in 2024, it drew hundreds of people to Pratt Street). 
“It really made perfect sense,” said AJ Martinez, who had launched a similar celebration at the Wadsworth with artist Carlos Hernández Chávez in the years prior. In 2024 and again last year, she remembered, Helena Martinez had made a short speech, assuring attendees that their presence was a sign of strength and resilience in a moment of political uncertainty. “She was like, ‘We’re here and we’re going to celebrate.’ It was beautiful and powerful.”
But the story of Helena Martinez’s own path to observing Día de Muertos takes root many years before that, during her childhood in Vernon and Manchester, Connecticut. The third of six siblings, Martinez grew up with an interest in crafting, cultivated during dozens of free workshops at craft stores that her mother took her to on the weekends. She didn’t think of herself as an artist until much later, but knew that something about creating made her feel at home.
When Martinez was a junior in high school, her older sister Charlie died suddenly, just weeks before her 18th birthday, after a freak accident sent her into cardiac arrest. It left the family reeling: Charlie was “our goth princess,” the sister who was opinionated and bookish, with a dark sense of humor and biting kind of snark that still managed to be funny and charismatic. When she died, “it was just very raw and heavy,” Martinez remembered. 

Helena Martinez’s ofrenda includes small figurines, children’s toys, and beverages and fruit that her relatives and loved ones once adored in life. Photo taken during a visit on October 22, 2026. Credit: Lucy Gellman / CT Mirror

“We grieved her death, but we were all comfortable on what to do,” she continued. Shortly before Charlie had died, she and several siblings had gathered to watch Peter Jackson’s film “The Lovely Bones,” based on Alice Seabold’s novel of the same name. In the book, the young narrator is murdered by a neighbor, and watches life on earth continue to unfold without her. Charlie, who had loved the book, wasn’t having it.
“She was like, ‘Don’t bury me in the ground for all the worms and bugs to eat me,’” Martinez remembered. “I want to be cremated.” 
Just weeks later, those words seemed strangely prescient. Martinez’s mother, Mary Martinez, built a shelf in her home to  hold an urn with Charlie’s remains. 
The year after Charlie’s death, Martinez and her siblings built an ofrenda for the first time, honoring the heritage that their mother held onto when her family migrated from Reina and Matamoros, Mexico several decades ago. Up until that time, she remembered, she had always leaned more towards her father’s Salvadorian side of the family, but something in the ritual called to her. She has made one ever since, in addition to the altar that remains up year-round in her home.    
Four years ago, “I felt like my sister was calling me” to do something bigger, Martinez remembered. By then, she had piloted a stationary company and lifestyle brand called Hecho by Helena, which featured language and imagery meant to honor the depth and breadth of Latinidad. She was working as a speech language pathologist in Springfield,  and had started hosting community crafting craft sessions (she now fondly refers to them as “Craft or Crash Out,” to recognize crafting as a form of emotional regulation). The celebration on Pratt Street grew organically from there. 

Helena Martinez’s ofrenda includes a station where people can dial a rotary phone and leave messages for relatives who have passed away. Photo from a visit to the Wadsworth on October 22, 2026.  Credit: Lucy Gellman / CT Mirror

This year, her second at the Wadsworth, the installation includes four different, intertwined stations, all designed with the idea of community participation and physical accessibility in mind. The first, visible from the museum’s lobby, is an archway covered in large crepe paper marigolds, the color so vivid it seems as though they have absorbed the sun itself. As she wove through the space last week, Martinez dipped in and out of the archway, inviting a trickle of visitors to do the same. The space is inherently a liminal one: families use archways during Día de Muertos to create a portal between the world of the living and that of the dead.  
Nearby, Martinez’s bright ofrenda sits beside an old-school rotary phone, painted off white with glittering gold numbers, on which people can leave messages for their loved ones. On the altar next to it, electric candles glow softly over fabric covers, beeswax, wooden and ceramic skulls, bowls of fake fruit (because of the museum’s policies, live flowers, burning candles and fresh fruit are a no-go) and small items once beloved by her relatives and friends. Around Charlie’s portrait, which sits prominently on the bottom rung, unlit red candles rise from inside empty bottles of Topo Chico, a fruity carbonated drink that her sister once loved.  
Above the altar, Martinez has invited community members, including staff at the Wadsworth, to include portraits of their loved ones, with a slideshow that rotates through each of their names and photos on loop. To its right, there is a place for attendees to write their loved one’s name on a small wooden heart, and add it to a collection of hearts that becomes a miniature community ofrenda of its own. 

Hartford Mayor Arunan Arulampalam and Helena Martinez, artist and founder of Helena’s Casita, during a visit to the Wadsworth on October 22, 2026.   Credit: Lucy Gellman / CT Mirror

On a walkthrough of the installation with Hartford Mayor Arunan Arulampalam last Thursday, Martinez said that she often feels Charlie’s spirit with her, and still calls on her in moments of exhaustion. Earlier this month, for instance, she was midway through installation, and so tired that she didn’t think she would be able to complete her work. She asked Charlie to give her the strength to push through. 
An hour later, Martinez felt a burst of energy. “I was like, ‘Oh, Charlie’s here,’” she said. 
Arulampalam, who has included the event in his “Mayor’s Day Out” programming, which provides free activities to Hartford residents through city sponsorship, pointed to the Wadsworth’s celebration as a chance for Hartford residents to both experience the museum, some of them likely for the first time, and observe the tradition in community. This year, that feels especially important: many members of Connecticut’s Latino population, including and especially Mexican and Mexican-American residents, are living in fear after increased activity from Immigration and Customs Enforcement earlier this year. 
As a father of five who has cherished many of his own family’s stories, Arulampalam said the day has become personal to him, too. Growing up in Los Angeles, he was continually surrounded by friends who observed the day. But it wasn’t until recently, when a caregiver in their home taught his kids about the tradition, that he thought deeply about its weight, and the chance to stop and remember the dead for the vibrant lives they lived. 
Now, he said, Dia de Muertos gives him a chance to think about his maternal grandmother, Kirupa Karunananthan, who lived with his family while he was growing up, and both of his grandfathers, whom he fondly remembers as Appu and Appuchi respectively. Each winter, he still dons the coat that his paternal grandfather wore after his family fled Sri Lanka, and migrated to England. After Arulampalam was elected mayor of Hartford for the first time in 2023, that coat and its story accompanied him to the White House, where he was able to share it with then-President Joe Biden. 
“I think there’s something so beautiful about living with the idea of death,” he told Martinez as the two walked through the exhibition.  
He remembered supporting his wife, the Rev. Liza Arulampalam, as she went through the grief of losing her mother several years ago. “People don’t know how to interact with you when you’ve lost someone,” he said, and Martinez nodded, one hand still extended toward something on the ofrenda. “We’re all so uncomfortable with our own sense of mortality.”
“It’s like, people shouldn’t ask, ‘What can I do?’” Martinez said. “Just bring food. Be present … I think the idea of death, because we’re not able to look it in the face, becomes a source of anxiety.”
The Wadsworth’s Día de Muertos celebration takes place Sunday Nov. 1 from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. at  600 Main St., at the museum’s website.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Ballotmania: Inside the flurry of measures upending Massachusetts politics
text:
SOMETIMES, A RAISED HAND is all it takes to kick off an 18-month campaign.
Framingham Democratic activists were celebrating their annual barbecue in July 2025 when 80-year-old Norma Shulman posed a simple question for the event’s special guest, Secretary of State Bill Galvin. What ever happened, she asked, to the proposal that would allow new voters to register on the same day they cast a ballot?
State law bars anyone from newly registering or changing the address at which they are registered within 10 days of an election. As a result, reform proponents argue, thousands of Bay Staters are disenfranchised each year when they head to the polls only to find out they are not registered or failed to update their address in time. Eliminating the blackout period has had major pockets of support on Beacon Hill for almost two decades — in fact, the Senate has approved some version of Election Day registration on three different occasions since 2008, but in each instance, the idea died because of resistance in the House.
Galvin, as Shulman recalls, made “a few little comments” about the repeatedly stalled effort and said he’d get back to her. Then, a couple of weeks later, her phone rang. It was the secretary, and he had a new idea.
“He said, ‘It’s just never going to get passed by the House. I’m doing something about it,’” Shulman recounted. Within days, the longest-serving secretary of state in Massachusetts history was standing in Shulman’s dining room, joined by some of her friends in Framingham, signing the paperwork to launch a campaign that would go directly to voters and ask them to write Election Day registration directly into state law.
Fast forward to today, and Shulman is chairing the main committee in support of the measure, circumventing a Legislature where the idea has long failed to earn the required support from all stakeholders. The question is one of nine on the ballot, tying the record for the most in a single year since Massachusetts wrote the option of direct democracy into its constitution 108 years ago.
It’s been more than three decades since voters last had this many significant decisions to make about state law. Across Massachusetts, while voters weigh reshaping how primary elections work and parse the particulars of the state tax cap formula, they find themselves asking another question: Why is all of this falling to us in the first place?
The surge in questions on the November ballot and the tens of millions of dollars being spent on them has revived debate about the process itself. Are initiative petitions a legitimate policymaking tool that citizens can wield when their elected officials are too resistant to public opinion? Or are they an outdated, poorly designed mechanism that can be exploited, especially in a post-Citizens United world, by those with a specific vision and money to burn?
Indeed, ballot questions have become the primary source of political kindling in a season when few races for elected office in Massachusetts are generating much heat of their own. Most of the people pushing the measures are not shy about bashing the Legislature, claiming they were forced into action because do-nothing politicians refuse to touch a widely popular idea. “It’s 1,000 percent the fault of the Legislature for not solving problems,” said Jim Stergios, executive director of the Pioneer Institute, which is backing a question that would overhaul the state’s tax cap and rebate law.
Legislators have responded with defensiveness and disdain, worried that a surge in spending and a fragmented media environment opened the door for financed entities with little regard for nuance to coopt a democratic option. House Speaker Ron Mariano, who has spent more than a year grumbling about both the number and types of decisions now handed to voters, said in a statement for this story that the initiative petition process is “fundamentally broken,” taken advantage of by “special interest groups and overly-ambitious politicians who refuse to retreat from maximalist positions.”
“The current initiative petition process is fundamentally broken. From a growing number of proposed questions that violate the state Constitution, to a lack of reporting requirements that allow ballot question campaigns to operate in the dark – the process is in dire need of reform,” said House Speaker Ron Mariano. (Chris Lisinski/CommonWealth Beacon)
Disagreement over ballot questions is fragmenting state government itself, too. Galvin, no stranger to tussling with lawmakers, is directly at odds with Democratic colleagues in the Legislature over the issue. So, too, is Auditor Diana DiZoglio, who led a successful campaign in 2024 for a ballot question empowering her to probe the House and Senate and is now following that up with a new measure that would subject the Legislature and governor’s office to the public records law. Concerned by the constitutional implications, Democrats in the Legislature have indicated they might substitute their preferred version of a records transparency bill for the one voters embrace, risking a worsening political fracas at a time when Beacon Hill’s transparency is already under fire.
Joshua Dyck, a political science professor at UMass Lowell who co-authored a 2019 book about direct democracy, called the trend a “spiral of distrust” between disgruntled constituents and irritated lawmakers.
“When people use the initiative [process] more, they’re signaling that they don’t trust the government,” he said. “Then, when voters show up and they see nine measures on the ballot — or 15 or 20 in other [states] — it also confirms to them that government isn’t doing their job because now they have to go and read this long voter guide and figure out how to vote on all these issues. They walk out of the voting booth no matter how they vote going, ‘Man, the Legislature’s not doing their job.’”
Stuck in the middle are voters, who will either need to make uninformed decisions with potentially permanent consequences, or form substantive opinions in the next week on nine proposals ranging from the fate of a 115-page gun control law to minimum lot size requirements for home construction.
In the birthplace of the American Revolution, is there such thing as too much democracy? 

The right for concerned voters to bring a policy change directly to their peers has been guaranteed since 1918, when Massachusetts joined a trend of progressive-minded democratic reforms that swept through the country in the wake of Gilded Age corruption and stagnation. 
It was a vastly different time — Massachusetts was still a year away from ratifying the Nineteenth Amendment, which guaranteed women the right to vote — and yet the arguments made in favor of enshrining a right to direct democracy appear familiar today. Ironically, it was a former House speaker, Joseph Walker, who led the charge after previous state leaders failed to win enough support for the change. At a months-long constitutional convention on the topic, Walker thundered that Beacon Hill was beholden to “sinister influence” from “lobbyists who appear yearly.” His campaign was eventually successful, and a new way of lawmaking business was born.
The nine statewide questions on the ballot this year tie the record for most in a single year, matching 1994, 1976, and 1972. It looked like we would smash that and set a historic high of 12, but judicial intervention wiped three questions from contention, whittling down the field. 
“We’re in a period of time where the whole system should be reviewed from top to bottom to figure out how to put the democracy, small-d, back into it and to have it balanced in relationship to our underlying system of representative democracy.”Former Senate president Stan Rosenberg
A citizen-originated ballot question these days hinges on a single early decision: instead of advocating for the House and Senate to take up the idea and perhaps change it along the way, proponents conclude they would rather spend several million dollars running a 15-month campaign, collecting tens of thousands of signatures, and convincing enough voters to squeak out a majority win at the polls.
Campaign leaders pull that lever for a host of reasons. Sometimes, the measure contains a proposal the Legislature has refused to advance despite little opposition; sometimes, it’s something so controversial the Legislature will never touch it; sometimes, a proponent files a question with the implicit goal of gaining leverage to pressure lawmakers on Beacon Hill, but winds up seeing it all the way through to Election Day anyway.
Lew Finfer, a veteran organizer who has been involved in almost every fight over the past four decades to improve life for working-class residents, recalled meeting with then-Senate President Therese Murray in the early 2010s, when labor groups were pushing for a minimum-wage increase and lawmakers seemed skeptical. At first, Finfer recalled, Murray told organizers, “I’ll do the best I can” — which he translates as, “I’ll decide, I have the cards.” Once union leaders said they were prepared to put the question on the ballot, the conversation changed. 
“We told her that, and she said, ‘Oh, that would be different. Oh, people would have to take a stand on this,’” the usually soft-spoken Finfer recalled with a rising voice, punctuating every syllable as he pantomimed Murray. “It was like you’d never seen her so animated.”
Much to the chagrin of Beacon Hill, ballot measures are a chainsaw method of policymaking instead of the more traditional chisel. It’s largely a structural feature: once a question clears eligibility and signature requirements, lawmakers can only approve it as written, take no action and allow it to proceed to voters, or broker a compromise in which the Legislature approves a bill tackling the same topic and proponents agree to drop their campaign. “That results in questions going to the voters that are overly simplistic, create more problems, in my view, than they solve, and give an artificial sense that this is a good way to make law,” said Rep. Alice Peisch, who co-chaired committee hearings on every initiative petition in the past two cycles.
While the most common response from legislative leaders over the years has been disdain, there have always been those who hewed more closely to former speaker Walker’s view, respecting ballot initiatives as a valuable offering that can complement the traditional lawmaking path. That’s the case for John McDonough and Stan Rosenberg, the two men most responsible for a landmark 1994 campaign finance and ethics law that took aim at many of the political ills animating ballot questions in the first place.
Auditor Diana DiZoglio (center), pictured here addressing a legislative committee helmed by Sen. Cindy Friedman (left) and Rep. Alice Peisch (right) on March 3, 2026, insists she could still expand the scope of her crusade to probe the Legislature down the line. (Chris Lisinski/CommonWealth Beacon)
In 1993, The Boston Globe put Beacon Hill’s top Democrats in the hot seat with a Spotlight series documenting, as the first story put it, “an insiders club that takes care of its own interests first and deals with public policy later.” For the second story, splashed across the front page were photos depicting then-House Speaker Charles Flaherty lounging on a Puerto Rican beach where, instead of attending a legislative conference in San Juan, he and a group of lawmakers indulged in a private four-day party on the other end of the island, funded by their campaign accounts and scores of lobbyists who were in attendance to bend ears. 
Incensed by the controversy, the good-government group Common Cause Massachusetts launched a ballot question that sought to crack down on lobbyist donations to politicians, significantly lower the cap on maximum campaign contributions a person can make toward a candidate, and require donors to disclose their job and employer. McDonough and Rosenberg, who together led the Election Laws Committee at the time, had extensive conversations with the question’s backers and ultimately produced a compromise bill that overhauled the state’s campaign finance law. Common Cause was satisfied enough to drop its ballot question charge. 
“The campaign election reform of ‘94 never would have happened were it not for the initiative petition process,” McDonough said.
He has long thought Massachusetts is better off with initiative petitions available, even if the system has flaws. “I was an outlier,” McDonough, who served in the House from 1985 to 1997 and penned a seminal feature about ballot questions for CommonWealth in 2002, said. “Most of my colleagues despised it and wished that it wasn’t there or that they could get rid of it.”  (McDonough, now a professor at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, also co-hosts CommonWealth Beacon’sHealth or Consequences podcast.)
“Importantly,” he added, “I haven’t been to another state where legislators in those states don’t feel exactly the same way. There’s nothing atypical about Massachusetts lawmakers’ annoyance with the process.”
His counterpart in those 1994 negotiations, Rosenberg, feels somewhat differently about ballot questions today than he did earlier in his career. Rosenberg rose all the way to Senate president before departing in 2017 amid a sexual harassment scandal involving his husband. During his tenure, he often positioned himself as a good-government reformist who was committed to small-d democracy, including both its representative and direct variations. In recent years, however, Rosenberg has become convinced that “money is too powerful a force” behind ballot measures.
“If there’s a 30-page piece of legislation that’s been put on the ballot, most people are not going to study that, not going to have enough information to know whether there are elements of it that are going to be unworkable, unmanageable, unfair, or downright unprincipled,” Rosenberg said. “I do not object to direct democracy as an element in our system. I believe that that system is no longer working as it should.”

Comparatively, it’s easier to place a proposed law before voters in Massachusetts than anywhere else in the country, at least in terms of gathering signatures to qualify. Only California, Colorado, and Louisiana will have more questions on their ballots this Election Day.
But why there are so many all at once — what it is about the state of our politics that led so many organizers to say, “Forget the Legislature, I’ll do it myself” — elides an easy answer. The most common theory, one floated by most people leading initiative campaigns, is that the Legislature has become particularly inefficient, and ballot questions are necessary to get movement on popular ideas.
Dissatisfaction with Beacon Hill, especially its pace of work, is clearly growing. Lawmakers have not sent the governor an on-time annual state budget in 15 years. In 2022 and 2024, the House and Senate kept their final formal sessions of the term going overnight and well past sunrise the following morning; somewhat abashed by the upheaval, the Legislature this time around granted itself permission to tie up any loose ends beyond the traditional July 31 date. Little has happened since then, and now more than a dozen major decisions will need to take place in the lame-duck weeks after the election.
“The volume of questions is a reflection of the degree of frustration,” said Danielle Allen, a Harvard University professor and longtime democratic reform activist leading the campaign to institute all-party primaries through the ballot box. “I think it’s a symptom, and I think people need to recognize it as a symptom.”
It’s a diagnosis shared by Galvin, himself a former state representative who has now served as secretary of state longer than any current counterpart in the country. “The people who are interested in these issues, whatever side they’re on and whatever issue it is, oftentimes have been attempting to get legislative action for years. They’ve spent money, significant amounts of money, on lobbyists to do that, not to mention grassroots efforts, and it’s all come to naught,” Galvin told CommonWealth Beacon. “As a result, they’ve concluded it might be cheaper to spend big money on an actual ballot campaign. History suggests that’s effective.” 
We asked: Does the surge in ballot questions reflect the system working as intended, or is it a sign that something is broken?






Danielle Allen, longtime democracy reform activist and backer of Question 3: “The volume of questions is a reflection of the degree of frustration. I think it’s a symptom, and I think people need to recognize it as a symptom.”








Auditor Diana DiZoglio: “It’s both. I think it’s the system working as intended — the ballot question process is a constitutional right of the people to protect against government tyranny and to hold their elected officials to account — and it’s also a sign that the Legislature has not been as effective as it could be.”








Senator Cindy Friedman: “I think something is broken and needs to be fixed, and I think it has to do with the influence of money and how, to a certain extent, we’ve lost a sense of common good. This may be good for you. Is it good for others? I see a trend, and that trend is money. It’s everywhere.”








Secretary of State Bill Galvin: “It’s both … The law is doing what it was intended to do: provide an alternative to those who want to advocate for an issue … None of that makes it less of a crude mechanism to effectuate policy changes.”








Rep. Alice Peisch: “I don’t think it’s either/or. The fact that there is legislation in conference at the moment that would establish a commission to look at the process — that is an indication that we think there may be some aspects of the process that could be improved.”








Stan Rosenberg, former Senate president: “I do not object to direct democracy as an element in our system. I believe that system is no longer working as was intended when it was established in the early 1900s because money is too powerful a force now in these ballot campaigns.”








Jim Stergios, executive director of the Pioneer Institute and a backer of Question 5: “The system’s working as it’s supposed to. I know it’s uncomfortable for people who are used to calling the shots from within one building. They don’t like to be questioned, or they don’t like to have extra variables thrown into their day. But honestly, every single person who lives in Massachusetts, they’re living a life that is variable. They’re trying to make ends meet. They’re trying to do stuff that gets their kids to move ahead. And what the Legislature’s doing right now, it ain’t working.”



Photo details and credits: Danielle Allen (Leise Jones Photography); Diana DiZoglio, Sec. Galvin, Sen. Friedman, and Rep. Peisch (Chris Lisinski/CommonWealth Beacon); Stan Rosenberg (MassINC); Jim Stergios (Rappaport Center/CC BY 2.0)

Many proposals have indeed existed in the legislative arena for years, but it’s not a universal truth. Two questions (Election Day registration and public defender unionization rights) came to be because sponsors grew tired of watching the proposals die in the Legislature. Two others (public records and all-party primaries) target electoral reforms or a degree of transparency to which the Legislature is unlikely to agree. One (tax cap reform) is more or less aimed at kickstarting a broader debate about state spending and the business climate, another (recreational marijuana ban) seems to originate with a national, secretly funded effort to undo drug legalization in states, and yet another (a gun law repeal) is led by citizens exercising their constitutional right for a voter referendum on a new law they dislike.
Evan Horowitz, executive director of the Center for State Policy Analysis at Tufts University who has studied each of the measures, thinks it’s a mistake to graft a single storyline onto the entire ballot. For evidence, he points to the measure that would earmark a share of sales tax revenue from sporting goods purchases and use it for conservation efforts.
“There was a bill there. The Legislature didn’t act on it. It’s now a ballot initiative. But it’s totally reasonable to me the Legislature didn’t act on it because they didn’t think it was a good idea,” Horowitz said. “That’s quite different than if they didn’t act on it because they were lazy or not responsive.” 
Lawmakers have argued the explosion reflects the growing, corrosive role of money in politics, with well-funded groups easily able to bankroll the work of gathering signatures and campaigning. “It’s definitely a question of money because getting 11 ballot questions at least certified to a certain extent with that many signatures that you have to get — that’s huge,” said Sen. Cindy Friedman, who joined Peisch to co-chair hearings on the ballot measures.
The proposals have indisputably gotten much more expensive. In 1994, the nine questions on the ballot generated a combined $11.8 million in spending over the course of the entire campaign. Adjusted for inflation, that’s about $25.5 million in 2025 dollars, a number that today seems quaint. Almost exactly that much money had already changed hands for the current crop of nine questions by October 15, two and a half weeks before the election. In five separate instances since 2016, a single question generated more than $35 million in spending, adjusted for inflation.
Opponents of a ballot question seeking to repeal the state’s 2016 legalization of recreational marijuana rally outside the State House on June 25, 2026. (Chris Lisinski/CommonWealth Beacon)
Massachusetts was almost certain to see its spending records vaporized two years ago. For years, ride-for-hire giants Uber and Lyft defined their sprawling networks of drivers as independent contractors, not employees. After then-Attorney General Maura Healey sued, claiming that classification violated state labor law, the companies and their allies launched a campaign for a ballot question that would have codified their drivers as independent contractors, essentially asking voters to rewrite the law they were alleged to be violating.
The companies put roughly $34 million into the campaign before dropping their effort in June 2024, after Uber and Lyft agreed to a settlement with Attorney General Andrea Campbell that forced them to increase driver wages but allowed them to retain independent contractor status. Had they kept going all the way to the ballot, the dollar figure would have grown much larger, especially because spending on campaigns tends to be heavily backloaded closer to Election Day. In California, gig economy giants spent more than $200 million on a similar measure voters approved in 2020.
Here in the Bay State, something shifted around 2014, and the trend has not yet reversed. Campaigns are spending way more to get proposed laws and constitutional amendments onto the ballot and to sway voters . In the three decades from 1992 to 2012, the inflation-adjusted average spend per question never exceeded $10 million. In every cycle since then, the same figure has soared into double digits, reaching as high as nearly $38 million in 2020, when a “right-to-repair” measure dealing with motor vehicle telematic data smashed individual question records. 
It’s hard to say exactly why ballot measures have gotten so much more expensive, and most likely, there isn’t a singular reason. Campaigns are more professionalized, which costs more. Many operations pay professional firms to collect the voter signatures needed to qualify a question; while paid signature-gatherers are far from new, it’s possible the growing demand has allowed them to charge more. 
Dyck, the UMass Lowell professor, believes the funding explosion reflects a broader trend. “Increasing spending is a signal of increasing conflict, which means initiatives are being contested over ‘hot’ or ‘highly contested’ issues,” he said. “That’s going to generate a lot of interest, a lot of advertisement, and bring a lot of pro and con money to the table.” 
Friedman thinks the amount of money now sloshing around is an obvious problem that “warps the notions of democracy.” When her predecessors embraced direct democracy as a lawmaking tool 108 years ago, she argued, a massive, corporate-backed spending blitz was not what they had in mind.
“The intent wasn’t to allow outside groups or people who had a lot of money but were disappointed by how things work to have an oversized influence on those policies,” she said. “I just don’t believe that that is what the intent was.”

Lawmakers are certainly aware of the narrative that the record-tying field is itself a referendum on the Legislature, a collective raised fist demanding more from government. Peisch, a top deputy to Speaker Mariano, thinks that idea is partly fueled by broader changes to the political climate, especially the fragmentation of debate ushered in by social media and the shrinkage of a once-robust State House press corps. 
“That has had an enormous detrimental impact on how the public views the Legislature,” Peisch said. “That’s related to these questions because some of them — not all, but some of them — are driven by this mistaken impression that we’re completely unresponsive. In my view, it’s not that we’re unresponsive. It’s that particular individuals and organizations don’t like the response.”  
At times, legislative irritation metastasizes into action to significantly alter or even nullify what voters order. In 2000, Massachusetts voters approved a ballot question to cut the income tax rate by almost a full percentage point over a three-year span. Two years into the transition, lawmakers voted to freeze the rate at the partially reduced level and condition the remaining step down on a series of economic triggers; that did not happen until 2019, nearly two decades after the question passed. In 1998, voters approved a “clean elections” ballot question providing for public financing of elections; five years later, lawmakers tucked language into the state budget scrapping the measure altogether.
Those maneuvers might be politically unpalatable, but they are not illegal — and lawmakers, many of whom run for re-election unopposed, rarely pay a price for them. A measure approved at the ballot box becomes state law on equal footing with anything that moves through both chambers and earns the governor’s signature. Legislators are empowered to adjust anything in state law as they see fit.
“I agree with the Legislature in hoping for a world with fewer ballot initiatives, but to have that requires responsiveness and accountability.”Danielle Allen, longtime democratic reform activist and chief proponent of Question 3
This time around, top Massachusetts Democrats might pull the trigger more quickly. A pair of bills, one subjecting the Legislature to a public records framework less extensive than the ballot question and another adding a new, stricter eligibility trigger for tax rebates, are tied up in House-Senate negotiations. If lawmakers choose to do so, they can surface either or both measures right before or right after the election, nullifying or dramatically changing what voters decide on Questions 1 and 5. 
Unsurprisingly, the chance of a ballot question rewrite or two has not gone over well in many corners. DiZoglio, the leader of the public records campaign who is years into a related fight over the not-yet-implemented audit law, has vowed to pursue legal action if Beacon Hill neuters Question 1. “They are trying to usurp our constitutional right as the voters of this Commonwealth in real time,” she told CommonWealth Beacon. 
Even former lawmakers gave the pending maneuver a less-than-favorable review. “Boy, that’s creative,” said Rosenberg, who spent two years as Senate president. “Either you cut a deal, or you fight it out on the ballot and then see what happens and then make your next moves,” added McDonough. “I think undermining it in that way is not an appropriate response. There are better ways to do this.”
Current legislators defended the potential rapid changes, arguing that they have both the right and responsibility to amend laws approved at the ballot when they have overriding concerns about the substance.
“While I agree that we should update the public records law, there are things in that ballot [question] that I would argue make it almost impossible for me to do my job,” said Friedman, a top Senate deputy. “If I want to fix that, I have to then take that ballot initiative once it passes, if it passes, I then have to change it. And then what happens is all those people start screaming, ‘You’re not following the will of the people.’ So I’m stuck in a very difficult situation because it’s my job to make law. That’s what you elected me to do.” 
Legislatures in other states have been even more aggressive in their battles against direct democracy. GOP lawmakers in Missouri unsuccessfully sought to require any citizen-led initiative to win a majority of votes in each of the state’s congressional districts, not just statewide. In both Utah and South Dakota, where voters previously embraced Medicaid expansion over the opposition of lawmakers, Republicans placed questions on this year’s ballot requiring at least 60 percent voter support for many future questions to pass.
While they disagree on the diagnosis, both Beacon Hill and many of the campaign leaders seeking to circumvent it find common ground on one point: having nine questions that touch on so many topics, some of which are intricate and dense, asks a lot of voters.  
“Why are you making us vote on these things? They’re too complicated,” Peisch recalls one constituent telling her. Shulman, the longtime organizer now working on the Election Day registration question, was out knocking on doors recently, and she heard from more than one voter who was struggling to make sense of the 88-page ballot question summary booklet mailed out by Galvin’s office. “They’re kind of tearing their hair out,” she said. 
For Rosenberg, the former Senate president, the attempt to reshape a tax cap and rebate law is particularly daunting. To understand that measure, one first needs to comprehend the 1986 voter law known as Chapter 62F that set a limit on state tax collections in a given year and the specific way that threshold is calculated, then decide whether it’s better to keep the cap tied to the prior year’s limit or instead change its basis to the prior year’s total revenue. 
“It’s a challenge for tax attorneys to try to explain that, never mind a volunteer, or never mind a voter sitting in their living room reading the secretary of state’s guide,” Rosenberg said. “Which is why a lot of people don’t vote on the ballot questions, and that’s a calculation that people who put questions on the ballot make.” 

So if a cocktail of sclerotic governance, interest groups with money to burn, and easy ballot access got us to this point, is a cascade of questions the new normal? Is Massachusetts on its way to becoming more like California, with 10 or more new laws decided every election? 
Perhaps not. There’s a very real chance this cycle brings about material changes to the process itself. 
Lawmakers are on the verge of codifying new campaign finance rules for ballot questions that would close an eight-month blackout period in which organizers do not need to disclose anything about their funders. If the House gets its way, Beacon Hill will also convene a new commission tasked with conducting a top-to-bottom review of the entire initiative petition process.
Some changes are possible through state law, which the Legislature and governor can achieve on their own. A more extensive overhaul would require an amendment to the Massachusetts Constitution, a dramatic step that, somewhat ironically, would culminate with a ballot question in which voters get the final say. 
It could be even more confusing for voters: in 1994, the last time Massachusetts had nine statewide ballot measures, ballots featured only the number of the question and a spot to select “yes” or “no,” with no title or description of what each measure would do, as seen in this sample archived by Secretary of State Bill Galvin’s office. (Chris Lisinski/CommonWealth Beacon)
Absent any real reconciliation, ballot questions will remain a political Rorschach test, a trend at which anyone can look and spot evidence for their preexisting arguments about the efficiency of the Democratic supermajority or the pernicious power of money in politics.
Many ballot question campaigns start because someone is irked about inaction or an undesirable outcome on a specific policy; when legislators respond by decrying campaigners, they can appear insulated and paternalistic, unwilling to engage with voter demands. That opens the door for a subsequent wave of initiative petitions pitched as tackling the issues lawmakers are unwilling to face. Over time, the dynamic can become an ouroboros of frustration begetting more frustration. 
Mariano declared earlier this year that the ballot question process is “fraught with peril.” To Allen, that line translates instead as, “You want to be heard, and I don’t want to listen.”  
“In an ideal world, you would always be able to do transformative change through the Legislature,” said Allen, who briefly ran for governor in 2022. “But the ballot initiative process is an important safety valve on the fact that, at the end of the day, insiders and gatekeepers will reach a point of entrenchment where they will protect the system as it is, even when people are manifestly frustrated with it.” 
In the meantime, voters will continue to have homework. A whole lot of homework.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska legislators press natural resources commissioner on no-cost state land transfers
text:
John Crowther, commissioner of the Alaska Department of Natural Resources, speaks to lawmakers at a joint meeting in Anchorage of the state House and Senate Resource Committees held on Aug. 20, 2026. Seated next to him is Haley Paine, director of the Alaska Division of Oil and Gas. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)As the Alaska Department of Natural Resources is deliberating on a controversial no-cost state land transfer in the Matanuska-Susitna Borough, legal questions remain around whether the transfer of public lands for private development qualifies as public or charitable use. 
The state could transfer 20,000 acres near Houston to its economic development agency, the Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority, for a proposed multi-use industrial and energy development district — a proposal that has sparked controversy because it could include data center development.
Under a rare legislative subpoena, DNR Commissioner John Crowther appeared before the Senate Resources Committee on Monday to answer questions about the department’s recent slew of proposed state land transfers to several state agencies at no cost under a “public and charitable use” statute, including the Mat-Su proposal.
The committee subpoenaed Crowther after he declined to appear at another hearing earlier this month. Department officials said at the time he did not have permission from Gov. Mike Dunleavy to appear.     

Senate Majority Leader Cathy Giessel, R-Anchorage, listens to a presentation about natural gas during a March 12, 2025, hearing of the Senate Resources Committee, which she chairs. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

Sen. Cathy Giessel, R-Anchorage, who chairs the Senate Resources Committee, questioned the uptick in no-cost state land transfers over the last year by DNR to a variety of state agencies and local municipalities, where they could potentially be leased instead for millions of dollars each year. 
“It feels like an appropriation,” Giessel said. “An appropriation of a very, very valuable asset, and that is Alaska land, Alaska public land. So that authority rests with the Legislature, and that raises questions.”
Senators pressed Crowther on whether a final decision from DNR is expected on the 20,000 acre Mat-Su proposal before a new governor is set to take office on Dec. 7, to which Crowther responded, “it’s certainly possible.”
However, Crowther said a final decision could be challenged by an administrative appeal or lawsuit. “It’s of course subject to judicial review,” he said. “So we anticipate moving through our process as expeditiously as possible. And some of those processes, we don’t have control over the timeline.”
A lawsuit filed Oct. 22 in state Superior Court is challenging the Mat-Su proposal as unconstitutional. The suit was filed by former University of Alaska Regent Eric Forrer and former Republican state Rep. David Eastman, and is intended to tie up the transfer and prevent DNR from pushing it through before Gov. Mike Dunleavy leaves office, Forrer told the Mat-Su Sentinel.
DNR issued a preliminary decision in July for the proposed transfer of the 20,000 acres near Houston to AIDEA. The proposal sparked public outcry, particularly as AIDEA’s list of potential development projects included data centers. 
DNR is now reviewing more than 2,100 public comments before issuing a final decision. The comments include opposition from nearby communities, the Mat-Su Borough Assembly and some members of the Senate Resources Committee who wrote letters criticizing AIDEA’s proposal as too vague and raising legal concerns around whether it serves a sufficient public purpose. 
Alaska senators question legality of state land transfer for possible Mat-Su data centers

DNR and AIDEA officials have maintained that AIDEA’s status as a state-owned economic development agency allows for the state land transfers under a “public and charitable use” statute. AIDEA officials have maintained that it is unlikely that data centers would be part of the development in the Mat-Su, due to a lack of a reliable energy source. No projects or contracts have been confirmed, AIDEA officials said.   
On Monday, Crowther said that state land transfers for private development is a priority of the Dunleavy administration. 
“I think it is very fair to say that using our land for development has been a governor’s priority, and consequently, the department’s been working on that in several different respects,” he said. 
Crowther said it’s a priority of the Dunleavy administration “to maximize use and development of state lands, and to look at how we can partner with these state agencies that have public purposes and public missions to make land that is in theory eligible for private use and development, but hasn’t seen that.” 
Officials with Dunleavy’s office did not respond to questions about the legality of the state land transfer, or local opposition to the Mat-Su land transfer proposal on Tuesday. 
Senators question regulation change for definition of ‘public purpose’ 
DNR recently changed state regulations to expand the definition of “public purpose” for state land transfers to include private development. 
Anchorage Democrat Sen. Forrest Dunbar wanted to know if the proposed transfers would have been legal before the regulation change. Crowther said the updated regulatory language clarifies existing state law and DNR’s authority. 
In March, DNR adopted changes in its regulations after a public comment period. Those changes included an expansion of the definition of “public purpose” to include supporting “private commerce or industry that contributes to the economic development of the state” and “is otherwise determined by the commissioner to be in the best interest of the state.”
At the same time, Giessel noted that the governor introduced a similar bill that included allowing state land transfers for commercial development parks, but it failed to advance in the Legislature. 
Crowther said DNR’s mission to promote development of state lands and resources has been ongoing, “for several years in several different avenues, and that regulation change was part of that.” 
He said that has included projects including renewable energy, housing, gravel mining and other development. 
“That theme runs throughout of: we need to use our lands and our resources in ways to address these, you know, in some ways very consistent, but in some ways very different cost access challenges that are stymying public interest across the spectrum,” he said. 
“Other states are trying to tackle these same challenges and are doing so through adaptive land offerings and land management approaches,” he continued. “And so that was a motivation both for that regulation change and some of these other initiatives.”     

A screenshot of a map by the Alaska Department of Natural Resources in a proposal for a no-cost state land transfer of 885 acres to AIDEA to develop a rail-support and cargo logistics area (Alaska Department of Natural Resources)
 

Giessel said she began to take notice of the number of state land conveyances over the summer, particularly the large Mat-Su parcel and another 885 acres at Port MacKenzie slated for transfer to AIDEA. The Port MacKenzie proposal includes developing a rail-support and cargo logistics area to serve a future railroad link between the port and the railroad’s mainline near Houston. 
Giessel questioned why DNR did not consider leases for agricultural use at the Port MacKenzie site. 
“This land is still productive, could be productive for farming, and yet you’re conveying it to AIDEA for apparently industrial uses,” she said.
Christy Collis, director of the Division of Mining, Land and Water, appeared at the hearing with Crowther and said the proposed use of the parcel is tied to obligations with the Mat-Su Borough but the department will evaluate farmers’ concerns in their review of the public comments. A decision on that parcel is also expected in the coming months, but there is no set timeline. 
Senators raise concerns with AIDEA, public input and oversight
Crowther told senators that officials with AIDEA approached DNR about the no-cost state land transfers before submitting proposals for the Mat-Su and Port MacKenzie parcels. 
AIDEA has drawn public scrutiny as it directs some of the most polarizing development projects in the state — from Arctic oil exploration to the proposed Ambler Road project. AIDEA is run by a seven-member board appointed by the governor, but does not report directly to the executive branch and manages investments independently. 
Dunbar asked Crowther how DNR weighs the benefits to the public of land transfers specifically for private development. 
Crowther said AIDEA is a state-owned agency that has a broad mission to promote economic growth and generate revenue for the state. 
“As long as their application (was) identifying a suite of activities consistent with that mission, and not identifying that they plan to abrogate that mission, I think we would interpret that as being cognizably appropriate under the conveyance,” he said. 
Anchorage Democrat Bill Wielechowski pressed Crowther on why DNR did not keep a reversionary interest in the Mat-Su proposal with AIDEA, which would allow land not suitable for development to be automatically transferred back to state ownership. 
Crowther said historically it’s been the state’s policy to maintain a reversionary interest, but it can also create challenges for developers to get financing for their projects.
“We wanted to provide flexibility for AIDEA as they develop options and plans, but it’s obviously been identified as a significant matter of legal concern and public concern,” Crowther said. “So we’re looking closely at it.”
Later in the hearing, Wielechowski criticized what he said was a lack of transparency and oversight of DNR’s no-cost land transfer to AIDEA for private development. 
“It’s a huge loophole that is being created here,” he said, pointing to how DNR’s land use proposals are subject to greater public oversight than AIDEA’s. 
“We’ve got a constitutional obligation to manage our resources, including our lands, and if you’re giving the lands away for nothing with no reversionary interest, very little protection for the public, to a board that’s not confirmed by the Legislature, has basically zero public oversight—it seems like it creates this giant loophole, for which AIDEA then has the ability to just go out and do whatever they want with the land, in a way that DNR would not have the ability, and that seems like, that’s what’s causing, I think, a lot of consternation and a lot of concern among the public and legislators.”

name: California
title: New poll shows billionaire tax falling behind as election nears
text:
A “Tax the Ultra-Rich Now” bus parked in San Francisco on Oct. 3, 2026. Photo by Manuel Orbegozo for CalMatters




Californians’ appetite for a first-in-the-nation wealth tax appears to be waning.
With less than a week before Election Day, support for Proposition 40, a proposed billionaire tax, is now under water, according to the latest poll by Public Policy Institute of California. Published Tuesday, the survey found that 46% of 1,086 likely voters support the tax, while 52% don’t.
That’s a notable change from last month, when Prop. 40 proponents held a slim 52% majority. The billionaire tax is by far the biggest and most expensive fight on the ballot. As of mid-October, wealthy people who oppose it have raised more than $205 million to fight the tax, including Google co-founder Sergey Brin, who has poured at least $102 million.
Still, Prop. 40 supporters remain undeterred. In response to the PPIC poll, Suzanne Jimenez, the chief of staff of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the union behind the measure, said “large majorities of Democratic voters” continue to support it.

Jimenez, in an email to CalMatters: “Even after months of the most controversial billionaires on the planet spending millions to spread misinformation about it, a clear majority of voters support asking about 250 billionaires to pay a modest, one-time tax to keep … healthcare affordable for millions of Californians.”

Meanwhile, a pair of related ballot measures intended to negate the billionaire tax could go either way.
Prop. 42, with 51% in support among those polled, holds onto a narrow lead. It would bar new taxes on personal property and assets and prohibit retroactive taxes. Prop. 41, which would impose limits to certain new state taxes, appears to be falling short with 48% support.
Voters seem to be more favorable on five other ballot measures. A majority of survey participants said they would vote yes on: 

Prop. 1, the $11.25 billion housing bond
Prop. 2, which would increase the amount of tax revenue the state can put in savings 
Prop. 3, which would permanently extend an income tax for high-earning households 
Prop. 37, which would create a $25 billion fund to help homebuyers
Prop. 38, which would dedicate $8 billion in bonds to fund immunology research

As for the governor’s race, Democratic candidate Xavier Becerra continues his lead in the polls with PPIC reporting that 61% of likely voters would vote for him, compared to 37% for Republican Steve Hilton.



We’re bringing our voter guide to life through VotingMatters events across California, in collaboration with on-the-ground partners. We’re holding two events today: In Mariposa at the Mariposa County Government Center and in Santa Barbara at the Louise Lowry Davis Center.

Other Stories You Should Know


Where Trump’s CA election lawsuit stands


A polling station clerk sanitizes a voting station at the Monsignor Ramon Garcia Recreation Center in East Los Angeles on Nov. 8, 2022. Pablo Unzueta for CalMatters




A federal judge appeared skeptical about the Trump administration’s demands that California set aside 20,000 ballots from alleged noncitizens, but won’t likely rule on the matter until after the Nov. 3 election, report CalMatters’ Ryan Sabalow and Nigel Duara.
In a potential setback for President Donald Trump, U.S. District Judge David O. Carter on Tuesday raised concerns that the administration’s efforts to stop noncitizens from illegally voting by ordering the state’s elections officials to sequester their ballots could disenfranchise “valid voters.” 
Though he’s expected to issue a formal ruling today, Carter’s final ruling might not come until after another hearing that will take place in two weeks. Carter also suggested that his ruling would prohibit federal authorities from threatening elections officials with criminal charges if they didn’t comply with Trump’s demands.
Read more.



Could election results help LA fire survivors?


Construction workers build a house in Altadena on Aug. 3, 2026. Photo by Jules Hotz for CalMatters




Survivors of the Eaton and Palisades fires are running out of money to rebuild their lives, and the outcome of the midterm elections may affect whether federal aid will come, writes CalMatters’ Levi Sumagaysay.
Nearly two years since the fires ripped through the Los Angeles area, the Trump administration has been slow to release funding to California, and it didn’t include L.A. County wildfire relief in its budget request for Congress this summer. 
It’s also unclear when the billions of dollars in long-term disaster recovery money the state has requested will come — if at all. Last week, outlets reported that the Federal Emergency Management Agency told states they will need to handle most disasters themselves.
U.S. Reps. Judy Chu and Norma Torres, both Southern California Democrats, said that if Democrats flip the House in November, federal aid could roll out to California and other states hit by disaster.
Read more.



And lastly: Fresno dad suddenly deported


Luis Arreguin stands at the Cathedral of Mexicali, in Mexicali, Baja California, Mexico, on Oct. 21, 2026. Photo by Daniel Resendiz for CalMatters




Luis Arreguin, a 54-year-old Fresno resident, was on his way to work as a skilled laborer on Oct. 1 when federal immigration enforcement agents arrested him. Sixteen days later, agents deported him to Mexico — where he hasn’t been since he was a kid — in a stunning example of the dizzying speed in which Trump’s deportation machine operates. Said Arreguin: “My whole life got destroyed.” Read more from CalMatters’ Wendy Fry.

name: VTDigger
title: State senator from Rutland County arrested, jailed on domestic assault charge
text:
Sen. Terry Williams, R-Rutland, at the Statehouse in Montpelier in Feb. 2025. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

A Vermont state senator from Rutland County has been jailed on a charge of domestic assault, according to Vermont State Police.
Terry Williams, 74, of Poultney, is set to appear Wednesday at 12:30 in court for an arraignment on the misdemeanor charge. Williams, a Republican, has served as a state senator since 2022 and is facing re-election on Tuesday. 
Williams was arrested after state police received a report around 5:40 p.m. Tuesday that a domestic assault had taken place in Poultney, according to a state police press release issued Wednesday morning.
An investigation revealed that Williams “had caused pain and injury to a household member one day earlier” on Monday, the release added.
Williams was placed in custody and taken to the Rutland state police barracks for processing, according to the release. He was then taken to the Rutland jail on $500 bail. 

READ MORE

No additional information was immediately available from state police. More information is expected to be made public following his arraignment and the release of the police affidavit filed in support of the charge.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Immigration restrictions are hurting already struggling Minnesota colleges, universities
text:
Gwamaka Mahenya, a junior political science and film and media studies major at St. Olaf College, sits in Boe Chapel on Oct. 27, with flags representing the nationalities of St. Olaf students hanging behind him. (Photo by Maya Betti/Minnesota Reformer)Gwamaka Mahenya knew studying in the United States would mean making sacrifices. The St. Olaf College junior applied to universities elsewhere, such as in the United Kingdom, and had been accepted to some. But coming to the U.S. made financial sense, he said, even if it meant being farther from home. 
Now, as federal immigration policies narrow international students’ opportunities to work and stay in the U.S., Mahenya said those sacrifices have grown beyond what he expected. 
“My younger brother is growing up without me, my pets are growing up without me,” he said. “Everything at home feels like it’s changing, and I’m just stuck here. I can’t go home.”
Tanzania, where Mahenya was born, is one of the 39 countries placed on the travel ban list the Trump administration announced in 2025. The restrictions partially suspend entry for Tanzanian nationals, meaning that if he were to leave the U.S., he could be barred from reentry. 
The travel ban paired with tighter federal rules around internships and jobs in his field after graduation have Mahenya feeling down about any future in the U.S.
