“This work will allow the port to accommodate modern, deeper-draft commercial vessels—significantly boosting shipping efficiency, lowering transportation costs, and enhancing navigation safety,” Darr told the Independent in an email comment. “Furthermore, a substantial portion of the dredged material will be beneficially reused directly within harbor to improve important fish habitat, enhance oyster grounds and build a new rock reef.”
Sally Kruse, the executive director of the New Haven Port Authority, welcomed the beginning of this project as “very exciting” not just for the port, but also for New Haven.
“It represents a major investment” by the federal and state governments in making ship transportation in and out of the port more efficient, she said. She said that larger vessels tend to be newer, more efficient, “more modern,” and even more eco-friendly — potentially allowing for “the same amount of material coming in” to the port with fewer vessels.
She said that the channel-deepening project should allow vessels to come in to New Haven’s port “without waiting for high tide. The current depth means that some of the largest vessels cannot come in without doing so.”
In an Oct. 21 press release announcing the start of the project, Darr wrote that New Haven is “the largest port of call in Long Island Sound, the third-largest port in New England by tonnage, and Connecticut’s busiest port.”
New Haven’s port is not a so-called “container port.” The products that are transported in and out of the city’s harbor are not, for example, big boxes of furniture or food.
Instead, the city’s port is a way station for “petroleum products, home-heating oil, aggregates, equipment, and scrap metal,” as Darr put it.
The Oct. 21 press release states that roughly 1.7 million cubic yards of dredged material will be used “to support aquatic ecosystem improvement of shellfish and reef habitat, including filling of relic borrow pits that have existed in the harbor since the 1950s.”
In addition to the deepening of the channel from 35 to 40 feet below Mean Lower Low Water (MLLW), this project will also see the widening of the entrance channel from 500 feet to 600 feet outside the breakwaters; the widening of the channel bend between the breakwaters from 560 feet to 800 feet; the widening of the main channel from 400 feet to 500 feet inside the harbor; and the “optimizing” of the turning basin “for more efficient use by larger vessels.”
“The improvements will support energy production with optimized delivery of critical petroleum, products such as gasoline, jet fuel, and heating oil as well as commodities such as road salt, steel and chemicals vital to our nations industry,” Craig Martin, senior project manager with the USACE New England District, is quoted as saying in the press release.
The work has been coordinated with the U.S. Coast Guard, Connecticut Port Authority, and New Haven Port Authority, among others.
Click here and here to read more about the project, including about how the Senate Committee on the Environment and Public Works authorized a feasibility study back in July 2007 regarding navigation improvements for the New Haven Harbor.
This story was first published Oct. 27, 2026 by New Haven Independent.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Starkville’s district consolidation is called the state’s most successful. County residents feel differently
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
STARKVILLE — In marbled rooms at the State Capitol, conversations about school consolidation often lead to Oktibbeha County. 
Many state leaders consider the 2015 consolidation of the Starkville city public schools and Oktibbeha County schools a success story. 
That’s because the consolidation — which married a failing district in the county to one that was middling in the city — resulted in more money, a temporary enrollment bump, a new state-of-the-art school with expanded academic offerings and what is now an A-rated district.
But some locals might argue that account leaves out another part of its legacy: Every school that closed belonged to the county district, where 90% of students enrolled were Black. By comparison, the city schools were 30% white.
Jackie Ellis pictured at the site of her former high school in Starkville, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Jackie Ellis, 70, attended county schools and graduated from B.L. Moor High School, which later became East Oktibbeha High School. Now the old school is home to an events venue and a boutique motel. 
Every time Ellis drives by the motel, she feels what she lost.
Early resistance ends with shared mission
When the consolidation was first introduced — by lawmakers from Hattiesburg, no less — Starkville residents grumbled, Haley Montgomery recalls.
“The community was fairly blindsided,” said Montgomery, who at the time was a volunteer with the local public school parents’ group and freelanced for the school district. She now handles communications for Starkville Oktibbeha Consolidated School District. 
Starkville parents worried how consolidation with the state-managed Oktibbeha County School District would reshape their C-rated schools.

A historical marker for B.L. Moor High School is pictured in Starkville, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
The former East Oktibbeha High School is now an event venue and boutique motel in Starkville, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today

Families wanted a seat at the table and asked the Legislature to let locals take the lead. Lawmakers formed a committee of Oktibbeha County residents to recommend ways to improve education in their community.
The committee stumbled early on, when it proposed sending Oktibbeha students outside of the county. Rex Buffington, who led the committee, said the group was trying to shorten commutes for students who lived closer to neighboring school districts than to schools in Starkville.
But the proposal was perceived as a rejection of students. “And of course it was,” he said, acknowledging the misunderstanding. “Why didn’t we see that?”
Rex Buffington, former chair of the consolidation committee, pictured in downtown Starkville, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Though painful, the incident helped change the committee’s perspective. No longer would they try to split up students. 
“These were all of our children,” Buffington said. “We were going to take responsibility for finding a plan to help children in both districts.”
When the committee visited the county schools, Buffington saw obvious disparities and, more importantly, the opportunities that lay before him.
“They didn’t have a lot of the extracurriculars that we take for granted,” he said. “I saw they were missing out on so much — in the classroom, yes, but even extracurricular activities. They didn’t have the things they needed and deserved. It was a moral issue to me.”
Many of the county students had grown up in the shadow of Mississippi State University but never visited the campus, Buffington said. The committee wanted to change that. 
The idea for the Partnership School was born. 
Partnership Middle School in Starkville, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
The university would partner with the district to train teachers at the campus, and would give sixth and seventh graders from across the county access to a sparkling new facility and extracurricular offerings that were previously unavailable to them, like an agriculture class and piano class.  
The school, lofty and spilling with light, opened in 2020 and serves 657 students on MSU’s campus. 
When history is erased
Orlando Trainer, who served as the county representative on the local consolidation committee, saw only benefits in merging the two districts. 
County supervisor Orlando Trainer pictured at the Oktibbeha County courthouse in Starkville, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Trainer attended Starkville schools, but he and his wife, a graduate of the county schools, chose to send their daughter to Oktibbeha County schools for most of her education. Over time, Trainer saw how much help county schools needed — facilities in disrepair, limited extracurricular and academic opportunities and low student morale. 
Trainer, a county supervisor, considered the condition of the county schools as shameful, particularly with a university just a few miles away. 
“Consolidation for us was an act of redemption,” he said. “I only wish we had done it sooner.”
English teacher Kasey Underwood goes over classwork with students at Partnership Middle School in Starkville, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
But for Ellis, the longtime Oktibbeha County resident and B.L. Moor High alumna, the loss of her school still hurts.
The only buildings that closed during consolidation belonged to the county district. Today, two former county buildings remain in use — an elementary school and another that’s an alternative school for students with behavioral problems.
East Oktibbeha High School was central to the community and a hub for civic life, Ellis said, including Juneteenth celebrations, ball games, fundraisers and concerts.
East Oktibbeha High School alumni and former school staff are memorialized in Starkville, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Julius Clark, a longtime Oktibbeha County Schools administrator before the consolidation, remembers the reaction when the closures were announced. 
“Of course, everyone felt that their children were being pushed aside or thrown into something that someone else wanted,” he said. 
Though Clark wishes those schools that were closed could have stayed in the community, he eventually came to support the consolidation. That’s because it gave county students access to extracurricular activities they didn’t have at their district, such as band and choir, and access to better resources, such as modern textbooks and technology. 
“They had been missing out on everything,” Clark said. “We didn’t have recognition or opportunities because of the money. Everything was based on money, and money is based upon your student body.”
Ellis, who works on historic preservation in Oktibbeha County, acknowledges that consolidation ultimately benefitted county students, improving their academic offerings and facilities through the Partnership Middle School. But she feels the community lost something important.
“The opportunity for the community to preserve (the East Oktibbeha school) property was given away to someone outside of the community,” she said. “It’s caused a great loss.”
A number of mementos such as class photos and trophies went missing during the consolidation, Ellis said. Some were found two years ago damaged or destroyed, she said. 
Artifacts that make up a school’s history and traditions are often overlooked during consolidation, said Carrie Hahnel, a senior associate with Bellwether, a national organization that works to improve education outcomes. 
The former East Oktibbeha High School is now an event venue and boutique motel in Starkville, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayA dedication marker for East Oktibbeha County High School is in place at The Hill and Moor boutique hotel Starkville, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayRex Buffington, former chair of the consolidation committee, pictured in downtown Starkville, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayThe Oktibbeha County courthouse in Starkville, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayConstruction at Partnership Middle School in Starkville, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayPartnership Middle School in Starkville, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayTrophies are on display at Partnership Middle School in Starkville, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayStudents complete classwork at Partnership Middle School in Starkville, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayStudents complete classwork at Partnership Middle School in Starkville, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayEnglish teacher Kasey Underwood goes over classwork with students at Partnership Middle School in Starkville, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Schools with more Black students are more likely to be closed, research shows. The logic of closing a predominantly Black school and moving students to a modern, well-equipped building makes sense, Hahnel said, it’s important to understand “that facility might be in disrepair because of a history of disinvestment.” 
A consolidation lesson: Listen to locals
In one Partnership School classroom in early September, Montgomery watched as seventh graders labeled vegetables on worksheets. Outside, a garden flourished under the summer sun. A fresh basket of sky blue eggs, gathered by students, sat on the counter.
“All things are difficult before they are easy,” read a cutout on the wall, a fitting reflection on the district’s consolidation.
For Montgomery, the consolidation was the right decision, one that ultimately brought the community together.
“There is something very special about serving your entire county,” she said. “If there were hurdles and challenges, our community is better for it.”
Haley Montgomery, Starkville-Oktibbeha Consolidated School District’s director of communications, poses for a portrait at Partnership Middle School in Starkville, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
As state lawmakers consider consolidating more districts, Buffington hopes they learn from Starkville-Oktibbeha’s successes — as well as its failures.
Above all, he said, locals should lead the process.
“You should really put local people and parents, in particular, in the forefront of deciding how the consolidation can be shaped to best benefit the students,” Buffington said.
“That way the community has ownership of it,” he said, “and it’s not something that is done to them.”
Jackie Ellis walks through her former high school building, now a boutique motel and event venue in Starkville, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
For Ellis, the loss of her former school offers an important lesson: Communities should have a say in preserving their history.
On a sweltering afternoon in September, Ellis walked through the halls of her old high school, now an event space and motel. Her eyes lit up as she pointed out the gym and cafeteria.
“That school had been there for over 50 years,” she said. “It was like home to the community. It was like home to me. And that history has been erased.”

name: Washington State Standard
title: Amid legal concerns, WA suspends contribution limits for candidates and PACs
text:
The Washington state Public Disclosure Commission has suspended enforcement of a law limiting the amount of contributions to candidates and committees in the final days of the Nov. 3 election. (Photo by Alan Schein via Getty Images)Washington state’s campaign finance enforcers are allowing candidates for legislative and Supreme Court seats to spend as much of their own money on their campaigns in the final days of this election.
And the state Public Disclosure Commission is also not enforcing caps on how much money political committees not tied to a ballot measure can accept in the run-up to next week’s election.
The citizen panel voted last week to suspend enforcement of the restrictions, amid ongoing concerns that the statute may not withstand a legal challenge.
“The law has not changed,” said Natalie Johnson, spokesperson for the Public Disclosure Commission. “The commission is concerned that the law on the books is not enforceable and is telling staff to not enforce it.”
At issue is a statute that limits contributions a committee can accept or a candidate can give themself in a short but critical period of time — seven days before a primary and 21 days before a general election. It sets the bar at $75,000 for those seeking legislative seats and statewide office, and $7,500 for a political committee or candidate running for a local office. 
Limits on individual contributions to candidates are still in place. And, in the 21 days before the general election, all candidates and political committees must report contributions totaling $1,500 or more from one source within 48 hours of receiving it.
Though the commission decision was the product of a public conversation begun earlier this year, its timing so close to the Nov. 3 election vexed election professionals and political observers. Some warned it enables large sums of money to flow to political committees actively engaged in supporting and opposing candidates on Tuesday’s ballot.
Dave Ammons, a retired reporter who served on the commission from 2017-21, said he was “perplexed and troubled” by the commission action in a post on Facebook.
“The trouble with huge late infusions of money is that they can influence outcomes that may not be known until after the election,” he said. “I wouldn’t bend the knee to court challenges unless there is a direct court order in a live case.”
Such an infusion appeared to have occurred Monday when Washington Needs to Compete, a business-backed committee that’s raised in excess of $13 million, funneled $100,000 to Jobs PAC, another business-funded committee that’s spent money supporting and opposing an array of legislative candidates.
Republican consultant Chad Minnick said while there may be a handful of contributions like that, he didn’t think this suspension of limits would matter much because it occurred so late. In the future, however, political committees can prepare and strategize.
“To have much impact you need to have money a few weeks out. At this stage most of the people have made up their minds,” he said. 
Dean Nielsen, a consultant for Democratic candidates this cycle, had a similar take.
“I don’t really think it will matter a lot this year because everyone was operating under the 21-day rubric,” he said. “But I do think it will have a major application for the future.”
In acting last week, commissioners sought fairness. They wanted to avert a situation where some candidates and committees are aware contribution restrictions are not being enforced and others are not.
Conner Edwards, a campaign finance activist who has filed hundreds of complaints in recent years, said it was “unfair” the decision came more than halfway through the 21-day pre-election period.
“Whether you agree or disagree with the courts, the reality is that if someone actually fought the PDC on this issue, the PDC almost certainly would have lost,” he said. “Considering that, I think the agency probably made the right decision.”
A conundrum for the commission
The decision to not enforce can be traced to a complaint filed against a judicial candidate in 2025 by a political consulting firm whose clients include Gov. Bob Ferguson.
Snohomish County District Court Judge Tam Bui and Superior Court Judge Karen Moore were competing in a special election for Washington Court of Appeals Division I, a contest that Bui won.
On Oct. 24, 10 days before the 2025 election, Bui paid $41,000 for last-minute mailers. That triggered a complaint from Erin Schultz of NWP Consulting, the firm founded by Christian Sinderman who was the architect of Ferguson’s 2024 gubernatorial campaign.
The in-kind contribution “gives the candidate an unfair advantage during the final days of voting and undermines the transparency and integrity” of the state’s campaign finance statutes, Schultz alleged.
Bui’s lawyers pushed back, pointing out the U.S. Supreme Court in Buckley v. Valeo in 1976 struck down federal limits on candidates funding their own campaigns.
That wasn’t the only reason commission staff had concerns. In 2011, the commission lost a case in which it tried to defend limits on contributions by individuals to ballot measure committees. As a result of that setback, those committees have been exempt.
In June, when the commission dismissed the complaint against Bui, the fallibility of the law came up again. 
“This case has presented a bit of a conundrum for us as staff,” said Executive Director Peter Frey Lavallee. He suggested asking the Legislature for clarification when it next convenes.
He said the attorney general’s office refrained from opining on the constitutionality but had cautioned that “this is not a great statute to be trying to enforce.”
Nielsen was Bui’s campaign consultant and knows commissioners have struggled with what to do with the law.
“I actually did not think they would do it,” he said of suspending enforcement. “I don’t think people were clamoring for it to end. They always push for transparency and accountability, I thought they’d be stubborn until somebody sued them.”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ’s low-cost health clinics see rising demand as insurance gaps widen
text:
New Jersey’s system of free or low-cost healthcare clinics will be even more important as the impact of federal funding cuts takes hold, advocates say. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)For Franz Murat of Irvington, the idea of getting sick or hurt at work is almost too much to think about.
The 24-year-old nursing assistant has no health insurance and is still paying off the $5,000 he owed after being hospitalized last year, when he said the cold weather overwhelmed his still-new-to-the-Northeast immune system. Murat was raised in Ecuador.
“For God’s sake, I hope that never happens because I don’t have insurance to go to the hospital,” he said.
Murat, a union member with 1199SEIU United Healthcare Workers East, is far from alone. More than 9% of New Jerseyans under age 65 don’t have health insurance, a percentage experts say will grow as cost-saving measures enacted by the Trump administration take full effect. These changes have already made Obamacare plans unaffordable for many and are expected to force more than 300,000 people from NJ Family Care, the state’s Medicaid plan.
The impact of these changes, many driven by a law Trump signed in July 2025 to reduce federal spending by trillions of dollars, reflects a national trend and a growing concern for healthcare advocates, lawmakers, and state officials nationwide, including in New Jersey.
“People’s lives are stressed enough, in terms of trying to just go to work every day, earn a living, and provide for their family. Now they have to worry about what happens if someone gets sick,” Sen. Joe Vitale (D-Middlesex), the Senate health committee’s chair, said during a meeting the panel held last week.
The federal changes are expected to reduce federal funding for hospitals and doctors here by as much as $6 billion annually by the end of the decade, state officials say, and create new bureaucratic barriers for those now on NJ Family Care.
“Now we’re going to lose literally thousands of people who have enjoyed that kind of coverage, like all of us enjoy that kind of coverage. We know when we put our head on a pillow at night that we can wake up in the morning and, God forbid there’s an issue, we can gain access to care,” Vitale said.
People like Murad often depend on free or low-cost clinics for medical services, a system advocates and state officials agree will be even more important as the impact of the federal funding cuts takes hold. The newly formed New Jersey Free Clinic Association represents five established no-cost providers that treat patients in Bergen, Camden, Cape May, Monmouth, and Ocean counties.

The five free clinics depend on small paid staff, volunteer doctors and nurses, and creative partnerships with hospitals, labs, and others to offer primary and outpatient specialty care at no cost. They do not take any insurance or receive federal funding, factors experts said insulate them a bit from the pending changes.
Suzanne Dyer is executive director of the Parker Family Health Center, a free clinic in Red Bank and chair of the new association’s board. Founded 26 years ago, Parker offers pediatrics, mental health, cardiology, and more, including a dental clinic that opened this spring in conjunction with Brookdale Community College.
The association is working with the state health department and others to raise awareness around the free clinics’ work, Dyer said. They are also developing a formal referral process so hospitals and other providers know where to send uninsured patients for primary care, and a toolkit for creating new clinics, something she said is now underway in Union County.
“As residents lose their insurance, or see their premiums escalate, many will delay care, or skip preventative or routine visits altogether. They may wait until their health conditions become very serious. When this comes, patients disproportionately tend to seek care through emergency departments, which is the costliest setting,” Dyer told the Senate panel Thursday.
But the reach of free clinics is limited. Patients must live in the same county, earn less than a certain amount, and meet other qualifications to get care. At some clinics, it can take weeks to get an appointment, something healthcare leaders said is likely to get worse in months to come.
The Bergen Volunteer Medical Initiative offers free primary and specialty care in Hackensack and recently opened a second location in Garfield. The practice had about 120 people on its waiting list last month, 27 of whom are now being enrolled as patients, according to Joanne Murad, who oversees their fundraising.
The initiative’s staff expects this to grow as more people lose insurance.
“We’ve already seen an increase in applications in the pipeline,” Murad told the New Jersey Monitor.
Murad said patients frequently come for routine care and are diagnosed with chronic conditions that require additional treatment, including undiagnosed mental health issues. Services are available in multiple languages, including Spanish, Korean, and Polish, and staff members work to link patients with other medical care and support as needed.
Nationwide, there are more than 1,400 free clinics in 21 states, primarily in the South and Midwest. Pennsylvania has more than 90. New Jersey has just a handful, but there are other models of low-cost care here — programs also threatened by the federal changes.
Medina Health Center began as a free care program that matched Mercer County patients with volunteer doctors, but in 2024 it opened a physical clinic in Trenton that also accepts insurance, executive director Mira Sadeghi told the New Jersey Monitor.
Medina serves many patients who are undocumented immigrants and do not qualify for NJ Family Care, Sadeghi said. Others think they have Medicaid coverage only to discover it has lapsed, something she anticipates will be increasingly common.
“It just puts the safety net healthcare organizations in a really bad position because every time someone shows up and their Medicaid’s not working, we’re getting paid significantly less for that visit. And it’s tough on the patients that are suddenly asked to pay on a sliding scale,” Sadeghi said.
New Jersey’s network of 24 federally funded clinics faces a similar problem. These clinics provide primary and some specialty care at 130 locations around the state, accepting Medicaid and other insurance or billing patients directly based on what they earn. This network received at least $32 million from the state under the current budget, plus federal funding, and cares for some 645,000 patients.
Selina Haq, president of the New Jersey Primary Care Association, which represents these providers, told the Senate committee that despite reimbursements from the state, federally funded clinics lose $142 on average on each uninsured patient. A majority of the clinics are struggling financially, she said, and several faced bankruptcy in recent years.
Medicaid now covers three-quarters of their revenue stream, Haq said, so the more patients that lose coverage, the bigger the financial gap clinics face. She urged the state to provide more funding.
“This is going to be even more devastating for our centers,” Haq said.
The state Department of Health created a website to help residents follow the federal shifts and find care, even if they no longer have insurance. NJ for Health Care, a coalition led by consumer advocacy group NJ Citizen Action, created its own website listing free and low-cost care options.
Dr. Stephen Cha, commissioner of the state human services department, which oversees NJ Family Care, told the health committee his goal is to limit the number of eligible members who lose their Medicaid coverage. He said his team has worked to alert people about the changes through multiple mailings and outreach through community groups. The department also launched a website to help NJ Family Care members navigate the new rules.
But benefits were eliminated on Oct. 1 for more than 10,000 noncitizens when the state was unable to confirm their immigration status, he said. That number is expected to grow significantly after new rules take effect in January that require more than 500,000 of the 1.8 million members to document that they are working, volunteering, in school, or providing care for others at least 20 hours a week. These members will also have to reapply for the program every six months, instead of annually.
Cha said he remembers caring for people without insurance before the Affordable Care Act, the 2010 federal law that provided extra federal money to states to expand NJ Family Care.
“I do not want to go back,” he said.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Comstock, Hosein face off for NU Regents District 1 in Lincoln, northwest Lancaster County
text:
Brent Comstock and Dr. Jeremy Hosein, both of Lincoln, are facing off for an open seat on the NU Board of Regents. (Photos by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — A founder of an advertising and marketing firm who also does political consulting and a neurosurgeon who is a former student regent are asking for voters’ trust for an open seat on the NU Board of Regents in Lancaster County this fall.
Brent Comstock and Dr. Jeremy Hosein, both of Lincoln, are seeking to succeed University of Nebraska Regent Tim Clare. Clare won election in 2008 and ran unopposed for reelection in 2014 and 2020. NU Regents District 1 includes much of Lincoln and northwest Lancaster County — Emerald, Malcolm, Raymond, Agnew and Davey.
Both candidates say they want to focus on affordability, lead NU into its next chapter, listen to campus voices and be more active in connecting with policymakers than previous regents. Each has faced criticism over their political party registration.
The 2026 candidates for University of Nebraska Board of Regents District 1 in Lincoln: Brent Comstock, left, and Jeremy Hosein. NU Regent Tim Clare declined to seek reelection to a fourth six-year term. (Photo courtesy of the candidate/campaign | University of Nebraska Varner Hall photo by Aaron Sanderford/Nebraska Examiner)
Comstock, 31, said voters are glad to know they would have access to their regent. He’s pitched quarterly town halls to work on practical solutions for NU’s future, including affordability.
“They care about the university being a resemblance of how strong our state is,” Comstock said. “If the university is succeeding and thriving, and we’re winning academically and in the arts and athletically, it’s perceived that the state is successful and vice versa.”
Hosein, 44, the 2013-14 University of Nebraska Medical Center student regent, said he views NU as being at one of its “inflection points.” He said regents and NU leaders “don’t have time to spin our wheels here” and that every Nebraska decisionmaker will know who he is if elected.
“If we don’t have the right leaders there that are making the right types of decisions, then we risk being one of those universities where we miss that opportunity for creating that next-generation workforce that we need,” Hosein said.
Both candidates sat down with the Nebraska Examiner in Lincoln to discuss how they would approach NU’s budget, tuition, community outreach, partisanship and more if elected.
Managing the state budget
Hosein said he has heard a disconnect as regents make cuts and raise tuition while investing mostly private dollars in large construction projects, such as UNMC’s Project Health or University of Nebraska-Lincoln athletic facilities.
“I think this just doesn’t square with the math that Nebraskans have here in our district,” Hosein said. “Trying to explain that and the funding sources does not work with our population.”
Dr. Jeremy Hosein, a 2026 candidate for University of Nebraska Board of Regents District 1, hosts a university community listening session at The Post bar in Lincoln on Sept. 30, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Hosein said slowing state support for NU, as well as a major projected state deficit, will require some “bold, innovative and fresh leadership.” He said NU can’t miss an opportunity to prevent itself from “continually sleepwalking into mediocrity.” He thinks NU should break down silos across campuses and eliminate redundancy, such as consolidating leadership roles across campuses.
“Rotating that model so it’s not so top-heavy, that’s where you can find a lot of cost savings at the university,” Hosein said.
Comstock is calling for a 10-year vision for NU that could allow legislators, the governor, regents, business leaders, philanthropists and more to be on the same page and decide where to invest in and build infrastructure.
“Some people may opt out,” Comstock said. “But we owe it to the constituents and to the voters, Democrats, Republicans, people that always vote, people that are disenfranchised from voting, we owe it to them to come together after this election and say, ‘this is where we want our state to go.’”
If tuition increases are a “lever” in that plan, “we cross that bridge, and we get there,” Comstock said. He said NU’s trajectory needs to be future-looking and growth-oriented.
Comstock said he would rather have consistency, even if that’s smaller year-to-year bumps, over volatility in the state budget for NU. He said he’s in favor of getting appropriators, the governor and NU on the same page about what would be needed for further investments.
“I like competition. I like to win,” Comstock said. “I think that we should be held to a standard, but that standard needs to be known, publicly known.”
Tuition, fees and affordability
Comstock, an Auburn native, said he is an example of a homegrown Nebraskan who wanted to go to NU. However, affordability and an out-of-state scholarship led him to North Carolina.
“Like a lot of people, I packed up and left, but there are so many people, myself included, who, when given the opportunity, would run towards that opportunity,” Comstock said.
Brent Comstock of Lincoln, candidate for University of Nebraska Board of Regents District 1, hosts a listening session with university employees at a coffee shop in Lincoln on Sept. 26, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Hosein said at NU’s current tuition rates — even if competitive in the Big Ten — he’s not sure his parents, an enlisted airman and a homemaker, could have afforded NU. He got his undergraduate degree from New York University and completed a pre-med graduate program at UNL before graduating from UNMC.
“Whether you’re 18 or you’re in your 50s, you should be able to pursue your dreams,” Hosein said.
Comstock said nearly half of the hundreds of parents he’s spoken to whose children also ended up leaving were “retainable,” yet other universities “headhunted” and recruited them first.
Hosein has pitched a “name, image and likeness” model for academics, bringing that incentive for recruiting student-athletes to “all-star” students, faculty and researchers. He is also interested in creating a greater bond between academics and athletics, such as a model from Vanderbilt where a donation on the academic side could lead to athletic benefits for donors.
The role of a regent
Comstock said NU needs to be a place where every student feels welcome. He said it’s not NU’s job or the job of a regent to tell someone what political party to belong to or to convince them that their personal opinion is right.
He said recruiting more international and out-of-state students could help with NU’s budget, because those students could earn a quality education at a slightly higher price than in-state students.
“The role of the regents, I do believe, is to be a good steward of the university,” Comstock said, “and even if it’s not politically popular with either side of the aisle, to say we stand up for students, faculty and staff, whether you are a Nebraskan or out of state, whether you are a person of color or not, whether you are gay, or trans, or straight, you belong here.”
Dr. Jeremy Hosein of Lincoln, a candidate for University of Nebraska Board of Regents District 1, talks with voters at the Harvest Moon Festival hosted by the Asian Community and Cultural Center in Lincoln on Sept. 28, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Hosein said campus should be welcoming, which he said means getting back to NU’s primary mission of education and personal and professional development. He said that parents shouldn’t fear their children’s political thoughts will be influenced, and that a student’s time at NU will offer a place where they can think freely. 
He said NU should be agnostic to someone’s faith or the color of their skin and be “institutionally neutral.”
“I don’t think that’s a violation of academic freedom,” Hosein said at a Sept. 30 listening session. “I think it’s a fundamental tenet of professionalism.”
An ad agency and political consultant
Hosein and Comstock have each faced partisan pushback for their ties to Republicans, in the case of Hosein, or Democrats, in the case of Comstock. Hosein is a registered Republican while Comstock is a registered nonpartisan.
Brent Comstock of Lincoln, a candidate for University of Nebraska Board of Regents District 1, attends the Harvest Moon Festival hosted by the Asian Community and Cultural Center in Lincoln on Sept. 28, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Comstock’s firm, BCom Solutions, works with corporations, chambers of commerce, rural health organizations, energy companies, nonprofits and capital campaigns for crisis prevention centers. It also does work with candidates, most Democrats but a few Republicans.
“If you have a conflict of interest, you disclose it, and then you move forward from it,” Comstock said. “But I’ve knocked on tens of thousands of doors, and not a single person has asked me about any conflict of interest that seemingly the other side spends a lot of time talking about.”
Hosein has said Nebraska deserves “better” than a political consultant in the office, and he’s alluded to concerns about Comstock’s nonpartisan party registration and “authenticity.”
“If you don’t have a relationship with our federal delegation or a statewide delegation, then you are in essence unable to fulfill the mission, and then you become more a talking head than an actual effectuator of outcomes,” Hosein said.
Comstock has worked on campaigns for former President Joe Biden, former Vice President Kamala Harris and various state and federal candidates nationwide. 
The boundaries of University of Nebraska Board of Regents District 1 in Lancaster County. (Photo courtesy of Nebraska Legislative Research Office)
For the 2025-26 election cycle, according to state records, BCom has been paid $321,000 by former Democratic state Sen. Lynne Walz of Fremont, who is challenging Gov. Jim Pillen, and $119,000 by state Sen. John Fredrickson of Omaha, a Democrat who is running for reelection.
BCom has received $3.6 million this election cycle federally, according to the Federal Election Commission. The top three FEC clients are the WelcomePAC, which supports center-left candidates ($378,000); the Blue Dog PAC, which supports center-to-center-right fiscal Democrats ($364,000); and Democratic Rep. James Walkinshaw of Virginia ($212,000). BCom has also worked with the Democratic parties of Virginia ($194,000), Alaska ($125,000), Nebraska ($98,000) and New Hampshire ($72,000) this election cycle.
But Comstock countered that he’s endorsed by Republican and Democratic regents, past and present, and that his organization employs people of all political stripes.
“I’m not worried about it because I know how to build relationships with people and my business is not running for Board of Regents,” Comstock said.
A policy adviser
Comstock’s campaign has criticized Hosein’s endorsers and financial backers, including Pillen and U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts, compared to more cross-partisan endorsers for Comstock.
“He claims to believe in bipartisanship, but he’s backed by a roster of partisan politicians and even campaigns as a ‘runs red Republican,’” a Comstock ad states.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates and the tools you need to cast your vote in Nebraska’s Nov. 3 general election, including NU Regents District 1.]
Hosein said his endorsements reflect those who have confidence in his judgment, character and ability to get the job done, not that he necessarily shares or agrees with all their views. Asked how he would be independent, he said, “It’s who I’ve always been, and it’s who I continue to be.” He noted that his wife, Dawn, is a Democrat and has supported him in the race.
“This isn’t a Unitarian executive position. It is working within a team to move the ball forward, and who has a greater chance to do that for a faculty than someone who has the ability to work with our elected policymakers to make that change happen?” Hosein said.
Hosein previously worked as a policy adviser to former Nebraska Govs. Mike Johanns and Dave Heineman, and he was selected for a prestigious, competitive White House fellowship during President Donald Trump’s first term. 
Comstock’s campaign has also sought to criticize the White House work as working on “presidential priorities” tied to Trump.
During the fellowship, Hosein said, he worked on nonpartisan priorities like kidney health, drug pricing, surprise billing and vaccines in Colombia related to the Venezuelan refugee crisis. The fellowships are awarded on a “strictly non-partisan basis” and often include military personnel prohibited from engaging in political activities.
“I trust the voters to decipher through that messaging. I really do,” Hosein said of criticisms.
Closing messages
Comstock said his elevator pitch to the NU community is that the university is Nebraska’s most important public institution and that he’ll listen to faculty, staff, students and constituents broadly, not because it’s a campaign slogan or talking point but because he believes in it.
“I think that we have a gem of a university system, and we need to do everything we can to protect it.”
Hosein said NU is facing an unprecedented “crisis” and the stakes are high. He said the most difficult challenges aren’t the budget but a “fundamental doubt about the power of higher education to transform lives.”
“I think selecting people with character and integrity and honesty, but more importantly, a workable vision,” Hosein said, “I think that’s what the university needs at this moment.”
The election is Nov. 3. Early voting is underway.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Commentary: On Nov. 3, the fight for democracy moves to the ballot box
text:
(Matthew Perschall/Louisiana Illuminator).In these midterm elections, let us ensure that the people’s voice — the most vital part of governing our republic — survives all the attacks at the state and national level that have been waged to weaken or silence it.
One of the most brazen act of aggression occurred on January 6, 2021, when a mob attacked the U.S. Capitol to prevent Congress from certifying the results of the 2020 presidential election. The mob was mobilized by the false and unsubstantiated claims that the presidential election had been stolen.
The conspiracy theories, blatant lies, misinformation and disinformation seem to have an endless life.
Despite repeated court defeats for efforts to overturn the election results, the  attacks on voting rights have continued.
Much has happened in full view. The Trump administration has sought to change election rules, including requiring proof of citizenship to register to vote and restricting mail-in voting. The FBI also seized 2020 election records in Georgia’s Fulton County.
Many other actions have been taken that didn’t make the headlines. They have included trying to usurp state and local control of elections, threatening officials who have spent their careers keeping elections free and honest, and overall undermining voting rights as protected by the U.S. Constitution.
Then there is the looming threat that the National Guard, some other military or para-military presence may be deployed to or around polling places during the upcoming midterm election, which is against federal law.
In recent years, many states have enacted laws restricting voting access. Since 2020, at least 31 states have adopted such measures, including tighter voter ID requirements and limits on mail-in voting.
What changes do you see in Missouri?
Missouri tightened its photo ID requirements in 2022, though the same law also allowed two weeks of no-excuse, in-person absentee voting.
Missouri voters face a different fight over citizen initiatives: whether legislators should be able to make it harder to put proposals on the ballot or overturn laws voters have approved.
Given what hangs in the balance both in Missouri and nationally, voting in these midterm elections is critically important. Our performance at the polls can send the message of a resounding victory if we are willing to show up for the fight by casting our vote no matter what.
Our vote or failure to vote will count. We cannot afford to remain on the sidelines.
It is not a cliché but an axiom: Election results have consequences. We live them daily in one form or the other.
Many of us will be eagerly and anxiously awaiting the election returns on Nov. 3, even in the hours and days afterwards — not only for who or what initiatives win in our city, county and state, but what has occurred in places across the country to garner some idea of what we can expect for the governance of our nation.
Now is not the time to be gullible, nor forget what the last few years have been like. Whether we have been in an environment of progress, pride and hopefulness for the direction in which our city, state and nation seem to be headed.
With all the effort to defeat or negate the people’s participation in how we are governed, these efforts need not win.
A lot is riding on our battle readiness and performance.
Our votes in these midterm elections will make the difference.
Are we ready to show up for duty?

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Federal government sues state over Idaho National Laboratory water rights
text:
An Idaho National Laboratory sign stands at the exit to the desert site during spring 2023. Much of INL’s research and experimental work supports the development of advanced nuclear technology, integrated energy systems and national security. (Photo courtesy of the U.S. Department of Energy)The federal government has filed a lawsuit against the state of Idaho, seeking to block the state from curtailing water use at Idaho National Laboratory and from administering federal water rights, court records indicate.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
On Sept. 11, the U.S. government filed a lawsuit against the state, the Idaho Department of Water Resources and Idaho Department of Water Resources Director Mathew Weaver in U.S. District Court. 
Arguing that the federal government has supremacy over the states, the lawsuit seeks to throw out a water curtailment order that would apply to Idaho National Laboratory and block the department and Weaver from administering any federal water rights in Idaho in the future.
There is also a legal question over whether the case should be heard in federal court or in state court. 
For purposes of the case, water curtailment means shutting off the water completely.
“Through the order, and (Idaho Department of Water Resources’) program of administering water rights, defendants are attempting to directly regulate federal agencies,” the lawsuit states. “However, federal installations are shielded by the supremacy clause from direct state regulation, unless Congress has provided clear and unambiguous authorization for such regulation.”
In a response submitted Oct. 16, attorneys for the state of Idaho denied the allegations in the federal government’s lawsuit and countersued the federal government. 
Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador said the U.S. Department of Energy and Idaho National Laboratory should have to follow the same water laws as any other water user in Idaho. 
Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador. (Photo courtesy of Attorney General Raúl Labrador)
“Water is the lifeblood of Idaho, and my office will protect the water rights of Idahoans who depend on it,” Attorney General Raúl Labrador said in a written statement Tuesday. “Our sovereign authority to administer those rights has been established for more than 100 years, and it applies to every water user in this state, including the federal government. The federal government gets no special treatment under Idaho law. We will work with federal agencies to meet their needs, but we will not sacrifice the water rights of Idaho farmers, ranchers, and families to do it.”
In their response to the federal lawsuit, state attorneys wrote that the feds’ lawsuit, “threatens injury to other decreed water rights, and threatens to fundamentally undermine the state’s sovereign authority to allocate and administer Idaho’s waters according to Idaho water law.”
Idaho Gov. Brad Little’s office also put out a statement saying Little will protect Idaho water resources.
“Gov. Little has a strong track record of fighting for Idaho’s water sovereignty, and he will continue to put Idaho first,” the governor’s office said in a written statement Tuesday. “The state of Idaho continues to work responsibly with the Department of Energy toward a mitigation plan that meets everyone’s needs and protects Idaho’s water resources.”
The stakes in the case appear to be high.
“This disputed issue is ripe for resolution because resolution of the issue will affect the administration of every other decreed water right in the coalition delivery call proceedings – both state law-based water rights and federal reserved water rights,” state attorneys wrote. 
With Idaho and much of the West experiencing drought and climate change, water is a precious resource in Idaho that farmers and water users have fought over for decades. 
Meanwhile, Idaho National Laboratory is ramping up nuclear projects at its 890-square mile complex in eastern Idaho and discussing adding data centers.
Idaho is also one of the finalist states to host a new U.S. Department of Energy Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus, though officials have not said where the campus might be built, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. 
 Why is the federal government suing Idaho’s state government?

According to court documents, the U.S. Department of Energy holds a water right in the amount of 35,000 acre-feet annually in Idaho. 



Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



An acre-foot is a unit of volume that expresses how much water it would take to cover one acre of land in water that is one foot deep. For comparison, one acre is a little bit smaller than a football field. 
The issue came to a head in May when Weaver issued an order curtailing water rights established after Oct. 11, 1900.
Idaho’s water laws are governed by a seniority-based framework. Simply put, when there is not enough water to go around, the oldest, or senior, water rights have priority over the newer, or junior, water rights. 
If the director of the Idaho Department of Water Resources determines that the junior water rights holders are injuring senior water rights holders by taking water that the senior water rights holders have a right to, then the director can issue a curtailment order cutting off the water for junior water rights holders. 
Under the terms of a 2024 state water settlement agreement, water users can protect themselves from water curtailment by joining a ground water district and participating in an approved mitigation plan, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. 
The U.S. Department of Energy did join the Big Lost River Ground Water District to participate in mitigation and protect itself from curtailment, but only joined for the 2026 water year, court records indicate. 
However, through the lawsuit, the federal government is challenging Idaho’s ability to enforce those water rights. 
“The (curtailment) order, and Idaho’s statutory scheme which authorized it, unconstitutionally and unlawfully seeks to require the United States’ participation in a state administrative proceeding for which the United States has not waived its sovereign immunity, and to directly regulate federal agencies contrary to the supremacy and property clauses of the United States Constitution and the principle of federal sovereign immunity,” the federal government’s lawsuit reads.
The federal government said there could be safety, economic and energy consequences if the state shuts off the U.S. Department of Energy’s water for Idaho National Laboratory.
“Curtailment of INL’s water right would disrupt this national nuclear energy momentum,” the lawsuit states.
“Forcing these facilities to curtail operations poses nuclear safety risks and would halt research support for the Navy’s nuclear-powered warships and commercial advanced reactor licensing,” the lawsuit continued.

name: WyoFile
title: Protect our vote: An open letter to our governor, secretary of state and attorney general
authors: Marguerite Herman, Rob Davidson, Barbara Chase, and Andrea Knutson
text:
Dear Gov. Mark Gordon, Secretary of State Chuck Gray and Attorney General Keith Kautz,
Before taking office, each of you swore an oath to support, protect and defend the constitutions of the U.S. and Wyoming. Both documents make clear that state and local officials, not the federal government, run and administer elections.

Opinion

We write to you as everyday Wyomingites. Three of us have served as election judges in numerous election cycles, and we can attest to the security and integrity of our state’s elections. We also write to you as members of Powder River Basin Resource Council, a group of people whose views span the ideological spectrum. Across our political differences, we come together around a shared commitment to the democratic principles and practices that give Wyomingites the power to determine our shared future. Nothing is more fundamental to that power than every eligible voter’s right to cast a ballot free of intimidation and interference, and to have that ballot counted.
We invite each of you to join us in this shared commitment to free and democratic elections by issuing a statement before Election Day that assures Wyomingites that you have full confidence in our state’s elections, election administrators and election results. Further, we ask that you state clearly that you will, if need be, use the power of your office to stand up to any outside political effort, including from the federal government, that seeks to disrupt the coming elections and intimidate voters and election workers, which would violate both constitutions you swore an oath to. 
Our request reflects an increasingly clear need for state officials to make such a statement. The federal government has already made numerous attempts this year to meddle in elections. One such attempt occurred right here in Wyoming during our primary elections, when U.S. Department of Justice observers appeared at a polling location in Cheyenne, trying to interview voters and access voting machines. They acted in ways that Gov. Gordon described as “aggressive, unexpected, disruptive — certainly didn’t seem to show respect for the state.” Laramie County Clerk Debra Lee said the DOJ observers showed a “complete disregard for our state laws and administration of our elections.”
“I feel very strongly about the federal government coming in and taking our guns — I don’t like that,” Gordon said. “And I don’t like the federal government coming in and taking our votes, either.”
We applaud and thank the governor for making this statement, and we ask that he issue another statement before the elections warning the federal government to stay out of our elections and reiterating his commitment to protecting our vote.
Gov. Mark Gordon speaks during the opening plenary of the Education Commission of the States’ 2026 National Forum on Education Policy on Wednesday, July 10, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Patrick Siebert/Office of Maryland Gov. Wes Moore)
Among Republican leaders who have stood up to federal meddling in state elections is Utah Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson, the state’s chief election official who has refused to comply with a DOJ order to hand over the state’s entire, unredacted voter database. Henderson has rightly argued that the order has no federal legal basis and violates Utah data privacy laws. Even as she now faces a lawsuit from the DOJ, which a federal judge dismissed last week and the DOJ quickly vowed to appeal, she has held fast to the oath she took to the U.S. and Utah constitutions. 
“Utahns can be assured that my office will always follow the Constitution and the law, protect voters’ rights, and administer free and fair elections,” Henderson said in response to the DOJ lawsuit. 
Also worthy of applause is Attorney General Kautz, who, alongside his Republican counterparts in Idaho, North Dakota, Utah and 11 other states, refused to back the president’s anti-mail-in voting executive order, knowing the chaos it would unleash and the federal interference it would enable in their states’ elections. We also thank him for his legal opinion released  this week that states that any monitors the department sends to Wyoming’s polling locations must remain outside, 100 yards from the polls and must not interview voters without their consent, in accordance with state law. Lee says the DOJ has informed her they will comply with that opinion.
At a time when the president himself has urged his supporters to “cheat like hell” in the coming elections, and the Department of Justice has told Wyoming it will again have observers at our polls, we sincerely hope that Secretary of State Gray finds the courage and leadership that the governor and attorney general have exemplified. We hope that all three of you issue a public statement before the election that shows or confirms your shared commitment to protecting our vote and are united in holding the DOJ accountable to the agreement it made to respect Wyoming’s voting laws.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: In Idaho, independent political polls are rare ahead of elections. Here’s why.
text:
Voters cast their ballots in the May 19, 2026, primary election at Emerson High School in Idaho Falls. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)How competitive is the race to represent Idaho in the U.S. Senate? It depends which poll you look at.
According to a poll released last week by the campaign for Todd Achilles, an independent running for U.S. Senate, Republican incumbent Jim Risch has only a six-point lead over Achilles. Eight percent of voters were undecided, the poll found.
The poll buoyed a claim by the Achilles campaign: Victory could be within reach. 
State Rep. Todd Achilles speaks from the House floor on the morning of March 10, 2025, at the Idaho Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
“That tight margin confirms what we’re hearing in every corner of Idaho: voters are tired of career politicians controlled by their party bosses,” Achilles, 58, said in a statement with the poll’s release on Oct. 23.
But the latest poll didn’t ask about support for the other two candidates in the race, which has drawn one of the most active attempts in years at unseating Risch, 83, who’s seeking a fourth, six-year-term. And Risch’s campaign polling — featuring the full line up of candidates — shows him pummeling Achilles.
In the run up to Election Day in a state without much independent polling, that’s the sort of divide in polling outcomes that some pollsters expect voters to see.
“Usually about this time, the candidates or the campaigns for ballot issues are publishing polls that show you that they’re going to win,” Stuart Elway, a longtime independent pollster in Washington state, said in an interview. 
In Idaho, independent political polls — which aren’t backed by a campaign or a special interest group — are hard to come by. They would offer a different perspective, Elway said. 
Stuart Elway, a retired longtime independent pollster in Washington state, speaks to journalists ahead of the 2023 legislative session in Washington. (Photo courtesy of Stuart Elway)
“An independent poll that’s not sponsored by any party or candidate or interest group gives you an objective measure of how the election is going, and I think more importantly, what the people are thinking about when they’re thinking about the election,” he said. 
Some polling experts say that Idaho lacks independent polls because the state is reliably Republican controlled, and independent pollsters aren’t willing to invest the high funds needed to conduct reliable polling. 
Instead, there are candidate and special interest groups polling in Idaho, like the back and forth of polls released by the campaigns of Risch and Achilles. 
The poll released last week by Achilles’ campaign, conducted by VoteNexus, had info on other races — including 54% opposition for Proposition 1, a ballot initiative to end Idaho’s strict abortion ban. In other key races, like for governor, and two U.S. House seats, Republicans were in the lead. The survey, conducted via online polls sent by text message of 700 likely Idaho voters, had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.5 percentage points. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 So, what makes for a good poll in politics?

How pollsters set up their surveys, from the questions they ask and the order they ask them in, is critical. That’s because certain wording or prefaces can push people toward certain answers. 
But there’s also a host of other survey design decisions to consider, such as whether the poll was done using a preselected online sample, which can have biases, or was done by phone calls, the most traditional method, or other avenues. 
Where are the debates? Idaho incumbents largely forgo debates and forums this year. 

If you’re looking at a poll yourself, you’ll also want to make sure that the survey is telling you its margin of error. That’s a value that tells you how much pollsters think that the results they reported could differ from the public’s actual opinions on the issues. Without that, a poll is “suspect,” said University of Idaho political science department chair Florian Justwan. 
Part of the draw of independent pollsters is, in theory, you have a firm without a vested interest in the issue gathering information. But good polling can be done by groups that have a perspective on an issue or candidate, said Jeffrey Lyons, Boise State University political science professor. 
“I would be hesitant to universally say ‘These polls, like issue group polls, are bad, or you can’t interpret them,’ because I don’t think that’s the case. I think they can be valuable. You just have to be a little careful with them,” he said. “And the same goes for polls done by political campaigns. … There’s a lot of questions to ask about that and what we can do with that information. For example, how many other polls did they do where they didn’t like the numbers and they just didn’t release them, right? So if they’re releasing the poll, they obviously like what they see.”
Campaigns also don’t benefit that much from inaccurate polling, said Lauren Goldstein, principal researcher at Change Research, which polled for independent Idaho gubernatorial candidate John Stegner’s campaign.
“While there might be some differences in goals and incentives of polls that are conducted by independent media outlets versus commissioned by campaigns, at the end of the day, accuracy is paramount for all purposes,” she said in an interview.
Another big hurdle for election polling is trying to ensure that the people they are surveying are actually going to turn out to vote in the election. To determine whether someone is a likely voter, pollsters may use different methods. One method might, Justwan said, count everyone who took the poll and voted in the last three elections, but another might just count anyone who indicates they will likely vote in the next election.
That’s part of the trouble in comparing the results of election polls.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
“Using these different filters as a way to remove all non-likely voters from the sample, depending on what your filter is, is going to give you very different responses,” Justwan said. 
Polling has also gotten a lot more difficult and expensive since the advent of cell phones and the shift away from landline phones, pollsters say.
But polls aren’t only helpful for horserace election coverage; they’re for understanding the public’s attitudes. 
The Idaho Public Policy Survey, conducted every year by Boise State University, releases information about how Idahoans feel about a range of issues, including their top policy priorities for the Legislature to address. The last iteration of the survey — which featured responses from 1,000 people, half of whom were through phone calls — cost $46,500, said Matthew May, the survey research director at Boise State’s School of Public Service. 
In the backdrop, many members of the public are losing faith in the polls, a decade after 2016 polls mispredicted that President Donald Trump would lose his first general election for the presidency. A national poll released in August by Rasmussen Reports found that half of voters don’t trust most polls about politics.
Lyons, with Boise State, acknowledged the huge gap in the results between Risch and Achilles’ polls. But he said he’d looked closely at the polls released in August and saw them as trying to do things differently. 
“I don’t view the two polls as being like they did the same thing and came to a different answer,” he said. “I tend to view them as more like they did different things and came to a different answer.”
 Are Achilles and Risch in a heated race for an Idaho US Senate seat?

In August, the Achilles campaign released results from an internal poll that made it seem like he has a chance against Risch. When likely voters were asked who they’d vote for, almost a third chose Achilles. Here’s how that broke down at the time:

Risch: 34%
Achilles: 30%
Matt Loesby, a Libertarian Party candidate: 4%
And unsure: 32%
*the fine print: The survey had a margin of error rate of plus or minus 3.97 percent, indicating how much actual public opinion could vary from the survey results it reports out. It sampled 608 likely voters. 

That poll — and the candidate options listed — was different from how Risch’s campaign pollster conducted its. For one, Achilles’ campaign’s pollster relied on largely text and online responses to the poll, rather than phone calls, the more traditional, but expensive polling method. And Achilles’ campaign’s poll didn’t include another independent candidate in the race, Natalie Fleming.
Achilles’ campaign manager Crispin Gravatt said in an email that the campaign was focusing on the big picture when asked about not including Fleming’s name on the candidate list.
“If we had unlimited time and resources, we would measure every possible combination and dozens of topics in the state [as I’m sure every data nerd would like!],” Gravatt said. “We do believe the trends in polling provide more insight than any individual poll- our polls and other polls we have seen show Todd’s voter share growing in Idaho, while even Jim Risch’s published polls show him losing steam.”
Brett Lloyd, head of the Bullfinch Group that conducted the survey for Achilles, said the only questions that came before poll respondents before they were asked who they’d vote for were typical demographic and screening questions.
Risch’s campaign, in a poll released days later in August, sought to clear the air. It found support for Risch was much higher:

Risch: 52%
Achilles: 18%
Fleming: 9%
Loesby: 2%
None: 1%
*the fine print: The survey had a margin of error rate of plus or minus 4 percent, indicating how much actual public opinion could vary from the survey results it reports out. It sampled 500 likely voters through phone interviews.

U.S. Sen. Jim Risch, R-Idaho, delivers remarks during the Virginia-class nuclear-powered fast-attack submarine USS Idaho’s commissioning ceremony at Naval Submarine Base New London in Groton, Connecticut, on April 25, 2026. Idaho is the newest fast-attack submarine and the fifth U.S. Navy vessel named for the Gem State. (Photo by Chief Mass Communication Specialist Darren M. Moore/U.S. Navy)
The pollster behind Risch’s survey, Erik Iverson who leads Peak Insights, did not release the question itself, or the full question list, which pollsters say is important to see to understand if pollsters might have pushed likely voters to respond in ways they might not have without a nudge. Iverson said only screening type questions, such as people’s likelihood of voting and favorable images of various candidates, came before the question of who they’ll vote for in the Senate race. 
“Our polling is not designed to shape any sort of a public narrative. It has one singular focus, and Sen. Risch has always been very clear about this,” Iverson said in an interview. “‘I need the most accurate polling possible so that we can develop a detailed campaign plan. We know exactly what we need to do, where we need to spend our money, and then go execute it.’”
A poll commissioned by Risch’s campaign conducted Sept. 28-30 found that Risch was still in the lead, but his support fell to 49%, and Achilles’ rose to 24%.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: In Tennessee, church mobilization efforts send message that voting rights attack is unacceptable
text:
A group marched from Edgehill United Methodist Church in Nashville to a early voting site as part of a weekend "Souls to the Polls" voting event. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)A crowd of no more than 20 at Souls to the Polls in Bordeaux, a traditionally Black North Nashville community, prayed with Rev. Paula Smith, who invoked the memory of voting rights activists and their sacrifice 60 years ago.
About half the crowd were organizers or co-sponsors of the event on Saturday. Even fewer had yet to vote, which is what the longstanding tradition in historically Black churches is meant to counteract. 
“We remember those who were beaten, threatened, jailed and even killed because they dared to believe that every person deserves a voice in shaping the future of this nation,” Smith, pastor of Gordon Memorial United Methodist Church (UMC), said in an opening prayer. 
That history is more pertinent this year after the U.S. Supreme Court gutted a key provision of the Voting Rights Act of 1965. Then, the state’s Republican supermajority legislature redistricted Tennessee’s only majority-Black congressional district in Memphis. 
“There’s a lot at stake. There are a lot of attempts to silence different perspectives and views,” resident Dara Ogelsby said at Souls to the Polls. “We are here to still be heard.” 
“We remember those who were beaten, threatened, jailed and even killed because they dared to believe that every person deserves a voice in shaping the future of this nation,” said Rev. Paula Smith, pastor of Gordon Memorial United Methodist Church in Nashville during a Saturday get-out-the-vote rally. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
Though Ogelsby already voted, she still thought it was important to attend. Her pastor, Rev. Perry Wiggins III, spoke at the event and their church is involved with Nashville Organized for Action and Hope (NOAH), which organized the march. When they arrived at the Bordeaux library polling location, members of Alpha Phi Alpha, a Black men’s fraternity, were also there for a voting block party. 
However, the lower turnout at Souls to the Polls illustrates a tension that pastors of historically Black congregations and other community organizers are observing. This November is an opportunity to send a message that the reversal of voting rights protections is unacceptable. Yet, the same barriers to voter awareness and education persist. 
“It could be the level of steepness of the mountain is so high that although we’re doing good, we’re not doing great,” Rev. Earle Fisher, Senior Pastor of Abyssinian Baptist Church in Memphis, said. “There are people who are motivated because they were angered by what happened in the state legislature several months ago. And I would like to believe our activism and advocacy is going to have a concrete impact on the ground.”
Fisher, who also leads a Memphis nonprofit for voter engagement and education, said he helped organize a recent Souls to the Polls in Memphis that was well-attended. Also, early voting turnout in Shelby County as of Oct. 22 was 70% higher than it was in 2022, according to recent state data. 
Still, Fisher said he feels like the enthusiasm and anger in response to the redistricting has “tapered off” since the August primaries. He’s gone as far as to identify precincts with historically low voter turnout and churches in those precincts. Then, Fisher touches base with pastors of those churches to urge them to host a town hall, Souls to the Polls, or a phone-banking event. 



Quotation







There are people who are motivated because they were angered by what happened in the state legislature several months ago. And I would like to believe our activism and advocacy is going to have a concrete impact on the ground.


– Don't forget to add author


Rep. Harold Love, a Nashville Democrat who has a foot in both worlds as both a lawmaker and a pastor, recently gave presentations on voter mobilization to a ministry for senior citizens and older adults and to a separate gathering of area clergy.
Rev. Perry Wiggins III, spoke at Saturday’s Souls to the Polls event. His church, Alameda Christian Church, is involved with Nashville Organized for Action and Hope, NOAH, which organized the march. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
 In both instances, he emphasized the importance of deputizing church members who are already registered to inform a “second wave” — be it children, grandchildren or neighbors — about the importance of doing the same. 
“If you think about it, isn’t that the same process that is used in the spreading of the gospel? I’m giving the members what the Lord gave me,” Love, pastor of Lee Chapel African Methodist Episcopal (AME) Church in Nashville, said. “They leave from here and they disseminate that information to those who may not be members of the church but are close to members of the church.”
A study that Love received from the nonprofit Black Voters Matter Fund showed that voters ages 50 and older, who are often more regular churchgoers, need less of a push to go vote, some motivated by the memory of their parents and grandparents who marched for the right during the Civil Rights Movement. Meanwhile, voters ages 18-49 are willing to vote insofar as they have information and a plan to go to the polls. 
Just as Love relied on different partner agencies to help with his presentation to different community groups, Dallas pastor Rev. Mike Waters said, “The work of the church does not end with the benediction.”
The Ride: Dallas pastor Rev. Mike Waters operates a nationwide tour that traces the steps of Freedom Riders. Waters brought the tour to Nashville on Sunday. (Photo: Liam Adams for Tennessee Lookout)
Waters is spearheading a nationwide tour called The Ride, which traces the steps of the Freedom Riders of 1961 and that made a stop in Nashville on Sunday. The group joined a service at Jefferson Street Missionary Baptist Church in Nashville. There, they handed out cards with information about the local history of the Freedom Riders and about early voting in Tennessee. Also, they invited Jefferson Street congregants to use markers to sign their names on one of the buses that the troupe is traveling on, emblazoned with, “When justice is loud, faith cannot whisper.”
In addition to churches, The Ride has gone to college campuses and set up a booth in the middle of Washington D.C, Waters said. “We need to connect with people in other places and spaces where they are gathered, where they are present. To invite them into the process,” he added. 
There are other examples of leaders of historically Black churches and denominations, several of which are headquartered in Nashville and Memphis, following in the footsteps of their predecessors — some of whom played key roles in civil rights demonstrations that helped secure the Voting Rights Act of 1965. 
To Fisher, that zeal is genuine. But achieving measurable change entails grueling work, like his recent effort to identify precincts with historically low turnout. That won’t change overnight.
“The concrete challenge is going to be what does it take to get the coalition of the willing to stay committed long enough to have a 10- or 15-year plan,” Fisher said. “And stop trying to scramble at the 11th hour every election cycle.”
