name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Groups push Gov. Landry to address Big Oil’s orphan wells
text:
Contractors with the Louisiana Department of Conservation and Energy's Oilfield Site Restoration plug an orphaned well. (Photo by Louisiana Department of Conservation and Energy)A coalition of environmental groups is asking the governor to address the risks of orphan wells, citing a new report detailing thousands of abandoned drilling sites throughout the state.
The groups sent a letter to the governor Monday asking if he would meet with them to discuss his vision for tackling what they see as a looming threat to the state’s vulnerable coastal areas and the ecosystems they host. 
“Louisiana should not have to clean up messes that are connected to some of the world’s richest oil corporations,” Rachel Mathews, a senior attorney at the Center for Biological Diversity, said in a news release detailing the letter sent to the governor. 
The letter references a new analysis Mathews authored. Other groups that co-signed the letter to Landry are the Deep South Center for Environmental Justice, For a Better Bayou, Habitat Recovery Project, Healthy Gulf, Louisiana Wildlife Federation, Mossville Environmental Action Network and Vessel Project of Louisiana. 
Mathews cites data from the LSU Center for Energy Studies that places the number of orphan wells in Louisiana at more than 6,300, up from 4,900 orphan wells in March 2025. They include at least 724 in state coastal waters that major oil companies once owned, with some having changed hands through acquisitions. 
“Orphan wells are those whose current operators are unwilling or unable to plug them — leaving the state responsible for them,” the groups’ letter reads. “Louisiana has never been able to reduce its orphan well population because the number of wells that oil companies abandon to the state is far outpacing the state’s ability to plug them.”
The governor’s office did not respond to requests for comment on the groups’ letter or their request to meet with Landry.   
The state government’s approach to oil well abandonment involves a financial commitment exploration firms are required to make before they obtain a state drilling permit. The companies must submit written proof that they have the resources to permanently shut down the well they are drilling, with costs averaging $113,000 per well according to a Louisiana Legislative Auditor calculation. Using that figure, it would cost nearly $712 million to plug all of the state’s current orphan wells.
It’s up to the state Department of Conservation and Energy to tackle orphan wells that the companies abandon. The agency permanently plugs about 125 sites a year, according to LSU data cited in the report. At that pace, it would take more than 50 years to erase the current backlog without any new orphan wells being added. 
The state had between $126 million and $250 million in combined state and federal money to put toward orphan well abatement as of July 2025, according to LSU research.
Department of Conservation and Energy officials were not available for comment before the deadline for the report.
An analysis from the Center for Biological Diversity found there are 3,231 inactive wells and 509 orphan wells within the boundaries of the Barataria-Terrebonne Estuary. (Illustration by Center for Biological Diversity)
The groups’ letter highlights what they see as an acute orphan well problem in the Barataria-Terrebonne estuary, which lies between the Mississippi and Atchafalaya rivers and touches 16 parishes. The area is home to 509 orphan wells and 3,231 that are inactive, a status that typically means the cost to operate and maintain the well exceeds the value that can be extracted from it. 
There are more than 22,000 inactive wells across the state. Oil and gas companies are only required to pay the state a few hundred dollars in annual fees for each one they take offline. The environmental groups say the system fails to encourage the industry to permanently plug their dormant wells, some of which sit inactive for decades with no indication they will be put back in production.
“If Louisiana is ever going to get ahead of this problem, it must focus on getting oil companies to comply with their obligations to plug the wells they’ve profited from before the wells are orphaned,” the letter reads. “This should start with requiring companies to plug their inactive wells.
Recommendations to the governor from the group’s letter include:

 Prioritize getting the industry to plug offshore and coastal wells, which are at high risk of failure, the most costly and complicated to plug, and most likely to impede coastal restoration efforts.
Develop a plugging plan based on priority oil and gas fields, not just by well.
Adopt a process for the Department of Conservation and Energy to require former operators to plug wells before they declare a site orphaned.
Close the loophole in state law that allows operators to pay an inactive well fee instead of plugging their idle wells.
Stop the transfer of state drilling leases to or from companies with overdue well-plugging obligations.

name: Michigan Advance
title: James’ departure opens up a political battleground in Michigan’s 10th Congressional District
text:
Democrat Christina Hines and Republican Michael Bouchard Jr. are vying to win the 10th Congressional District on Nov. 3, 2026. (Campaign photos)U.S. Rep. John James’ announcement that he would be leaving Congress to seek a new role as governor of Michigan sparked concern and frustration among party leadership over who would succeed the two-term representative in the southeast Michigan swing district.
Encompassing southern Macomb County and a sliver of Oakland County that includes Rochester and Rochester Hills, the nonpartisan Cook Political Report initially rated Michigan’s 10th Congressional District as “lean Republican” but has shifted its assessment to “toss-up” meaning either party has a chance to win the seat.
In August, Republicans nominated U.S. Army Capt. Michael Bouchard Jr., the son of Oakland County Sheriff and former state Sen. Mike Bouchard, as James’ potential successor. Christina Hines, a former prosecutor in Wayne and Washtenaw counties, heads the Democratic ticket.
While Bouchard carries the backing of President Donald Trump, U.S. Speaker of the House Mike Johnson (R-Louisiana) and Republican officials including former Gov. John Engler, Democrats at the state and national level are determined to claim control of the district, with U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-New York) joining Hines for a campaign event earlier this month. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In an interview with Michigan Advance, Jason Roe, a former executive director of the Michigan Republican Party and Republican political strategist working with U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett’s (R-Charlotte) campaign said the seat would likely still have its “lean Republican” rating had James decided to pursue reelection.
He pointed to multiple factors that made the district more competitive, including the open seat and the fact that both candidates were pursuing their first congressional bid.
“I think to call it a toss up is fair, but I still think at the end of the day it is a Republican seat,” Roe said. 
If Bouchard’s campaign is going to pull out a victory, Republicans need to do a better job of conveying that Hines is someone on the political left, Roe said. 
“Even when Macomb in that part of Metro Detroit was Democrat, it was always a very conservative Democrat,” Roe said, pointing to former state Sen. Gilbert DiNello, who identified as a Democrat for most of his political career before switching parties in 1992, as one example.
While Democratic candidates of the past were opposed to abortion, supporters of  the Second Amendment and more culturally conservative, Roe said the Democrats of today are not those Democrats. 
“But guess what? Macomb County is still those people,” he said. 



Quotation







I think it’ll shake its reputation as being a swing area permanently.


– GOP consultant Jason Roe on how the perception of Macomb County as a swing district will change if Republican Michael Bouchard Jr. wins on Nov. 3.


However, Bouchard, like many other congressional candidates, faces headwinds in the form of the war in Iran and President Donald Trump’s 31% approval rating.
Over the course of the campaign, Hines and her supporters have sought to paint Bouchard as a rubber stamp for Trump’s policies, pointing to an Inside Elections article from Feb. 19, prior to the start of the war with Iran, where Bouchard was unable to point to any areas where he has disagreed with the president.
“Mike Bouchard doesn’t have any ideas of his own,” Democratic political consultant and Sterling Heights councilman Michael Radtke told the Advance. “He absorbs other people’s. And one thing he’s done is he’s tied himself to the boat anchor that is Trump, and he’s tossed himself over there into Lake Michigan. Sorry, Lake America.”
Christina Hines, the Democratic nominee for the 10th Congressional District, addresses supporters and Democrats at a rally featuring former President Barack Obama at Cass Technical High School on Oct. 24, 2026, in Detroit, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)
While Bouchard’s campaign did not respond to multiple emailed requests for an interview, he told The Detroit News’ Political Insider podcast that he would like to see an end to the U.S.’s trade conflict with Canada and to find a way to end the war in Iran “that makes sure that terrorists don’t have nuclear weapons and that gas prices come down very quickly.”
He did not provide a direct answer when asked whether he would support a war powers resolution to halt military action in Iran. 
“I’d have to look at what the actual legislation is. I mean, I’m not going to comment on a hypothetical,” Bouchard told The Detroit News. 
Roe told Michigan Advance he was skeptical over how much Bouchard’s ties to the president would hurt his campaign, saying that a Trump endorsement was baked into the Republican brand.
“I think anyone knows that the Republican president supports Republican candidates and vice versa. They’re in the same party,” Roe said. “If you hate Trump so much that you’re going to vote for a Democrat, I don’t know that Trump being publicly supportive of that Republican or not makes a difference.”
Although Republicans have delivered on some of their 2024 campaign promises, like cracking down on immigration, Roe said these gains will likely be overshadowed by the war in Iran.
“There was a lot of promise out there, and then all of a sudden we woke up one day and we were at war,” Roe said, noting that the interruptions to the global oil supply that followed and the downstream effects have been disastrous for most households.
Candidates running in an open seat can also position themselves as change agents, Roe said, noting that both Hines and Bouchard were both taking that approach.
As a result, Bouchard may not carry as much baggage as a sitting member of Congress would, Roe explained. 
“Mike Bouchard does not own any of the decisions of this current Congress,” Roe said. “He’d start with a clean slate, and you know I think no matter what happens in this election, we’re going to see a pretty seismic shift in what happens in Washington over the next two years.”
While speaking with the Advance, Radtke called Bouchard’s ability to reach voters on issues like grocery and housing prices into question given that Bouchard had returned from combat deployment last October. On the other hand, Hines has kids and understands how hard times are for families, Radtke said.
“It costs us over $90 now to fill our minivan up, and our utility bills are higher than ever,” Hines said in an interview with Michigan Advance. “Costs are like issue number one, two and three for pretty much everybody in our district.”
Additionally, Bouchard’s lack of a plan around Social Security was a no-go for working people in Macomb County, Radtke said, pointing to the Detroit Free Press’ endorsement of Hines which said Social Security was “just one of many policy matters Bouchard was unable to address” in an interview with the editorial board.
“People who are out here at the assembly line, their hands are hurting, their knees are hurting, their backs are hurting,” Radtke said, calling the idea that these people could work a few more years “a fantasy.”
“Hard work breaks your body,” Radtke said.
Michael Bouchard, the GOP nominee for Michigan’s 10th Congressional District, at the GOP Unity Luncheon on Aug. 5, 2026 (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)
Hines said ensuring the program was fully funded was a key passion of hers, joking that she “might be the only 36-year-old in the country that’s obsessed with Social Security.”
There is only about five more years until the Social Security Trust fund dries up, Hines told the Advance, resulting in an automatic 22% cut to benefits that Hines said is a matter of life and death for some folks in her district.
“We have people that live exclusively on Social Security, and we could fully fund it for at least 35 years by simply removing the loophole that allows the richest people in this country to not pay their fair share into it,” Hines said.
Bouchard’s campaign website lists Medicare and Social Security as among his top priorities, stating “You paid into these safety-net programs and they need to be there for you. I will always protect Medicare and Social Security. We need to root out the waste and the fraud that threatens these critical programs.”
Radtke also pointed to Bouchard’s residence in Oakland County’s Rochester Hills as another factor working against him, with working-class Macomb County making up the vast majority of the district. 
Roe offered a similar assessment noting that “folks in Macomb don’t much trust anyone that’s not from Macomb.”
While there is a threshold to cross in order to gain Macomb residents’ respect, Roe pointed to Bouchard’s military experience.
“It goes back to service and I think that’s the kind of DNA that you see in Macomb,” Roe said.
If Hines takes home the win, Republicans can lay the blame at Trump’s feet, Roe said, but if Bouchard wins the 10th District, a redefinition may be in order.
“I think it’ll shake its reputation as being a swing area permanently,” Roe said.

name: VTDigger
title: As flooding increases and federal aid shrinks, Vermont is not prepared to manage disaster recovery
text:
This story is part of The Coming Storm, a yearlong investigation by VTDigger, in partnership with FRONTLINE (PBS), into Vermont’s ability to help communities recover from natural disasters.


BARRE CITY, VT — Shayd Pecor loves his home, but he wants to leave. For good.
On July 10, 2023, up to nine inches of rain pummeled Vermont. Pecor and his wife, Laurie, evacuated as the water overtook their front porch. 
That night, floodwaters inundated more than 130 towns across the state, killing two people, tearing through thousands of homes and destroying roads and bridges. The storm left an estimated $600 million in damage. 
The next morning, the Pecors found that their kitchen appliances had floated into the living room. Their furniture, pictures and family heirlooms were ruined. During the four months it took to repair their home, the Pecors slept on their daughter’s couch, then moved into a camper. 
One year to the day later, another flood came. Another four feet of water in their basement. 
“When it rains, we’re on edge,” Shayd Pecor said. “It’s continuous worrying, prepping, getting clothes ready. I don’t know how many times I’ve taken my camper out of the driveway and brought it to dry ground since the ‘23 flood.”
“It’s not a matter of ‘if’ it happens, it’s ‘when’ it happens again,” he said.
Shayd Pecor was among 67 homeowners who applied for FEMA buyouts in Barre City. The city blocked his application. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
The Pecors thought they had a way out: They would apply for a “buyout” from the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), which would fund the purchase of their home at its pre-storm value if the city of Barre agreed to demolish their house and not develop the property. 
The Pecors were among 67 homeowners who applied for buyouts in Barre, home to about 8,200 people. But officials there decided the city could not survive if it lost the tax revenue from all of those properties. They blocked the Pecors’ application, along with those of 39 others in flood-prone homes. 
“We feel trapped,” Pecor said.
Vermont was once considered a climate haven. But average rainfall has increased 21% since 1900, repeatedly swelling the state’s more than 7000 miles of rivers, accelerating erosion – and threatening its mostly rural residents. Flood damage in the state is projected to cost billions in the next century. In the past, Vermont has relied on the federal government for disaster help – more than almost any other state.
Now, the Trump administration aims to slash disaster support, shifting more recovery responsibility to the states. But Vermont does not have a disaster reserve, or traditional county governments that can help with recovery. Most of Vermont’s towns have fewer than 5,000 people, and their annual budgets are often less than $5 million. 
All this means Vermonters are facing a precarious future. Without federal aid, another massive storm could gut the state’s savings  – and pose an existential threat to some communities.
If FEMA cuts aid to states, Vermont is “not going to be able to provide what we need for our people,” said Sen. Phil Baruth, president pro tempore of the state Senate. “Without putting too fine a point on it, that will mean death and destruction in my state.” 

 

About The Coming Storm: VTDigger obtained emails from state officials regarding assistance to flood survivors, reviewed state and federal disaster funding and risk-reduction plans, examined federal proposals to change FEMA, and analyzed FEMA data on disaster aid, with assistance from Eric Sagara of Big Local News at Stanford University. VTDigger also interviewed flood survivors, frontline recovery workers, state and local officials, lawmakers, emergency management experts, scientists, and social services providers, among others, for this series.
Taking on more debt
Across Vermont, flood recovery bills have overwhelmed small town budgets. 
On July 10, 2025, Jim Sullivan, the town administrator in Burke, watched anxiously as the clear afternoon skies gave way to a billowing rain cloud. Sullivan was still struggling to pay for flood damage after floods in 2023 and ‘24 when 2025 brought more flooding. The three-year flood damage total came to almost $1.6 million. The town’s annual budget is $3.3 million.
A few miles away, in neighboring Sutton, home to fewer than 1,000 people, road damage totaled $1.4 million in 2025, more than twice the town’s nearly $600,000 highway budget that year. The town clerk, Patricia McClure, and road foreman, Shane Heath, had learned the ropes in 2023, then again in 2024. 
Sutton town clerk Patricia McClure and road foreman Shane Heath struggled to manage recovery after the town was flooded three years in a row. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
“Each year, we’ve taken out a line of credit from the bank,” McClure said. In 2023 and 2024, FEMA reimbursed them just as that line of credit was coming due. 
Even with money from the state to cover some of the cost of 2025 damage, the town may need to take out a loan to pay off its existing line of credit. That could raise taxes for residents, many of them farmers and older Vermonters who live on fixed incomes.
The town of Lyndon, just six miles south of Burke, was still waiting for FEMA funds to repair damage from the 2023 floods when the July 10, 2024 storm hit. 
As floodwaters poured into the town office building, the staff of four fled to a different building. They crammed into a small office to field call after call from residents whose homes or offices were flooding.
Then, another torrential rainstorm brought more flash flooding on July 30. Four houses washed away, displacing several families. By morning, two of the town’s major roads were almost completely gone. 
“We’re talking in numbers that we don’t deal with,” said Justin Smith, the municipal administrator. “We had a bill a couple different weeks that was $750,000. Our highway budget, in a year, is in the $2 million range — $2.1 million, $2.5 million, depending on what we’re doing in a given year. And we’re seeing bills, absolutely legitimate, but close to half of our annual budget range in a week.”
The town of Lyndon was still waiting for FEMA funds to repair damage from the 2023 floods when the July 10, 2024 storm hit. Photo courtesy of the Vermont Agency of Transportation.
Lyndon started borrowing money. First, it took out a $8 million line of credit, then another $6.8 million from one bank. But the town still needed more money. It turned to the Vermont Bond Bank, which was created by the state to help local governments finance projects, for additional funding.  By September 2026, the town was still repairing damage, and Smith estimates it will have spent about $20 million in total.
When the 2024 flood hit, FEMA asked Smith what the town needed. 
“You can get me some money coming, because we are out,” he recalled telling the agency.
As of September, Lyndon was still waiting for FEMA to reimburse more than $13 million that it has already spent to repair roads.
Without outside aid, towns can either take on more debt when disaster strikes, potentially risking bankruptcy, or allow public infrastructure to deteriorate. That leads to “a town with worse public services, worse infrastructure, likely causing population drain as a result,” said Tatyana Deryugina, an associate professor of finance at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign who studies environmental risk.
“Do more with less”
Vermont’s small towns have often faced funding gaps following natural disasters. But in past federally declared floods, FEMA has filled those gaps. 
In 2025, for the first time, the federal aid never came.
President Donald J. Trump denied Republican Gov. Phil Scott’s request for a Major Disaster Declaration, saying that aid was “not warranted.” The president makes the final decision on all declarations, and none are guaranteed.
In his second term, Pres. Trump has denied more disaster requests from states that voted against him in 2024 – such as Vermont – than from states that voted for him, according to an analysis by the Associated Press. 
FEMA declined an interview with VTDigger for this series and did not fulfill a Freedom of Information Act request for details about the federal government’s decision to deny Vermont’s major disaster declaration for July 2025 flooding.
In an emailed statement from an unnamed spokesperson, FEMA said that the agency has sent almost $20 million in funding through the agency’s Hazard Mitigation Grant Program and more than $160 million in public assistance to Vermont since January 2025, when Trump took office. But those funds were unlocked when President Joseph R. Biden issued disaster declarations.
“FEMA remains committed to supporting survivors of the Vermont (sic) and to the locally executed, state managed, and federally supported approach to disaster recovery,” the statement said.
Last November, the governor appealed the Trump administration’s decision, and in his request, he included written pleas from town officials.
“Vermont is not an easy place to live, but it’s our home,” Sullivan, Burke’s town administrator, wrote. “It’s hard to earn a living and many of us have to farm, log, mill, hunt, and barter our trades to make ends meet and feed our families. The disaster we had this past July 10, 2025, has cost our town about $300,000.00 so far just for the roads and bridges. Without FEMA assistance that additional tax burden is going to hit our residence (sic) hard. Especially our seniors, farmers and single parents.”
Jim Sullivan said Burke would have been “a bankrupt town” without FEMA funds after the 2023 and 2024 floods. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
The 2025 flooding hit towns like Burke that were least equipped to deal with FEMA’s retreat. The town is in Vermont’s Northeast Kingdom, where poverty rates are the highest in the state.
Without FEMA funds after the 2023 and 2024 floods, Sullivan said, Burke would have been “a bankrupt town.” He’s watched residents count out change to pay their taxes.
The Trump administration has long been planning to shrink FEMA and require state and local governments to manage and pay for more disaster relief.
Soon after he took office in January 2025, Trump issued an executive order, forming a council to conduct “a full-scale review” of FEMA.
“We’re looking at the whole concept of FEMA,” Trump said in January 2025. “I like, frankly, the concept when North Carolina gets hit, the governor takes care of it. When Florida gets hit, the governor takes care of it, meaning the state takes care of it.”
The notion of gutting the agency drew ire from critics including U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt.
“Clearly, we need to protect FEMA,” he told reporters in July 2025. “The idea of dismantling FEMA, or cutting back, at a time when communities are going to see more and more flooding and other types of disasters, is a terrible mistake.”
In May 2026, Trump’s council recommended in its final report that federal assistance only be used “for truly significant events,” and states can and should pay more for disaster recovery. 
“It is time to close the chapter on FEMA,” the council wrote. It proposed creating a new agency that included existing programs with “a proven track record of effective federal-state-local partnership” while giving states direct funding and more responsibility to distribute it.
The proposals have a long road to becoming real, permanent changes to FEMA. Many of the proposals are not specific, and so far, Congress has not altered the Stafford Act, which governs how disaster aid is distributed. 
But they all point in the same direction, said Eric Forand, director of Vermont Emergency Management: “The states have to do more with less.”
Sue Minter, Vermont’s chief recovery officer after Tropical Storm Irene in 2011, watched federal money pour into the state to fund all aspects of recovery in the wake of that disaster. 
“I’m very alarmed by the possibility that FEMA may reduce its commitment to funding responses to disasters,” she said. “I know full well that those who will be most hurt and aggrieved by this are those least able to manage.”
Without those federal dollars, the state is “so, so facing crisis,” she said.
No disaster reserve
Experts say Vermont could not cover the cost of a large disaster without federal aid.
The state doesn’t have enough money in its reserves — its savings account — to pay the bills for most storms. Vermont’s reserves are about equal to the cost of one large storm, which makes it the most financially vulnerable state in the country to swings in federal disaster aid, according to a 2025 report from The Pew Charitable Trusts. 
Vermont’s budget is $9.4 billion, and as of 2025, it had a little over $300 million in its reserves. State officials estimate the final damage tally from the 2023 flood to be around $600 million. 
It’s not only the large disasters that concern state emergency management officials. Historically, Vermont has received federal aid for smaller disasters. 
That’s because the threshold to unlock FEMA aid for the most expensive recovery projects — repairs to roads and bridges — is calculated based on a state’s population. With some 645,000 residents, Vermont can qualify for aid when storm damage exceeds $1.2 million. (For comparison, California, with its 39.4 million residents, has a threshold of about $76 million.) 
“Towns have lower budgets because they have a lower amount of taxpayers, which means that a road washout that’s $100,000 is much more significant in Sutton than it is in, you know, New York City or a larger place, like the suburbs of Massachusetts,” said Forand, Vermont’s top emergency management official. 
The Trump administration wants to raise that threshold. Last year, Cameron Hamilton, who is now the FEMA administrator, proposed quadrupling the current threshold for all states. Under that plan, Vermont’s threshold would be $5 million.
Earlier this year, the FEMA council pitched a smaller increase, which would raise Vermont’s threshold to around $2 million.
In addition to the higher threshold, the council also recommended that states pay a minimum amount, like a deductible, before federal aid kicks in, but did not specify how much it should be. Even a relatively small deductible could have a big impact on Vermont, making the majority of disasters in the state ineligible for any federal disaster aid. Since 2002, 53% of Vermont’s disasters have cost less than $5 million, and 79% have cost less than $10 million, a VTDigger analysis of FEMA data shows.
Congress will have to weigh in on many of the council’s plans. But the proposals would “reduce the amount of money that community, state, and local government would be eligible to receive from FEMA post disaster, with no indication for how states and locals might be expected to make up for that loss of funding,” said Samantha Montano, associate professor of emergency management at Massachusetts Maritime Academy.
In October, Hamilton said states should prepare to take on more of the recovery cost. 
Cameron Hamilton testifies during a Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Government Affairs Committee hearing to examine his nomination to be Administrator of the Federal Emergency Management Agency, Wednesday, June 17, 2026, on Capitol Hill in Washington. He was confirmed in August, 2026. (AP Photo/Mariam Zuhaib)
“What I would tell states is that, if there’s concern over whether they’re able to have the financial resources able to meet that mission space, we’d like to see them invest early,” he said in an Oct. 19 interview with Spectrum News. 
U.S. Senator Peter Welch (D-Vt.) issued a press statement after POLITICO reported that Hamilton, at a private conference in Arkansas, told state officials to increase their reserves and prepare to receive less federal help. 
“Vermont’s catastrophic floods of 2023 and 2024 would have been impossible to recover from without the immediate, lifesaving response efforts provided by FEMA,” Welch said. “I have no doubt our next flood or natural disaster will be harder to recover from because of President Trump’s misguided, reckless policies.”  
FEMA’s decision not to help after the 2025 floods offers a glimpse into what may be coming. The state sustained more than $1.8 million in damage, which would have been enough to trigger FEMA aid in previous administrations. The denial left the towns desperate for alternative funding.
Gov. Scott and lawmakers eventually agreed to cover some of the damage through the state budget. Scott said that he wants “to be careful about the precedent, because once we start that, then we have to continue from a parity standpoint.”
Between 2011 and 2024, Vermont had 25 federally declared climate disasters and every county had at least five disasters. Gov. Scott and other state officials have acknowledged that they don’t have a comprehensive plan to recover from future climate disasters without federal aid. 
VTDigger sent multiple requests to Gov. Scott’s office requesting an interview for this series and did not receive a response.  
In an interview, Doug Farnham, Vermont’s chief recovery officer, said the state is “reacting to the individual events.”
“For each situation that comes up in the next two years, we’re going to evaluate it and respond,” he said. “If federal law changes, then Vermont needs to change its structure, but we can’t shift our structure based on the current president.”
Doug Farnham, Vermont’s chief recovery officer, said Vermont doesn’t have the funds to prioritize disaster recovery. “If we were in a healthy position,” he said, “that would be something that would make sense.” Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Emergency management experts say states should create a disaster reserve to have immediate access to recovery funds. 
“That is a bare minimum thing that every state should have,” Montano said.
A state task force to address reductions in federal aid called creating a disaster reserve “a clear policy priority.” But leaders across the political spectrum say Vermont cannot afford to fund it, and there is little appetite in Montpelier to raise taxes for such a reserve. 
“If we were in a healthy position, that would be something that would make sense,” Farnham said. “From a macro perspective, I don’t think that disaster recovery at this point in time can take priority over things that are having a much bigger human and financial impact.”
“Should we be saving up a billion dollars in the event that we’re flooded similarly next year?” asked Baruth, Democratic president of the state Senate. “We literally don’t have that money.”


Senator Phil Baruth (D/P-Chittenden-Central), president pro tempore of the state Senate, said Vermont is “not going to be able to provide what we need for our people,” if FEMA cuts aid to states. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger


Rep. Robin Scheu (D-Middlebury), the chair of the state’s House Appropriations Committee, said lawmakers should work on creating a disaster relief fund, but – unless they’re storm victims – voters say they don’t consider it a high priority. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger


Vermont is struggling with an array of economic challenges, including a severe housing shortage that has driven up rents and home prices, especially for lower-income residents, and led to a sharp rise in homelessness. Gov. Scott, a popular Republican in one of the nation’s bluest states, has repeatedly vowed to reject any policy proposals that contain new taxes or fees.

READ MORE

Rep. Robin Scheu (D-Middlebury), the chair of the state’s House Appropriations Committee, said lawmakers should be talking with the governor about creating a disaster relief fund – “that’s a conversation that needs to happen” – but acknowledged that many voters have other priorities.
“If you talk to Vermonters, unless they’ve been impacted by the floods themselves, this doesn’t rise to the top for them,” Scheu said. “This is an election year.”
Sullivan, in Burke, says the state needs to be prepared for damaging storms that are coming “every year.”
It’s frustrating “to go through this number of disasters, and to not be hearing more about how they’re going to build a reserve,” he said.
In the absence of a disaster reserve, he’s working to ensure “that our town budget is really bare bones.” 
FEMA doesn’t cover all of the flood damage costs, and the town’s portion, though a fraction of the overall bill, is still “a huge hit,” Sullivan said.
“The next year, you get whacked again,” he said. “And it’s like, we didn’t budget for that, you know? You just start sinking.”
“Save Shadow Lake”
In Glover, Theresa Perron-Janowski is selling t-shirts to fix her town’s leaking dam.


Theresa Perron-Janowski’s job as Glover’s town administrator has been almost entirely “flood-related and FEMA-related, looking for grants, writing grants,” she said. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger


Should the Shadow Lake dam fail on the 210-acre body of water, the resulting flood could be catastrophic. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger


It’s been more than three years since state inspectors found a small hole, the size of a mouse, piercing the main wall of the Shadow Lake dam. A year later, more floods made the problem worse, creating a 5-foot by 5-foot sink hole. It was a “huge red flag,” she said.
Should the dam fail on the 210-acre body of water, the resulting flood could be catastrophic for the people downstream. A nursing home and senior housing both sit in the path of the river. 
When Perron-Janowski started as Glover’s town administrator – a week before the 2023 flood — she didn’t know then that she’d soon be carrying the weight of the town on her shoulders.
“I was brand new to the ropes, and was waiting for somebody to tell me what to do with that,” she said. “Then, I realized, nobody’s going to tell me what to do. I got to do this myself then.”
She scrambled to organize temporary fixes, which, she said, made the dam safer. But it still needs permanent repairs, which could cost millions of dollars. She expects FEMA will cover the bulk of that. But Glover will have to pay about 18%  of the cost, and there is no room for that expense in the town’s annual budget of $2.3 million.
To avoid raising taxes in her economically challenged town, Perron-Janowski has searched long and hard, with no luck, to find another source of funding. A member of Vermont’s flood recovery office has joined in her efforts, and together, they keep a long list of rejected grant applications. 
Of the state’s roughly 800 dams, Shadow Lake is just one of around 150 listed as a “significant” hazard. Another 74 are considered “high” hazards.

READ MORE

Perron-Janowski has begun fundraising, holding auctions and selling t-shirts that read, “Save Shadow Lake.” As of October she had raised close to $40,000, which she expects will go toward a $100,000 analysis that will map out how to do the repairs -— not fund the repairs themselves.
Perron-Janowski was 70 when she took the town administrator job three years ago.
“I took this job to get less stress,” she said with a laugh.
She thought her days would consist of managing the town recycling center and overseeing other basic services. Instead, the floods have “been consuming,” she said, and her job has been almost entirely “flood-related and FEMA-related, looking for grants, writing grants.” When she receives a donation check in the mail, she dances around the town office and often sheds a tear, she said. 
Though FEMA officials have assured Perron-Janowski they’ll stick with the project, she watched in horror as her neighboring towns failed to get federal aid in 2025. 
“It’s devastating. It puts the community in debt,” she said. 
She often stays awake at night, fretting over the cost of the repairs. When it rains, she worries about the residents who live downstream from Shadow Lake. 
Her own home sustained flood damage in 2023. She’s not sure how much longer she wants to keep working, but she plans to stay until the dam repairs are complete.
“You know, maybe you could put a little plug in your paper,” she said. “We will be looking for a town administrator, if anyone is interested.”
No county governments
Much like Glover, other small towns in Vermont struggled to retain staff with the expertise to work with federal disaster officials and manage flood recovery. 
In Wheelock, two key town employees quit after consecutive July storms, leaving the volunteer selectboard chair, Ann Lawless, to become the town’s primary contact with FEMA. “You can’t run these giant projects just on volunteers,” she said. “We’ve made many mistakes because we’re volunteers.”
More than 100 miles south, in Ludlow, flooding in 2023 damaged the town’s grocery store and wastewater treatment plant. Brendan McNamara, then the town municipal manager, relied on FEMA to coordinate recovery through its Public Assistance Program Delivery Managers. But during his two-and-a-half years with the town, Ludlow had 13 different program delivery managers, McNamara said, which meant town officials had to “re-explain and reinvent the wheel every time.” 
Flooding in Ludlow damaged the town’s grocery store and wastewater treatment plant in 2023. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
McNamara came into the job with “aspirations of moving things forward” in Ludlow. But after years of managing the aftermath of the storms, he quit in December 2025. 
In many states, county governments would fill these gaps, connecting small towns in a region with a pool of resources. So when a road crumbles in one town in a county, there’s a larger bucket of money and more staff at the county level to step in and help. 

READ MORE

In Vermont, regions are technically split up into counties, but they don’t have governments. Six other states have versions of county government that are roughly as limited as Vermont’s, according to the National Association of Counties.
In lieu of county government, Vermont’s has 11 regional planning commissions which were created by state law and get their funding mostly from grants, with small contributions from their member towns. They help towns with everything from economic development to housing to emergency management, and they are one of the most significant resources that exist for towns after disaster hits. 
But that support varies. Some regional planning commissions have flood experts on staff and are well-poised to help towns with flood recovery. Others have fewer resources.
Experts say that Vermont has likely missed opportunities to get federal funding because of its lack of county government. A comparison of Vermont’s Covid-era federal funding to that of other New England states showed the state received a fraction of what other states with strong county governments got from the federal government.
Installing county government would be a radical shift for Vermont, where towns and cities maintain local control by relying on rituals of direct democracy. Many hold an annual Town Meeting Day where residents gather to vote on town business, often before or after a potluck. Changing this would require large-scale legislative approval. 
While such a big change is unlikely, lawmakers have met in recent years to discuss forming some other regional system that could provide towns with more support. A state law created a County and Regional Governance Study Committee to look into the question. It is expected to file its report in December 2026. 
If proposed changes to FEMA move forward and towns are left without help to pay for repairs from the damaging floods, an increasing number of Vermont towns may not be able to fund the basics of civic life.
Vermont’s more affluent towns are “going to be fine,” said Pete Fellows, a certified floodplain manager at Two Rivers-Ottauquechee Regional Commission in eastern Vermont. “But parts of Vermont are going to start to fall off the edge more than they have been.”
“Terrible decisions”
In Barre, city officials created a plan to purchase flooded homes directly from residents, which would remove FEMA from the equation and allow the city to keep the development rights. That way, people like the Pecors could walk away with the pre-flood value of their homes, and the city could build more housing on the land, taking measures to reduce flood risks. 
The plan hasn’t worked for a familiar reason: City officials don’t have the funding.
Barre asked the state to pay for the buyouts, using money from a flood relief program. But the state rejected that proposal – twice. State officials said Barre’s plan didn’t create housing outside of the floodplain.

READ MORE

In October 2026, the state approved and funded a final application from the city. With $4.2 million, Barre plans to replace a city park with new housing and buy out two commercial buildings. The plan only included one residential buyout, which Mayor Thom Lauzon said was likely to be a home along Route 302 — not the homes of Pecor or his neighbors. 
“We just feel really disappointed,” Pecor said. “We feel let down by the city government, and it’s not just me. It’s everybody I speak to on the North End, that it wasn’t taken seriously.”
“When it rains, we’re on edge,” Pecor said. “It’s continuous worrying, prepping, getting clothes ready. I don’t know how many times I’ve taken my camper out of the driveway and brought it to dry ground since the ‘23 flood.” Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Recently, Pecor turned 59. He’s been working since he was 14 years old, he said. He and his wife had planned to sell their house to fund their retirement. But that plan has evaporated.
Pecor said he wouldn’t be able to sleep if he sold his house to someone else, “knowing that it would happen to them possibly soon,” he said. “No one’s going to buy it anyway.”
Mayor Thom Lauzon said flood recovery is his biggest focus. 
“Driving through Barre, there are certain areas, mostly on the North End of town, where it’s very clear that people are still struggling and trying to recover,” Lauzon said. 
It wasn’t easy to deny the FEMA buyout applications, he said. But the goal of that program is to reduce the costs and risks from future flooding, not to compensate flood survivors for their losses.
The city denied 40 FEMA buyout applications, including the Pecors, but approved 27 buyouts in areas where the newly opened land would create floodplain and measurably reduce flood risk to the rest of the city.  
“Their stories were just as compelling, but because we couldn’t make the case that this would benefit the city as a whole, as opposed to just that individual property owner, we had declined to buy them out,” Lauzon said. “Those were terrible decisions to make.”  
This story was reported with support from FRONTLINE’s Local Journalism Initiative, which is funded by the John S. and James L Knight Foundation.

The series continues. Next in The Coming Storm: River erosion, the greatest naturally occurring threat to Vermonters, causes the vast majority of the state’s flood damage. As climate change intensifies, the problem is expected to worsen — yet solutions are complex and expensive. In the meantime, many Vermonters remain in harm’s way.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Opinion: President Donald Trump came to Kansas and enraptured an audience with bunkum. I fear for us.
text:
Fans cheer as President Donald Trump takes the stage at an Oct. 19, 2026, rally at the Heartland Credit Union Arena in Park City, Kansas. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)With midwestern naivete, I thought I could attend the rally in Park City on Oct. 19, hear President Donald Trump speak and determine for myself the validity of the “news.”
Was Trump a doddering, senile shell? Was his MAGA base cheering barely controlled bloodhounds on the hunt for immigrants? Were the radical left lunatics bent upon disrupting a sitting president?
First, I didn’t get in, due to the aforementioned naivete. I thought I could just download my ticket, follow the timeline, stroll into the Heartland Credit Union Arena a couple of hours before Trump spoke, chat with the attendees and have the answers. I did not plan on people camping out at the site the night before, or the devotion of those willing to arrive many hours early.
However, the trip and the parking lot provided ample food for thought.
Blue skies and dramatic clouds filled the landscape through the Flint Hills during the two-hour drive to Wichita. On my flawed timeline, I believed I had plenty of time to try one of the barbecue restaurants involved in a hot Facebook debate.
Station 8 was closed, so I settled on Bite Me BBQ, located in Wichita’s Old Town. Walking in, the aroma of decades of woodsmoke seeped from the walls. Promising. A chalkboard offered the Monday special: all the fish tacos one could eat. Not so promising.
My brisket dinner convinced me that, yes, America is great and it is immaterial whether Republicans or Democrats or immigrants or billionaires or unions or the Supreme Court is responsible. Food had already entered our political debate this fall with the U.S. Senate race in Texas veering off into who is a vegetarian or vegan. In Kansas, Adam Hamilton was accused of preaching against beef consumption.
No one from either party could caucus against that brisket.
Bite Me was about half full this Monday. Workmen in safety vests dined and joked about their jobs. Reluctant to leave, I decided to question the young customer service manager who stopped at our table.
Business was pretty good, she said, but they were watching expenses. On a personal level, she felt her life was going well. Her husband had made smart decisions years ago. He had bought a small house when he was only 21 and it was almost paid off, she explained. They plan to parley their equity into a larger place as their family grows.
Midwestern manners precluded me from asking how she would vote in the midterm, but she noted she may not cast a ballot at all due her son’s needs and her work schedule.
By 2 p.m. I headed toward Park City, four hours before the scheduled time. Turning into the facility, there was a line of cars but it only took 10 minutes to arrive at the designated casino parking lot. Inching along in the line, a steady stream of attendees walked along a sidewalk toward the venue
Surprisingly, I saw only two red hats. Many did wear red Kansas City Chiefs shirts. Red is red. The was calm, orderly and focused on reaching the arena.
My parked car faced a line of standing people waiting for the shuttle busses. Sitting in the car, sun-basked and drowsy, the prospect of standing for hours lost appeal. The line did not move, although small groups sometimes leave the line and return to their cars.
One refugee told me the arena was full. They wouldn’t let any more people in, but I could stand outside and watch the rally on a screen,
A man parked beside me rolled down his window and said: “It’s not worth it. Download the Rumble app and watch live.” I did.
What I saw was enlightening and disturbing. Wholesome-looking families cheered and waved flags as the president of the United States rambled and lied. He called Derek Schmidt “Eric” and people cheered.
Protesters heckled, and the devout crowd tried to drown them out, chanting “USA.”
Trump said, of the hecklers: “I can tell by the voice they get paid.”
People cheered. He used the word hate frequently. People cheered.
I don’t know much about business, but I was jarred by Trump’s explanation of Roger Marshall’s reasons for suing his patients for back payments. Trump claimed it was the law. I asked my physician friends if this was a law. They laughed and simply said no.
And I cannot even bring myself to discuss his claims that public schools transition children to different sexes without parental knowledge. As I watched the cheering, red-clad crowd, all I could think was: What is wrong with these people?
What made the “it’s the law” segment so much more terrifying rested in the delivery. Trump spoke sincerely, forcefully, eloquently, with conviction. Had I not known the words were false, I would have believed.
My mind abruptly shifted to a the public radio show “Car Talk,” featuring “Click and Clack, the Tappet Brothers.” Hosts Tom and Ray Magliozzi would respond to particularly stupid ideas with laughter and the refrain: “Unencumbered by the thought process.” They saying was funny when all that hung in the balance was a 1974 Dodge Dart’s transmission, but less so when when one values morals, freedom and democracy.
I quit watching. I left the parking lot, heading to get coffee. Questions raced through my mind. What was happening to our democracy? Free press? Ethics? The truth?
What to do? I closed my eyes for a moment and could see the sea of red. How could they not see?
I thought of Little Red Riding Hood, dressed in red and questioning the identity and motives of that terrible wolf. According to the spreading power of AI, the tale is about 2,000 years old, so the problem of identifying evil is not new. Little Red Riding Hood’s fate has changed over the centuries. Sometimes she dies, sometimes she is rescued.
What will our fate be?
Marsha Hayes is a retired rural mail carrier, retired community college English teacher and award-winning equine journalist. name: Georgia Recorder
title: Fleming, Brown Reynolds compete to be Georgia’s next top elections officer
text:
The two candidates for secretary of state, Republican Tim Fleming (left) and Democrat Penny Brown Reynolds (right) face off at a debate hosted by the Atlanta Press Club. Photo by J Glenn PhotographyThe race to become Georgia’s next top elections official is heating up as Election Day nears, and the two candidates on the ballot are offering starkly different visions for the future of voting in the Peach State.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
On the Republican ticket is Covington state Rep. Tim Fleming, a two-term lawmaker and the former deputy secretary of state under then-Secretary of State Brian Kemp. He also currently serves on a special committee dedicated to helping select Georgia’s next voting system.
Democrat Penny Brown Reynolds is a former Fulton County judge, reality TV show star and member of the Biden administration. She helped lead the Office of the Assistant Secretary for Civil Rights in the U.S. Department of Agriculture.
The role soared to national prominence in the aftermath of the 2020 election when Republican Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger resisted President Donald Trump’s request to overturn his loss in Georgia. Georgia’s status as a battleground state means the next secretary will likely continue to administer elections with national consequences, including the 2028 presidential race.
Lawmakers weigh seismic changes to Georgia’s voting equipment

The next secretary of state will also be responsible for overseeing the implementation of Georgia’s new election system. The state’s decade-long contract with its current ballot-marking devices is coming to an end, and lawmakers are expected to select a new system during the 2027 legislative session.
Both nominees have pledged on the campaign trail to improve the state’s election system, but the two candidates are offering contrasting visions of what voting should look like in the future.
Fleming has been a staunch opponent of Georgia’s current ballot-marking devices, introducing a key amendment during the state’s June special session that requires the special election committee to focus exclusively on hand-marked ballot systems. He has also sought to restrict no-excuse absentee voting and “defend” the state’s voter ID laws.
Brown Reynolds has focused more on expanding voting access, pledging to defend absentee voting and coming out against the federal SAVE America Act, arguing that Georgia’s current laws already require voters to present their ID at the polls and prevent non-citizens from voting. She has also highlighted her mother’s experience as a poll worker, promising to expand voting rights and support local election officials.
With the potential for mid-cycle redistricting on the horizon in Georgia, Cathy Cox, a Democrat who served as Georgia’s secretary of state from 1999 until 2007, said that whoever leads the office will likely play a key role in carrying out the Legislature’s redistricting plans and defending them in court.
“There’s probably going to be some effort toward reapportioning legislative districts outside of the normal 10-year reapportionment cycle,” she said. “Those reapportionment efforts always go back to the Secretary of State’s office because the Secretary of State is the one who ultimately has to administer elections.”
Cox also said the secretary of state plays an important role in certifying election results for statewide races and turning federal results like for the presidential race over to the governor’s office for certification. 
Efforts from the GOP-run State Election Board to delay certification of election results became a flashpoint of the 2024 election cycle, and the Trump administration has already sought to block certification of election results in states like Alaska if Republican candidates lose.
And in Georgia’s secretary of state race, perhaps more than any other contest on Georgia’s ballot this year, the memory of Trump’s efforts to overturn the 2020 election by urging Raffensperger to “find 11,780 votes” for him looms large.
Raffensperger’s refusal to overturn Georgia’s election results likely helped him gain support from Democrats and independent voters and defeat a Trump-backed GOP challenger in 2022. 
Trump urges supporters to ‘pretend’ he’s on the ballot as he campaigns with Georgia Republicans

But Fleming has taken a different route, downplaying Trump’s claims of a stolen election in 2020 and appearing alongside the president during a recent rally in Dalton.
“I’m not here to relitigate 2020,” he said during an Atlanta Press Club debate earlier this month. “I’m here to focus on the future and focus on Georgians to make sure their right to vote is secure, fair, transparent and trusted moving forward.”
Brown Reynolds has sought to capitalize on Fleming’s close association with Trump, arguing that she wouldn’t hesitate to stand up to pressure from federal officials.
In a recent campaign ad, she highlighted Trump’s call with Raffensperger and pledged to “do what’s right for Georgia, no matter who’s calling.”
And during the Atlanta Press Club debate, she questioned Fleming for failing to oppose a March executive order from Trump that sought to restrict mail voting.
“He’s doing everything in his power not to be able to say ‘what Donald Trump did was wrong,’” Brown Reynolds said during the debate. “You need an independent Secretary of State, not somebody that’s running to Washington trying to get an endorsement.”
Fleming has doled out criticisms of his own, attacking Brown Reynold’s decision to resign from the bench before the end of her term as a Fulton County judge and film her reality TV show, “Family Court with Judge Penny,” which ran from 2008 to 2009. 
“She chose Hollywood instead of Georgia,” Fleming said at Trump’s October rally in Dalton.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Data center bans, a high-profile DA race and other things to watch for on Nov. 3
text:
The polls at the Woodfords Club in Portland on Election Day, Nov. 4, 2025. (Photo by Jim Neuger/ Maine Morning Star)[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: How to register, key dates, who’s on the ballot and where the candidates stand on the top issues facing Maine.]While much of the focus this election cycle has centered on high-profile races for statewide and national office, Mainers also have the opportunity to weigh in on several local races and referenda on Nov. 3. 
Some feature candidates who do not fall neatly within party lines, or recently switched or disaffiliated from a party. That’s part of larger trends of Republicans trying to defy political headwinds during a midterm and attempts to reach beyond the two-party system as Americans increasingly ditch labels. 
Depending on where voters live, they may be able to weigh in on several municipal or county-wide ballot questions, including on lot rent stabilization, restrictions on syringe service programs and bans on data centers and Flock cameras. 
While at the polls, voters may also come across petitions to repeal recreational cannabis, publicly fund universal healthcare and restrict transgender rights in schools, which groups are seeking to get on ballots next year. 
Here are some notable contests and questions:
Cumberland County district attorney
Current Cumberland County District Attorney Jackie Sartoris, a Democrat, is seeking reelection against independent Stephanie Anderson, who previously held the role as a registered Republican. 
Anderson served as district attorney for 28 years, first elected in 1990. She is now a town councilor in Cape Elizabeth. Sartoris was first elected in 2022.
Coming out of retirement to run, Anderson has argued Sartoris has destroyed her legacy and endangered public safety. Meanwhile, Sartoris has claimed a return to Anderson’s leadership would set the district back after she’s made major progressive changes. 
Sartoris has broadened the use of restorative justice programs, worked through a backlog of untested rape kits, and publicly shared her willingness to prosecute illegal use of force by federal immigration agents. 
Some of that work has been opposed by police unions, who are backing Anderson, along with several attorneys. Meanwhile, Sartoris is endorsed by several city councilors and Democratic state legislators, including Speaker of the Maine House of Representatives Ryan Fecteau, as well as former Democratic candidates for national and statewide office.
While Anderson was district attorney, she was known for her toughness. She established Maine’s first drug court, juvenile unit and domestic violence unit.  
Anderson has out-raised Sartoris, with $89,707 to $49,969 total contributions, respectively. Regarding independent expenditures, Sartoris has received more than $12,000 from the Working Families Party political action committee, and Anderson has received $6,400 from Bright Future Maine PAC. 
Hancock County sheriff’s race
A local contest where party lines are blurred can be found in Hancock County. 
On face value, a Republican is running against a Democrat for sheriff. However, cross party endorsements in the race paint a more complicated picture. 
Three Democratic state legislators endorsed Republican Corey Bagley, a detective with the Ellsworth Police Department and former sheriff’s chief deputy, over Democrat Dakota Dupuis, who is currently a lieutenant at the Hancock County Sheriff’s Office.  
In their endorsement letter, Reps. Nina Milliken of Blue Hill and Gary Friedmann of Bar Harbor and Sen. Nicole Grohoski of Hancock County pointed out that Dupuis only recently switched party affiliations and that the current sheriff, Scott Kane, a Republican, is supporting Dupuis. Whoever wins will replace Kane, who is not seeking a fourth term.
“As Democrats, we definitely expect to disagree with Bagley on policy positions down the road,” they wrote. “But we would not be serving our communities honestly if we failed to say this plainly: we believe Corey Bagley is the better choice for Hancock County Sheriff. Clear independence from the current sheriff, experience, good judgment, and leadership matter more than party branding in a race like this.”
Data center bans
After Gov. Janet Mills vetoed a temporary statewide data center moratorium, some could be coming on the local level.
Voters in Peru, a town in Oxford County, will decide whether to adopt a 180-day moratorium on data center development and permitting. 
Wiscasset voters will get to decide whether to temporarily stop the town from  accepting, processing, reviewing, or approving applications for new or expanded data centers. Unless lifted earlier or extended, it would expire six months after enactment.
Amid housing crisis, Maine mobile home residents make strides to protect themselves

In York County, voters in Wells will be asked if they want a 180-day moratorium on development of data centers 100,000 square feet or larger, and in North Berwick they will consider an outright ban on data centers larger than 25,000 square feet. 
Lot rent stabilization
Several municipalities are considering ordinances to stabilize the cost of rent for mobile home lots. 
Affordability is a concern for people in various types of housing across Maine, as a massive shortage in supply confronts stagnant wages, high building costs, and an influx of residents in part due to an increase in remote workers.
While mobile home residents often own their physical homes, they have to rent the underlying land, leaving them vulnerable to skyrocketing monthly lot rents, especially when corporate or out-of-state investors buy parks. 
Augusta, Farmington, Jay, Wells and Wiscasset each have ordinances on their ballots. 
In Augusta, the ordinance would cap annual lot rent increases at either 3% or the rate of inflation, whichever is lower. In Farmington, the measure would cap annual rent increases at 3% for occupied lots and 5% for vacant lots. In Jay, the ordinance would limit most mobile home park lot rent increases to the Northeast Consumer Price Index. In Wells, it would cap annual lot rent increases to the rate of inflation plus 1%. In Wiscasset, voters will decide whether to temporarily prohibit lot rent increases exceeding 3%.
State’s first peer-led harm reduction community center opens in Lewiston

Syringes
Lewiston voters will decide whether to implement restrictions on syringe service programs.
Lewiston has one of several syringe service programs in the state. They are aimed at harm reduction, offering sterile needles and other supplies and connecting people to services such as substance use treatment.
Currently in Lewiston, people can receive up to 100 clean needles per visit. The ballot question asks if Lewiston residents want to amend the program to mandate a 1 to 1 needle exchange with a 20-syringe daily limit per person, require each provider to operate from one fixed location and ban mobile units. 
Portland rejected a similar proposal two years ago. 
Flock cameras 
As municipalities in Maine and across the country are increasingly relying on Artificial Intelligence for policing, some localities are considering bans. 
Voters in York will decide whether to ban automated license plate readers, such as Flock cameras. 
Auburn voters will eventually get to decide on their own petition to ban such cameras, but not until early next year in a special election. Over the summer, a group of bipartisan legislators collected enough signatures for the petition, which the city council decided in September to send to the voters (not enough time to put the question on the Nov. 3 ballot). 
Local efforts to ban Flock cameras gain steam

South Portland disabled and removed its Flock cameras in June following concern about data sharing and surveillance.
Circulating petitions
Voters may also come across people gathering signatures for several petitions at the polls because three statewide petitions are currently in circulation. 
One seeks to roll back cannabis legalization (which signature gatherers have been accused of misrepresenting in the past). 
Another would direct the Maine Legislature to develop a healthcare system that would ensure that all Mainers have “comprehensive, publicly funded healthcare coverage.”
And another would limit what sports and school facilities transgender students can access. It is a renewal of a failed attempt to get the initiative on the Nov. 3 ballot, after Maine’s highest court ruled the group did not clear the signature threshold.
