name: Georgia Recorder
title: Commentary: Bookman: This midterm election could reshape Georgia politics
text:
Former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms and U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff campaign together earlier this month in Cobb County. Alander Rocha/Georgia RecorderIf you believe the polls, Jon Ossoff will easily win re-election to the U.S. Senate, and Keisha Lance Bottoms is right on the heels of Rick Jackson in the governor’s race despite being badly outspent. She might even have a slight lead.
Once upon a time in a not-too-distant past, this whole thing would have been unthinkable. For some, it still is. But Georgia has changed, the times have changed and under Donald Trump, the Republican Party has changed. 
After Tuesday, even more change is likely. 
First, though, a note of caution: Polls can be wrong. Never put your faith in polls.
But can polls be wrong everywhere, all at once? I ask because national polls and polls in other states are producing results much like those predicted here in Georgia. They project significant Democratic gains even in deep red states such as Texas and Kansas. Overall, polls suggest a fairly consistent 8 to 10-point swing toward Democrats, which would be larger than in most midterms. If that proves to be the case come election night, a lot of unemployed Republican politicians will be lined up outside Fox News trying to get contributor contracts.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
But back to the question: Yes, theoretically all the polls can be wrong, everywhere and all at once, if pollsters are all making the same mistakes.  
So let’s examine the 2026 electorate from another perspective. Early voting totals here in Georgia show big turnout from Democratic counties, and slow turnout in Republican areas. While that data would seem to offer real-life validation of what the polls are finding, caution again reminds us that we won’t know for sure what those ballots contain until they’re opened and counted. Voters can be tricky.
However, we also know roughly who those voters are. Black and minority Georgians are turning out at a higher pace than white Georgians, who tend to vote Republican. Urban voters and independent suburban voters are voting in larger numbers than rural voters. In other words, polls, early voting numbers and voter demographics are all pointing us in the same general direction.
And if that turns out to be true, if Ossoff sails to reelection and Bottoms gets elected as governor, it’s hard to imagine the impact on Georgia politics in general and specifically on the Georgia Republican Party. Everything would have to change.
It has been an article of faith that Georgia is and always will be a conservative state. Even when the state was dominated by Democrats, they were culturally conservative, pro-business Democrats who had no problem whatsoever adopting the Republican identity when the time proved right. Even when Ossoff and Raphael Warnock won statewide races for the Senate, it was possible to dismiss those results as accidents of bad timing and bad candidates.
If the pollsters prove to be right, that’s no longer the case, and the power structure in the state will be shaken to its core.
The catalyst for that change, the catalyst for most of the political chaos of the last decade, is of course Donald Trump. In his second term as president, Republicans abandoned whatever restraints they once put on their president and have let Trump be Trump. Voters everywhere seem determined to make them pay for that failure.
If Tuesday delivers a broad rejection of Trump’s leadership, how do Georgia Republicans respond? For years they’ve been fed this delusion that Georgia hasn’t changed, that America hasn’t changed, that the only reason they’re losing elections is because they’re being cheated of their birthright to rule. That mindset, if it persists, will not allow them to make the necessary adjustments to compete in this emerging Georgia. 
They have a ready role model in Brian Kemp, the popular governor who leaves office with a nearly 70% job approval rating. However, part of Kemp’s appeal beyond the MAGA base is his refusal to embrace and act upon that “election integrity” delusion. For many MAGA Georgians, that is a disqualification.
Republicans would also have a lesson to the contrary in Mike Collins, the MAGA-approved Senate candidate who bet his future that a base-only strategy could still win a general election in this state. As Georgia voters are about to confirm, you cannot.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Beyond Bars celebrates writing and writers reaching out from inside prison walls
text:
Louise K. Waakaa'igan reading her poems at Beyond Bars: Voices of Incarceration. (Frank Zufall/Wisconsin Examiner)The Wisconsin Examiner’s Criminal Justice Reporting Project shines a light on incarceration, law enforcement and criminal justice issues with support from the Public Welfare Foundation.
Louise K. Waakaa’igan, a poet and member of the Anishinaabe (Lac Courte Oreilles Band of Lake Superior Chippewa) tribe in Sawyer County, Wisconsin, spent 16 years at the Shakopee women’s prison on the outskirts of the Twin Cities. Waakaa’igan was one of the 19 writers featured at a program called Beyond Bars: Voices of Incarceration.
The event, held on Oct. 24 at Hamline University in St. Paul, was the 15th public reading organized by the Minnesota Prison Writing Workshop, made possible by a grant from the Minnesota State Arts Board.
Some of the writers, like Waakaa’igan, had been released and now have jobs on the  outside. Waakaa’igan is the event coordinator at Lac Courte Oreilles Ojibwe University in Wisconsin. Others are still incarcerated and their writings were read by other authors or by a writing mentor or instructor.
More than 500 people filled the large, open venue at Hamline University overlooking the campus. The mood was upbeat. Writers who had recently been released got standing ovations, and all who had spent time in prison received flowers.
All of the writers in attendance who had been released from prison received flowers. (Frank Zufall/Wisconsin Examiner)
Waakaa’igan, who has participated in several of the past events since 2020, said she started writing when she was young as a way to “survive early adolescence,” but had stopped writing as an adult until she was in prison and a volunteer group encouraged her to start writing again in 2004.
“That’s really where my voice solidified, where I had an actual writing community for the first time in my life,” she said.  “Just a circle of writers where we would give each other feedback, where we’d be able to share, learn different aspects and different pieces of the craft, which was really beneficial.”
In 2014 Jennifer Bowen, the founder of the Minnesota Prison Writing Workshop, came to Shakopee, and helped expand the prison writing program with support from a large group of mentors who give feedback to incarcerated writers and instructors who teach in the prisons and provide a “creative community” to encourage writers.
“It’s just a creative, collaborative, supporting community that recognizes the writer, whether they’re incarcerated or not, recognizes the writer as an essential part of our creative life,” Waakaa’igan said of the Minnesota Prison Writing Workshop.
Bowen spoke of her appreciation for the writers and those who came out to support them.
Jennifer Bowen, the founder of Minnesota Prison Writers Workshop, talked about her admiration for the writers and also the people supporting them (Frank Zufall/Wisconsin Examiner)
“The incarcerated writers you all have sent thousands, literally thousands, of notes of feedback to, have long written under pressure, under surveillance, and toward change,” she said. “They’ve told us stories about 600 days in segregation, about surviving the Khmer Rouge, about missing their daughter on her birthday every single year for 21 years. Many of those writers are home now, joining us as citizen artists on pages and stages and in the streets, showing up to offer change as artists and the art when it’s most needed, which is now. And they are building nonprofits that connect and organize and heal this community.”
The readings kicked off with a student introduction by an incarcerated writer named Andrew  (read by Tarik Dobbs) who described himself as serving more than one life sentence. He recounted not caring about writing when he joined a workshop in prison just to pass the time, but then found something more:
“Writing gave me my life back, or at least made my fate and future possible, tolerable. And more often than one might think, for someone serving multiple life sentences, enjoyable — the  kind of joy and serenity only possible when one finds a sense of purpose, a reason for being. For me, this meant, in some part, the self-expression, the catharsis that comes from any writing, as small as one word on a post note or a magnum opus on the meaning of the universe.”
Waakaa’igan read “East of Cicero,” a poem that recalls memories of abuse and struggles experienced after leaving the reservation:
“The year was 1999. They just buried half my identity. I refused to attend the ceremony after talking with Ni maama (Ojibwe word for mother). Instead, I sat in the dark, carving scars on my anemic body, dirtying my pale skin blending tears with Mad Dog 20/20, burning stale cigarettes in my nephew’s sandbox. I began driving alone back then, replacing reservation roads for out-of-state freeways…I met my first demon there on I-94 east of Cicero. He silenced me like those drunk hands did in Six Mile. I laughed as I flicked my Newport out the window. I’m not a little girl anymore. I bragged. I’ll fight back this time. It was his turn to laugh, and he did, mimicking that drunken slur that left boozy saliva on my five-year-old body? …It wasn’t until I slept in that cement cell block in Minnesota that he let my tears dry on their own. Those saltless tears pulled next to me on that cement floor pitied me, just as that demon den east of Cicero.”
Louise K. Waakaa’igan (left) with her daughter Janey Trepanier and granddaughter Arya House. (Frank Zufall/Wisconsin Examiner)
Commenting on her poem, she said, “There are traumatic events in people’s lives, that I think, unfortunately, happen when we’re young that we learn how to recover and heal from, and I’m not exempt from that, and there have been things that have happened in my life that I’m still trying to recover and heal from, and my writing has definitely been a way to make sense of some of that and move on and heal in a way.”
She also read a poem written in prison about the place that shaped her:
“…I’m from Packer games on Sundays, Greyhound trips for Christmas, and Easter baskets with Karla. I’m from women with the same last name and a father none of us knew. I’m from the woods, northern, where pines and birch bark blanket both ends of tribal roads, paved and gravel. I’m from a single parent household. Michael Jackson cassette tapes, Purple Rain posters, and latchkey kids. Title V programs, commods (commodities, federal government issued food) on pantry shelves, cucumbers from Grandpa Jake’s garden and a mean ol’ dog named Turkey. I’m from ‘crying won’t change anything,’ and ‘you should have known better.’ I’m from punitive silence and where it’s normal, hugs are warm, forced Catholicism still weighs heavy on Imam’s shoulders. This is where I will always return.”
The poem, she said, was a kind of “sweet lamentation,” of the place she couldn’t return to because of incarceration.
Von Johnson, a writer recently released from prison and now on supervision, read his poem “Here Now!” describing the hardships in prison and then being released into society where he was adjusting to the freedom, figuring out who he spend his free time with,  learning new technology, enjoying his first savoy steak, but also the continued accountability to the criminal justice system living with an ankle monitor:
Von Johnson read his poem “Here now.” (Frankj Zufall/Wisconsin Examiner)
“I have to fill out a pass to go everywhere, even to come here tonight. Noting the time to leave, how long the drive will take, the moment I arrive, the purpose of being in each destination. My selfie game is out of control, except there’s always some address or giant logo next to my face to identify that I reached my destination, as if this ankle monitor wasn’t enough, right? How long I will stay, the minute I leave, my travel time, the next logo-slash-address field, you get the picture. I have to have permission to see my mother. Rules on how long I can hold my significant other, but I guess I’m here now. I need permission to drive a car, own a car. I’m not allowed to finance a car. Hell, get into a car. But I’m here now…”
Mark Altenhofen, called Red because he formerly had a red beard, read his  poem, “Do you remember,” written in prison upon learning a life-long friend outside was dying of leukemia:
“…Do you remember the feel of fist against flesh when we fought? The bitter tears on our lips with “I love you” and “I’m sorry” still foreign to us. Do you remember tumbling through the dust, our blood mixing with it until we fell side by side, too exhausted to do anything but laugh? Your mom compared us to Huck Finn and Tom Sawyer. We acted out the stories written until we nearly drowned…”
After his reading, Altenhofen talked about how  the Minnesota Prison Writing Workshop helps remind people in prison that  “we’re still human beings.” That  is “huge,” he said, “because it’s really easy to lose your humanity in there, and to be reminded we’re still people. We still have people that care about us, and there’s a community out here we can come back to. … It gives us something to hold onto and to look forward to, and to make ourselves better men.”
He added, “I was one of those guys I didn’t know how to talk about emotions. I treated emotions like I was a diabetic and that was sugary cereal for kids.” Writing, he said, was “a way to get to deal with the stuff I never had a chance to deal with, I never had the courage to talk to anybody about.”
Peter Schilling has mentored seven writers through the  Minnesota Prison Writing Workshop.  He said writers in prison often are processing their experience in a way that helps them cope. He noted one of his mentees wrote a Western, with wide open spaces that speak of unrestricted freedom as a counterpoint to his confinement, and another wrote a horror, modeled on a Steven King novel, transposing real struggles into the stories of fictional characters.
Will sang his original song “Among these Voices.” (Frank Zufall/Wisconsin Examiner)
Michael Kleber-Diggs, a writing instructor in prisons since 2015 and board president for Minnesota Prison Writing Workshop, said the evening event represented an effort to “transcend prison walls and reach the community,” and also to “tear down the distinction between incarcerated writers and community writers.”
One of the evening’s last offerings was an original song written by a man named Will, who had recently been released. He performed  “Among these voices,” an anthem to living courageously: “Justice, burn my lips come roaring off my tongue. Set me alight to set me free. This tide has risen to make many voices one. Among those voices you’ll find me.”

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Commentary: Voter registration update: Pa. Dems show strong gains ahead of 2026 midterms
text:
Voter registration trends in Pennsylvania as of October 19, 2026. Key: Navy - D+5,000 or more, Blue - D+1,001 to D+4,999, Light Skyblue - D+1 to D+1,000. Light Salmon - R+1 to R+1,000, Red - R+1,001 to R+4,999, Maroon - R+5,000 or more. Yellow - No Net Change. (Map by Nick Field via Dave’s Redistricting)
Pennsylvania Democrats have all the momentum at their backs as they hope for a Blue Wave to sweep the November 3rd midterm elections. 
Since 2015, I’ve examined the voter registration trends in the Keystone State across dozens of articles over the last decade-plus. In that time, I’ve never created a map as blue as the one above. For the most part, Pennsylvania  Republicans have consistently gained ground on their Democratic counterparts in the Trump Era.
To illustrate, a month before Trump descended the escalator to run for president, Democrats held a registration advantage in the state of 999,427. By the end of 2024, in the wake of Trump’s second Presidential victory, that lead had dwindled to only 170,975. 
In October 2025, however, the tide began to turn as Trump’s approval ratings  dropped and there was new leadership in the statewide Democratic Party. By last May, thanks to gains in the southeast and south central portions of the commonwealth, Dems were able to improve their margin to 188,381. 
Over the course of the summer, Democrats experienced strong growth throughout the state, to the point that their statewide margin now stands at 247,724. These numbers will likely buoy Gov. Josh Shapiro, who is aiming to win re-election with enough coattails to flip four U.S House seats. The governor’s also looking to become the first Democratic incumbent to sweep in elected majorities in the state House and Senate since Milton Shapp did so during the 1974 Watergate midterms.  
Beyond our borders, political observers are always eagerly watching a swing state like Pennsylvania to get a sense of the national mood. So let’s take a deeper dive into these numbers to see what they can tell us about the upcoming midterms! 
A quick note: I explore our changing voter trends by tracking the gains one party accumulated in registrations over the other party. For example, R+500 means that the Republican Party gained a net 500 more registered voters in that county than the Democratic Party did over this period, while D+500 indicates the opposite.
A sign directs voters to where they can cast their ballots at Allegheny County Election office in Pittsburgh Oct. 19, 2026. (Photo by John Beale/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)

One of the most-debated topics of the 2026 campaign is whether Trump’s tariff and Iran policies are hurting him with his rural voters. Well, in largely rural central Pa., we’re seeing Democratic gains in core GOP counties. Moreover, the influx of new students to Penn State flipped Centre County from a Republican plurality to a Democratic plurality, reversing a GOP accomplishment from 2024.

Among the quartet of competitive Congressional contests in our commonwealth is the match-up between freshman Rep. Rob Bresnahan and Democratic challenger Paige Cognetti in the Northeast’s 8th Congressional District. Over the past decade, Donald Trump converted thousands of ancestral Democrats in the Scranton/Wilkes-Barre corridor, to the point that Bresnahan was elected off Trump’s coattails in 2024.
In 2026, however, it looks like some of those voters are returning to the Democratic fold, as the party posted four-digit gains in both Lackawanna and Luzerne counties. The Luzerne numbers in particular must be especially worrying for the Bresnahan campaign, as his eight point margin there was pivotal to his 2024 victory.

I always keep an eye on bellwether Erie County, which has supported the statewide winner in 19 of the last 20 Presidential elections. If Democrats bounce back there it could be a sign that they’re likely to perform well throughout the Midwestern United States.

The southcentral region is home to another critical U.S. Houe  race, the rematch between Republican incumbent Scott Perry and his Democratic opponent Janelle Stelson in PA-10. Perry can’t be happy with these numbers, as not only did blue Dauphin and purple Cumberland move left, but Dems also gained ground in York, traditionally the Big Red Machine of Pa.counties. Furthermore, the shift in Lancaster suggests Josh Shapiro could become the first Democratic gubernatorial nominee to win that county since Bob Casey Sr’s landslide back in 1990.  
Southeast

SEPA is home to the other two key U.S. House races: Incumbent GOP Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick vs Democrat Bob Harvie in PA-1, and Democrat Bob Brooks vs incumbent GOP Rep. Ryan Mackenzie in PA-7. The 1st District mostly consists of Bucks County, where Democrats are trying to build on their 2025 victories to finally upset the Fitzpatrick dynasty there. Meanwhile, Dem gains in Lehigh and Northampton Counties are a strong sign for Brooks’ hopes of flipping the bellwether 7th District.
Even further down the ballot, there are several state Senate and state House races in this area that Gov. Shapiro is targeting. For instance, the Montgomery County native is aiming to flip the Southeast trio of SD-6, SD-16 and SD-24 in his quest to earn that aforementioned Pa. Senate majority. Recent polling from State Navigate suggests Shapiro’s coattails may indeed be strong enough to win these crucial legislative races. 
Southwest

Allegheny: D+7,291

Since 2016, Donald Trump has depended upon the voters in the Appalachian southwest to power his statewide efforts in Pennsylvania. Yet even here, the PA GOP is seeing erosion. While it’s not a surprise to see Democrats gain in Allegheny County, the degree of their improvement is nonetheless notable. What might most worry Republicans, however, is the poor performance in Allegheny’s neighboring counties, where they’ve gotten used to posting terrific margins on Election Nights.  
Why these trends mnatter
All historical and contemporary indicators suggest Democrats will enjoy plenty of victories on November 3rd. Of course, ever since Donald Trump shocked the world and defeated Hillary Clinton in the 2016 presidential contest, any positive poll results have elicited the same reaction from shell-shocked Dems: Are these numbers actually for real?
While anything could still happen, it’s worth going over how the Pennsylvania voter registration trends have generally been predictive of future results. Republicans initially saw gains throughout Trump’s rise in 2015 and 2016; and they only began to lose momentum midway through 2017 and on into the 2018 midterms, when Dems won the House. GOP growth then resumed in the run-up to the 2020 election, foreshadowing Trump’s surprising performance in that contest (despite losing in 2020, Trump out-performed his polls the most that year).
During the summer and fall of 2022, Republican registration gains noticeably slowed, an indication that those midterms would ultimately disappoint them, as Democrats held up well for a party with an incumbent president. Yet the PA GOP resumed their strong growth in 2023 and 2024, a sign that Trump would soon return to power.
Given all this context, these past two years have unfolded as you might expect. Coming out of 2024, Pennsylvania Republicans continued to make gains through 2025, only for the tide to begin to turn that fall. Since then, state PA Dems have gained exponentially more strength over the course of 2026, suggesting they’ll do quite well in these upcoming midterms.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Final Ohio campaign finance report shows Acton raising more, spending less than Ramaswamy
text:
Democratic candidate for governor Dr. Amy Acton, left, and Republican candidate for governor, Vivek Ramaswamy, right. (Photos/graphic by WEWS.)Campaign finance reports filed last Thursday give Ohio one final look at the governor’s race ahead of Election Day. Outside groups like Super PACs will continue reporting independent expenditures with the Federal Election Commission, but Thursday’s report is last window into Ohio campaigns’ direct fundraising and spending.
Over the summer, Ohio campaigns report what they raised on a monthly basis, but not what they spent. So, when it comes time to make their final filing ahead of Election Day, they’re reporting two weeks of fundraising but more than four months of spending.
The gulf between the two in Republican Vivek Ramaswamy’s report is large. While his campaign brought in $1.5 million, it spent $51.1 million. Ramaswamy also reported making another $5 million loan to his campaign. That brings its total outstanding debt to $41.3 million.
Continuing a recent trend, Democratic candidate Amy Acton reported raising far more than her Republican competitor. Acton’s campaign reported bringing in $3.9 million — more than double Ramaswamy’s take — while spending $26.2 million.
Ramaswamy’s report
Among Ramaswamy’s donors making contributions of $10,000 or more are American Electric Power, the Ohio branch of the National Federation of Independent Businesses, Elevance Health — formerly Anthem, and a political committee representing Ohio banks.
Outside groups pour hundreds of millions into Ohio races for governor, U.S. Senate

The Winkelvoss twins, who notably almost invented Facebook, both made maximum donations to Ramaswamy’s campaign. The brothers now run a venture capital firm and head up a cryptocurrency Super PAC called Digital Freedom Fund.
That PAC has spent another $5.9 million in Ohio attacking Democrat Sherrod Brown or boosting his Republican opponent U.S. Sen. Jon Husted.
Ramaswamy’s campaign spent more than $35 million on media and television ad placements between July and Oct. 14. The biggest single media expenditure is the most recent — nearly $8 million on Oct. 8.
From the outset of his campaign, Ramaswamy faced criticism for crisscrossing the state in a private jet. In September, NBC reported on growing unease among GOP officials who urged him to “park the damn jet.”
Ramaswamy didn’t take their advice.
The pre-general report includes nearly $870,000 in charges related to Ramaswamy’s private jet travel. The campaign maintained two concurrent aircraft leases totaling almost $386,000. In addition, Ramaswamy’s campaign reports spending nearly $484,000 with the private jet charter company Talon Air.
Ramaswamy also reports making two in-kind contributions to Secretary of State Frank LaRose’s campaign to fly to campaign events.
Acton’s report
The biggest contributions Acton reports are a pair of donations totaling about $262,000 from the Ohio Democratic Party candidate fund. She also got donations of $10,000 or more from committees representing Franklin County Engineer Adam Fowler, Columbus teachers, the Ohio life sciences industry, and the Ohio Hospital Association.
But the OHA appears to be hedging its bets. Every contribution its PAC has made since Oct. 2025 has gone to Republicans. And although it gave Acton $10,000, it gave Ramaswamy a maximum donation of $16,615 two weeks prior.
Two notable individual donors backing Acton are executives with the defense company Anduril, which is building a manufacturing facility called Arsenal-1 just outside Columbus. CEO Brian Schimpf and COO Matthew Grimm both gave Acton maximum donations.
Acton’s campaign reports spending about $22.3 million on advertising placements and production. Roughly $1.7 million of that was later refunded to the campaign bringing the total closer to $20.6 million.
Like Ramaswamy, Acton’s campaign logged a lot of flight miles. But because they fly commercial it cost a lot less. Despite scores of airfare reimbursements, Acton’s total bill was about $57,600 — or less than a month and a half of Ramaswamy’s cheapest aircraft lease.

title: Charleston port chief says recovery underway, but more work must be done
text:
Micah Mallace, president and CEO of the S.C. State Ports Authority, delivers the 2026 State of the Port speech at the North Charleston Convention Center on Tuesday, Oct. 27. 2026. (Photo by Jeni Becker/Courtesy of the S.C. State Ports Authority)NORTH CHARLESTON — With the promise of a 6% increase in containerized cargo already on the books and a better financial footing to build on, the South Carolina State Ports Authority is now in the second phase of a three-part comeback plan that will restore its competitiveness in the South Atlantic region, its president reported.
“Where last year I personally could not have stood up here and said I saw light at the end of the tunnel … today I do,” Micah Mallace, the authority’s president and CEO, said Tuesday during his annual State of the Port address at the North Charleston Convention Center.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“It’s not some rose-colored glasses or hopeless optimism, but we are on the next steps toward overcoming some of our largest obstacles,” Mallace told a record audience of 1,150 people at the event hosted by the Propeller Club of Charleston.
Mallace — who took over as CEO a year ago following the abrupt resignation of the agency’s previous leader — outlined a three-phase comeback plan for the authority, which owns and operates the Port of Charleston.
Following a year of regaining competitiveness, which Mallace termed the first phase, the authority is looking to improve service and build on what has been accomplished.
“We have kick-started our momentum story,” Mallace said, adding that while “we have arrested negative momentum” the effort still needs help from the entire maritime community to move forward.
“It’s fragile and still requires attention,” Mallace said of the recovery. “The kindling is burning. The logs are ready to go on. Walk away, and it goes out. Tend to it, work together, and it grows.”
Mallace said the authority had been spending too much money while chasing too little cargo and charging container ship operators and other customers high rates that exceeded the amount competitors like the Port of Savannah were asking.
Operating expenses have been trimmed by more than 20% in the past year — savings that have been passed on to customers and a pledge Mallace made during his first State of the Port speech a year ago.
SC Ports shifting focus to growth with immediate benefits, new CEO says

That hasn’t yet shown up in a year-over-year increase in cargo volumes, which were down 5% at the end of the most recent fiscal year.
Still, Mallace said businesses have committed to bringing an additional 159,000 containers through the port in the coming year, roughly 6% of the port’s annual total, due largely to financial and operational improvements the port has made.
Unlike previous years, where the port’s cargo mix was largely manufacturing based, the new business coming online through 2027 represents a broader mix of industrial products, consumer goods and export commodities.
“This new business is a direct result of the port team’s willingness to rethink how we operate, find innovative solutions and deliver the exceptional service our customers need to grow,” Mallace said, adding that while cost cuts were largely across the board the agency’s sales staff was doubled.
“We are building momentum,” he said. “We have a clear strategy, and we are committed to turning this momentum into sustained growth.”
While continuing to cater to the state’s manufacturing base, the authority will sharpen its focus on luring new retail distribution centers to South Carolina.
Retail goods continue to outpace other import categories throughout the Southeast, but a statewide lack of distribution and warehouse space has hindered growth here. Consumer goods account for 81% of the value of containerized goods nationwide, but only about 50% at Charleston’s port.
“Where distribution centers locate, the ships follow,” Mallace said.
SC Ports temporarily halts Leatherman operations in face of high costs, waning demand

The authority also intends to hold costs steady while improving service, including truck turn times, in the coming year.
Getting to the third phase of the recovery plan will take time and a sustained effort, but Malllace said he will know it has been successful when the port reopens its Leatherman Terminal in North Charleston.
The authority on Aug. 1 indefinitely paused operations at the $1 billion terminal, which has been underutilized because of its high unionized labor costs. The port’s other container terminals do not have the same labor structure.
“That will signify that we have achieved volumes and an operating cost structure that suggests the terminal stays open, not for another year or two but for good,” Mallace said, adding this is not the time.
“We are not rushing any of these things,” he said. “We want to be intentional. We want to do it right.”
The same is true of the Navy Base Intermodal Facility, a near-dock rail yard in North Charleston where trains from Norfolk Southern and CSX Corp. will move cargo boxes.
Mallace said the authority is still negotiating contracts with those railroads and an opening date for the rail yard is not scheduled.
“The first phase was to get competitive again,” Mallace said of his three-pronged plan. “The second phase of the comeback plan is to strengthen the core and deliver on some of the commitments we’ve made. And the third phase — make it stick.”

title: Ohio Democrats outraised Republicans in home stretch of key U.S. House races
text:
The U.S. Capitol. (Photo by Jennifer Shutt/States Newsroom)Democrats outraised Republicans in five of the six competitive U.S. House races in Ohio as the midterm election season enters its final days.
That includes Ohio’s 10th Congressional district, where 12-term Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Turner faces a late surge from Democratic challenger Kristina Knickerbocker for a chance to represent the Dayton area in Congress. 
The data from Ohio reflects a national trend of both parties redirecting spending to newly competitive battlegrounds in traditionally Republican areas.
House Majority PAC, a super PAC aligned with House Democratic leadership, released a poll Wednesday showing Democratic nominee for the 15th Congressional district Don Leonard up 3% over Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Carey. It was one of six polls showing Democratic challengers leading in Republican strongholds.
Both districts were rated “Solid Republican” by Cook Political Report until August. On Oct. 16, the election forecaster shifted both to “Lean Republican.”
“For the first time in years, Democrats have genuine pickup opportunities deep into Trump territory, in districts that were once considered entirely out of reach,” House Majority PAC said in a press release.
Congressional candidates must file several financial disclosures throughout the year of their election. Reports for the first two weeks of October were due Oct. 22.
Democrats widened cash advantages in the 7th and 9th Congressional districts, which are rated “Toss-Up” by Cook Political Report, and in the 1st and 13th Congressional districts, which are rated “Likely Democratic.” Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Carey, who represents the 10th Congressional district, was the only Republican to outraise his opponent.
Even as independent polls of the Congressional generic ballot point to a favorable environment for Democrats, National Republican Congressional Committee spokesman Zach Bannon said the GOP is “on offense” across the state. 
Although the NRCC spent on ads supporting Turner in recent weeks, neither incumbent is on the organization’s list of vulnerable Republican congressmembers.
“Congressmen Mike Turner and Mike Carey are battle-tested leaders who have delivered real results for their communities and earned Ohioans’ trust,” Bannon said.
Democrats had the largest fundraising advantages in the two districts rated as toss-ups.
Democratic nominee for Ohio’s 7th Congressional district Brian Poindexter reported over $3.1 million in direct contributions from July through the first half of October, far more than incumbent Republican U.S. Rep. Max Miller’s $180,000 in reported donations.
Miller put $1 million of his own money into the race in August after allegations of domestic abuse prompted several national Republicans, including both of Ohio’s U.S. Senators, to call for him to drop out. 
He spent almost $2.4 million in the third quarter, but just over $22,000 in the first two weeks of October, leaving him with around $135,000 in cash on hand. Poindexter reported a cash balance of around $793,000, making Miller the only incumbent in any of Ohio’s competitive Congressional districts with less cash on hand than his opponent.
“After Max Miller loaned himself $1 million to try to buy himself out of trouble, tens of thousands of grassroots supporters stepped up to help send a union ironworker to Congress,” Poindexter said in a press release. “I am grateful for their support.”
Meanwhile, Democratic U.S. Rep. Marcy Kaptur spent over $3.2 million in the third quarter of her rematch with Republican nominee Derek Merrin. It’s the most Kaptur has spent in a single quarter over her 44 years representing Ohio’s 9th Congressional district, and more than her spending in all but two election cycles.
Kaptur beat Merrin by 0.7 percentage points in 2024 despite President Donald Trump winning the district by seven percentage points. The Ohio Redistricting Commission redrew the district’s boundaries in 2025; had the 2024 election used the new map, Trump would have won the new 9th Congressional district by 10.6 percentage points.
Kaptur is spending more of her own committee’s money and getting less outside help compared to the third quarter of 2024. Back then, super PACs spent over $4.4 million to support her or oppose Merrin while she spent just $2.2 million. Super PACs make independent expenditures, meaning that they are barred from coordinating with candidates by federal law.
Kaptur reported around $697,000 in cash balance to Merrin’s $430,000 cash on hand.
Ohio’s 1st and 13th Congressional districts were within Republicans’ sights at the start of 2026. 
Democratic U.S. Rep. Emilia Sykes won reelection to the 13th Congressional district by just 2.2 percentage points in 2024. Democratic U.S. Rep. Greg Landsman’s 1st Congressional district was redrawn from one that favored Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris by seven percentage points to one that would have favored Trump by three percentage points.
Cook Political Report rated the 1st Congressional district “Toss-Up” and the 13th Congressional district “Lean Democratic” in March. The National Republican Congressional Committee added 1st Congressional district nominee Eric Conroy to its “MAGA Majority,” a list of challengers to vulnerable U.S. House Democrats, in April.
As the national environment deteriorated for Republicans in the summer and fall, the outlook for Republicans in both districts worsened.
Democrats and Republicans cut back on previous commitments to spend in the 1st Congressional district in October. The Congressional Leadership Fund, a super PAC aligned with House Republican leadership, pulled all remaining advertising after announcing it would spend $4 million in the district. Their Democratic counterpart, the House Majority PAC, canceled around $192,000 in future advertising on Oct. 19.
A significant portion of that money is instead being spent on two ruby-red Congressional districts that Democrats believe they could flip.
Turner is in his 24th year of representing the Dayton area, which the 10th Congressional district encompasses entirely. He won all 12 of his regular Congressional election campaigns by 10 percentage points or more.
He was outraised from July through the first half of October by Democratic nominee Kristina Knickerbocker, who reported around $642,000 in direct contributions to Turner’s $417,000. He still has around $191,000 more in cash on hand from previous campaigns.
Carey reported around $772,000 while Democratic challenger for the 15th Congressional district Don Leonard received around $550,000 in campaign contributions over the same span. Carey had a cash advantage of around $272,000 as of Oct. 14. 
Although the NRCC spent on ads supporting Turner in recent weeks, neither incumbent is on the organization’s list of vulnerable Republican congressmembers.
“Congressmen Mike Turner and Mike Carey are battle-tested leaders who have delivered real results for their communities and earned Ohioans’ trust,” said Bannon, the NRCC spokesperson.
Independent polls are yet to be conducted for either district, but outside spending from both sides soared in October. Independent-expenditure groups spent a combined $5.4 million on ads in the two districts just in the week between Oct. 16 and Oct. 23.
[Voter Guide: 2026 Ohio General Election Voter Guide: Races, deadlines, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
A Democratic dark money group called Your Community PAC has spent close to $3.9 million in both races, making it the second-biggest spender in the two districts behind the party leadership-affiliated House Majority PAC. Knickerbocker and Leonard reject corporate PAC donations, and both have called for campaign finance reform.
Neither have any control over outside groups’ decisions to boost their campaigns, said Atiba Ellis, a Case Western Reserve University professor who studies campaign finance. 
“Candidates certainly could denounce ads that cut against their message. But at the same time, that could spin off into other misunderstandings that could affect the electorate,” he said. “So, even if it’s not a contribution, the outside spending and the commercials that result define the campaign in ways that it’s really hard for politicians to fight against.”
It reflects a larger trend of outside groups holding increasing influence on elections, even for campaigns with mostly grassroots donor bases, Ellis said. Republicans hold a large spending advantage in Ohio’s U.S. Senate and governor’s races despite being outraised by Democrats, largely because of outside groups.
These outside groups often spend on attack ads against candidates’ character, Ellis added, which can take attention away from important policy issues.
“Their premise is to motivate people using the least common denominator they can find concerning the candidate they oppose,” he said. “It’s ironic that in the name of getting out the vote, we’re being distracted from having serious debates about the issues that should guide people on how to vote.”

title: Commentary: Standing alongside a personal attack on a victim of child rape, Ohio politicians reveal themselves
text:
U.S. President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance. (Photo by Drew Angerer/Getty Images)When you stand with vile you reveal yourself. A political ad that ran in Ohio last week sparked nationwide revulsion as perhaps the vilest in American history. It is that bad. 
Republican Vivek Ramaswamy’s morally incomprehensible hit piece against Democrat Dr. Amy Acton in the Ohio race for governor will be studied and deconstructed (in all its atrociousness) long after the 2026 midterm elections are over. You know why. 
The decision to platform a mother complicit in the rape of her daughter — as an obscene strategy to blindside a political opponent — went way beyond the pale of personal attacks in the heat of a campaign. It was a sick act by a struggling candidate to capture voter attention that few saw coming. 
The ad featured the estranged mom of Ramaswamy’s gubernatorial rival. Donna Arthur fled Youngstown 48 years ago with Acton’s alleged rapist after the then 12-year-old victim testified against him in court.
The 80-something woman in Ramaswamy’s toxic ad chose to live on the lam with Acton’s fugitive stepfather, Cledith Arthur, until he died in 2004. Neither Acton nor her younger brother saw or spoke to their mother since she skipped town in 1978 with the man arrested, charged, and indicted by a grand jury for raping Acton. 
It was this troubled character, who abandoned her daughter and son as children, that Team Ramaswamy brought direct to camera with scripted venom. Arthur delivered. The performance was staged in a cozy, softly lit kitchen to exude warmth in chilling scene from a twisted story. 
Acton, whom Arthur rejected as a shattered tween in a courtroom, called her now 60-year-old daughter a serial liar with mental health issues who needed help. She warned Ohio voters “don’t let her become your governor.” The message was meant to stop people cold. It did. But after the bombshell went viral so did the backstory. 
The tables turned. So did stomachs as viewers (across the political spectrum) realized how next-level despicable the ad was in elevating an aging abusive mother with a checkered past who ditched a traumatized daughter to run off with the child rapist who assaulted her. 
The Ramaswamy obscenity, thrown on the air less than two weeks before the election, has been widely vilified as the re-victimization of young Acton to win power at any cost. 
Imagine the buried pain it must have triggered. The ad is still running in a shortened version — as if that sanitizes reprehensible. Tellingly, not only does Ramaswamy stand by his viral outrage, but vows to promote it with more than $4 million in bought airtime across the state. 
As disgust grew (and grows by the day) over the exploitation of a tortured childhood for political sport, Ohio’s finger in the wind Republicans responded on a scale from minimal to militant. 
“I would not have run the ad” was the mealy-mouthed comeback from Ohio U.S. Sen. Jon Husted, running in a tight race with former Democratic candidate Sherrod Brown to keep his seat, and Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose, running for a placeholder spot as state auditor against Annette Blackwell, a third-term Cleveland-area mayor. 
“I hope the ad will be taken down,” said an equally mincing former Ohio U.S. Sen. Rob Portman, who added the rising incivility in politics “should concern us all.” 
It took Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine a full day to denounce the weaponization of childhood sexual abuse that gut punched his former state health director who was instrumental in helping Ohioans navigate a frightening and fatal pandemic. 
“It’s just plain wrong,” he said. Finally. “Deeply, deeply troubling.” DeWine also said he stood by his endorsement of Ramaswamy despite the vileness manifested in his contemptible ad for the ages. Ever the profile in cowardice. 
Notably, all the Ohio Republicans who had something to say about the appalling Ramaswamy ad that revictimized the girl who grew up to become the Democratic nominee for Ohio governor — still stand with the GOP nominee for governor who launched the unconscionable clickbait and has never stopped defending it.
Ramaswamy blames backlash to the ad, which has generated massive national and local attention, on (wait for it) a “flawed and failed media” that is “lying about an ad that is about lying.” 
JD Vance, a confessed liar who admitted creating stories out of thin air to command similar exposure, piled on by declaring his disgust not with the vicious strike against a child rape survivor but with Republicans “whining” about it. 
The ad is “not really my concern,” sniffed the smug, amoral veep from Middletown. Couldn’t care less about whether resurfacing Acton’s MIA mother to score political points was appropriate or abhorrent. 
Vance, who also survived an abusive childhood, summoned no compassion or moral clarity about the depravity that drove Team Ramaswamy to malign yesterday’s abused and neglected child for political sport. With JD, power trumps principal. Winning is paramount. Decency is an indulgence. Republicans can’t get hung up on humane if they want control.
Vance’s boss doubled down on defense of the indefensible. Trump embraced the Ramaswamy ad as a gift from heaven and urged the candidate to leave it up. 
He was thrilled the ad blowing up on social media “was hitting pay dirt” and insisted his party own it. But when you stand with vile — smearing a child rape victim to win dirty — you reveal much about yourself. 
Which Ohio Republican will stand with Trump when he returns to Ohio Wednesday? The president welcomes vileness as a means to an end. He demands supporters follow suit or be branded as “disloyal to the Republican Party. Watch who joins him on the stage at the Chillicothe rally. Always revealing.

title: Commentary: Ohio voters, casting a ballot is our foundational right and responsibility
text:
Voting booths. (Photo by Seth Tupper, States Newsroom.)I am among the many Americans who did not vote in our elections at one time. I believe I was wrong not to do so and I will attempt to convince you current non-voters to change your mind.  
And there are many of you. Even among those registered, ten percent do not cast ballots. In the 2024 national elections, fully ten percent of registered voters did not turn out. That is 18 million registered non-voters in a closely fought election decided by two million votes. 
When I was quite a bit younger and before I knew much history I had little understanding about the long struggle for the right to vote and the democracy of which it is a key part. Most of humanity for most of our history has been governed by narrow cliques of thieving oligarchs or autocratic royals, many of whom relied on violence and terror to retain power. 
[Voter Guide: 2026 Ohio General Election Voter Guide: Races, deadlines, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
At the start of the democratic era it took great courage to stand against the powers that be. But many thousands of people did so anyway, even realizing that they might well pay with their lives to resist. Great numbers of them had to know that they themselves would be unlikely to ever live to exercise the right to vote. They sacrificed their own lives and welfare so that the rest of us could live in a democratic society. Among those epic struggles were the American and French revolutions, but they were not the first. The people of ancient Athens also rose up against tyranny for democracy. Of course there were also many others.  
So I argue that we owe a debt to those who struggled on our behalf. We have a duty to them to vote, and to do so intelligently as best we are able. It is easy to forget that women and minorities were excluded from voting in the United States for long periods of time, and had to struggle mightily for the voting franchise. Some of them paid with their lives. By voting, we can show respect their sacrifices. 
Another argument against voting is that our votes do not count for much. Well, there is some truth to that in the United States, especially with an Electoral College winner-take-all presidential system in which our votes do not count at all if our candidate loses in our state. But on the other hand, there are many state and local offices, as well as school, park, health, safety and other local levies, for which our votes can matter a great deal. And in fact, local elections have a significant impact on the quality of our lives. 
We also hear it said that politicians in general are corrupt and “all the same”. There is a grain of truth to that point of view. Many politicians are indeed narcissistic sociopaths to whom the idea of the public good is close to meaningless. But they are not all like that. In fact, politicians and parties vary in their truthfulness and honesty – at least a third of them are reasonably honest and worth supporting. It is your job as a voter to do some research and support the best of them. If you do not vote, you enable the bad guys. Nowadays it is hard to argue that there are no differences in the two major US political parties.  
To be fair, there are real barriers to voting including onerous registration procedures, long lines at the polls, billionaire dark money in campaigns, and lazy “horse race” journalism that avoids issues. Negative ads and hate media increase public cynicism and increase polarization, of which we have too much already. The consultants who produce untruthful and fear-inducing media know exactly what they are doing.  
It is your job to meet these challenges and support those who are working hard to address them.
If your vote did not matter, they would not work to keep you away from the polls. With freedom comes responsibilities. Voting is one of them. 
Arnold Oliver is Professor Emeritus of Political Science at Heidelberg University in Tiffin, Ohio, and is a member of Veterans For Peace. He is grateful to his former students and colleagues who taught him about the importance of voting.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Can this film change our understanding of the climate and migration crises?
text:
A still from The Welcome Table. (Image courtesy HBO.)
This story was originally published by Capital & Main.
Filmmaker Josh Fox has racked up a lot of miles covering the climate crisis. Sparked by a confounding business offer at his family home nearly two decades ago, his latest project took him around the world to tell stories of people uprooted by extreme weather and natural disasters.
It started in 2008 when a fracking company approached Fox, whose family has long had a home in northeastern Pennsylvania, with a $100,000 offer to lease minerals beneath the property for natural gas development.
Attempting to make sense of the offer, Fox turned to a nearby town already on the frontlines of fracking: Dimock. In that rural Pennsylvanian hamlet, he found families complaining that the natural gas extraction technique had ruined their well water and caused stomach aches and other sicknesses.
That spurred Fox to go deeper and take a road trip, documentary gear in tow, to natural gas-producing areas across the United States where, over and over, he heard testimonials from landowners living near operations of the nascent industry.
He discovered people who would hold a match up to their kitchen faucets — and light their tap water on fire. He strung together such images in the Emmy-winning, Oscar-nominated documentary “Gasland,” a cautionary tale about the risks of the booming industry, which saw the number of fracking wells nationwide multiply 13-fold between 2000 and 2015.
In the years since, the industry has continued to grow, even as climate change-fueled natural disasters have surged in frequency and severity.
In the shadows of “Gasland,” which was pivotal in paving the way for what developed into a potent protest movement against fracking, Fox’s latest film, “The Welcome Table,” shows the result of continued fossil fuel development.
The HBO Original Documentary takes viewers into communities on six continents that Fox visited over a nine-year period. It follows climate migrants who are victims of wildfires — like the 2018 blaze that nearly wiped the town of Paradise, California, off the map — floods and hurricanes, back to the homes from which they fled or to the new ones to which they relocated.
The film visits residents in communities ravaged by drought and mudslides where locals are holding out after fearful neighbors took off. It also features climate migrants who, among the growing number of people seeking refuge in other countries, are hampered or blocked entirely by tightening border policies that don’t take into account the gravity of their hardships.
The film argues that solving the climate crisis and the vast global migration intertwined with it will require collaboration, not division.
Ahead the film’s Oct. 25 national tour kickoff, Fox spoke with Capital & Main about the new film, how it fits into his larger body of work and what it says about the state of the climate crisis.
This interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.
Capital & Main: Some of the first shots in this movie are from the Paradise fire in Northern California in 2018, where you follow a couple who lost their home as they wade through the rubble of their old lives. That was eight years ago. When and how did you know you had a movie on climate migration — a departure from your earlier films on resource extraction?
Josh Fox: So, with “Gasland,” there’s this image of people lighting their water on fire. Ninety-nine percent of people have a kitchen sink. So, when you light the water on fire, they’re like, “Oh f—, that’s just like my kitchen sink.” And people would tell me that they went home to try to light their water on fire, even though they were living nowhere near fracking.
But nobody has [a visceral concept] of their “climate” [the way they have a concept of their tap water]. This is a problem.
“The Welcome Table” is not a climate movie. I think climate change is the background, the backdrop. I felt like what we needed to look at was: How many people are going to lose their homes? How many people are going to be displaced?
I realized that these two issues [climate and immigration] were on such a collision course. And the film focuses on people losing their homes because home is so intrinsic to everyone. Everyone should have a home, or at least has an idea of home, right? Even if they don’t have an idea of “climate.”
“Gasland” was really about one thing — fracking. “The Welcome Table” is about climate change, but also nationalism, border policies and colonialism, and these three things get their own attention in the movie. Was that intentional? 
We have made a tragic error about what the cause of climate change was by focusing on parts per million of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. That’s a symptom. Colonialism is the real cause, and the ideology that goes along with it. What I wanted to show was people’s reaction to loss and crisis. As [a Brazilian community leader named] Gabriel says at the end of the movie, “Home is not a place; home is the people around me.” That’s the only home we have left.
“Gasland,” which came out in 2010, in the early days of natural gas extraction, was a cautionary tale about fracking. “The Welcome Table” is about not listening to that cautionary tale. As our societies have extracted and burned more natural gas, these people who have seen their homes threatened by climate change are living proof of the result.
This is the result of 100 years of influence of the oil industry on our politics. It’s more powerful than anything. Our leaders didn’t want to take it on, and as a result, the world is burning and it’s a disaster. The question is: Can we move on from this extractive ideology, or will it destroy the planet? There are these giant questions that I don’t know the answer to, but it does feel very dire at this moment.
“Gasland” created a lot of buzz, including in and around Dimock, where, 12 years after the film came out, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, then-attorney general, secured a plea deal from a fracking company charged with polluting the area. The deal saw the company agree to pay for a clean water line for residents. Yet, the same day, regulators lifted a vital protection preventing fracking in the town that had been in place for 10 years. Is this the justice you expected for that area, and what does justice for the communities you feature even look like? 
It’s a betrayal in every sense. It would be very helpful to redefine rural Pennsylvania as a place that has been colonized by the oil industry, by the powers that be, and whether you have a Democratic label, like Josh Shapiro, or a red one like [former pro-drilling Republican Gov.] Tom Corbett, this is not what we need.
Josh Shapiro, not only is he politically a hypocrite, but he is a better agent for the oil industry than somebody like Tom Corbett. Josh Shapiro is trying to pretend to be the good guy. Pennsylvania has a history of people who are mealy-mouthed corporate centrists who love to pretend that they are on the side of the working class, but they ignore the working class. It’s incredibly condescending and it’s dehumanizing. The first thing you do when you colonize the place is you dehumanize those people.
After “Gasland,” you faced a broad backlash from the natural gas industry, which argued the film contained falsehoods. That effort included a campaign to disqualify your film from Oscar consideration after it was nominated for best documentary. The disinformation ecosystem has changed a lot since then.
What we’re seeing right now in the arena of truth and misinformation is the toxic data that is everywhere, and it’s polluting the landscape of journalism. Misinformation is more prevalent than fact. Propaganda is more prevalent than journalism.
Right now, we need to imagine. We need to indulge that poetic part of us that is much more human and true. When I started “The Welcome Table,” we were in a different era.
The ideas that sort of bind the movie to what I imagine its audience would be are still there. The principles in there are: human rights and love and generosity. It’s better to share than to be greedy, and be accepting of people, rather than bigoted. Those things I would hope we still have a consensus about.

title: Catching Our Eye News Roundup, Oct. 28, 2026
text:
The Ohio burgee. (Getty images file photo.)Every morning in the Ohio Capital Journal’s free newsletter, The Eye-Opener, we round up the news and commentary from across Ohio and around the country and world that is catching our attention. We call this feature Catching Our Eye, republished here.
Please subscribe to our free daily newsletter to get all the Ohio news you need to know right to your inbox every weekday morning.
If you already subscribe, please share with your family and friends so they know about the Ohio Capital Journal too: https://ohiocapitaljournal.com/subscribe/
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Catching Our Eye

• Federal election monitors. The Statehouse News Bureau’s Karen Kasler reports, “Feds will send election monitors to three Ohio counties next week.”
The US Department of Justice has informed three Ohio county boards of elections that the federal government will be sending monitors to observe next week’s election. It’s part of what is expected to be the DOJ’s largest-ever election monitoring effort, with the agency planning to send monitors to all 50 states.
The Boards of Elections in Franklin, Medina and Cuyahoga Counties were emailed letters informing them the Civil Rights Division of the DOJ intends to send election monitors to those jurisdictions.
• Gerrymandering. The New York Times reports, “An Extremely Detailed Ranking of the Most Gerrymandered States in America.”
Which state has America’s worst gerrymander? After a year of redistricting battles, we have an answer.
We’ve ranked all 44 states with more than one district by the fairness of their congressional maps. Many of the most notorious gerrymanders are ranked near the top of the list. But there are also some oft-derided maps that we judge to be fundamentally fine. (Ohio ranks No. 7 most-gerrymandered.)
• Ohio Supreme Court. Signal Ohio’s Jake Zuckerman reports, “Is Ohio on the cusp of an all-Republican state Supreme Court?”
Since Statehouse Republicans passed a law in 2021 requiring Ohio Supreme Court candidates to run under party labels on the ballot, reversing a century-old nonpartisan approach, Republicans have gone six for six.
If their undefeated streak continues, they’ll achieve the historically rare feat of total one-party control, a first since 2010.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Brewers blow 12th inning lead, still chasing first World Series title
text:
Fans at the World Series watch party at American Family field react to Cooper Pratt's go-ahead home run in the 12th inning. (Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)The Milwaukee Brewers came tantalizingly close to winning their first World Series title in franchise history Tuesday evening before the Tampa Bay Rays’ Ben Williamson hit a walk-off single to score the winning run in the bottom of the 12th inning, giving the Rays a 4-3 victory. 
A Cooper Pratt home run in the top of the 12th inning had the team just three outs away from the championship but a throwing error with zero outs in the top of the inning sparked a rally for the Rays, who for the first time in the series were able to string together a series of hits. Brewers pitcher Shane Drohan, who had previously pitched just one inning in the playoffs, gave up the game tying and winning runs. 
At American Family Field in Milwaukee a sold out watch party was standing, clapping, cheering and groaning along with the game as if it were happening on the field in front of them and not on the massive screen in center field. 

The game ended around 11:30, with kids out far past their bedtime and lifelong fans on the edge of their seats to watch their hearts get ripped out. 
Watching from the third deck was Chrystal Glynn-Skipini who drove down from Neenah to watch the game in the atmosphere with her niece and great nephew. 
“Why not, how awesome to be with all the other fans,” she said, double crossing her fingers that the team would close out the sweep Tuesday. 
Game five of the series is Wednesday at 7 p.m.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Trone Garriott, Nunn respond to attack ads on Epstein, transgender issues at debate
text:
Democrat Sarah Trone Garriott, left, and Republican Zach Nunn, are competing to represent Iowa's 3rd Congressional District in the 2026 general election. (Photos by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch, photo illustration via Canva)Meeting for the sole debate in Iowa’s 3rd Congressional District, U.S. Rep. Zach Nunn and state Sen. Sarah Trone Garriott responded Tuesday to attacks from their opponent on issues like the Epstein files and transgender athletes and students.
The debate, hosted by KCCI in Des Moines, was aired just a week before Election Day, and follows weeks of the campaigns criticizing one another for being unable to come to a scheduling agreement. The contest is one of the most competitive U.S. House races in the country, according to political forecasters,
While Tuesday was the first time Iowans saw Trone Garriott and Nunn on stage together, many viewers had likely seen campaign ads about the candidates — more than $10.6 million in spending from outside groups was poured into the race, according to Federal Election Commission reports.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Moderators gave the candidates the chance to address some of the claims made in attack ads, including ads criticizing Nunn for his votes related to publicizing files related to Florida financier and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Nunn voted to pass the “Epstein Files Transparency Act” in 2025, but Democrats have criticized Nunn, as well as other members of Iowa’s federal delegation, for not signing off on the initial discharge petition to force the House to vote on the bill, or voting for an amendment on another measure to compel the release of the Epstein files.
Nunn says votes against releasing files was to protect victim identities
Nunn said he voted against the earlier efforts to release Department of Justice information on Epstein and collaborators, because the proposals would have released the names of Epstein’s victims, which he said would “revictimize the victims.” Some Epstein survivors had their identities revealed in unredacted documents released by the DOJ in early 2026.
“I want to make sure Jeffrey Epstein and all of his accomplices are held fully accountable. He’s a disgusting human being and we’ve been able to lead that legislation here in Iowa,” Nunn said. But “simply opening up and making the files transparent for the victims — their names, their addresses, their background — that’s not fair to the victims.”
He said his vote was to “hold the people who actually did the crime accountable,” and referenced his work in Congress to advocate for providing more federal funding for programs and services for victims of domestic abuse and sexual assault. He said he believed Iowa Republicans were also taking on this issue at the state level.
“It’s not just Jeffrey Epstein,” Nunn said. “This kind of stuff happens right here in Iowa, let’s get after it.”
But Trone Garriott said Nunn’s vote to release the Epstein files only came “when the president had given him permission that he finally joined in and voted to release them.”
“We’ve only gotten half of the files out there, so much is still unknown, and no one has been held accountable,” Trone Garriott said. “We need to make sure that we’ve got someone standing up for us in Washington to make sure that kids are safe.”
Trone Garriott says she voted to give parents a ‘voice’ on transgender issues
Trone Garriott was asked to respond to attack ads criticizing her votes on legislation related to transgender Iowans, including her vote against a 2022 law banning transgender women from participating in women’s sports, and against a 2023 law banning transgender students from using school restrooms that do not align with their sex assigned at birth.
The Democrat said as a mother with two children in Iowa public schools, she cared “deeply about their safety, about health, about fairness” — and said the laws she voted on in regards to transgender students and school athletes were in an effort to allow parents to “have a voice in the decisions that are impacting their children.”
Sand, Lahn call for increasing mental healthcare access, Medicaid oversight in debate

“I believe that we make much better decisions when parents are involved, because parents are the ones who are there, who can see the circumstances, they can understand what’s at stake — and they make the best decisions for our community, that actually help us address the issue,” Trone Garriott said. “Every single one of the bills that was put before me in the Iowa state Senate took away a parent’s voice. I have to stand up for parents’ voices in this process to make sure that things are safe and fair for our kids.”
Nunn claimed Trone Garriott was in the “extreme element of her party” on issues related to transgender issues. The Republican referenced comments from Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Josh Turek, who he said “highlighted the fact that this is wrong and should be stopped.”
He also said Trone Garriott “authored the bill that would teach transgender ideology to kindergartners.” The legislation Nunn referenced has been referred to by Townhall, a conservative news organization, as a bill to “teach sex education in kindergarten classrooms.” The measure relates to Iowa’s Area Education Agencies and does not mention sex education.
Trone Garriott said some of the criticism comes from her support of “Erin’s Law,” a proposal with bipartisan support that would require the state Department of Education to develop guidelines on how schools can teach students in kindergarten through sixth grade about child sexual abuse, with the goal of awareness and prevention.
“Because I was a sexual assault crisis counselor, I also worked to help bring education into classrooms,” Trone Garriott said. “It’s incredibly important that kids have age-appropriate education so that they can ask for help when something is wrong, when they’re being abused. Some of the bills that I’ve been attacked on are bills … to make sure kids have the language to ask for help when they’re being abused.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Our job is to protect your right to vote. Your job is to use it.
text:
Lately, when I talk with Connecticut residents about the upcoming election, they tell me they’re afraid.
Sometimes, they can tell me exactly what they’re afraid of: federal immigration agents showing up at polling places, protesters interfering with voting, their personal information being seized, or even the federal government attempting to stop the election altogether.

Secretary of the State Stephanie Thomas

Other times, people can’t quite put their finger on what’s worrying them. They just know they’re scared.
I understand. For years now, we’ve heard repeated claims about stolen elections, widespread voter fraud, and ineligible people casting ballots. We’ve seen alarming headlines and social media posts predicting everything that could go wrong. Some concerns deserve serious attention. Others are based on speculation or misinformation. But when all of it gets mixed together, it can leave people wondering what to believe and worrying about what might happen next.
But here’s what concerns me most: That fear could accomplish the very thing people are afraid of, which is keeping them from exercising their right to vote.
And that’s why I want Connecticut voters to understand something.
It’s our job to worry about the what-ifs. It’s our job to prepare for them. It’s our job to take the steps necessary to protect voters, election workers, and our elections.
And when I say “our,” I don’t just mean the Secretary of the State’s Office. I mean the Attorney General’s Office, the Connecticut Department of Emergency Services and Public Protection, local election officials in all 169 towns, law enforcement, and the many other state and local agencies and people who have responsibilities for keeping our elections safe, secure, and accessible.
We take those responsibilities seriously. We plan, we prepare, we work together, and we have procedures in place to respond when something doesn’t go as expected.
Our job is to think through what could go wrong before it happens. And most of that work happens long before anyone walks into a polling place.
Earlier this month, election offices in several states received suspicious letters, some containing powder. Federal authorities told us a letter addressed to our office had been intercepted. But before we knew about that letter, we’d already reminded local officials how to handle suspicious mail safely.
We’ve also helped towns prepare for 2026 election law changes, including to help law enforcement understand a new state law establishing restrictions within 250 feet of polling places and other designated election sites. The goal is to protect voters and election workers while making sure officers can still respond to emergencies and perform their lawful duties.
I wish I could promise that nothing unexpected will happen between now and when the polls close at 8 p.m. on Election Day, November 3. But what I can tell you is that we’ve spent months working with state, local, and federal partners to be ready if something we hope never happens does occur.
This is the kind of work most voters never see. And none of it begins the week before an election. It happens year-round, and it involves people from different agencies, political parties, and communities working together.
That’s our job. Your job is to vote.
In the 2018 midterm election, about 65% of Connecticut’s registered voters cast a ballot. In 2022, that figure fell to about 58%.
What will voter turnout look like in 2026?
I hope it will show that Connecticut residents understand what’s at stake; that they realize that the people we elect make decisions about our nation, our state, our towns, the services we rely on, and how public money is spent.
Eligible Connecticut voters have three ways to cast their ballots. They can do it in person during Early Voting through November 1, in person on Election Day November 3, or by absentee ballot.
Find our 2026 Voter Guide in English or Spanish at MyVote.CT.gov. It contains everything you need to know about voting in Connecticut, from how to find your polling place, to the candidates on your local ballot, to the rules about who can legally handle and return someone else’s absentee ballot.
We’re doing our job, Connecticut.
Now it’s time to do yours.
Stephanie Thomas is Connecticut’s Secretary of the State.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Turnout surging in Maryland, as ‘jacked up’ voters head to the polls for early voting
text:
Campaign signs lined up near Wayne K. Curry Sports and Learning Center in Prince George's County during early voting Tuesday. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)Early voting in Maryland is surging, with turnout 67% higher through the first five days of in-person voting than it was at the same time four years ago, according to data from the Maryland State Board of Elections.
Higher voting was recorded in every county in the state, with 309,190 voters having cast ballots through Monday, compared to 185,121 voters after the first five days of voting in 2022. The surge mirrors a national spike in early voting, with more than 34 million Americans already having cast ballots, a week before Election Day on Nov. 3.
Democrats in Maryland have been particularly motivated to vote early, with their numbers up 81% over four years ago, compared to 33% for GOP voters, according to an analysis of state data by Jim Burton, the founder of political and public affairs consulting firm Burton Research and Strategies. 
“They are jacked up to vote,” said Burton, the former executive director of the Maryland GOP. “On the Democrat side, they’re willing to run through a brick building to cast their vote.”
Early voting surges in midterm elections as millions cast their ballots

Monday saw the biggest increases, with Democratic voting up 84% and Republican voting up 49% compared to the fifth day of early voting in 2022. Frederick County saw the biggest surge Monday, with Democratic voting up 146% and GOP voting 67% than four years ago.
Burton said the higher numbers could be voters expressing their displeasure with the administration of President Donald Trump. He added that while the biggest increases appeared to be in suburban areas, the increases could be also be due to local or regional issues, since the surge is being seen everywhere in the state.
Nikki Tyree, the executive director of Maryland’s League of Women Voters, said she thinks big issues like data centers, the cost of living, or Question 3, the proposed constitutional amendment on congressional redistricting, are driving voters this year.
“We’re looking at a midterm that is hanging on so many critical issues that people have been focused on,” Tyree said. “Marylanders have really shown that they’re paying attention to what’s going on.”
In addition to the more than 300,000 who had voted early in person so far, state election officials said voters had returned 305,690 mail-in ballots as of Sunday, about half of the 645,962 mailed out this year.
Early voting began last Thursday and continues through this Thursday. Burton said the first few days and the final day of early voting tend to see the heaviest traffic.
“The candidates and campaigns are still trying to drive turnout,” he said. “I tell my clients … just because what the early-vote demographics are showing doesn’t mean we’re handing in the towel. We have to continue to do our job, and we still have seven days to do it.”
A Burton Research and Strategies analysis of Maryland State Board of Elections early voting data shows it is surging in every county and in both parties, when compared to turnout four years ago. (Graphic courtesy Burton Research and Strategies)
Burton said that even though the increase in Democratic voting is much higher than that of Republicans, it’s too soon to read much into it, as it could simply be the result of differing personal preferences between the parties.
He said Democrats tend to vote by mail of hit the polls early compared to Republicans, who historically tend to stick to voting on Election Day, as they might be “set in their ways.”
Heading into the final days of early voting, and only a week out from Election Day, Tyree thinks the increased turnout is a good sign for the rest of the country.
“I think Maryland is always sort of a microcosm of what’s happening across the country,” she said. “Our little state has so much of what other states encompass…. If our voters are paying attention to the issues that are affecting their daily lives, I think that’s just a small example of what some of the voters who are facing widely publicized races are engaging in as well.”
