name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Lamont, Fazio lively in last debate while breaking no new ground
text:
Buoyed by positive polls and a favorable tailwind generated by an unpopular president, Gov. Ned Lamont soldiered through his second and final debate with Republican Ryan Fazio on Tuesday, hewing to a central message of him steering Connecticut to fiscal stability and growth after a lost decade of chronic crises.
Fazio, a 36-year-old state senator from Greenwich seeking statewide office for the first time, once again was the aggressor, this time emphasizing mandates, property taxes and other issues of particular interest to the live audience: the Connecticut Conference of Municipalities convention at Mohegan Sun.
Lamont was more relaxed than in last week’s debate in a largely empty TV studio, playing off an audience with familiar mayors and first selectmen, addressing several by name — and reminding them of their role in shaping a revised housing bill at his invitation after vetoing an initial effort.

Gov. Ned Lamont, who prefers to go without neckties and didn’t wear one in the first debate, answers questions following the Connecticut Conference of Municipalities Gubernatorial Debate at Mohegan Sun’s Earth Expo and Convention Center on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT MIrror

The 72-year-old governor displayed a crispness and a willingness to volley with Fazio largely missing last week, challenging Fazio and other Republicans as failing to oppose President Donald Trump on tariffs, a war in Iran driving up gas prices, and a crackdown on immigration that Lamont called cruel and overreaching.
“I don’t know what happened to the Republicans in the state,” said Lamont, whose home is Greenwich, where local officials plan to erect a statue in the wealthy enclave in tribute to its native son, President George Herbert Walker Bush. “The old Republicans, the Bush Republicans, would stand up. They’d be outraged.”
Fazio distanced himself from Trump without offering comment on a Bush family that has produced two presidents and a U.S. senator but whose brand of politics has lost standing in a GOP dominated by a president who equates the party’s interests with his own, even if he becomes a lame duck next week.

State Sen. Ryan Fazio, Republican challenger, answers a reporter’s question following the Connecticut Conference of Municipalities Gubernatorial Debate at Mohegan Sun’s Earth Expo and Convention Center on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT MIrror

“I’ve criticized Trump administration policies and Democratic administration policies since before I was even in office, and that’s why Gov. Lamont called me bipartisan and objected to others calling me extreme before this general election campaign started,” Fazio said. “I’m an independently minded leader.”
WTNH Channel 8 televised the debate live with two anchors, Dennis House and Kathryn Hauser, posing most of the questions with one wrinkle: Joseph DeLong, the chief executive of CCM, and two members of its “citizens’ assembly” had turns posing difficult questions that neither candidate answered directly.
DeLong challenged Fazio to explain how he could deliver on his promise to cut state taxes and cap municipal property tax increases at a 2% cap or the rate of inflation, whichever is greater. 
“If a city or town school and special education costs rise faster, who covers the difference?” DeLong asked. “Is it the state, local taxpayers, or is the school district going to be required to do drastic cuts?”
Fazio did not reply to those choices but insisted his overall plan would lower costs for municipalities by eliminating unfunded state mandates — and gigged the governor as unreliable on special education reform. 
“The problem is he’s had eight years to accomplish it and hasn’t,” Fazio said.

Gov. Ned Lamont answers a reporter’s question following the Connecticut Conference of Municipalities Gubernatorial Debate at Mohegan Sun’s Earth Expo and Convention Center on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT MIrror

Lamont did not engage on a separate question about mandates, framed around a requirement that municipalities and not the state must advertise public meetings. Instead, he pivoted to dollars his administration has provided, including funding for free school meals.
“I think the answer from Gov. Lamont that those costs are just not that big a deal is not an acceptable answer,” Fazio said. “It’s not just one of these costs that the state is imposing. It’s over 1,000 of them, and the governor increased the number of those costs by over 100 more in just the last five years.”
Hauser pressed Fazio on his opposition to the Lamont administration using surplus state funds to replace expiring federal credits before their expiration caused dramatic increases in premiums.
“Does that remain your position, even for a family that cannot afford coverage, while your proposed cost-cutting reforms take effect?” Hauser asked.

Republican gubernatorial candidate Ryan Fazio at a debate at Mohegan Sun on Oct. 27, 2026. Credit: courtesy WTNH

Fazio said his opposition was about process, not policy.
“The problem with the proposal is that it went outside of the spending caps and would have caused tax increases,” Fazio said. “We can provide this funding through the normal budget process in a state with a $30 billion budget, and I would favor that.”
Fazio pivoted to blame the Lamont administration for approving premium increases.
“Gov. Lamont’s own insurance commission has approved increases in health insurance premiums of 11% and 16%. That’s on his watch. That is the record, and that is not sustainable,” Fazio said.
But he acknowledged to reporters after the debate he was not suggesting they should have been rejected — something that could lead to plans being withdrawn from the Connecticut market.

Gov. Ned Lamont at a debate at Mohegan Sun on Oct. 27, 2026. Credit: courtesy WTNH

Lamont offered the state premium subsidy as one of several examples of Connecticut acting to offset actions or inactions by Trump.
“The Trump administration jacks the price of health insurance on the exchange by $800 a month, pushing people off of health insurance, but not in Connecticut,” Lamont said. “We stepped up, and we are providing support for that. Ryan Fazio did not support that. Those people would be uninsured today.”
Neither candidate warmed to a proposal by CCM’s Citizens’ Assembly to impose tolls and use the money to eliminate the property tax on motor vehicles. A tolls proposal by Lamont in 2019, his first year in  office, fell flat and drove his job approval rating to the bottom of all U.S. governors.
“Joe, you may have heard I actually tried something like that a while back. Nobody wanted to do that. We’re not going to do that,” Lamont said. “But it gets to a bigger story. When I came into office, we had a special transportation fund that had nothing in it, zero. It was on fumes.”

State Sen. Ryan Fazio, Republican challenger, pauses before answering a reporter’s question following the Connecticut Conference of Municipalities Gubernatorial Debate at Mohegan Sun’s Earth Expo and Convention Center on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT MIrror

Lamont turned the question on Fazio, who has proposed a gas tax holiday.
“That’s just the type of mentality that got this state in a pickle eight years ago, and I’m not going to let it happen again. I’m happy to work with the assembly on other ways. We think we can mitigate taxes there. I’m not sure that’s what I’d go for,” Lamont said.
It was an example of the governor and his challenger falling back on messages little changed since the start of the election season.
“After eight years, Gov. Lamont’s had his chance,” Fazio said. “He promised to hold the line on taxes, but he increased your taxes. He promised to cut your property taxes, but property taxes have risen 30 percent on his watch. Now, it’s time for a change.”
Lamont also asked voters to take a closer look.
“Look back, eight years ago, we were lurching from deficit to deficit,” Lamont said. “We had three tax increases in a row. Your mayors and first selectmen, remember, they couldn’t even get a budget done in 2017 until three or four months late. So I do disagree that we’re not in a better place today than we were before.”

Gov. Ned Lamont and Republican gubernatorial candidate Ryan Fazio at a debate at Mohegan Sun on Oct. 27, 2026. Credit: courtesy wtnh

Applause was discouraged during the debate, but the governor got a laugh when he recycled an oft-used line that his opponent in the Democratic primary attacked him for refusing to raise taxes on the wealthy and Fazio cast him as a spendthrift.
“Maybe these two guys should have a debate and then come in and tell me what they’ve decided,” Lamont said, as the municipal officials tittered, then laughed. He landed a punch line, saying loudly, “I do what I think is right every day.”
That got applause.
Did either man hear anything new?
“From him, I really didn’t,” Lamont said. “I just heard him say over and over again, ‘Eight years. What have you done?’ And I said, ‘Eight years, this is what we’ve done to improve our school systems, improve our budget, improve our roads and bridges.’”
Asked the same question, Fazio just smiled and replied, “No.”
CT Mirror reporter Keith M. Phaneuf contributed to this report.

BILOXI – Former U.S. Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg on Tuesday pleaded for Mississippi voters to “send shockwaves” by voting for Democratic nominee Scott Colom and rejecting Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith next week. 
Buttigieg was the latest national political figure to campaign in Mississippi in the homestretch before the Nov. 3 midterm elections. The Senate race has also attracted a last-minute barrage of spending as Democrats see an opening and Republicans worry that reliably conservative Mississippi could become a casualty of President Donald Trump’s sinking popularity nationwide. 
Trump hosted a rally for Hyde-Smith in Corinth on Monday, days after former Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris campaigned for Colom in Columbus last week.
People hold up signs as former U.S. Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg speaks at a rally for Democratic Senate nominee Scott Colom in Biloxi on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026. Credit: Michael Guidry/Mississippi Today
Trump’s approval ratings have plummeted nationally amid opposition to increasing consumer prices and an unpopular war in Iran. Democrats have grown optimistic that Colom could pull off an upset in a state that hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate in more than four decades. 
READ MORE: Trump rallies for Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi: ‘You like me’
“When you win in Mississippi, it is going to send shockwaves,” Buttigieg told a galvanized crowd in Biloxi. 

 Speaking to hundreds of people at a community center, the Biden administration transportation secretary said Trump and Hyde-Smith are directly responsible for soaring gasoline and grocery prices because of the president’s tariffs and other policies and the Iran war. 
“It’s happening because of decisions that were made in Washington,” Buttigeig said. “This time it’s not because Vladimir Putin decided to start a war. It’s because Donald Trump decided to start a war.” 
Colom repeated his campaign pledges about the need to raise the federal minimum wage and his desire to advocate for policies that help deliver access to affordable healthcare to rural Mississippi, which has some of the most dire health outcomes in the nation. 
“My commitment to you is that I am going to fight to do everything in my power to save our healthcare and save our hospitals,” Colom said.  
Buttigieg said healthcare issues show the Trump administration and Republicans are out of touch.
“Folks are saying, ‘We need help with healthcare,’ and they are saying, ‘OK, let’s build a new ballroom in the White House,'” Buttigieg said. “Folks are saying, ‘I need help affording the things that I buy at the store every week,’ and they are busy protecting whoever is in the Epstein files.”
Earlier in the day, Colom and Buttigieg had a press conference at the Coast Transit Authority in Gulfport, where the two celebrated the 2025 restoration of Amtrak’s Gulf Coast route from Alabama to Louisiana, called the “Mardi Gras Service.” 
The route was shut down after Hurricane Katrina and likely wouldn’t have been resurrected without a significant injection of federal money from Congress’ passage of the bipartisan infrastructure bill in 2021. 
Mississippi Sen. Roger Wicker was one of 19 Republican senators and the only Republican in Mississippi’s congressional delegation who voted for the federal legislation. Both Buttigieg and Colom praised Wicker’s support of the program and denounced Hyde-Smith’s opposition.  
“Let’s be very clear, there was a Republican U.S. senator from Mississippi who voted and acted to bring those dollars to this state,” Buttigieg said. “Just not Cindy Hyde-Smith because she was incapable of doing something without the permission of the then-former president.” 
Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Scott Colom speaks outside the Coast Transit Authority in Gulfport on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026. Credit: Michael Guidry/Mississippi TodayPeople wait in line outside a community center in Biloxi before a rally featuring Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Scott Colom and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026. Credit: Michael Guidry/Mississippi TodayScott Colom, Democratic nominee for a U.S. Senate seat in Mississippi, speaks at a rally in Biloxi on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026. Credit: Michael Guidry/Mississippi Today
Hyde-Smith at the time said she opposed the infrastructure legislation because it would increase the national debt, something Colom on Tuesday said was hypocritical because Hyde-Smith hasn’t voiced concerns about the debt increasing under Trump. 
“She doesn’t care about debt,” Colom said. “She cares about politics.” 
Colom also criticized Hyde-Smith for appearing with “Mardi Gras beads” at a ribbon cutting celebrating the reopening of the rail line, calling her dishonest for not disclosing to the public that she voted against the infrastructure bill. 
Buttigieg’s visit to the Magnolia State comes one day after Trump rallied for Hyde-Smith in Corinth in northeastern Mississippi, where he called Colom a “Democrat communist” and accused him of being soft on crime and overly supportive of transgender rights.
Colom called Trump’s description of him lies and pointed to his track record as a district attorney in north Mississippi as evidence that he’s tackled violent crime while in elected office. 
“Can you fill your gas up with those lies?” Colom said of Trump. “Can you pay your grocery bill with those lies?” 
Democratic leaders from outside of the state, such as Harris and Sen. Raphael Warnock of Georgia, have campaigned for Colom in hopes of energizing Democratic turnout on Election Day. 
Hyde-Smith and the GOP have sought to tie Colom to the far-left of the Democratic Party and criticized him for welcoming national Democratic leaders to the conservative state. 
But Colom said Mississippi voters should ask themselves why people such as Buttigieg “care more about roads and bridges” in Mississippi than Hyde-Smith does. 
If Colom wants to pull off an upset, he would need to make significant inroads in the Gulf Coast area, which has become a firewall of support in recent years for Republican candidates. Colom told reporters he believes he’s gained support there because he’s had multiple events in the region and listened to voters’ concerns.
Buttigieg last visited Mississippi in 2024 while he was transportation secretary, to help break ground on a $20-million renovation of Medgar Evers Boulevard in Jackson. He also toured the Medgar and Myrlie Evers Home National Monument and visited the Mississippi Delta, Laurel and Meridian. 
Buttigieg is a potential 2028 Democratic candidate for president and would likely need to shore up support among Black voters to capture the party’s nomination. Mississippi has the largest percentage of Black voters in the nation, but the national party often overlooks Mississippi because of its overall conservative electorate. 
Buttigieg said the national party needs to spend more time in conservative states such as Mississippi because “there’s no such thing as a permanently red state, district or county” and that Southern states deserve better than the incumbents serving them. 
“I think it’s always been a mistake to overlook Mississippi,” Buttigieg said.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Teen found not guilty of homicide in Lincoln Hills counselor death
text:
Lincoln Hills, the youth prison plagued by problems in Wisconsin. (Photo courtesy of the Wisconsin Department of Corrections)The Wisconsin Examiner’s Criminal Justice Reporting Project shines a light on incarceration, law enforcement and criminal justice issues with support from the Public Welfare Foundation.
A jury has found Javarius Hurd, 18, not guilty of reckless homicide in the death of a youth counselor at the Lincoln Hills School for Boys. Hurd was, however, found guilty of battery by a prisoner. 
Hurd had been charged with reckless homicide in the death of Corey Proulx, who died after a confrontation with Hurd in 2024. Prosecutors said that Proulx chased Hurd after the then 16-year-old threw a cup of soapy water in another staff member’s face. Proulx chased Hurd into an outdoor recreational area where, in a scuffle with Hurd, he hit his head on a hard surface. 
After Proulx’s death, the Department of Corrections issued a statement that staff members were collectively mourning. In a press release sent out after the incident, the DOC said that Proulx’s fiancee and daughter “would like everyone to know that Corey was an amazing partner, father, and human being.” 
Hurd’s case became a flashpoint both in and outside of the courtroom. While his attorneys battled prosecutors unsuccessfully to prevent the case from being tried in adult court, Proulx’s death was used by Republican lawmakers to take shots at the approach to juvenile justice taken by Gov. Tony Evers.
Lincoln Hills had become notorious as one of the nation’s largest juvenile prisons where youth suffered abuse and excessive force while guards and counselors were under pressure from  staffing shortages. Recently, Lincoln Hills was found to be in compliance with the requirements set forth after a class action lawsuit over those conditions. As a result, court-ordered monitoring of the facility was halted as new, smaller facilities are being opened around the state. 
A sentencing hearing for Hurd has been set for Friday morning, Oct. 30.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Tennessee hosts first gubernatorial forum in eight years. GOP frontrunner no-shows
text:
The 2026 Gubernatorial forum with candidates Jerri Green (D), Lauren Pinkston (I) and David Hatley (I) Republican nominee, U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn did not attend the event
on October 27, 2026 at MTSU in Murfreesboro, Tennessee. Sponsored by Tennessee Press Association and Middle Tennessee State University. (Photo: 
John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Three of the four major Tennessee gubernatorial candidates appeared at a forum one week before the 2026 election and answered questions on a range of topics, including private school vouchers, data centers and toll lanes. 
U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, the Republican nominee and favorite to win the race, declined to participate in the forum, continuing a trend among Tennessee GOP candidates of avoiding appearing on stage against their campaign opponents.
Democratic candidate Jerri Green and independent candidate David Hatley both attacked Blackburn at the forum hosted by the Tennessee Press Association and Middle Tennessee State University on the school’s Murfreesboro campus.
Green, a Memphis City Councilmember, said it was a shame the only other candidate with a “path to victory” wouldn’t debate. 
“I’m the only candidate on this stage that won a primary,” Green said.
The press association invited Blackburn, Green, Hatley and Lauren Pinkston, another independent candidate. Blackburn was the only one of the four who declined the invitation.
Hatley is a Washington County hot tub mogul running as a “conservative.” He has put nearly $12 million of his own money into the campaign and refuses to take donations. Hatley is trying to find a lane where he can get enough votes to win without splitting the conservative vote, which could allow Green to win the governor’s race with a plurality.
In his closing remarks, Hatley attacked Green for not supporting the Memphis Safe Task Force and criticized Blackburn for allowing campaign donors to “buy the governor’s office.”
Spoilers or contenders? Two independent candidates for TN governor try to shake up the race

Pinkston is running as a moderate, emphasizing that most voters don’t affiliate with a political party and are fed up with the two-party system. 
Blackburn also refused to debate her Republican gubernatorial primary opponents earlier this year and didn’t debate during her 2024 U.S. Senate reelection campaign. U.S. Sen. Bill Hagerty hasn’t debated in either of his U.S. Senate campaigns. Gov. Bill Lee refused to debate his Democratic Party opponent in 2022. 
The last time Tennessee held debates for statewide offices was in 2018, when Lee debated former Democratic Nashville Mayor Karl Dean and Blackburn took the stage with former Tennessee Gov. Phil Bredesen in their U.S. Senate race. 
Whoever becomes Tennessee’s next governor will face a range of policy decisions
America’s leading artificial intelligence companies started hiring lobbyists earlier this year, ahead of the 2027 legislative session and amid growing backlash to data centers.
The debate over data center expansion has led some local communities to impose construction moratoriums because they worry it’s driving up electricity prices and has negative environmental impacts.
Lawmakers and the next governor are likely to debate whether to pass a state law that preempts local moratoriums on data center construction, paving the way for more. Officials could also look into repealing the generous tax incentives the state offers data centers. 
Green said she would go the other way and implement a statewide moratorium on data center construction, adding that she fought the construction of XAI’s data center in Memphis.
“Elon Musk and his like need to go,” Green said, referring to the CEO of the company that owns XAI.
Pinkston agreed with Green on the moratorium. 
Hatley said he only wants data centers in Tennessee under the right deal.
“We have to have guardrails,” Hatley said. “They need to pay property taxes.”
Blackburn hasn’t publicly taken a stance on whether the state should preempt localities over data centers or whether the state should implement a moratorium.
The candidates on stage differed most from Blackburn’s public position on private school vouchers, where she has called for expanding the program. Blackburn has received million of dollars in support during the gubernatorial primary and the general election from a political action committee, PAC, pushing for private school voucher expansion in the state. 
Blackburn moves $4.8M from US Senate campaign account in apparent legal ‘workaround’

Private school vouchers cost Tennessee taxpayers $310 million a year. Lawmakers expanded the private school voucher program to 35,000 students, funding roughly $7,300 per student to enroll in private schools. The state’s first voucher program provides about $9,000 for about 5,000 low-income students only in Nashville, Memphis and Chattanooga.
Hatley and Pinkston pointed out that most rural counties don’t have private schools and can’t take advantage of the program. 
Green said the whole thing was a “scam” funded by out-of-state interests. 
“Public dollars should go to public schools for the public good,” Green said. 
The next governor will also have to make executive decisions on whether to pursue more toll-lane projects to address a structural deficit in how the state pays for roads. An intergovernmental agency report recommended that state lawmakers consider raising taxes or passing a law that would allow the state to borrow money to cover a $400 million shortfall in the state department of transportation’s budget.
All three candidates at the forum Tuesday also agreed that the state shouldn’t pursue more toll lane projects. 
Green said toll lanes were just “fast track lanes for wealthy people.”
Hatley said he had no idea why the state would pursue toll lane projects after they “failed” in other states.
While Blackburn wasn’t on the stage, her campaign continues to talk on conservative-friendly media.
Blackburn has continued to emphasize that she wants to implement a program similar to President Donald Trump’s Department of Government Efficiency, DOGE. 
Details of the specific cuts are sparse, but when Lee became governor in 2019, he hired the consultancy firm McKinsey to produce a report on ways to reduce government size. During Lee’s eight years in office, the number of state employees modestly increased.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Sand, Lahn call for increasing mental healthcare access, Medicaid oversight in debate
text:
Democratic Auditor Rob Sand and Republican businessman Zach Lahn are competing to become Iowa governor in the Nov. 3, 2026 general election. (Photos by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch, photo illustration via Canva)Both Democrat Rob Sand and Republican Zach Lahn said Tuesday in their final gubernatorial candidate debate that  more work was needed to address mental healthcare and the impact of Medicaid privatization on healthcare providers, but the candidates offered different solutions to improving Iowa’s health system.
Tuesday’s debate, hosted by KCRG-TV9 and The Gazette in Cedar Rapids, was the third for Sand, Iowa’s current state auditor, and Lahn, a businessman with a farm in Belle Plaine. The candidates originally planned four debates but they were unable to reach an agreement on rescheduling a debate with “Iowa Press” on Iowa PBS that had originally been scheduled Oct. 21. Sand withdrew from the Iowa PBS debate following the death of his brother-in-law.
Though Sand did not mention his brother-in-law, Walter E. Lauridsen II, by name, the Democratic candidate said at the debate his family was one of many in the state who have struggled to find psychiatric services in Iowa for people in need. Lauridsen, the brother of Sand’s wife, died earlier in October in a traffic incident near Lucas. Sand said in a social media post sharing the news that “Walter lived with mental health complexities. While this is a difficult and painful time for all of us, we know he is now at peace.”

“If you’re one of the families that struggle to find a bed for people, we’re there with you,” Sand said during the debate. “We’ve struggled too. It’s a real problem in our state. We don’t have the availability that we need, and people suffer because of it needlessly.”
Sand also shared another personal story on mental health struggles, speaking about a 2025 incident when a man broke into Sand’s home in Des Moines while his family was away for Thanksgiving. Court records show the man was homeless at the time of arrest, and was later sentenced to two years probation after pleading guilty to burglary and two counts of interference causing injury. He was ordered to receive mental health treatment at an Iowa residential mental health facility, but was set to remain in custody until space was available.
Sand says he remembered having a conversation with the man’s sister after the crime.
“We reached out, and she was just happy to know that he was alive, because she hadn’t heard from him for three years,” Sand said. “This is a man who was living outdoors, saw a warm place. The problem is that we haven’t been paying enough attention to people who are struggling with mental health issues. And then sooner or later, their mental health issue becomes our problem, too, whether it’s because of crime or accidents or anything else. We’ve got to do a better job with this for everyone in this state, because it’s public safety, not just mental health.”
As of a 2023 report, Iowa had two available psychiatric beds per 100,000 individuals, ranking Iowa 51st among all states and Washington, D.C., in availability for state hospital beds available for adults with serious mental health issues.
Lahn says economic growth is key to improving mental healthcare
Lahn similarly said he believed Iowa needs to open additional mental health facilities, and said he believed “there are people that are in prisons in our state that need to be in mental health facilities — and actually, that’s hurting everybody involved.” However, he said the larger conversation on how to address this problem starts with growing Iowa’s economy.
“One thing I’ve learned in running for governor is clearly that we’re dealing with the allocation of scarce resources in the state,” Lahn said. “… I think as we look at, how do we improve access to this, we have to look at priorities that will help us grow as a state. But we cannot just continue to depend on, you know, funding from the federal government for things like this. We have to prioritize growth. If we don’t, we’re just gonna be continuing to put money at something that is not getting the return that we’d like it to have, and not serving the people, and not being able to open up more of these facilities to serve people that do have the mental health needs that need it.”
Sand calls for ending Medicaid privatization
But Sand argued there was a more direct fix for the issue — ending the privatization of Medicaid. Iowa Medicaid was privatized in 2016 under former Gov. Terry Branstad, but Sand said Iowa has seen the privatization of the public health coverage program fail over the past decade. He attributed shortages for mental healthcare and other healthcare to high rates of denied Medicaid coverage and reimbursements by the private managed care organizations (MCOs) that manage the state program. These denials lead to providers shutting down, he said, because they are not being paid.
In 2021, Sand released a report as state auditor which found the percentage of appeals in which judges overturned a reduction or denial of services increased 891% after Medicaid privatization. Sand said these denials not only lead to healthcare facilities closing, but raise healthcare costs across the board.
“It’s not just that people are closing down, because they can’t get paid — other healthcare practitioners have hired new full-time employees, where their entire job is to talk on the phone all day long with these MCOs, to argue about getting paid for the care they provided to people,” Sand said. “Who’s paying that person’s salary? We are. … Privatization of Medicaid in the state of Iowa has driven up costs. It is driven down the quality of care. It has led to mental healthcare practitioners closing their doors.”
Lahn said he understood there were problems with Iowa’s Medicaid system, and called for more oversight of MCOs. But he also said did not believe reversing privatization was the correct solution.
“I think there’s better oversight that we can have with this, but I do not believe the people of Iowa want the government running their healthcare,” Lahn said.
For government oversight, Lahn said he believed the government could take steps to ensure payments to healthcare providers are paid on time, and said the priority would be to pay large bills first.
“One of the issues that I hear from practitioners and hear from providers that sometimes that their largest bills get pushed down to the lower part of the bucket,” Lahn said.
He also said he believed MCOs should not be allowed to have “vertical integration,” meaning the companies involved cannot own healthcare facilities or pharmacies, as well as saying there should be a ban on the use of artificial intelligence when denying claims.
However, Lahn warned removing managed care oversight from Iowa Medicaid would remove “about $1 billion in federal funding” that currently goes to MCOs.
“I do believe there’s better oversight for this,” Lahn said. “I do believe there’s changes we can make to this, but I also believe that the private sector can handle these things better than the government can. But the government has a very distinct role to play in oversight in being the watchdog of these organizations, and I would like to increase that oversight over these organizations, to make sure they are providing the right type of care, they’re paying promptly, and people can have something they should be able to count on — which is just a good service from these companies.”
Agreement on Medicaid work requirements
Despite different opinions on privatization, both candidates said they generally support Medicaid work requirements, implemented on the federal level through the “One, Big Beautiful Bill” Act and similarly placed in Iowa law through a 2025 measure. Lahn said he fully supported work requirements and said he believed Medicaid expansion through the Affordable Care Act “didn’t close this loop” and allowed some able-bodied adults to receive benefits without seeking work.
“I think the people of Iowa just understand, look, if you’re an able-bodied adult, that can seek work, you should be seeking work,” Lahn said. “… But I think one other part of this that we need to make sure we’re focused on, too, is to make sure that only the citizens of the state that are eligible for these programs are getting these programs. I do not believe benefits should be going to illegal immigrants that are in the state.”
Lahn referenced a report from the Center for Immigration Studies, a D.C.-based research organization that advocates for reducing both legal and illegal immigration, which found 59% of “non-citizen households” used one or more public benefit program. Undocumented immigrants are largely banned from receiving any public benefits, but the report argued immigrants, including people in the country illegally, have received “welfare benefits on behalf of U.S.-born citizen children.”
“I think that there’s protections that we can put in place, technology that we can use to make sure that only the people who are eligible for these benefits are getting these benefits,” Lahn said. “And (for) the people who deserve these benefits, that we’re not creating endless bureaucratic paperwork for them, but we’re making it easy for them to be able to get the benefit that they deserve.”
Sand said he believed able-bodied individuals should work. “It’s not an option. If you want to have income, if you wanna have health insurance, that just makes sense,” he said.
He also said because Medicaid work requirements were a federal obligation, and “we are going to follow the law.”
However, Sand said he had concerns about people legitimately in need — who often are working — getting denied access to healthcare because of they were unable to file needed paperwork proving their work history in order to receive health coverage. He referenced a case that received national coverage when Arkansas implemented Medicaid work requirements. A man with a chronic obstructive pulmonary disorder, who was working 30 to 40 hours a week at a poultry plant, meeting the state work requirements, was unable to navigate the monthly reporting system. Because he was unable to report his work hours, he lost Medicaid coverage and could not afford his medication, leading to him losing his job — and eventually losing his life.
“I want able-bodied people to be working, but I want to make sure that what the government is doing is putting in a work requirement and not a paperwork requirement,” Sand said. “It should be simple. It should be straightforward. It should be something that very busy people who do not have a lot of free time on their hands can get done and get done quickly, and the government should take responsibility for making sure that that is happening.”

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Murkowski and Murkowski endorse Alaska’s Democratic governor candidate
text:
Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, speaks to the Alaska Federation of Natives conference in Anchorage on Oct. 22, 2026. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)Republican U.S. Sen. Lisa Murkowski and her father, Republican former Sen. Frank Murkowski said Tuesday that they are endorsing the election of Democratic candidate for governor Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins.
Kreiss-Tomkins and three Republicans — Dave Bronson, Treg Taylor, and Bernadette Wilson — are running to replace incumbent Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy, who is term-limited and cannot run for re-election this year.
Polling indicates Kreiss-Tomkins, widely known as JKT, has a significant lead, in part because Republican votes are being split among three candidates.
Lisa Murkowski announced her endorsement in an interview with KTUU-TV on Tuesday afternoon.
“JKT is a young Alaskan with a view and a perspective that I think Alaska needs right now,” Murkowski told reporter Rebecca Palsha.
Murkowski has a reputation for bipartisanship in the U.S. Senate and has endorsed the re-election of her colleague, Republican U.S. Sen. Dan S. Sullivan. 
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Frank Murkowski, who served as one of Alaska’s two U.S. senators before being elected governor in 2002 — whereupon he appointed his daughter, Lisa, to his vacated Senate seat — joined former Democratic Gov. Tony Knowles and former independent Gov. Bill Walker in endorsing Kreiss-Tomkins via an Anchorage Daily News op-ed published Tuesday.
“We come from different political backgrounds, have different perspectives and have not always agreed on issues facing our state,” the three men said. “But we share a deep commitment to Alaska and its future. That is why we are coming together to support Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins for governor.”
Former Republican Gov. Sarah Palin has not endorsed any of the candidates in this year’s governor race, nor has former Republican Gov. Sean Parnell.
President Donald Trump endorsed Wilson on Oct. 13 during a rally in Wasilla. Speaking at that rally, Dunleavy declined to endorse any specific candidate but said Republican voters should rank all three Republican candidates.
“You need to get out and vote for your governor candidates. There are three of them. I need you to vote for each one of them. Ranked choice voting has foisted this on our shoulders, and the only way we’re going to win is if we all vote for the Republican candidates for governor, and that’s very important,” Dunleavy said.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Medicaid fraud task force recommends more staff, utilizing false claims act
text:
Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird and Solicitor General Eric Wessan present recommendations the final Iowa Medicaid Fraud Elimination Task Force meeting Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) Iowa’s Medicaid Fraud Elimination Task Force is sending a draft of recommendations to Gov. Kim Reynolds that suggests the state more than double the fraud investigation and civil enforcement unit to hold fraudsters accountable. 
The task force, which was initiated by Reynolds in July, met for the final time Tuesday and outlined their findings on how to end instances of fraud in the tax-payer supported healthcare system. 
Former state officials who have been vocally opposed to the task force said Tuesday that the initiative was “political theater” and that the conclusions it came to were the same recommendations the former officials suggested months ago. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Kevin Techau, former Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing director, said Attorney General Brenna Bird, who led the task force, could have long ago directed her staff to pursue cases under a state law that allows for lawsuits against parties who have defrauded the state. 
Techau said Bird and Reynolds have been “sitting on their hands” instead of directing staff to file claims under the state’s civil False Claims Act, which he said other state attorneys general have used to pursue cases of fraud and failure to provide Medicaid-funded healthcare.
“Suddenly, they wake up, just before an election, and decide Medicaid fraud is a big issue,” Techau said. “…So, hallelujah! They finally found the answers, but the answers were always sitting there right in front of them.”
Former state officials Kevin Techau, left, and Dean Lerner, right, talk to reporters after the final Iowa Medicaid Fraud Elimination Task Force meeting Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
Techau said Iowa nursing homes continue to collect Medicaid funds without providing the care they promise. A recent review of Center for Medicare and Medicaid Services data revealed that Iowa had more insufficient staffing citations at nursing homes in 2025 than any other state.
The task force recommended, according to an executive overview released Tuesday, establishing a “civil fraud team” in the Iowa Attorney General’s Office to make use of the Iowa False Claims Act to recover Medicaid funds from fraudsters. 
“Today, Iowa doesn’t have lawyers that are dedicated to suing these Medicaid fraudsters for the money they took, and the task force is recommending a civil fraud team in my office, something I very much support, to use the Iowa False Claims Act to allow triple damages plus penalties,” Bird said during the meeting. 
Recommendations 
In addition to adding a civil fraud team, the task force recommended growing the Medicaid Fraud Control Unit staff from 9 people to 24 people, including “dedicated prosecutors, investigators, data analysts and a nurse investigator.” 
Eric Wessan, solicitor general for the state, said that “person for person, Iowa’s unit brings more criminal cases than any other unit in the country,” but he said the unit has not grown since 2013. Wessan said that while Medicaid spending has grown 129% since 2013, the Medicaid Fraud Control Unit’s budget has grown 31% in the time period.
“The bottom line is simple: Iowa already does more with less than almost anyone,” Wessan said. “With the right tools, the right people, and the right structure, we can do a great deal more yet.” 
The task force also recommended tougher penalties for Medicaid fraudsters and the establishment of a “Medicaid Fraud War Room” to suspend payments to providers within 24 hours when fraud is suspected, and while it is investigated. 
Stephan Bayens, commissioner at the Iowa Department of Public Safety and a member of the task force, said the investment into the investigation and prosecution side of the issue was “much needed.” 
“In at least some of the public comments that we received, there (were) concerns about staffing levels, and I believe that this is an appropriate recommendation to kind of recognize the good work that’s being done, but also recognize there is capacity that could be addressed with more people.” 
Another section of the task force recommendations calls for revalidating high-risk providers and deactivating providers who are not serving patients. 
It recommended increasing technology and analytical tools for the fraud unit and related departments so they can use data to target reviews of high-risk areas such as in-home care to help ensure, for example, that a caregiver actually showed up to provide the care that was billed to Medicaid. 
Wessan said the task force was also recommending a “program integrity technology unit” within the Iowa Department of Health and Human Services to measure what is spent on “fraud-fighting technology” and what the technology has recovered. 
The task force was also directed to investigate ways to enhance fraud awareness and public reporting of suspected instances of fraud. The task force recommended the state release a video that clearly explains Medicaid fraud and how to report it to the state through avenues such as IowaFraudFighters.gov. 
Wessan said some of the recommendations “can start tomorrow under existing authority” but others will require legislative approval or funding. 
Bird said the draft of the recommendations will be submitted to Reynolds who, upon approval of the recommendations, will release the draft to the public. 
Bird thanked the task force for its work over the past several months. 
“Adopting this report, too, I want people to know this is not the finish line,” Bird said. “This is the starting line. Our message today is unmistakable: Iowa has zero tolerance for anybody who would steal from the taxpayers or exploit vulnerable people who are on Medicaid.”

name: California
title: What local election officials found in Trump’s new claims about California voters
text:
In summary
The Trump administration is demanding that almost every California county review its claims that noncitizens are registered to vote. Some of the information appears outdated, officials say.


Election officials from across California questioned the accuracy of the federal government’s methodology for finding noncitizen voters after the Trump administration threatened them with criminal charges last week.
The counties on Friday were given 48 hours to commit to working with federal authorities and to segregate ballots from a list of people federal authorities claimed were likely noncitizens. 
The letters said the list of names were from the same group of 20,000 people that the Trump administration flagged as noncitizens and then sued California over, demanding that state officials not count those ballots until they verify the voters’ citizenship.
State officials have questioned the accuracy of the data and have refused to comply, saying the federal government risks disenfranchising thousands of voters in an attempt to illegally meddle in state elections. On Tuesday, a federal judge appeared skeptical of the Trump administration’s legal arguments.
Meanwhile, the letters counties received last week threatened potential criminal charges for election officials who “knowingly tabulate ballots cast by individuals identified by federal agencies as noncitizens.”
Butte County Clerk-Recorder Keaton Denlay said he received one such letter and a demand to not count ballots from a list of 47 people.
“Upon inspection of the list of names, it appeared to be a print screen of a poorly formatted excel spreadsheet with missing and jumbled information,” he said in a statement. 
Denlay said he reviewed the list and found that 32 of the people were not on Butte County’s active voter rolls and were not sent ballots. Seven others “did not have sufficient information … to match to our voter list with confidence” since the list only contained partial names, partial addresses, no dates of birth, no drivers’ license numbers or Social Security numbers.
Six of the names belonged to people who may not be eligible to vote, but Denlay said California law requires those challenging a voter’s eligibility to have extraordinary levels of proof.“Given the overall inaccuracy of the list provided and its lack of specificity, I believe the Department of Justice has not met that burden,” Denlay said. “There will be no further action taken at this time.”
Fresno County Registrar of Voters James Kus also received a letter, but he said he couldn’t tell how many ballots federal prosecutors wanted him to segregate, since the “not particularly legible” list was a printed sheet, in small font, and “not in a format that facilitates counting or reviewing.” He said the county already follows state and federal voter registration laws.
“We will not be deviating from those legal requirements for this letter,” Kus told CalMatters in an email.
Francisco Diaz, San Benito County registrar of voters, said his office received a demand with 33 names. A preliminary review found that some on the list weren’t registered to vote.
“Hand-delivering a letter via armed federal agents with an arbitrary 48-hour deadline does not circumvent state law,” Diaz said in a statement. “We will not be intimidated by agents with guns for simply doing our jobs, nor will we be rushed into compromising confidential voter data.”
Orange County Registrar of Voters Bob Page said he wasn’t notified of a letter alleging his county had 1,754 “likely aliens” on the voter rolls until after business hours on Friday.
That’s because, he told reporters in an email, federal prosecutors had addressed and hand-delivered the letter not to Page but to Orange County Clerk-Recorder Hugh Nguyen, who handles such documents as marriage licenses and property deeds. 
On Monday, Page said federal agents delivered a correctly addressed letter to his office, along with a “data storage drive.” 
Page planned to respond by the Wednesday deadline, he said.
The messy voter lists counties described fits a pattern, said David Becker, executive director of the Center for Election Innovation & Research, a nonprofit whose mission is to restore trust in the American election system
He noted that the Department of Homeland Security recently claimed that Nevada had nearly 16,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls. DHS sent the state the names of only 185 voters. Nevada officials confirmed the voters had attested they were all U.S. citizens.Becker said the Trump administration has been making “broad political claims made with great fanfare” only to have them “fall apart as they’re subjected to scrutiny.” 
“I’m not entirely sure the DOJ wants to get into court and defend its evidentiary claims because I think they would fall apart, just as we’ve seen in other states,” said Becker, a former U.S. Justice Department attorney.
In federal court on Tuesday, Bill Essayli, the first assistant U.S. attorney in Los Angeles, insisted the federal list of 20,000 people was accurate.
“We stand by the reliability of the information,” he said. “We take our obligations and ethics very seriously.”

name: California
title: Judge says Trump could disenfranchise voters in purge of noncitizens from election rolls
text:
In summary
A federal judge is unlikely to issue a final ruling on the Trump administration’s claim that noncitizens are registered to vote in California until after Election Day.


Saying he had concerns it could disenfranchise voters during the midterm election, a federal judge on Tuesday seemed skeptical of the Trump administration’s demands that California election officials set aside 20,000 ballots that it claimed could have been mailed to noncitizens.
“Some of these may be very valid voters, and that’s my concern about disenfranchisement,”  said U.S. District Judge David O. Carter, an appointee of President Bill Clinton.
Carter said he would issue a formal ruling by Wednesday, but he told the courtroom he was likely going to appoint a special master to weigh the evidence both sides present at a hearing in two weeks. That means his final ruling might not come until after the election.
He said he didn’t want to “just wing it with a ruling” based on last-minute evidence the federal government submitted to the court the night before Tuesday’s hearing.Carter also suggested that his ruling would order federal authorities to stop telling election officials that they could face criminal charges if they didn’t comply with the Trump administration’s demands. The Trump administration on Friday sent letters to California election officials telling them to set aside ballots from suspected noncitizens, and threatened them with criminal charges if they allowed those people to vote.“This court believes it would be wise that any threats to state or county (election) employees cease immediately,” Carter told the courtroom.
Carter’s remarks point to yet another likely legal blow to the Trump administration as it seeks to validate President Donald Trump’s longstanding claims of widespread election fraud favoring Democrats. Experts and election officials say those claims are meritless. 
Bill Essayli, the first assistant U.S. attorney in Los Angeles, acknowledged that the government’s list of 20,000 people may contain citizens, but he said the possibility that noncitizens were voting illegally was too great a threat.
“I would ask the state how many illegal votes is OK for them?” Essayli said. “It cannot be that the state has a right to facilitate the counting and tabulation of noncitizen votes. There’s no right to that.”
The Trump administration sued California earlier this month saying election officials refused to comply with a 48-hour federal deadline to set aside the ballots of up to 20,000 people the administration had flagged as possible noncitizens until the voters’ citizenship could be verified.
The administration sought a temporary restraining order forcing the state to comply.
California officials argued there was no way they could since they were busy overseeing the election. They also called the demand an illegal effort to meddle in state-run elections that could disenfranchise legal voters.“I just want to make sure the stakes are clear: that what we’re talking about is stripping voting rights from thousands of people until proven otherwise,” said Anne Bellows, a deputy attorney general with the California Department of Justice. 
Judge points to immigrant arrests
State and county officials also have questioned the methodology the federal government used to flag possible noncitizens.
In a court filing, Los Angeles County officials said that a sampling of 200 names from the federal list, which included people from all over California, found that many of them were likely citizens and that most had not voted before and were not sent ballots.  Federal investigators re-reviewed those 200 names and found that only four were citizens, Essayli told the judge.“We stand by the reliability of the information,” he said. “We take our obligations and ethics very seriously.”
Carter noted that, last week, federal prosecutors charged 28 California green card holders for allegedly voting or registering to vote in violation of laws prohibiting noncitizens from participating in elections. 
He said that if noncitizens really are voting in as large of numbers as the Trump administration claims, there’s nothing stopping federal prosecutors from finding them and charging them without the risk of blocking legal voters from having their ballots counted.
“If it’s this big, you’ve got a remedy for goodness sakes,” Carter told Essayli. “Go out and indict.”
After the hearing, Essayli said from the courthouse steps that the state could “resolve this today.”
“They just seem disinterested in getting to the bottom of this,” Essayli said, noting that the number of ballots in question could tip smaller elections. “A lot of elections are decided by tens of votes or hundreds of votes.”
9th Circuit ruled against Trump
The hearing came a day after two judges on a three-judge panel of the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals rejected an emergency effort from the Trump administration to bypass Carter’s courtroom. 
The Trump administration sought an emergency order from the appellate court, claiming that Carter didn’t schedule a hearing fast enough. The two judges said prosecutors’ arguments about urgency didn’t hold up.
Their ruling noted that the prosecutors have been making claims about illegal voters on California’s voter rolls since July and could have taken action any time since, so their “claimed emergency, at least in part, is a self-constructed one.”Judge Mark Bennett, a Trump appointee, noted in a concurring opinion that he had “serious doubts” about the federal government’s claims that prosecutors could “superintend or intervene in a state’s election administration.” 
He wrote that Congress granted states — not the executive branch — authority over elections.In a dissenting opinion, Judge Patrick Bumatay, another Trump appointee, argued that “federal law precludes California from commingling ballots likely cast by aliens with legitimate ballots, because it encourages and induces illegal voting.”
“Stopping that practice for those identified as likely noncitizens is the bare minimum,” Bumatay wrote.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Governor signs bill allowing security spending with campaign funds
text:
Gov. Mikie Sherrill signed a measure, introduced after political killings last year, that lets candidates and elected officials pay for security upgrades with campaign cash. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)Gov. Mikie Sherrill on Tuesday signed legislation allowing candidates and some other fundraising committees to use political contributions to pay for security upgrades needed because of a campaign.
The bill, which won unanimous passage in the Senate but met with a 51-12 Assembly vote divided largely along party lines, allows certain political fundraising committees to fund security upgrades like cameras, gates, and personnel to meet threats that have become increasingly common for individuals seeking or holding office.
It prohibits using campaign funds to pay for firearms or ammunition, and it bars any payments to family members or entities they operate.
Under the new law, security upgrades paid for by campaign accounts are the property of the campaign and must be dissolved once the campaign account closes or an officeholder leaves their position. That can be done by selling devices and equipment at cost or for another reasonable value.
The New Jersey Election Law Enforcement Commission will set regulations further governing the use of campaign funds for candidate security.
The bill’s introduction in February came after a rising tide of political violence in 2025 that included the assassinations of former Democratic Minnesota House Speaker Melissa Hortman and her husband and the conservative activist Charlie Kirk.
Despite its bipartisan sponsorship by Sens. Paul Sarlo (D-Bergen) and Carmen Amato (R-Ocean) and Assemblyman Rob Karabinchak (D-Middlesex), the bill had met with Republican opposition in the lower chamber from members who worried campaign donors were the wrong source to fund security.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Louisiana’s bond rating improves, which should save the state money
text:
Fitch Ratings moved Louisiana’s credit from “AA-” to “AA" last week, which is expected to save the state money. (Photo by Wesley Muller/Louisiana Illuminator)One of the three national credit rating agencies upgraded Louisiana’s bond rating at the end of last week. The state should now expect to pay less in interest when it borrows money for roadwork and other construction projects.  
Fitch Ratings moved Louisiana’s credit from “AA-” to “AA,” according to a statement released by the global agency Friday. It attributed the upgrade, in part, to new tax laws Gov. Jeff Landry and the Louisiana Legislature approved two years ago. 
“The upgrade reflects the state’s successful implementation of 2024 revenue policy changes, which reduces a projected structural gap,” said the Fitch report. 
Landry and state lawmakers skirted a major state budget deficit by eliminating an automatic sales tax cut before it took place in 2025. Instead, the governor and legislators raised the sales tax rate further to offset a new income tax reduction. They also freed up more money by shifting revenue dedicated to major transportation projects into accounts for expenses such as healthcare and higher education. 
State Treasurer John Fleming, R-Minden, said the credit rating improvement should be celebrated. 

“We must continue building on this progress to ensure that Louisiana’s finances remain strong for years to come,” he said in a written statement. 
Louisiana Senate President Cameron Henry, R-Metairie, and House Speaker Philip DeVillier, R-Eunice, said the legislature will continue to focus on bringing long-term fiscal stability to the state. 

“We are not done yet, but we are making the changes necessary to secure our state’s fiscal future,” Henry said in a written statement.

A reversal of the new tax policies — for example, a future sales tax rate cut — could cause the rating agency to downgrade Louisiana’s credit in the future, Fitch said in its report. 
“Slow economic growth, the planned partial rollback of the 2024 sales tax increase and the relocation of certain revenue from the general fund to transportation projects could constrain long-term revenue growth,” the report states. “These factors will be important determinants of future financial performance.”

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho reports second influenza death, as health officials report early start to flu season
text:
An influenza vaccine is pictured at the Ellis R. Shipp Public Health Center in West Valley City on Thursday, Sept. 17, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Idaho health officials on Tuesday reported the state’s second flu death in the 2026-27 influenza season.
The death was of a resident of Elmore County, a rural area outside Boise, who was in their 80s, the regional health agency, Central District Health, announced. The first death, reported last week, was of an Owyhee County man who was older than age 65. 
The deaths come as public health officials say that influenza is spreading earlier in the year than usual. In recent weeks, emergency department and urgent care visits related to the flu have been higher than they were during the same time last year, state health officials say.
Idaho has averaged about 60 reported influenza-related deaths annually for the last five flu seasons, with most reported deaths among people over 50, according to the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare.
Officials at Central District Health say vaccination is the best way to reduce the risk of severe flu illness.
“While most people who get the flu recover without serious complications, some groups are at higher risk for severe illness, hospitalization, and death,” said Dr. Jaime Butler-Dawson, the health district’s epidemiology program manager. “These include adults age 65 and older, pregnant people, young children, people with obesity, and those with weakened immune systems or chronic conditions such as asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), diabetes, or kidney disease.”
According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, this year’s vaccines are designed to protect against three different influenza viruses expected to circulate during the flu season.
Symptoms of the flu include fever, cough, sore throat, runny nose, body aches, headache, chills and fatigue. Although most people who get the flu recover after a few days, some can have serious complications that can lead to hospitalization or death.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Montana Public Service Commission postpones vote on NorthWestern Energy merger
text:
(Photo by Scott Olson | Getty Images)The Montana Public Service Commission postponed a decision on the pending merger of NorthWestern Energy and Black Hills Corp until Nov. 10.
Commissioner Jennifer Fielder, who proposed the postponement Tuesday, said staff analysts addressed many of her concerns about the $15.4 billion merger proposal.
However, Fielder requested more time to propose an additional condition to address a concern that two of the groups who have opposed the merger still had.
“I think that there might be some good work we could yet do on that,” Fielder said.
Commissioners Jeff Welborn and Randy Pinocci supported Fielder’s motion to postpone the final decision. Commissioners Annie Bukacek and Kirk Bushman opposed it.
Most of the parties that participated in the case ended up in support of the merger — or agreed not to oppose it — after the utilities addressed their concerns. But 350 Montana and Montana Farmers Union continued to oppose it and suggested conditions the PSC should place on any merger.
Fielder said she wanted to propose one condition the groups had recommended: To reserve a portion of NorthWestern’s acquisition at the coal-fired plant in Colstrip for Montana customers if it would be the most affordable.
Fielder said the additional time would allow members of the public and the parties to review the condition, and it would allow them time to review any additional conditions commissioners wanted to propose.
Bukacek, who has voted to support NorthWestern, urged against the delay.
She said the merger proposal was made more than one year ago, and the PSC should vote this week as scheduled to avoid more staff time and travel costs.
“Enough’s enough,” Bukacek said.
NorthWestern Energy and South Dakota-based Black Hills announced plans to merge in August 2025 pending approval from regulators.
Regulators in Montana will be the last to vote on the deal.
At the meeting Tuesday, roughly 30 people urged the PSC to oppose the merger, citing concerns including the costs more data centers might have on Montana customers.
PSC legal and regulatory staff recommended approval.
Staff cited support from the Montana Consumer Counsel and restrictions aimed to protect NorthWestern’s Montana assets from financial activities of the parent company.
Based on statute, the final day for the PSC to act is Thursday, Nov. 12.
If approved, the new company, to be called Bright Horizon Energy, would operate in Montana, South Dakota, Arkansas, Colorado, Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska and Wyoming.
This story will be updated.

name: Daily Montanan
title: University of Providence to shutter in 2027
text:
The University of Providence (University of Providence photo)The University of Providence, a private liberal arts Catholic school in Great Falls, will close Aug. 20, 2027 the university announced Tuesday, citing ongoing financial struggles.
University President Caroline Goulet said falling enrollment and financial pressures as the reasons for the school closing its doors in a video posted to its website.
The school “pursued multiple paths to secure the university’s future,” she said in a video.“Despite those efforts, we could not find a financially sustainable way forward.”
The school’s board of trustees voted unanimously on Tuesday to shut down the university, which is located on a 44-acre campus made up of 17 buildings near Benefis Hospital. 
“While this chapter of the university’s history is ending, its mission and impact will endure through the generations of graduates, faculty, staff, Sisters and partners who have carried the spirit of Providence into their communities,” Terry Cosgrove, the chairperson of the board, said in a press release. “We are committed to honoring that legacy with the same compassion, dignity and integrity that have guided the university since its founding.”
The board said that a planned closure would be easier than an abrupt one. 
Several webpages created by the university added details about the decision.
“The university’s circumstances also reflect broader pressures reshaping small private colleges across the country, particularly institutions serving smaller and rural communities,” a webpage said, adding a merger and acquisition were also discussed.
In 2025 the university had $28.6 million in revenue and $35.6 million in expenses, with total assets valued at $48.6 million, according to ProPublica.
“The board concluded that closing the university with care was the responsible path forward,” the university said in its communications released Tuesday.
  ‘Questions about what comes next’ 

The university has separate student and facility webpages with additional information about the closure. Students will face decisions about transfers, credits, and degree recognition; whether they can graduate and what happens if faculty leave before the end of the year. 
The Montana University System said in a press release that it would support Providence students seeking to find a new school. The school had 630 students and 244 total employees.
“We know University of Providence students have invested significant time, effort, and resources in their education, and this news brings difficult questions about what comes next,” Montana Commissioner of Higher Education Clayton Christian said in a press release. “Our message to those students is simple: You do not have to navigate this transition alone. The Montana University System is here to help you find a path forward that builds on your progress and supports your goal of earning a degree.”
Staff now face questions dealing with benefits and employment details.
What to do with the school’s endowment is still under consideration, according to the university. Reports show the university having about $20 million in its endowment.
The school is still taking donations, and those will be used to help current students — specifically offering scholarships to cover the cost of tuition for students during the summer 2027 session, and reducing graduate tuition for students.
Existing donors will also be contacted to discuss alternatives true to the “original intent and purpose” of those endowment and scholarship funds.
“The university is working with legal counsel on the steps required to permit use of endowment funds as scholarship support for continuing students, consistent with donor intent and applicable law,” a school webpage says. “These funds would help students complete their education before the university closes.”
  ‘Times change’ 

The school is a private, Roman Catholic liberal arts university, founded in 1932 by the Sisters of Providence.
That religious order, which was founded in 1842 in Montreal, opened schools and hospitals in Montana as early as 1864, according to the university. The Sisters of Providence came to Great Falls in 1892 to open the city’s first hospital and four decades later, the school in cooperation with the Diocese of Great Falls-Billings. 
It was called the College of Great Falls at the time, before changing to the University of Great Falls in 1995 and finally the University of Providence in 2017.
However, about 10 years after the school opened, the Diocese of Great Falls-Billings relinquished control of the university to the Sisters of Providence. 
The Sisters of Providence also grew into a major hospital provider across the West — the healthcare branch of its work, Providence Health & Services, now includes 51 hospitals, 1,002 clinics and 119,000 employees across five states. 
The university said the healthcare service had provided “substantial financial support to keep the university open while it searched for a viable and sustainable operating model.”
Issues at Providence Health also contributed to the university’s demise, as they were contributing about $8 million annually to the school, which was cut, according to the Montana Free Press. 
The school formally declared a financial exigency in December 2025 and sought to address the issues.
Providence Ministries, which is also associated with the university, said the Sisters of Providence saw a need in Great Falls and looked to fill it.
“Because of this ministry, thousands served in hospitals, classrooms, businesses, and communities throughout Montana and beyond,” Mary Anne Sladich-Lantz, president of Providence Ministries said in a press release. “But times change. The path forward for many small, private universities across the country is uncertain. Financial sustainability is no longer feasible.”
  ‘Cannot be measured in dollars alone’ 

The university was known for its nursing program and also had majors in criminal justice, biology, healthcare administration and psychology, among others.
In Great Falls, the news was met with sadness by Mayor Cory Reeves, who called it a “huge loss” for the city.
“For me, this one is personal,” Reeves said in a statement. “It’s where I went to college, earned my degree, and met my wife. The University of Providence will always hold a special place in my heart, and I’m grateful for the role it played in my life.”
He added it was more than losing a college.
“Its impact on Great Falls and Montana cannot be measured in dollars alone,” Reeves added, who said he was “truly saddened” by the news.
The school mostly competed athletically in the Frontier Conference, which also includes a number of other Montana schools. Some sports, including wrestling and soccer, competed separately in the Cascade Collegiate Conference.
The University of Providence had successful sports programs including a volleyball program that has won five Frontier Conference titles — four of which came in the last six years — and advanced to multiple NAIA national tournaments in the last two decades. 
The women’s basketball team made the NAIA’s Final Four during the 2023-24 season, and the school also notably had one of the few wrestling programs in the Mountain West.
Frontier Conference Commissioner Scott Crawford did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico students walk out of classes to protest data centers, US Sen. Heinrich’s permitting bill
authors: Matt Mondschein, Joshua Bowling, Patrick Lohmann
text:
Students from the New Mexico School for the Arts in Santa Fe marched to the Capitol for the "Pull Out the Plug" protest on Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo by Matt Mondschein/Source NM)Hundreds of students from New Mexico School for the Arts in Santa Fe and the University of New Mexico in Albuquerque — some donning Halloween costumes — walked out of classes Tuesday and joined protests organized against data centers, pipelines and fossil fuel projects.
The protests, organized by Youth United for Climate Crisis Action (YUCCA), followed a Sunday protest on the Las Cruces campus of New Mexico State University and a coordinated campaign to support a data center moratorium during next year’s legislative session.



“We will not get back the last 20 years of climate progress Project Jupiter will undo,” Isabelle Taylor-Ault, a student organizer and junior at NMSA, said to the crowd outside the Roundhouse in Santa Fe. “You, the adults, the ones supposed to be fighting for us, you may get the privilege of dying of old age, but our children will die from climate change.”
A handful of state lawmakers sitting on the interim Water and Natural Resources Committee — which was meeting on the Capitol’s third floor — headed down to watch the protest unfold.
State Rep. Micaela Lara Cadena (D-Mesilla), a vocal critic of Project Jupiter and one of the first state lawmakers to call for a statewide data center moratorium, told Source NM she was thrilled to see teenagers across the state opposing the development.
Last month, Democratic gubernatorial nominee Deb Haaland said if elected on Nov. 3, she plans to enact a statewide data center moratorium as an executive order immediately upon taking office. Lara Cadena acknowledged that the Dec. 7 public hearing on whether to give Project Jupiter’s power source an air quality permit — one of the last hurdles the data center needs to clear to become fully operational — could result in a decision before then, but said she plans to continue using her office to hold the industry to account.
“Those permits haven’t been issued yet,” she said.
Protesters — bearing signs with messages like “El agua es vida,” “This sign was not made by AI” and “Make Orwell fiction again” — stood in a circle around the perimeter of the second-floor rotunda, where they began a “Stop Project Jupiter” chant.
As the chant echoed across the rotunda, they marched upstairs to Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham’s fourth-floor office. Standing outside Lujan Grisham’s office, they shouted in unison: “MLG, you can’t hide. You support ecocide.”
