title: Sharpton, Gilchrist join Detroit effort amid voter intimidation concerns ahead of Election Day
text:
The Rev. Al Sharpton and Michigan Lt. Gov. Garlin Gilchrist speak outside an early voting site at Wayne County Community College District’s Northwest Campus on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026, encouraging voters to exercise their right to vote as volunteers prepare to help address intimidation concerns across Wayne County. (Photo by Janelle D. James/Michigan Advance)DETROIT — As concerns about voter intimidation and election interference grow ahead of Election Day, civil rights leader Rev. Al Sharpton and Lt. Gov. Garlin Gilchrist reassured voters that they can cast their ballots without fear. 
The two spoke Tuesday morning outside of Wayne County Community College District’s Northwest Campus, an early voting site, alongside volunteers from Vote Safe, an organization that helps minority residents overcome fears of voting. 
Statewide early voting began Saturday and runs through Nov. 1. Registered voters can cast their ballots in person at their local early voting site. 
“You can be confident that we’ll be on the ground … all over this city to make sure that they won’t be allowed to intimidate you, block you or stop you from voting,” the Rev. Sharpton said during the press conference. “Do not have any fear because we are here to …  protect your vote.” 
The Rev. Al Sharpton urges Detroit voters to exercise their right to vote without fear amid concerns about voter intimidation ahead of Election Day. Sharpton was speaking during an event at Wayne County Community College District’s Northwest Campus on Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo by Janelle D. James/Michigan Advance)
The press conference came just days after Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel announced in a press release that the U.S. Department of Justice will send federal election monitors to polling locations in Detroit, East Lansing, Flint, Grand Rapids, Hamtramck, Lansing and Warren on Election Day. 
The DOJ also sent federal monitors to Detroit, East Lansing and Lansing in August during the primary election. 
And in September, Markwayne Mullin, the U.S. homeland security secretary said that federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers could also be sent to polling sites across the country. 
Sharpton urged voters not to let concerns about intimidation keep them from the polls. 
“People cheat and part of cheating is to scare you,” he said. “They don’t have to rob you if you don’t show up but if you don’t show up, you rob yourself.” 
“I’m telling you to ‘melt the ICE’ and come out and vote. It is time to make democracy work,” Sharpton said. 
As part of those efforts, Vote Safe, a project of the Save America Movement, will deploy volunteers outside of polling locations across Wayne County through Election Day to combat voter intimidation. Volunteers will be available to answer questions, document wrongdoing and de-escalate tense moments if necessary. 


“Voting is important and in a time where there is a lot of suppression happening, a lot of fearmongering happening, people need to feel safe to do their civic duty,” said Ellarose Preston, a volunteer for the project.  “We’ll be a friendly face to make people feel comfortable.”
Federal election monitors have a different role. They are only allowed to observe from 100 feet away from a polling location, though local clerks can grant them additional access. Monitors are also prohibited from talking to voters, touching ballots and interfering with the administration of the election.  
Gilchrist also warned against efforts to discourage people from voting, arguing such tactics are an attempt to undermine voters’ political power. 
“Make no mistake about it, the people who lie about our elections, the people who try to scare people out of voting, what they’re really afraid of is the power of those voters,” said Gilchrist, the Democratic candidate for Michigan secretary of state. 
“Nobody asks powerless people to do powerless things and powerful people never pass up a chance to use their power,” he said. 
Lt. Gov. Garlin Gilchrist warns against efforts to intimidate voters, saying attempts to discourage people from voting undermine their political power. Gilchrist was speaking during an event at Wayne County Community College District’s Northwest Campus on Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo by Janelle D. James/Michigan Advance)
Ruby Farmer, 68, of Detroit said that she’s noticed voter intimidation has gotten more prominent under President Donald Trump. 
“The people that we have in office now are liars. They cheat and they do anything to win,” she said. ”You have to just believe that you have a right to vote … and you should do your duty.” 
Farmer, who typically votes by mail, sent in her ballot three weeks ago. 
Michigan is just one of many states that the Trump administration has targeted during the midterm elections.  On Friday, the president said he ordered the DOJ to file a lawsuit which would block Alaska from certifying the election if Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan loses his race. Attorneys representing the state of Alaska have since asked a federal judge to dismiss the lawsuit.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Trump, along with several other Republicans, alleged that Dan J. Sullivan, also a Republican, is running a fake campaign to confuse voters and steal votes from Sen. Dan Sullivan. 
“The Dumocrats know how good he is and have put up an imposter of the same name. Vote for the ‘INCUMBENT SENATOR.’ Don’t let these fraudsters get away with this hoax,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post. 
The Republican incumbent’s name will appear as Dan S. Sullivan on the ballot while his challengers’ name will appear as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. 
U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche defended the DOJ’s lawsuit in a post on X, formerly known as Twitter. 
“This litigation seeks to ensure that after Alaskans cast their ballots, they are preserved in a manner that only Alaska’s governing officials have the information necessary to make a determination as to whether Alaskan voters were confused or misled,” he wrote.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: An electric utility wants to fix Pa.’s competitive energy market; regulators say more study needed
text:
State-by-state figures from monthly utility bill data show, on average, American households paid roughly $110, or 6.4%, more for electricity in 2025, compared to 2024. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)When Pennsylvania’s largest electric utility proposed a change to the commonwealth’s competitive electricity marketplace, saying it could save customers millions of dollars, consumer advocates said they were on board.
Utility regulators, however, said last week they want to study the issue on a statewide basis – a move that the commonwealth’s independent utility watchdog said will delay protections for millions of FirstEnergy Pennsylvania ratepayers.
“What FirstEnergy was trying to do was something that my office and others have been trying to do for a very long time,” said Darryl Lawrence, the state’s consumer advocate.

SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Since 1996, consumers in Pennsylvania have been able to compare the rates offered by their local electric utility to those offered by generation suppliers on the open market and select the most attractive price or their preference on how the power is produced. 
As part of the state’s deregulated utility market, the Electricity Generation Customer Choice and Competition Act was intended to increase competition among electricity generators and spur innovation in the products and services they offered. 
Typically, electricity suppliers have offered a choice of plans of varying lengths and prices allowing consumers to lock in a low rate or choose a longer-term contract as a hedge against rising energy costs. 
“Customers are signing up for what’s often been very short term offers … and you get a very competitive price, sometimes a very low price for three months of generation service. But at the end of those three months, you need to do something,” Lawrence explained.
Those who don’t take action to switch back to the utility’s default rate or don’t select a new contract are automatically rolled onto variable rate plans at much higher costs.
“Consumers, by and large, have not affirmatively taken action,” Lawrence said. “They’ve missed the notice. They’ve forgotten about it. They misplaced the notice they got in the mail … these things happen.”
Constellation Energy’s Eddystone Generating Station in Delaware County. (Photo by Peter Hall/Capital-Star)
Collectively, that has been a very expensive mistake for Pennsylvania ratepayers.
In its February filing with the Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission (PUC), FirstEnergy said it cost its customers alone $82 million more in aggregate last year than if those customers had used the same amount of electricity at the default rate. The proposed default service plan in the filing outlines how the utility would set electricity rates for customers who don’t shop for a supplier. FirstEnergy is the parent company of WestPenn Power, PennPower, Penelec and Met-Ed, which collectively serve more than 2 million customers. 
“The commission is doing the right thing to continue to look at this,” Energy Association of Pennsylvania President Andy Tubbs said, adding that the group supports electric choice. “But customers need guardrails so they are not overpaying for their energy service.”
While not every supplier engages in the practice, some market short-term teaser rates that come with a sweetener, like a gift card or other benefits.
“If the customer is not diligent in paying attention to energy prices and when the contract ends inattentiveness can very quickly eat into any savings in a month or two,” he said. 
By a 3-2 vote Thursday, the Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission rejected part of FirstEnergy’s proposal that would require customers to be switched back to the default rate when a supply contract ends, rather than allowing suppliers to move customers to a higher rate.
Another rejected part of the proposal would require suppliers to have customers who are paying more than the default rate to affirm their choice on a quarterly basis.
Separately, the proposal would modify how suppliers get paid to reduce the amount of uncollectable debt that the utility and its customers must pay for. 
Under the existing arrangement, FirstEnergy buys consumer debt from suppliers and must absorb any that can’t be collected. The commission approved provisions Thursday that would make debts incurred at rates above than the default ineligible.
In his motion to modify the settlement on the proposal, PUC Chair Stephen DeFrank, said he was reluctant to make “such a profound revision” to the retail electricity marketplace for a single electric company. He noted the commission’s regulations permit electricity suppliers to retain their customers when a contract expires provided they give required notice.
Additionally, DeFrank said it’s necessary to do a more comprehensive review of the issue to determine what portion of the excess costs are due to customers choosing more costly plans that prioritize renewable energy over fossil fuels, longer term contracts versus costs attributable to “customer inertia.”
DeFrank’s motion directed the PUC’s Office of Competitive Market Oversight to conduct an expedited review of those concerns by June.
Commissioners Kimberly Barrow and Kathryn Zerfuss cast the dissenting votes.
“We find ourselves squarely in the middle of an affordability crisis and customers are rightfully asking for relief,” Barrow said in a statement she read at the meeting, adding that the rejected provisions would provide immediate help for customers to avoid exorbitant rates.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Citing evidence submitted by the Coalition for Affordable Utility Services and Energy Efficiency in Pennsylvania, Barrow noted that FirstEnergy’s residential electricity shoppers are cut off 10 times more often than non-shopping customers. And the average per-customer write off of about $2,200 for shopping customers is more than double that for non-shopping customers.
Zerfuss added that the $82 million in excess payments accounts for the FirstEnergy customers who did save money by choosing their rates.
“That finding should carry real weight when we decide whether an additional consumer safeguard is warranted,” she said. “I do not know how much longer we need to study a problem that this record already documents, and quite thoroughly.”
State lawmakers, meanwhile, have been divided over how to approach the issue.
House Energy Committee Chair Elizabeth Fiedler (D-Philadelphia) and committee Secretary Heather Boyd (D-Delaware) urged the PUC earlier this month to adopt the FirstEnergy’s proposal, saying it “better reflects consumer behavior and ensures that rate changes occur only through informed, affirmative consent.”
Boyd and Fiedler are co-prime sponsors of House Bill 2131, which would require consumers to be returned to their utility’s default rate. In the Senate, Sen. John Kane (D-Chester) is the prime sponsor of similar legislation. With only two voting days remaining in the legislative session for each chamber, the bills are unlikely to be considered. 
The chair of the Senate Consumer Protection and Professional Licensure Committee, Sen. Patrick Stefano (R-Fayette), said the case signals a significant problem and state officials have a responsibility to ensure consumers have choices and that the process is as efficient and cost-effective as possible.
“The Commission’s action acknowledges these affordability concerns while allowing a broader review of the retail electricity market to move forward,” he said in a statement.
Senate Energy and Environmental Resources Committee Chair Gene Yaw (R-Lycoming) said the framework that has governed Pennsylvania’s electricity market for decades reflects deliberate policy decisions of the legislature.
And while the PUC has authority to execute the law “significant changes … should be authorized by the General Assembly rather than created through administrative proceedings,” Yaw said in written comments to the commission.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Chris Jones says his unconventional campaign is a ‘referendum on water’
text:
Democratic candidate for Iowa secretary of agriculture Chris Jones speaks at the Greater Des Moines Partnership Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) Chris Jones, the Democrat running for Iowa secretary of agriculture, said Tuesday that his campaign, which has largely focused on water quality, has shown a “different way” of running for office. 
Jones spoke at the Greater Des Moines Partnership candidate forum Tuesday morning and said he knows he is a “peculiar” candidate that doesn’t “fit the mold.” 
Jones, who is running against incumbent Republican Mike Naig, said he has not run television ads, or “begged” people to donate to his campaign, but has instead relied on social media marketing and a message of “inspiration.” 
“We’re trying to inspire people,” Jones said. “I’m trying to show candidates there’s a different way of doing this. You can compete here if you have an inspiring message, and you have at least a little bit of money.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Candidates on the Nov. 3 ballot have raised millions of dollars for their campaigns. Iowa’s gubernatorial race between Democrat Rob Sand and Republican Zach Lahn raised a combined record breaking amount of $81 million. 
Jones said the amount of money in a campaign has almost become a “self-fulfilling prophecy” where candidates who win, and raised a lot of money, attribute it to the funds and those who lose feel their fate was tied to not raising enough.
“I think the campaign is demonstrating how to effectively do something different here and still be competitive,” Jones said. 
Naig is scheduled to speak at the forum Thursday morning. 
Meet Iowa’s secretary of agriculture candidates

Jones, who has called his candidacy a referendum on Iowa’s water quality, joked that the “experiment about a candidate running on water and winning has been ruined” because water quality has become a top issue for many candidates on the Nov. 3 ballot. 
Jones has called for changes to Iowa’s dominant agricultural systems, with policy proposals to fund “off ramps” for producers who want to stop growing things like corn and soybeans and instead move to other, more diversified crops. 
He suggested this method, and a more diversified agricultural system would boost Iowa’s economic vitality, especially in rural farming communities. 
“We need to diversify our farming system,” Jones said. “That’s how we bring jobs to rural Iowa.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Debate on fuel price hikes filtering into Kansas campaigns for US Senate, governor
text:
U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall, a Republican seeking reelection on the Nov. 3 ballot, speaks during an Oct. 26, 2026, campaign rally featuring Vice President JD Vance rally in Topeka. (Photo by Thad Allton for Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Vice President JD Vance blamed “tinpot dictators” in the Middle East, former President Joe Biden and other Democrats for surging gasoline and diesel prices in Kansas.
Vance didn’t attribute higher U.S. fuel prices on President Donald Trump or Republicans controlling Congress during his Tuesday speech in Topeka designed to bolster the campaign of Republican U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall, who finds himself in a tight race with Democrat Adam Hamilton.
Vance pointed to loss of 20% of California’s refining capacity while Biden was president and Democrats’ proposals for the Green New Deal emphasizing greater reliance on renewable energy, including wind and solar, and less dependence on fossil fuels like oil and coal.
“They talk about affordability, but they are the ones supporting the green new scam,” Vance told the crowd in Topeka. “The Biden administration shut down 20% of America’s West Coast refineries, leaving us more reliant than ever on tinpot dictators in the Middle East.”
“You all will hear a lot of people say that gas prices are too high. I understand that. It’s true. But it’s also true that the price of gas goes up each time a foreign leader in the Middle East throws a tantrum,” the vice president added.
In Kansas and in other states, the Nov. 3 election prompted political disputes about factors influencing fuel prices. Marshall has argued the true culprit was Ukraine’s defense against the Russian invasion in 2022 and the affinity of Democrats for energy policy reform tied to climate change. Hamilton blamed Trump’s war against Iran.
“The real problem with the cost of diesel in particular is, No. 1, the Ukraine war,” Marshall said. “Beyond that, why are we dependent upon diesel imports? It’s because of the Green New Deal policy that my opponent supports. We have not had a new refinery built since 1978. We’ve lost 90 refineries since 1990. The problem right now is refining capacity.”
Marshall predicted ending the Ukraine-Russia war would promptly lower gasoline and diesel prices in the United States. However, he said, placing Democrats in control of the U.S. House and U.S. Senate would prevent consumers from benefitting from potential price declines.
Hamilton, who founded the largest United Methodist congregation in the United States, said he supported elements of energy policy contained in the Green New Deal. He said Marshall’s insistence on blaming Ukraine for defending its sovereignty was designed to mislead Kansas voters into believing the Trump administration’s attack on Iran wasn’t linked to the rising price of fuel.
Before the United States attacked Iran in February the price of diesel was about $3.62 per gallon but climbed to $6.53 per gallon by September. The escalation in diesel costs forced Kansas farmers to spend an extra $83 million during the spring planting season.
“This happened in response to the war in Iran that didn’t need to happen,” said Hamilton, who has called for an end to the conflict. “It’s an unnecessary war. This is why the prices went to record highs, and Roger Marshall supported that. I support the Ukrainians being able to defend themselves. This is something Roger Marshall has waffled on.”
Democrat Adam Hamilton, the Democratic Party’s nominee for U.S. Senate, speaks with potential voters during an Oct. 12, 2026, campaign event in Lawrence. He blames President Donald Trump’s war with Iran for escalation in U.S. fuel costs. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)
Hamilton said the president’s decision to drop economic sanctions against Russia to allow importation of diesel to the United States was a blunder.
“It’s a disaster,” he said. “Why in the world would we agree to do this with Russia? Many Republicans are saying the same thing. This is selling out our allies and Ukrainians.”
These military conflict and global energy market pressures, as well as other affordability issues confronting Kansans, bled into the Kansas race for governor.
Republican Ty Masterson, who endorsed the U.S. attack on Iran, said during a recent forum in Baxter Springs that fuel pricing was a piece of the affordability conversation along with property taxes, insurance, housing and grocery costs.
“The big problem with diesel prices is not Iran,” Masterson said. “We haven’t built a refinery in this country in 50 years. We have a bottleneck in refinement and that is legacy policy.”
Masterson said Democrats “hate oil and gas” and he linked the refining capacity shortage to political advocacy of the Green New Deal.
“I’m gonna be the most pro-oil-and-gas governor we’ve seen,” Masterson said.
Cindy Holscher, the Democratic nominee for governor, said Kansas families were paying $4,700 more on fuel and essentials due to the Trump administration’s imposition of tariffs and the war with Iran.
“Ty Masterson has championed the war in Iran that sent diesel prices skyrocketing, and now he is lying to rural Kansans about why they are paying so much at the pump,” Holscher said. “Once again, Masterson is surrendering to his party bosses in Washington and the oil and gas lobby instead of standing up for the Kansas farmers and rural communities who are bearing these costs. Kansans deserve a governor who will tell them the truth.”
On Wednesday, the nonpartisan Cook Political Report changes its prediction in the Kansas governor’s race from lean Republican to toss up. The report followed a Holscher campaign poll indicating the gubernatorial race was deadlocked at 47% to 47% and the infusion of about $1.5 million in new data center industry contributions to Masterson’s campaign.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Lamont’s overdue food assistance slows down further
text:
Nearly five months after Gov. Ned Lamont pledged $300 grocery gift cards to 25,000 poor residents who’d lost federal nutrition benefits, his administration has delivered just 2,000, the Department of Social Services reported Tuesday.
And while the administration vowed to intensify efforts on Oct. 2 when the Connecticut Mirror disclosed the relief program had bogged down, distribution has slowed since then.
Meanwhile, anti-hunger advocates predicted Tuesday that the breakdown would expand legislative support for a new state-funded nutrition grant to assist some of the tens of thousands who’ve stopped receiving federal Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits, commonly known as SNAP.
“We are almost a year into the SNAP crisis caused by the federal budget, and Connecticut still has not come up with a plan to get people fed,” said Meghan Holden, communications director for The Connecticut Project, a philanthropic research group focused on economic opportunity and affordability.
The governor, a Democrat campaigning for a third term, announced on June 3 that grocery store cards would be released in early August to complement millions of dollars in supplemental state contributions to food banks and pantries.
“Here in Connecticut, we’re stepping up and looking out for you,” Lamont said at the time.
But the social services department didn’t provide local nonprofits assisting with card distribution with full contact information for all eligible recipients until early September, a department spokeswoman said. Officials wanted to ensure that transfer wouldn’t violate federal privacy rules.
By early October, two months after the program had started, only 1,425 former SNAP beneficiaries had received a collective $427,500, with 23,570 food-insecure residents still awaiting about $7.1 million.
Despite pledges to intensify efforts, the department, which got relief to an average of 712.5 residents during the first two months of distribution, reached only about 575 more during the bulk of October, spokeswoman Christine Stuart said Tuesday.
The department also announced several new steps to streamline distribution.
Though residents eligible for gift cards were notified via text this summer, the department is sending notifications again, this time through post cards and regular mail.
Those notified earlier this year about gift card eligibility don’t have to make an appointment but can simply visit any of the nine nonprofit Community Action Agencies helping with distribution “and receive a gift card immediately upon quick verification.”
Though the agency staff still can explore options to restore card recipients’ access to federal benefits — such as enrolling in job training or volunteer work — that is not necessary to receive the $300 benefit.
And while gift cards were transmitted electronically in the past, the agencies now will be providing physical cards.
“DSS will continue working closely with the agencies to remove barriers to keep the process simple and respectful,” the department wrote in a statement.
Rhonda Evans, executive director for the Connecticut Association for Community Action, added that “we encourage individuals who have received notification that they are eligible to visit their local agency to verify their identity and receive their card. Our goal is to ensure eligible individuals can access the support they need as easily as possible.”
Lamont has faced increasing pressure to intervene since July 2025, when Congress and President Donald Trump ordered major cutbacks to SNAP and other federal human services programs.
Veterans, people experiencing homelessness, former foster youths and parents with children older than 14 all face tougher work requirements. Many lawfully present immigrants, including refugees, lost eligibility. And critics say tougher error penalties from Washington have led states to unfairly disqualify many SNAP applicants.
The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, a fiscal policy group based in Washington, D.C., reported earlier this month that SNAP enrollment is at its lowest point nationwide in 17 years. Connecticut Voices for Children, a local policy and research organization, noted in August that nearly 63,000 Connecticut residents, including almost 19,000 children, have lost federal nutrition benefits since July 2025.
Lamont’s critics, on both sides of the aisle, said there are lessons to be learned from the grocery card situation.
“It’s surprising and a bit frustrating that DSS hasn’t been able to get these cards out the door,” said Sen. Matt Lesser, D-Middletown, co-chair of the Human Services Committee and advocate for a state-funded nutrition benefit. “We really do need to set up a more permanent program.”
Sen. Cathy Osten, D-Sprague, co-chair of the Appropriations Committee and another advocate for a state-funded nutrition benefit, said “gift cards don’t change the dial” enough in a hunger crisis.
“We need to get people food,” she said. “We shouldn’t be waiting to hand out gift cards months later.”
Republican gubernatorial candidate Ryan Fazio has opposed using state funds to offset federal human service cutbacks. But he also has chastised Lamont for touting the assistance at campaign press conferences while failing to deliver the actual relief to many.
“Gov. Lamont got the headlines, took credit for fighting the federal government, and then what?” Fazio said, noting that 92% of those the governor pledged to help feed five months ago have received nothing.
“This isn’t just an administrative delay. It’s failed leadership. … The governor must be held accountable for his broken promises.”
But Lamont and his fellow Democrats in the legislature’s majority have used hundreds of millions in state reserves to offset federal cutbacks in healthcare, heating assistance and other social services.
Lamont also has criticized Fazio for opposition to any state intervention and for failing to speak out against cuts that analysts say will remove more than $1 trillion from federal human services programs by 2034.
“Talk is cheap,” Lamont campaign spokeswoman Lauren Gray said Tuesday. “When Connecticut families needed help, Gov. Lamont proposed the Federal Cuts Response Fund to protect them. Ryan Fazio said no. That’s the difference between talking about helping people and actually showing up for them.”
Note: The Connecticut Project is a funder of The Connecticut Mirror.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Free speech or threat? Brantley County activist faces court after arrest at county meeting
text:
Tanya Tomanek poses for a photo outside of the Brantley County Courthouse on Sept. 23, 2026. Credit: Justin Taylor/The Current GA/CatchLight/Report for AmericaFor most of her life, Tanya Tomanek thought of herself as a businesswoman, mother and grandmother, someone who moved to her quiet 13-acre land in Brantley County three years ago. She was more concerned with her family than politics.
That changed this summer, when Tomanek was led out of a county commission meeting in handcuffs and spent three nights in jail after delivering an impassioned plea for transparency and accountability over the hot-button issue of data centers.
On Wednesday, Tomanek, 53, is going to court to fight charges of criminal trespass. She says the accusations are politically motivated and meant to silence her coalition of residents against tech firms and developers that are scouring Georgia for places to build data centers and the local officials tempted to bring them to her county.
 A new view on government

Tomanek’s journey from an apolitical citizen to a frontline warrior in Georgia’s data center wars illustrates how voters across the state are becoming more civically engaged around an issue that many see as an existential threat to their way of life.
At the same time, grassroots campaigns popping up across traditionally Republican rural counties like Brantley illustrate why election polls suggest that Georgia’s statewide races are so tight ahead of Election Day: voter anxiety about affordability and the potential end of their way of life is intertwined with a widespread perception that elected officials aren’t listening.
“I guess God woke me up,” Tomanek said about her relatively new political activism. “I saw good versus evil” and “ knew that I couldn’t stand by.”
The sheriff’s deputy who handcuffed Tomanek viewed the matter differently. In his incident report he wrote that Tomanek was using threatening language and refused to comply with demands that she sit down before the end of her allotted five-minute public comment.
Tomanek was “ejected from the meeting because she broke the rules” that had been posted prior to the session,” Brantley County Manager Joey Cason told The Current GA. “Chairman Skipper Harris asked her to sit down; she said no. The officer asked her to leave, and she said that he would have to take her out in handcuffs. So the officer handcuffed her and took her out.”
Tomanek concedes that she used an expletive as her emotions ran high at the podium but denied making any threats. She says that heavy-handed tactics against voters like her will likely blowback against the political establishment at the ballot box.
“I’ve never been in politics. I don’t know politics. I didn’t participate in my local government” until this summer, she said. “They didn’t take the power from us; we gave it away. And we’re the only ones that can take it back.”
 Taking a hard look at artificial intelligence

Tomanek, who grew up in Illinois and lived in Camden and Brantley counties for close to two decades, has lived through turbulent times in American history but the advent of the Artificial Intelligence era has hit home differently, she said.
As someone who helped care for elderly parents and now helps raise grandchildren on her farm, Tomanek was too busy to get in the weeds of national economic policy, or local government issues. That changed in January of 2026. She and a friend went to a local discussion group at the Waynesville Baptist Church where the topic was data centers.
The technology’s potential to disrupt America’s economy and her grandchildren’s lives frightened her enough to drastically change her life. Her free time was concentrated in research about data centers and conversations with neighbors. She and her partner, Matt McGrath, sought to raise awareness of their concerns by using a digital billboard the two installed on GA 82.
In February, she christened her coalition Citizens United for Brantley County’s Future. Their first formal meeting, she said, was at Waynesville Primary School, where around 150 people showed up.
Later that month, a man who attended the monthly Brantley County Committee meeting was escorted out by police after speaking against a proposed zoning change to allow the construction of a data center. He was not charged.
A subsequent meeting of the Citizens United group in Nahunta attracted nearly 100 Brantley County residents, all “blue collar people,” according to Tomanek. Residents, including young families and retirees, used the opportunity to air all sorts of grievances against county commissioners. Data centers were among the topics, she said.
Tomanek and McGrath were thrilled at the unexpected turnout. The sense of community — and anger — heightened soon after when wildfires destroyed over a hundred homes and forced families to evacuate.
Some in Tomanek’s anti-data center coalition started the rumor that tech companies or developers had started the fires deliberately to clear land for such a facility. County commissioners have denied they were considering a data center in Brantley.
But anger about the slow pace of help and rebuilding after the fire merged with frustration over higher costs and growing perception that local elected officials were ignoring urgent problems.
Tomanek felt the backlash growing in her social media chats with the Citizens United collective. By summer, her own ire concentrated on the county’s elected officials.
Her emotions led her to sign up to speak at the July 7 county commission meeting, where residents are allowed five minutes to discuss issues of importance.
 Taking a stand

A video taken of Tomanek’s speech shows her at the podium, amid a room of around 20 neighbors including a sprinkling of Citizens United allies. She started by telling the commissioners her philosophy of government. Local government, she said, is like a business, and elected officials, she said, are employees of the voters. The people of Brantley, she continued, have been “really shitty business owners,” meaning that the voters have done a poor job of holding their commissioners accountable.
“They didn’t take the power from us; we gave it away. And we’re the only ones that can take it back,” she said to some cheers in the crowd.
As her emotions grew, she used an expletive. “Our county’s going fucking bankrupt,” she said.
By that, she meant that she was worried that the commissioners were going to change the rural face of Brantley with large-scale economic development, such as data centers, a new landfill or solar farms.
At that point, a commissioner signaled for the sheriff’s deputy to remove her from the room, according to the incident report of Tomanek’s arrest.
“Tomanek began speaking, and as she continued into her speech, her tone and demeanor became noticeably more aggressive specifically towards Board Chairman Skipper Harris,” according to her arrest report. “About 2 minutes into Tomanek’s speaking, she began verbally berating and cursing loudly for everyone in the room to hear.”
 ‘Terrified’

Tomanek felt a mixture of surprise and fear as she was put in the county lockup that Tuesday afternoon. “I’m terrified. If I said I wasn’t scared, I’d be lying,” she said.
Another woman already in the holding cell told her the sheriff processed people on a Wednesday, and Tomanek prepared herself for an uncomfortable night.
The next day, her cell mate was processed. Tomanek, however, had to wait until Friday, when she was released on a $1,000 cash-only bail while she awaited a hearing on charges of criminal trespass.
She considered both decisions a symbol of retaliation for what she sees is a crusade to speak truth to power, a mission she said she feels called to perform. “None of this is me. This is nothing but the Lord,” she said about her political activism.
So far, she has not convinced the courts of her divine calling. Before her first court hearing scheduled Sept. 23, her assigned public defender told her he had to recuse himself from her case because of a conflict of interest. In private practice, he apparently does work for the county, she said.
That has delayed Tomanek’s quest for justice. At her court appearance on Oct. 28, she’s hoping that the judge will throw out the charges.
“I’ve had a target on my back since jump,” she said.
“Before January, nobody stood up. Nobody was here. They could do what they wanted because we were silent,” said Tomanek. “My voice holds no more weight than the next. They didn’t do it to me. They did it to everyone. I just happened to go to jail.”

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Utah couple to spend four days in jail after admitting to helping a man flee ICE
text:
The Orrin G. Hatch United States Courthouse is pictured in Salt Lake City on Wednesday, May 7, 2025. (McKenzie Romero/Utah News Dispatch)A Utah couple who admitted to helping a man escape as immigration officers tried to detain him was ordered Monday to serve four days behind bars, a sentence prosecutors say will help deter others from doing the same as the Trump administration continues its immigration crackdown. 
“This crime merits more than just a probation sentence, a public scolding, or some finger wagging,” federal prosecutors wrote in a sentencing memo. “Defendants and the general public need to understand that if they interfere with lawful ICE arrests, they will go to jail.”
Utah couple accused of helping man flee immigration agents face federal charges

Kelzie Ryann Luna and George Sanchez-Juarez both pleaded guilty Monday in U.S. District Court to a class A misdemeanor count of theft and disposal of government property, along with aiding and abetting. 
In October 2025, the couple was in their car at a gas station in Salt Lake City when a man ran into traffic and came up to them, saying “help me please” in Spanish, prosecutors said in court filings. 
From the passenger seat, Luna recognized him as a past customer at the McDonald’s nearby where she used to work. She later said in an Instagram post that he had a gash on his arm and a black eye, prosecutors alleged, and that “we brought him to safety and made sure he was okay.”
In another post, Luna was accused of posting a video of a man sprinting into traffic and another clip of someone cutting off handcuffs with the caption, “(Expletive) ice viva Mexico,” followed by prayer hands emojis. 
The immigration officers had gone to a Salt Lake City Home Depot looking for four people previously deported, court documents say, with one agent saying the escapee “looked like one of the four targets.” He got away from a vehicle while officers were arresting someone else. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In federal court in Salt Lake City on Monday, Magistrate Judge Dustin Pead sentenced the pair to four days of imprisonment, which they’re expected to serve in a jail within the state. Pead also imposed six months of supervised release and a $600 fine on both Luna and Sanchez-Juarez. 
In addition, the judge ordered them to pay $28 in restitution to cover the cost of the handcuffs they were accused of destroying with a bolt cutter.  
The U.S. Attorney’s Office for Utah did not say in a news release announcing the outcome whether immigration agents eventually found the man who got away with help from the couple. 
In the sentencing memo, prosecutors said the couple in their early 20s have young twins, are employed and have no prior criminal history. They said a sentence of four days or two weekends behind bars is sufficient. 
Charles Engle, special agent in charge for Homeland Security Investigations in Denver, said in a statement that the couple’s actions “were not harmless. They undermined public safety, obstructed justice, and showed blatant disregard for the rule of law.” 
“Those who choose to take the law into their own hands will be held accountable,” U.S. Attorney for Utah Melissa Holyoak added in her own statement, noting the consequences include a permanent federal criminal record.
The judge ordered the couple to report to the U.S. Marshals Service to serve their sentences at different times next month. Attorneys representing them declined to comment on the decision.
An analysis released last week by the nonpartisan Migration Policy Institute counted 980,000 deportations from the start of the second Trump administration through July, Stateline reported. The total included arrangements to leave voluntarily after an arrest.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: How Trump’s ‘Big Beautiful Bill’ is playing in Maine’s US Senate race
text:
U.S. Sen. Susan Collins (R-ME) at the U.S. Capitol Building on June 30, 2025 in Washington, D.C as Republican leaders worked to get U.S. President Donald Trump's "One, Big, Beautiful Bill" Act through Congress before the July 4 Independence Day holiday. (Photo by Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: How to register, key dates, who’s on the ballot and where the candidates stand on the top issues facing Maine.]Hospital and birthing center closures. Healthcare workforce shortages. Rising insurance premiums. As Mainers grapple with increasing health-related costs and dwindling access to care, those issues have become a focal point of the U.S. Senate race. 
Incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic nominee Troy Jackson have sparred over healthcare during debates and on the airwaves. The candidates differ in their overarching approaches to healthcare — Jackson, a proponent of Medicare for All, and Collins, a critic of a “big government” healthcare takeover.
At the center of many of their arguments over healthcare is President Donald Trump’s signature spending package, known as the “One Big Beautiful Bill,” which is expected to slash Medicaid funding in Maine and across the country.
Jackson, like many Democrats across the country, has tried to pin the healthcare cuts on Collins. Collins, who voted for a procedural motion to advance the bill but against the final package, has in turn touted the rural healthcare fund she secured in the bill during negotiations. 
The Rural Health Transformation Program could mitigate but will not fully offset the larger cuts in the law, said Zachary Levinson, project director of the KFF project on hospital costs. 
Maine was awarded $190 million in initial program funding in fiscal year 2026, which has all been committed as of this fall for a range of projects such as hospital financial sustainability, workforce recruitment and training, and technology improvements. 
While the program was established in part to address concerns about the impact of Trump’s spending law on rural hospitals, the funding is being used for broader purposes than that and has restrictions that limit its ability to address urgent needs, Levinson said. 
The votes
Ads from Jackson’s campaign and supportive super PACS claim Collins cast the deciding vote on the “One Big Beautiful Bill.” 
In late June of 2025, Collins voted to advance the bill, a 59-49 vote. Throughout the negotiation process, Maine’s senior senator expressed concern about the impact the bill would have on rural hospitals and on some Medicaid recipients, though she supported adding work requirements to the low-income healthcare program. Days later, Collins voted against the final package, which narrowly passed in the Senate with Vice President JD Vance casting the tie-breaking vote. 
Collins has repeatedly justified her vote to advance the bill, arguing that she otherwise would not have been able to include the $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program that she authored in the package. 
Collins has also highlighted the program in a campaign ad, which touts the funding without mentioning the “One Big Beautiful Bill.”.
Jackson equated Collins’ approach to “an arsonist who helped set the fire, and then she wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put it out” during a debate on Oct. 6. He has also pointed out that her Republican colleagues had called her a “team player” for advancing the legislation. 
At the time, Sen. John Hoeven, a Republican from North Dakota, told the Boston Globe that Republicans knew that when it came to the final vote, Collins likely “couldn’t get there just because of her state.” 
Democratic U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York weighed into the matter during her visit to Portland last week. 
“There’s a lot of procedural votes that say, ‘You can go ahead, you can go ahead.’ It doesn’t just show up on the floor one day,” Ocasio-Cortez said. “At every single moment, you have an opportunity to stand up and say no.”
Snags
Maine applied for $200 million through the program last November and was awarded $190 million at the end of December. 
In late March, Collins claimed that the funding had been in jeopardy because “the state missed milestones and provided inadequate information to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services.” Collins said she spoke with CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz and that CMS worked with the state to bring it into compliance.
Collins leans on familiar playbook in hopes of defying political headwinds

However, according to Lindsay Hammes, press secretary for the Maine Department of Health and Human Services, at no point had CMS indicated to Gov. Janet Mills’ administration that Maine’s responses were untimely, inadequate, or that the funds were potentially at risk. Hammes said the department submitted a fully allocated budget for the program to CMS that was approved in March. 
On Oct. 15, CMS confirmed that the totality of Maine’s grant award was obligated, meaning the state has legally committed its allocated funds. The program uses a cost-reimbursement model, so funds will be drawn down as expenses are accrued. 
CMS did not respond to questions about whether Maine’s funding had ever been at risk. Instead, an unnamed spokesperson said in an email that it is standard procedure for CMS to request states amend budgets and adjust initiatives during grantmaking. CMS maintains ongoing oversight through reporting, monitoring, and annual progress assessments, the spokesperson said. 
Maine and several states had to change their initial plans to fit CMS guidelines. 
For instance, Maine initially proposed using some funding for uncompensated care payments and provider payments for essential health services to people who are uninsured. However, those plans were removed from the final budget. 
While not included in the text of the law, CMS guidance says the funds are not intended “to be used for perpetual operating expenses, rather for investments… that will have sustainable impact beyond the end of the program.”
Also, payments to providers for services have a number of limits. They cannot exceed 15% of a state award in a given budget period, be used for short-term relief, or supplement existing funding sources, including Medicaid.
CMS is viewing the rural healthcare fund as an “opportunity to transform how healthcare is delivered in rural parts of the country,” Levinson said. “But the trade-off is that they’re really not focused on providing short-term, immediate relief to rural hospitals or other providers, and that means this fund is less targeted towards these more immediate concerns about rural hospitals closing their doors or eliminating certain service lines.”
Nearly half of Maine’s 24 rural hospitals are considered “at risk” of closing, according to an analysis by the Center for Healthcare Quality and Payment Reform. Labor and delivery units are often the first to go. Since 2015, 12 birthing centers in the state have closed.
Impact 
The “One Big Beautiful Bill” is projected to slash Medicaid funding nationally by $911 billion and by nearly $3 billion in Maine over the next decade. Considering only rural areas, the law is estimated to cut $137 billion nationally. 
That means the rural healthcare program could offset about 5% of the total estimated cuts to federal Medicaid spending and 37% of the estimated cuts in rural areas, according to a KFF analysis of the Congressional Budget Office’s estimates released shortly after the law’s enactment.
“It’s also worth noting that the reductions in Medicaid spending will become much more significant in later years after the rural health fund has started to dry up, and many of those cuts are permanent,” Levinson said. The rural healthcare program is primarily being distributed over a five-year period.
In Maine, $66 million of the state’s $190 million will go toward improving hospitals’ financial sustainability, such as $35 million for the Rural Hospital Efficiency Fund and regional planning activities, and $29 million for helping providers transition to alternative payment models. 
The next largest share of the funding, $53 million, will go toward technology, including telehealth hubs and services, cybersecurity and Artificial Intelligence. The Hallowell-based MCD Global Health is leading this work.
Community care is another component of Maine’s approved plan, with $34 million going toward things like evidence-based practices, nutrition education, and school-based care. Another component is workforce recruitment and training, with $31.5 million obligated for rural clinical training, simulation equipment and workforce transportation, among other efforts.  
With this work just beginning, Jeffrey Austin, president of the Maine Hospital Association, said it is too early to speak to actual impacts of the rural healthcare program. As for the overall effect of the “One Big Beautiful Bill,” Austin said, “We certainly have some concerns in the short-term that some cuts will absolutely materialize, but decades-long projections are something I avoid.”
Austin said there are “plenty of ways the federal government could help in the future,” including “no additional cuts.”

title: Mississippi State expands housing for upperclassmen
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Upperclassmen at Mississippi State University will have more on-campus housing options after state higher education officials approved a $63.9 million dormitory expansion that would add 527 beds in two years.  
The expansion would increase the College View housing capacity from 656 beds to 1,183 beds, reviving plans for the second phase of the project that was postponed during the COVID-19 pandemic. 
The Mississippi Institutions of Higher Learning board of trustees unanimously approved the project expansion plans on Monday. 
A private developer will finance the project through a partnership with the university, IHL spokesperson John Sewell said. The estimated construction completion date is August 2028. 
The university needs more modern housing for upperclassmen that is close to campus and connected to campus life, MSU spokesman Sid Salter said. 
The university also plans to take older residence halls out of service or repurpose them to better serve students’ needs, Salter said. He did not specify when those changes would begin. 
Mississippi State has 18 residence halls on its main campus in Starkville and requires freshmen to live on campus. The university enrollment has also increased from 22,649 students in fall 2022 to 23,563 last year.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Oshkosh middle school teacher detained by ICE
text:
Wendy Mendez (back row right, holding cup) receives an employee of the year acknowledgment in 2025. (Screenshot | Oshkosh Area School District YouTube video.)An Oshkosh middle school teacher has been detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement. In a statement, a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson confirmed that on Oct. 14, ICE arrested Wendy Mendez, a Spanish teacher at the Vel Phillips Middle School in Oshkosh. 
The spokesperson said that Mendez entered the United States in August 2020 “on a temporary basis, but in violation of our laws, failed to depart by Feb. 9, 2021.” The statement continues that on Feb. 18, 2026, Mendez was “placed into removal proceedings, and on Sept. 9, was ordered removed by an immigration judge for failing to show up for her removal proceedings. She received due process and will remain in custody pending her removal from the United States.” 
DHS did not clarify the type of visa or permit which Mendez may have had during her time in the United States. Although President Donald Trump campaigned on sending ICE to apprehend “the worst of the worst,” Mendez appears to be the latest example of someone who does not fit that description. A check of online court records showed that the only thing linked to Mendez were divorce proceedings, suggesting that she has no criminal record. 
Wendy Mendez receives an employee of the year acknowledgment in 2025. (Screenshot | Oshkosh Area School District YouTube video.)
Reports about Mendez’s detention first emerged on social media.  Facebook posts by someone who said she is a friend of Mendez’s  described Mendez as a woman of Afro-Caribbean descent who was raised in Costa Rica, and who moved to Oshkosh six years ago with her husband and two sons. The posts claim that one of her sons has Down syndrome and doesn’t understand why his mother is missing. The post states that Mendez had no knowledge of her deportation proceedings because notices from the court were sent to an old address. The post claims that while in detention, Mendez was placed in solitary confinement and made to sleep on concrete floors and mold-covered beds. According to the post, Mendez was deported after being moved among multiple detention facilities in different states without having the opportunity to appear before an immigration judge.
Mendez’s story was first reported by the independent University of Wisconsin-Oshkosh student newspaper, the Advance-Titan. 
A spokesperson for Voces de la Frontera, an immigrant rights group that runs a statewide network to verify ICE activity, told the Examiner that the group had not received any information about the case.
The Facebook posts mention details about Mendez that later appeared in official statements from DHS and the school district. However, the original poster has not responded to Wisconsin Examiner’s requests for comment. 
Federal immigration officers at the Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport in March (Photo by Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder)
In an emailed statement, the Oshkosh Area School District confirmed that Mendez “is an employee in good standing who has been placed on an unpaid leave of absence due to unforeseen circumstances.” A district spokesperson added that “at no point was this a school safety or performance-related issue. Our primary focus remains on supporting our students and staff and keeping learning moving forward in our classrooms.”
On Monday, the district sent a letter to the families of students about Mendez, saying that although it normally follows privacy laws regarding employee matters, “this situation has become public and is felt across the community. We are sharing this update directly to address her absence, reduce uncertainty, and outline the support available.” The letter reiterates that Mendez has been placed on unpaid leave due to “unforeseen circumstances,” and that she was in good standing with the district. “The district is working through the process of obtaining more details and will provide more information if we are able.”
The letter explains that students in Mendez’s class were informed of her absence last Tuesday. “We know this situation brings heartbreak, frustration, and worry for many in our community,” the letter states. “Additionally, whenever a sudden absence occurs, it naturally brings up questions or concerns for students. Our primary responsibility is to ensure every student feels safe, supported, and grounded.” 
School counselors and support staff are being made available to listen to students, and help them process what’s happening. 
Mendez was named employee of the year last year by the Oshkosh Area School District. A video posted to the district’s YouTube page showed a surprised Mendez receiving a balloon and coffee thermos as her students applauded. 
A masked U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent knocks on a car window in Minnesota. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)
“We are keeping Mrs. Mendez and her loved ones in our thoughts during this difficult time,” the letter states. “If you feel your child needs additional support during the day, please contact our Vel Phillips Middle School counseling office directly.” The letter is signed by Oshkosh Area School District Superintendent Dr. Bryan Davis, and Vel Phillips Middle School Principal Amanda Patza. 
Oshkosh is situated in Winnebago County, where the sheriff’s office is part of the 287(g) program which deputizes local law enforcement to participate in immigration enforcement and detention. Since last January, ICE has reported 25 arrests in Winnebago County, almost all of which originated from the jail, Wisconsin Watch reported.
In September during a town hall meeting, Sheriff John Matz said that his office’s participation in 287(g) “needs to continue.” Matz said, however, that he isn’t interested in street enforcement or in renting jail beds to ICE. This year, voters will decide whether to support Matz or his Democratic opponent Jason Ripple, a patrol officer. Ripple told Wisconsin Watch that he would void the 287(g) program, stating that the program “may be an open door for additional involvement with (ICE)…and I think that by any modern law enforcement standards, we’ve seen pretty clearly that their tactics are sloppy.”

name: Daily Montanan
title: Commentary: A legacy in waiting: Let’s pass the ‘River Runs Through It’ Act
text:
Sisters cool off in the Blackfoot River. (Brockton Gnose for the Daily Montanan)When I was a boy, the fishing expeditions to Montana’s Blackfoot River launched from our family cabin at nearby Seeley Lake were the high points of summer.
The trips followed a ritual that began with a period of longing during the cold winter months. Once the family re-established itself for the summer at the cabin, as we did every year, anticipation turned to action.
“The barometer’s up; tomorrow will be a good day for fishing,” my father would declare, glancing at the barometer on the mantlepiece that’s still there more than a half century later.
We gathered rods, reels, and the worn-out work clothes we fished in, and stacked them on the kitchen porch. God help the poor soul who left out an essential item: He did not deserve to fish. We packed into the car, sometimes just father and son, but family, friends, uncles, aunts and cousins, too. We fished other rivers, of course, but the waters of the Blackfoot carried so many of our dissolved memories from times past that we regarded it as our family river.
By the time I returned to Montana in middle age, while writing a series of books about the West, the Blackfoot had become everyone’s river. My father Norman Maclean’s novella, “A River Runs Through It,” had made the Blackfoot famous, especially after Robert Redford produced a movie based on the book. Pilgrims by the thousands came to what had been “our” river, many sporting hats and vests like the ones they’d seen in the movie.
The Blackfoot, to be honest, fished better than it had in the old days, thanks to the millions in restoration dollars generated by book and movie and put in local hands. There was a catch. The old Blackfoot had been a “tomahawk” river, a secondary weapon where guides took clients if bigger, better known rivers like the Missouri and the Clark Fork weren’t fishing well.
The new Blackfoot became a must stop for those who bought a non-resident fishing license along with their airline ticket. “A River Runs Through It” is a story of a troubled, loving family lived out against the backdrop of a primitive Eden. Many came yearning for a vanishing way of life, and some found reason enough to remain. Others saw their own family problems mirrored in the tragic story of the younger Maclean brother, Paul, and came for solace, and sometimes they found it.
Their arrival, though, brought change. Scores of boats with fishermen and sightseers process down the river on popular days, which means most days in high season.
The river has troubles of its own. Warm temperatures and low water flows have stressed trout populations and impacted insect hatches the fish – and fishermen – rely on. The important October and early season caddis hatches have been almost non-existent the last couple of years. The low water flows have exposed rocks that serve as insect spawning grounds, and the caddis larvae dry up in their pebbly cocoons and die.
“We’re happy to see a mosquito anymore,” a fellow fisherman remarked during a fall hot spell.
Now, Montana’s Congressional delegation – two senators, two representatives, all Republicans – has an opportunity to take a significant step to protect the Blackfoot’s cold water and many other resources. For two retiring members, Sen. Steve Daines and Rep. Ryan Zinke, it’s also a chance to leave behind a worthy legacy. And it’s good business. Sport fishing is a $1.2 billion a year industry in Montana, no small thing for a state with a general fund budget this year of only $3.5 billion.
After more than two decades of struggle, residents of the Blackfoot Valley and other “stakeholders” this year produced a bill combining two previous efforts, the Blackfoot Clearwater Stewardship Act and the Lincoln Prosperity Proposal. My family supported calling the combination the A River Runs Through It Act. Affecting about 430,000 acres in the Blackfoot Valley, the act has “something for everyone” — wilderness advocates, ranchers, loggers, snowmobilers, the works. A whopping 80%- plus of Montanans support it, according to a University of Montana survey.
Zinke introduced the act this fall, and Rep. Troy Downing quickly joined as a co-sponsor.
“This proposal was built by the people who live, work, hunt, and recreate in the Blackfoot, and after decades of work they found a way forward that keeps this landscape working for everybody,” Zinke said.
Daines spoke eloquently earlier this year about how his family cherishes “A River Runs Through It” and its evocation of the Montana spirit. They often watch the movie or read the book at family get-togethers, he said at an event for Montana supporters in June in Washington, D.C., which I attended. Facing retirement after more than a decade in Congress, Daines said he looks forward to spending more time with his children and grandchildren.
This year is the 50th anniversary of publication of the book. If Montana’s Congressional delegation gives its full support and the act is passed, we could all look our children and grandchildren in the eye and say, we did our best for the river that runs through it.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: WV contributes federal health funds to breast cancer screenings, substance abuse recovery, more
text:
Gov. Patrick Morrisey speaks to an audience in Bluefield, West Virginia, about the Rural Health Transformation Program in November 2025. (Photo courtesy of the West Virginia Office of Gov. Patrick Morrisey)The state of West Virginia will contribute millions of federal health dollars to help those in substance abuse recovery return to work, expand breast cancer screenings and more, Gov. Patrick Morrisey’s office has announced recently. 
West Virginia received $199 million in federal dollars from the Rural Health Transformation Program for 2026. The five-year program from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid was part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which made historic cuts to healthcare and food assistance spending. 
The Rural Health Transformation program aims to “empower states to transform the existing rural healthcare infrastructure and build sustainable healthcare systems that expand access, enhance quality of care and improve outcomes for patients,” according to CMS. 
Here’s a breakdown of recent Rural Health Transformation funding announcements: 

$1.5 million to help West Virginia residents in recovery return to work. The award includes $500,000 to the United Way of Harrison and Doddridge Counties for RecoveryWorks Appalachia and the Work Bank program; $499,500 to the Mountain State Educational Services Cooperative; $250,000 to the Williamson Health & Wellness Center, and $237,000 to the West Virginia Ministry of Advocacy and Workcamps. 
$1.3 million to the WVU Cancer Institute to replace the Bonnie’s Bus mobile mammography unit, which provides cancer screenings in rural communities across West Virginia.
$3.4 million to WVU Health to expand care for patients with chronic health conditions and help rural hospitals address staffing shortages. Of the award, $2.5 million will expand support for West Virginians living with diabetes and high blood pressure, and $900,000 will help WVU Health create a statewide pool of healthcare professionals who can be deployed to hospitals experiencing staffing shortages. 
$500,000 to the Potomac Highlands Guild to strengthen mental health and addiction recovery services in eastern West Virginia. The project will provide new technology to help healthcare providers identify patients who need additional support, reduce paperwork and spend more time caring for those struggling with mental health challenges and addiction, Morrisey’s office said. 
A $1.5 million to Ascension Recovery Services for a program designed to help West Virginians who have lost their jobs — or are at risk of losing them — due to substance use disorder re-enter the workforce and maintain long-term employment.
$2,000,026 to the West Virginia University (WVU) Eye Institute to establish a statewide teleophthalmology network to bring advanced medical technology and specialized eye care to patients across West Virginia.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Top Republicans keep visiting Kansas and encouraging people to vote
text:
Vice President JD Vance speaks to a crowd on Oct. 26, 2026, in Topeka, urging voters to reelect U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall. (Photo by Thad Allton for Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Before Vice President JD Vance was finished speaking Monday in Topeka, Republicans announced President Donald Trump would make his second visit to the state in as many weeks. 
The White House has made itself visible in Kansas, drawing thousands to Olathe, the Wichita area and Topeka, and Trump is expected to do the same Saturday morning in Salina.
Top Republicans in the Trump administration have cycled through Kansas in the lead-up to the Nov. 3 midterm election, mostly to campaign for U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall and other Republicans running for public office, including gubernatorial candidate Ty Masterson.
“We’re here to get these guys elected,” said U.S. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum ahead of Vance taking the stage Monday.
It’s a numbers game. Of Kansas’ more than 2,027,500 registered voters, nearly 902,000 are registered Republicans, and more than 521,000 are registered Democrats. Nearly 579,000 are unaffiliated. 
Early voter turnout is up by nearly 50% compared to the 2022 midterm elections, according to IKE Lab, an elections data and analysis service from two Wichita State University professors. 
Compared to the 2024 election, however, turnout this year is down by nearly 30%, particularly among Republicans.
In late October 2024, more than 170,600 Republicans had already turned out to vote while more than 120,500 Democrats had turned out. 
But the lagging Republican turnout hasn’t caused Republican candidates to shy away from stumping across the state. 
“If there’s a big blue wave, it’s going to crash into a big red wall in Kansas,” said Kansas Attorney General Kris Kobach, who is running against Democrat Chris Mann, at the rally.
Vance directly addressed undecided voters Monday. He acknowledged gas prices are up, but blamed it on foreign leaders in the Middle East, who he said drive the price of gas up each time one “throws a tantrum.”
He asked the audience: “In one week, are we going to tell the country that Kansas supports America first? Are we going to support a candidate that is fighting for our faith instead of against it? Are we going to support a candidate fighting for American sovereignty?”
Marshall faces a competitive reelection bid for the seat he’s held for a term, facing the Rev. Adam Hamilton, a Democratic Methodist pastor in the Kansas City area.
Marshall has struggled since the primary to outrun scandal. He has faced criticism for medical debt collection practices during his time as an OB-GYN in central Kansas, his time spent in Florida and alleged misuse of public funds.
“I’m asking you to send me back for one more term,” Marshall told the crowd Monday. “Six more years.”
Vance urged attendees not to judge Marshall by what he says but by his actions.
“I don’t want you to just judge him by what he says, because — of course he’s got great ideas, and he says them very well — I want you to judge him by what you couldn’t possibly see, but I do,” Vance said.
He said what’s more important is how Marshall has behaved and acted and “how he fights when the cameras aren’t on.”
Trump, Vance, Marshall, Masterson and others have encouraged their crowds to vote, bring their friends to the polls and pretend Trump is on the ballot.
“The only votes that count are the ones cast,” said U.S. Rep. Derek Schmidt, who is running for reelection in the 2nd District against veteran and veterinarian Don Coover, at the Topeka rally.
Marshall and Burgum told the crowd their vote “defends freedom” and the political trajectory of Kansas.
“In all of these races, and particularly the Senate race, it’s going to defend the direction of this country, and that changes the direction of the world,” Burgum said. “That’s how much your vote matters.”

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Judge strikes down parts of North Dakota Beef Commission membership law
text:
South Central District Judge Jackson Lofgren is seen Feb. 3, 2025, presiding over a trial in Bismarck. Lofgren has ruled that parts of North Dakota's Beef Commission membership law violate the state constitution. 
(Photo by Mary Steurer/North Dakota Monitor)A North Dakota judge has ruled that the law for nominating people to the panel that promotes the beef industry violates the state constitution because it gives nominating power to specific trade groups and no one else.
“That is arbitrary and unreasonable,” South Central District Judge Jackson Lofgren wrote in his Friday decision.
Three cattlemen – Kenneth Graner, Michael Heaton and Jeremy Maher – who are the directors of the Ranchers Rights Initiative challenged the law last year as unconstitutional. The state sought to have their claims dismissed. The judge heard arguments from both sides in a July hearing.
Lofgren said the law “deals out an advantage by name,” granting the named groups “the exclusive power to choose who may be considered for six seats on a public commission.”
“By specifically naming private entities, rather than listing criteria for entities to meet to be eligible to submit nominations, (the law) creates a closed class that prohibits accession into it,” the judge wrote.
The Beef Commission consists of nine members, including three beef producers, one cattle feeder, one dairy producer, one representative of a public livestock market and three at-large members, all appointed by the governor. Six of the nine members are nominated by four cattle-related groups, including the North Dakota Stockmen’s Association, named in the law.
Naming specific organizations to make nominations creates a special law that treats similar people and groups differently and is prohibited by North Dakota’s constitution, the judge wrote.
North Dakota judge weighs decision in Beef Commission membership lawsuit

The Beef Commission decides how to use the money raised from fees on cattle sales of $2 per head – $1 apiece to the state and federal government – known as the beef checkoff. The money is mainly used for beef promotion, education and research. The commission raised more than $1.5 million of assessment revenue in 2024-2025, according to an annual report.
The challengers said the law favors certain private associations and creates a “closed class” or different treatment that is not allowed by the state constitution.
In a statement Tuesday, the Ranchers Rights Initiative said: “For years, independent cattle producers were barred from serving on the NDBC because of the Stockmen’s Association’s complete control over nominations. The North Dakota Legislature rejected multiple attempts to correct and reform the law. Today, that barrier has finally come down.”
The state had argued the challengers lacked legal standing for their claims and waited too long to sue, and that the law applies equally to everyone and doesn’t require membership in specific organizations.
The judge wrote: “Even if there were specific or unique qualifications that only these organizations have, (the law) does not list these requirements or qualifications; it just names the organizations. The classification is based solely and arbitrarily on being a specific organization. Thus, the classification in (the law) bears no relationship to the Commission’s purpose of promoting the cattle industry in North Dakota.” 
An attorney for the challengers said the decision means the Beef Commission is now open to all in the industry and opens doors to 20 other state boards with the same selection process.
“If you’ve been excluded because you weren’t willing to pay the dues to join some trade group, you now have the chance to say, ‘Hey, that’s illegal. You need to stop doing that,’” attorney Robby Dube said.
The law keeps the industry-specific seats but now anyone can nominate for them, and the governor can pick from any nomination, Dube said. The executive branch will have to change its nomination form, he added. The Legislature doesn’t have to take action, but might consider how it could make the selection process more democratic, perhaps by election and not appointment, he said. 
The ruling applies to future appointments. The judge made clear that nothing in his decision “prevents the Governor from accepting recommendations from any person or group, including the named associations.”
Gov. Kelly Armstrong “respects the court’s ruling, which provides the Governor’s Office additional discretion in appointing members to the Beef Commission,” spokesman Mike Nowatzki said via email.
The North Dakota Monitor left phone messages seeking comment for Commission Executive Director Nicole Wardner, Chairman Brian Amundson and a spokesperson for the Stockmen’s Association. The association president planned to put out a statement Tuesday afternoon.
The commission could appeal to the state Supreme Court.
The judge did not decide everything in the challengers’ favor. They said an eligibility requirement that commissioners are barred from receiving a checkoff refund in the last three years is punitive and discriminatory. Lofgren said the Legislature can set the time limit for the requirement and conditions to the refund. He said lawmakers would rationally want commission members who have paid into the program to be deciding how to spend the money.
