name: Nevada Current
title: Lawmakers mulling cannabis tax revisions
text:
(Photo by Amanda Watford/Stateline)Nevada lawmakers are pondering whether the state’s “maturing” marijuana industry needs to update its tax structure.
Revenue from the state’s cannabis excise tax, which flows into the State Education Fund, peaked in 2021 and declined 40% by 2025. The decline is “in part due to price compression attributed to a maturing market,” according to a new report by a committee tasked with reviewing potential tax changes.
After an initial rush of a new market in 2017 when the state legalized cannabis, the industry has leveled off to more sustainable numbers. Customers and transactions have increased, and the price of cannabis has continued falling, signs the industry is maturing.
For example, the retail price of flowers/buds in Nevada went from $9.02 per gram in 2019 to $4.46 in 2025, a 50% drop. Similarly, infused edibles went from $19.77 per item to $11.81 over that same time span, a 40% drop.
“Overall the annual price trends indicate that Nevada’s cannabis market became less expensive for many of the product categories analyzed,” said Erica Scott, an economist in the Nevada Department of Taxation and chair of the subcommittee that put the report together. “This price compression could be reflective of a combination of factors, which could include market maturation, increased competition, production efficiencies, technological advancements, or greater availability of lower priced products, which in this market would be illicit products and intoxicating hemp.”
The State of Nevada since legalizing marijuana in 2017 has collected a 15% tax on the fair market value of wholesale cannabis and a 10% excise tax on the retail sale of recreational cannabis. Additionally, the retail sale is subject to standard state and local sales taxes, which vary from 6.85% to 8.375%.
The formula the state uses to calculate “fair market value” has been the subject of consternation among cultivators, who have argued the metric has lagged as prices quickly falling, resulting in them being heavily overtaxed. One proposed solution, pitched most recently by Assemblywoman Danielle Gallant (R-Henderson) during the 2025 Legislative Session, was to eliminate the current wholesale tax and increase the retail excise tax to offset the lost revenue.
Gallant’s bill never advanced out of committee but language to study such a proposal was amended into another cannabis bill. That bill created the subcommittee, which presented their final report was presented to the Interim Legislative Committee on Revenue last week.
The report, which emphasized that it was only studying impact and not recommending any specific changes, found the state would need to increase the retail tax to between 12% and 15% in order to offset the eliminated wholesale tax.
Additionally, the state would need to address the impact on local governments, regulatory operations and the State Education Fund, which all currently receive distributions from the wholesale cannabis tax.
So what could this mean for consumers?
Recreational consumers are currently paying a combined retail tax rate around 18%. The tax paid by wholesalers is passed along to consumers as part of the retail price.
Under the proposed restructuring, consumers would be paying a 23% combined retail sales tax rate in Clark County, the county with the highest local sales tax rate. In other counties, it’d be a little less.
Medical card holders are exempt from the state retail excise tax, meaning their prices would likely not change in the short term.
Scott explained that the “assumption is cultivators would not be dropping the price immediately and instead maintaining the previously paid 15% (wholesale) tax as profit.”
But Scott and leaders from the state’s Cannabis Compliance Board added that industry representatives believe wholesale prices would drop in the long term.
“We are getting rid of one big tax – a 15% excise tax on wholesale — and increasing retail tax anywhere from 2 to 5%,” said CCB Executive Director Michael Miles. It’s “not guaranteed it’s going to even out, but the idea is that it should even out.”
Miles noted that Nevada is actually considered “average or below average” when it comes to its taxation rates of cannabis across the country.
The revenue committee took no action on the study but may revisit the issue next year when it meets for the 2027 Legislative Session. Several lawmakers flagged additional data or information they wanted on consumer behavior or the impact other states have seen from raising the retail excise tax. One suggested the proposed changes would be more transparent to customers.
The cannabis subcommittee also explored the emerging “intoxicating hemp” market, which popped up out of a loophole in the federal Farm Bill in 2018 that allowed for the sale of edibles and drinks containing THC. Such products can now be found in smoke shops and gas stations.
The cannabis subcommittee estimated Nevada’s intoxicating hemp market to be about $45 million annually but emphasized that local and national data is scant.
Clark County earlier this year attempted to crack down on unregulated, intoxicating hemp products. But it remains an ongoing issue, Miles acknowledged.
The future of the industry is “rife with uncertainty.” Congress is expected to consider legislation to ban intoxicating hemp later this year.
But, assuming it sticks around, the state should aim for tax parity between intoxicating hemp products and cannabis products, the subcommittee recommended.

name: California
title: California is about to overhaul the way it runs K-12 schools. Will it fix a fragmented system?
text:
In summary
For more than a century the state’s K-12 system has been fragmented between the state superintendent of public instruction, State Board of Education, governor’s office, the Legislature, local school boards and a dozen other entities.


California is on the brink of a total overhaul in the way it governs K-12 schools, but whether those changes actually happen or fade into irrelevance will come down to one person: the next governor.
“We used to ask, who’s in charge here? It was everybody and nobody,” said Michael Kirst, former head of the State Board of Education. “Now we know. It’s the governor. That’s a total sea change – I never thought I’d live to see it.”
In January, Gov. Gavin Newsom proposed a realignment of the education governance structure, which for more than a century had been fragmented between the state superintendent of public instruction, State Board of Education, governor’s office, the Legislature, local school boards and a dozen other entities. That system was so diffuse, according to the think tank Policy Analysis for California Education, that policies were rarely implemented evenly and it was easy to blame someone else when things went wrong.
Newsom’s proposal, Assembly Bill 181, passed overwhelmingly in July. It calls for a new governor-appointed education commissioner, who will oversee the California Department of Education and ensure that policies set in Sacramento are enacted in classrooms. It also strips most duties from the state superintendent, a voter-elected position that will soon have few job responsibilities besides championing various education policies.
The idea is that one person – the governor – will be in charge. Most other states, particularly those with high test scores like Mississippi and Massachusetts, have a similar system.
But that alone won’t fix California’s convoluted K-12 governance, according to researchers Heather Hough and Jason Willis, who recently published a report through a state agency called the California Collaborative for Educational Excellence on what the state needs to do next. 
The new education commissioner needs to simplify and clearly communicate goals for schools, provide stricter oversight and offer more direct assistance for struggling schools. Basically, the state needs to take more responsibility for improving student outcomes, Hough said.
“Right now, if a district is performing badly, there’s not a lot of clarity about what should happen,” said Hough, an education policy consultant. “The state has to be able to step in.”
For example, if a school has persistently low scores on standardized tests, the education commissioner should intervene, Hough said. That could mean bringing in experts, tutors or other resources, or removing barriers. If all else fails, the commissioner should have the power to take drastic action such as replacing the superintendent, she said.
So far, California’s gubernatorial candidates have offered few hints about their plans for education commissioner or K-12 schools generally. 
Xavier Becerra, a former state attorney general and cabinet member under President Joe Biden, said in a recent televised debate that he thinks schools are mired in too much bureaucracy, and schools should hold back students who are failing. Steve Hilton, a former Fox TV commentator, said in his platform he favors education savings accounts that would allow parents to use public funds to pay for private school.
Neither campaign responded to requests for more information.
Pressure on new education commissioner
The next governor will name an education commissioner after they take office Jan. 4, and there won’t be much down time. By early June, the commissioner must produce a draft report for the Legislature on how he or she plans to reshape the system. A final report is due in the fall.
Among the commissioner’s priorities should be strengthening – and expanding – the Department of Education so there’s more oversight and assistance for schools, said Marshall Tuck, executive director of the advocacy group EdVoice.
“We will not have a state that is effectively educating all students unless we have a highly effective state Department of Education,” said Tuck, who ran for state superintendent in 2014 and 2018. “It’s just not possible. And it’s something we have not had.”
Overall, he’s hopeful that the new education commissioner and governor will have the political clout to persuade all the major players in education policy, including the powerful California Teachers Association, to support changes in governance. Previously, the teachers union had opposed Newsom’s plan because its members thought it shifted too much power away from voters and toward the governor. In the past, the teachers union spent heavily on superintendent candidates – including those running against Tuck. 
“This is a real opportunity to change things,” Tuck said. “But it’s very, very important that the governor makes this a top priority and appoints the right person.”
California Teachers Association President David Goldberg said his organization is looking forward to working with the new commissioner, regardless of the union’s past opposition to the idea. 
“We’re hoping for an ally,” Goldberg said, “someone who will advocate for the same things we do and elevate the voices of families and teachers.”
‘An extraordinary opportunity’
In Humboldt County, Superintendent Michael Davies-Hughes is optimistic about the possibility for positive change, and how it could bring about better outcomes for students. A more streamlined system, with a stronger state Department of Education, could reduce the paperwork burden for local schools. That, he said, would give teachers and administrators more time to help students in the classroom.
“Educators spend too much time navigating the bureaucracy. If we can remove those barriers, students will benefit,” said Davies-Hughes, who’s the incoming head of California County Superintendents.
School staff often spend hours a week filling out state-mandated paperwork. For instance, every three years school districts are supposed to make a report describing their finances and goals. One from a small district could top 100 pages. Los Angeles Unified’s is nearly 800 pages. The reports are supposed to be updated regularly.
The new commissioner will have a difficult job balancing policy in Sacramento with the needs of local school districts, Davies-Hughes said. The commissioner will also have to take risks and be willing to stand up to powerful political interests, if necessary.
“This person will have to break through a system that’s been in place for decades,” he said. “Otherwise the current problems will just be exacerbated.”
El Dorado County Superintendent Ed Manansala said that the new commissioner’s role will be important, but it’s only the start. Larger changes in governance could have a long-lasting, beneficial impact on schools and students.
“It’s an extraordinary opportunity to rethink how the whole system works,” Manansala said. “But we need to be able to speak openly about what’s working and what isn’t, and collaborate to create a more focused and coherent system.”
Kirst was an architect of the Local Control Funding Formula, which in the early 2010s shifted the bulk of budget decisions from the state to local school boards. Even though the new structure calls for more power concentrated at the state level, Kirst feels it’s the right path forward.
“I don’t think it affects local control. It adds efficiency,” said Kirst, who’s an emeritus education professor at Stanford. “It’ll actually improve local control because it gives teachers and schools clearer guidance.”

name: California
title: The final stretch: Catch up on what’s happened in the California governor’s race so far
text:
In summary
For weeks, Republican Steve Hilton has tried every trick in the book to boost his candidacy in the California governor’s race. It doesn’t appear to have made a big difference.


With Election Day a week away, the two-years-long race to succeed Gov. Gavin Newsom is winding to a predictable end. 
Polls released throughout the summer and fall show Democrat and former Attorney General Xavier Becerra maintains a commanding double-digit lead over Republican former Fox News host Steve Hilton since they finished in the top two spots in the June primary.
The latest, conducted by Emerson College from Oct. 17 to 19, places Becerra 27 percentage points ahead: 60% of likely voters supported him compared to 33% for Hilton. When pressed, nearly two-thirds of the small share of undecided voters in the survey leaned toward Becerra. 
In Sacramento, policy advocates have for weeks been scrambling for a chance to meet with the presumptive next governor.
If the results hold as expected, it won’t be for a lack of trying on Hilton’s part. 
The GOP candidate, a first-timer in California politics, has tried everything and more to boost his candidacy: barnstorming the state, flooding social media with provocative ads, using AI to portray himself as a gladiator in Becerra’s colosseum and texting selfie videos from Los Angeles’ Skid Row. 
He’s proposing a wide and eclectic range of policies, from $3 gas and steep tax cuts across all income levels to building 10 new cities and establishing an “Office of Fun and Freedom.” (Responsibilities would include loosening regulations on nightlife and allowing dogs in more state parks.) His latest proposal would require animal shelters to notify the public before euthanizing dogs so that someone might adopt them instead. He’s said little about how he would get Democratic supermajorities in the Legislature to support his many plans that would require their approval.
The try-it-all approach has led to some stumbles: His ad series aimed at courting liberals who should “just try” voting Republican triggered a conservative backlash. Days later, he accused Becerra of lying about his parents’ immigrant backgrounds because his father was born in Sacramento, brought to Mexico as a child and then worked as a young person on both sides of the border before settling again in California. Latinos said the accusation misunderstood the common Mexican American experience of families moving back and forth across the border. Hilton, who is British American, moved to California with his wife, a Silicon Valley executive, in 2012.
Republican strategist Mike Madrid said it made Hilton, whom he otherwise praised as a “substantive” candidate, look out of touch: “He’s literally saying, ‘I’m not one of you.’”
Becerra’s approach couldn’t be more different. Careful to avoid flashy promises, he rolled out few specific policies, instead speaking generally about how his decisions would prioritize middle- and working-class families. 
Some of his proposals represent incremental adjustments to what the state already is doing under Newsom, like reducing bureaucratic hurdles for developers to get housing projects approved. His most ambitious campaign promise is for California to continue covering everyone who would lose Medi-Cal healthcare under steep federal cuts of up to $30 billion annually; he won’t say where he’ll find the money, but has said he could cut some wasteful and administrative spending. He also wants to provide certain low-income households two hours of free electricity during off-peak daytime hours, and expand down payment assistance programs.  
He’s leaned hard on his opposition to Donald Trump, who is widely unpopular in California. Trump endorsed Hilton in the primary; Hilton has since tried in the general election to court Democratic voters by saying he wouldn’t align with the president on everything. 
Becerra has been eager to tie Hilton to the president at every turn. The tactic was on full display during a CNN debate last month; it was the only debate Becerra agreed to and did not appear to change much about the race. 
At a Bakersfield rally for Democratic House candidate Randy Villegas, Becerra told reporters he would lead the state to sue federal immigration agencies over their aggressive enforcement. Asked by reporters what he would do about gas prices, Becerra acknowledged that state policies on oil drilling and refining could affect prices, but pointed out the immediate cost issue was Trump’s war in Iran.
“The first thing, obviously, we have to do is get Trump to end his crazy war abroad,” he said. “But what we can do in California is make sure we don’t allow the spikes to come because of anything we do in California.”
Becerra makes appearances in final weeks
After a summer with few public appearances or media interviews, Becerra has been back on the campaign trail in recent weeks rallying voters and volunteers around the state, but often not on his own behalf. With a comfortable lead in the polls, he instead spent most of his time holding press conferences with fellow Democrats to oppose Proposition 39, the Republican-backed voter ID measure, and boosting Democrats running for legislative seats. 
He appeared with several Democrats running in competitive House districts in Southern California and the Central Valley, where Becerra’s campaign believes he could help turn out an important group of Latino voters. 
Perhaps Hilton’s biggest impact in the race has been to force Becerra to answer for Democratic policies that he blames for the high cost of living, and to run on a message of changing “16 years of one-party rule” in an attempt to appeal to the majority of California voters who want the state to go in a different direction. 
In Bakersfield, which sits in a Republican county that supported Hilton in the primary, Becerra said his experience in government sets him apart. He also took care to distinguish himself from Newsom, who has had generally favorable approval ratings, pointing to both his time in Biden’s cabinet and his personal background. 
“I am different from every governor that we’ve ever seen because no one brings the experience or the credentials that I bring, and no one brings the life experience,” he said.
Tim Rosales, a GOP consultant, said Hilton has done the best he could given the Democratic advantage in California, and shown “that a unique Republican personality can influence the political debate to some degree.” He has raised $33.6 million to Becerra’s $40 million — double what the leading Republican candidate raised in 2021 during the failed Newsom recall election.
“He’s run a good race,” Rosales said. “The fact is that Democratic voters in California, which there are a lot of them, can agree with Hilton on the issues. They just want a Democrat to try to solve them.”

name: California
title: Californians revolt against police drones after rapid adoption across state
text:
In summary
Across California, police departments are rapidly expanding “Drone as First Responder” programs, triggering intense public backlash over warrantless surveillance and corporate overreach. 




Public pushback over municipal police drones is boiling over across California, turning routine local policy hearings into high-stakes battles over the boundaries of neighborhood surveillance.
The increasingly heated public debates are driven by landmark privacy litigation and a 2021 law that mandates explicit local board approvals for the use of “military equipment,” including drones. Those disclosures make clear that police are increasingly looking to drones as potential “first responders” in cities like San Francisco, Berkeley, Santa Ana and Stockton — forcing local leaders to face skeptical residents in public hearings required before drone programs can expand. 
At those appearances, law enforcement agencies are pushing to broaden their drone use beyond emergency-only response to aid in everyday patrols, while citizens are concerned  about drones conducting warrantless searches, if municipalities are hoarding too much data collected by drones, and whether drone makers have too much power and information.
Those tensions  were on stark display earlier this month in San Francisco, when a policy  debate at a police commission meeting drew a packed room of opposing residents.
The San Francisco Police Department asked commissioners to approve a policy allowing drones for a wide array of uses, including “public safety response,” active investigations, training, and “community outreach.” While prohibiting random “general surveillance” or tracking activities protected by the First Amendment, the draft stipulated that public footage would be retained for 30 days unless tied to an open investigation.
“With drones, you can fly at much lower altitudes, you can get thermal imaging, you can get tracking.”Katie Inman, attorney at Holland & Knight
Supporters argued the technology is vital for modern crime-fighting. “Public safety and personal privacy shouldn’t be competing interests,” said Anna Carney, president of Stop Crime SF, urging commissioners to give officers every responsible advantage to save lives.
But privacy advocates and skeptical residents saw a slippery slope toward unchecked surveillance, drawing explicit parallels to the contentious rollout of automated license plate readers across the state. In recent years, cities like San Francisco and Stockton built extensive fixed camera networks supplied by vendors like Flock Safety. Now, communities fear that attaching drones to those same networks creates an inescapable, multi-dimensional dragnet — one that tracks citizens not just by car on the street, but from the air above their homes.
“We are all here today because these drones are impacting all of our communities, ” said Manny, a member of the privacy advocacy group DeFlock SF, who urged the commissioners to cancel the department’s contract with drone manufacturer Skydio. “If SFPD truly cared about operating these drones with any respect to privacy, the very least that can happen is one of you make an amendment to require a warrant,” he added, referring to language used in the department’s proposed policy. 
Although commissioners voted to advance the policy to labor negotiations without adding a warrant mandate, the friction displayed in San Francisco reflects a statewide reckoning.
Legal uncertainty and the policy vacuum
The 2021 rules governing military equipment in law enforcement still leave a policy vacuum confronting municipalities across California: Local agencies that deploy drones are stepping  into a legal gray area where technology is far outpacing  state regulation.
A lawsuit against Sonoma County underscores the uncertainty. Privacy concerns  festered for years in the county after officials launched a \drone program in 2019 for code enforcement. But investigators with the American Civil Liberties Union later uncovered hundreds of warrantless searches over private yards, homes, and windows — all conducted without a published policy in sight. In 2025, the ACLU of Northern California sued Sonoma, and last month, the county settled. Sonoma pledged to reel in its drone use, obtain warrants or consent before conducting residential property code inspections, restrict data retention, and directly notify residents if their property was subjected to aerial surveillance.
The case brought to the forefront the complex legal matrix officials must navigate in deploying unmanned aircraft. 
“There’s three main buckets,” explained Katie Inman, a drone policy expert and attorney at Holland & Knight who previously worked at the Federal Aviation Administration. “You’ve got the broad…constitutional law principles, then you’ve got state statutes, and then you’ve got the third bucket, which is FAA operating rules.”
Inman noted that California belongs to a category of states that lack a comprehensive state statute explicitly governing law enforcement drone use, leaving municipalities on their own to read and comply with constitutional Fourth Amendment case law, which protects against unreasonable search and seizure.
She said the Supreme Court has ruled that aircraft surveilling areas that are visible to the naked eye from lawful altitudes do not violate Constitutional protections.
“But those were manned aircraft; they are not drones,” she said. ”With drones, you can fly at much lower altitudes, you can get thermal imaging, you can get tracking, you can get just a lot of hovering — a lot of surveillance potential there that you would not normally have.”
Across the state, nearly 60 law enforcement agencies use drone programs, according to the Los Angeles Police Department. Most foundational policies, including those in Chula Vista, Fremont, and the policy proposed in San Francisco, prohibit random surveillance, but programs diverge when it comes to deployment triggers and public oversight. Departments like Chula Vista deploy automated “Drone as First Responder” units broadly ahead of ground officers for routine 911 calls, whereas newer or more heavily scrutinized frameworks, such as San Francisco’s proposed policy, attempt to draw tighter lines by limiting flights to active criminal investigations, vehicle pursuits, or specific, incident-based emergencies.
Officers with the Los Angeles Police Department  at an active crime scene outside a Superior Grocers in the LAPD’s South Bureau in Los Angeles, on Dec. 7, 2024. Photo by Mark Abramson for CalMatters
Multimillion-dollar contracts and unproven safety claims
Beyond constitutional and policy questions, the rapid growth of drone programs is closely tied to an aggressive push by defense and surveillance technology vendors.
Both the San Francisco and Los Angeles police departments rely on hardware manufactured by San Mateo-based Skydio, while industry peers like Axon, which makes body cameras, and license-plate-reader manufacturer Flock Safety have also aggressively expanded into the market. Skydio originally launched to give extreme sports athletes a way to track and film themselves doing parkour or snowboarding. But after the U.S. government labeled Chinese drone maker DJI a national security risk in 2020, Skydio pivoted to fill the void for military, police, and enterprise customers.
At a recent customer conference, Skydio CEO Adam Bry laid out an ambitious roadmap: small drones for tactical flights inside buildings, mid-range aircraft for vehicle pursuits, and high-speed models capable of traveling 100 mph up to a 30-mile radius. Bry also outlined a future driven by AI, envisioning software that analyzes 911 calls in real time to automatically recommend dispatching an autonomous drone to a scene.
“SFPD should tie deployments to specific incidents… No general routine patrol. No general surveillance.”Jesus Gabriel Yanez, recently-retired police commissioner
Executing that vision requires major investments — from taxpayers and billionaire backers alike. Santa Ana recently greenlit $682,900 for its Drone as First Responder initiative in partnership with Skydio, while the Stockton City Council approved a $3.15 million contract expansion with Flock Safety to integrate six drones into its existing network of 120 license plate reader cameras. In San Francisco last year, the police department received a $9.4 million donation from the crypto billionaire and Ripple cofounder, Chris Larsen, to expand its drone program and surveillance systems, Mission Local reported. 
“The premise of the Bill of Rights is respect for liberty of the individual, and that used to mean something in this city,” a San Francisco resident named Ilona said at the Oct. 14 Commission meeting, lambasting officials for accepting Larsen’s drone donation. “But it doesn’t anymore because now we have sold out to tech billionaires…. SFPD has been sloppy and reckless with our privacy. How can we trust them with these tools?” 
Venture-backed drone vendors have spent heavily to influence local officials to support their expansion — Flock Safety, for instance, has reportedly spent millions of dollars on local and federal lobbying, claiming its technology helped “solve” a million crimes last year alone. Yet researchers are increasingly skeptical of what vendors and law enforcement say the technology can  help accomplish. 
Police argue that drones help them respond to incidents more quickly, help them deescalate potentially dangerous situations, and improve crime clearance rates. A February 2026 study by the UC Berkeley Criminal Law and Justice Center found that while first-responder drones can improve response times, there is no evidence they reduce officer-involved shootings, lower overall use of force, or improve case resolution rates.
The rapid rollout has also intensified community anxiety over interconnected surveillance networks, and intensified the brewing nationwide backlash against AI-powered police tech. 
Jesus Gabriel Yanez, a recently-retired police commissioner, spoke at the San Francisco commission meeting. He briefly read a passage from George Orwell’s dystopian novel “1984” before expressing his opposition to the drone use policy outlined by his former peers.
“SFPD should tie deployments to specific incidents that cannot be addressed without compromising officer safety — period,” Yanez said. “Those are the only times when we should allow for the deployment of a drone. No general routine patrol. No general surveillance.”
Opponents like Yanez point to past instances where California law enforcement agencies illegally shared license plate tracking data with federal immigration authorities, as well as technical missteps like a recent leak that exposed live police drone video feeds online due to vendor misconfigurations. That anxiety over vendor overreach and AI surveillance isn’t confined to California—similar resistance is bubbling up across the country. In Minneapolis, the city council voted to reject a police drone contract with Skydio following community protests over privacy and dual-use military technology. In New Orleans, advocacy group Eye on Surveillance successfully mobilized against a proposed policy that would have allowed weapons on police drones.
Whether through public city council debates sparked by AB 481 or court-enforced settlements like Sonoma County’s, California communities are trying to make it clear that adopting cutting-edge public safety technology will not come at the cost of privacy. The automated eye in the sky may arrive in seconds, but citizens are demanding to know exactly who is watching — and who holds the remote.
CalMatters Technology Reporter Khari Johnson contributed to this report.

name: California
title: AI and social media bans won’t make California kids safer online. It may even be harmful
text:
Guest Commentary written by

Gillian Hayes
Gillian Hayes is a professor and computer scientist at the UC Irvine where she co-directs the CERES Center for Children and the Digital World.


For more than two decades, my research group has been studying and supporting young people with disabilities, as they create and use digital technologies.
In one study of Autcraft, a Minecraft server built for autistic kids, a 13-year-old boy described a rich social life there that included friends he trusted, builds he led, other kids he comforted when they were struggling. 
And yet, when describing this rich social life, he asked, “Will I always be not social?”
This quote has stayed with me. This sweet, social child was measuring his life against a definition of “social” that was not built for him. And the way his parents, schoolteachers and other well-meaning adults were using that definition made him feel terrible about his own experiences and the things that made him happy.
Californians are right to worry about kids online. We are right to demand of our lawmakers, teachers, administrators and tech companies responsibility for what we are all collectively bringing into the world. The lawsuits behind this year’s chatbot bills involve real children who were harmed. 
Somehow, though, we keep behaving as though there is only a binary choice to either ban technologies, whether phones or AI, or keep the status quo. Both options fail the kids who need support the most.
Access bans sound protective, but the evidence so far mostly suggests they are not. 
Australia’s under-16 social media ban, evaluated after three months by both the government’s own regulator and a peer-reviewed medical journal study, found more than 80% of kids still using restricted platforms. They fake their ages, borrow logins and find ways around the ban.
Worse, even when bans do reduce usage, evidence indicates they don’t actually improve things we care about, like mental health and academic performance.
What concerns me most is the possibility that we are now undoing the decades we have spent destigmatizing the use of a variety of assistive technologies and participation in online communities.
We know that many kids go online because these are some of the few communities in which they truly feel comfortable, like the 13-year-old who used Autcraft as his primary social space. Research consistently shows LGBTQ youth find identity support and community online that isn’t always available at home or school. 
Autistic and other neurodivergent kids often find their best friendships in text-based or game-based spaces, where eye contact and improvised small talk aren’t the price of entry.
To be clear, the status quo is not the answer. There are substantial problems with these platforms, even if we restrict our thinking to adults. And none of them were built with childhood or disabilities in mind. 
Change needs to happen. It’s just that we should design better platforms for everyone, rather than banning or restricting them for some.
Recently, with the passage of Assembly Bill 1709, California lawmakers attempted a design-oriented framing, which I greatly appreciate. The law requires social media companies to stop using some of the more problematic design features, such as infinite scroll. 
The problem, for me and for groups like the Electronic Frontier Foundation, is that this law effectively bans social media for people under 16, given how broadly things like “addictive features” are defined. It also requires age verification, which largely doesn’t work and allows the same companies we are worried about to amass even more data about not only kids but all of us, with limited ability to mitigate these risks.
We already have examples of alternative, optimistic futures that don’t create a surveillance state. 
Autcraft is safe by design, with community-enforced rules, trained volunteer moderators and a culture built around acceptance. Likewise, other online communities that focus on popular media and games enable connection and learning that looks very different from what young people encounter in traditional schools. 
Rather than have their curriculum, ideas and social opportunities dictated to them with adult preferences and neurotypical norms, these “neurodiversity oases” allow youth to be in charge of learning and to be driven by an ethos of acceptance within a framework of passion for shared interests. 
The success of these platforms shows we don’t need to ban children from well-designed platforms. Good design can and does work. 
We should hold platforms accountable for what they design and encourage them to make better experiences for everyone, rather than banning some people while creating a surveillance infrastructure that risks harming us all.
California has a real choice this year: pass bans that push youth further from spaces they feel safe or start setting standards for platforms so those spaces actually are safe. The 13-year-old who wondered if he’d always be “not social” was asking us to see his social life, not to take it away.

name: California
title: Will Republicans block Democrats from Congress if they win the midterms? We asked them
text:
In summary
CalMatters asked the nine Republican members of Congress from California whether they signed a pledge agreeing to abide by the midterm elections results. Here’s what they said.


Will President Donald Trump’s MAGA Republican allies in Congress try to block newly elected Democrats from taking their seats after the midterms, claiming the election was rigged?
That worry prompted a bipartisan pair of lawmakers to urge their fellow members of Congress to sign a pledge promising to accept the results of the midterms.
As Trump and his allies aggressively push claims of widespread election fraud, its authors are hoping to head off a scenario similar to Trump’s pressure on congressional Republicans to not certify Joe Biden’s 2020 presidential victory. That triggered the deadly U.S. Capitol riots on Jan. 6, 2021.
California’s current congressional delegation has eight Republicans and one independent who caucuses with them. CalMatters reached out to their offices to learn whether they signed the pledge. 
Only one, Rep. Kevin Kiley, the Republican-turned-independent representing the Rocklin area, said that he had signed it. 
“When the election’s over, we should get things certified and get started on the important work Congress has to do,” Kiley said, adding that he would accept the results should he lose his race to Dr. Richard Pan, a Sacramento Democrat running against Kiley in a newly drawn Democratic-leaning district.
Rep. Young Kim, who represents the Anaheim area, hasn’t seen the pledge, but she “will seat new members,” said her spokesperson, Ellie Gilchrist.
“I can’t answer that,” said Natalia Jovovich, a spokesperson for Rep. Jay Obernolte when asked whether the Republican representing the Hesperia area had signed the pledge.Bakersfield-area Rep. Vince Fong and his wife had a baby last week, so Fong wasn’t available to comment on whether he would seat new members of Congress, his spokesperson, Ryan Gardiner, said in a text message.
Jonathan Wilcox, a spokesperson for San Diego Rep. Darrell Issa, responded to CalMatters’ inquiry but did not say if Issa had signed the pledge.
Spokespeople for the other Republican California U.S. Reps. — Ken Calvert, James Gallagher, Tom McClintock and David Valadao — didn’t respond to CalMatters. 
The Wall Street Journal first reported on the pledge authored by Reps. Don Bacon, a Nebraska Republican, and Josh Gottheimer, a New Jersey Democrat. 
What does the pledge say?
The signatories pledge to oppose “efforts to undermine free and fair elections or override the will of the voters, including any attempt to refuse or delay the seating of any Member-elect who presents a validly issued election certificate.”
The signatories also agree to recognize “the election winners certified by each state pursuant to that state’s law,” according to the Wall Street Journal.
The signers have not been made public, and Gottheimer’s office didn’t respond to CalMatters’ requests to learn which other members had signed it. Bacon’s office referred CalMatters to Gottheimer’s. On Friday, Gottheimer announced that 17 Republicans and Democrats had signed the pledge, but he didn’t say which ones. The U.S. House of Representatives has 433 members and two vacant seats. 
Sacramento-area Rep. Kevin Kiley signed a pledge agreeing to seat newly elected members of Congress. Photo by Anne Wernikoff, CalMatters
Republicans have a razor-thin majority in the U.S. House of Representatives going into November, so even a small number of Republicans sticking to the pledge could block a far-right effort to not seat new Democrats after the midterms. The newspaper reported earlier this month that two Republicans — Reps. Mike Lawler of New York and Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania — had signed it.
The letter comes as federal investigators have been aggressively attempting to validate Trump’s claims of widespread election fraud in Democratic-controlled states, including in California.
Federal agents have arrested a few dozen people across the country in recent weeks for allegedly voting illegally, but so far, they haven’t turned up proof of a widespread conspiracy that Trump has claimed for years is rigging elections in favor of Democrats.
Heritage Foundation pushes Congress
The Heritage Foundation, a think tank that’s influential in Trump’s Make America Great Again movement, in April argued that Congress has the power to investigate elections that members believe to be fraudulent.“Congress can ferret out fraudulent votes of all sorts — not just voting by noncitizens,” wrote Scott Yenor, a senior research fellow at the foundation. “Congress can then declare elections invalid and order a new election when it judges elections to be fraudulent.”
Earlier this month, WNYC, a New York public radio station, asked Rick Hasen, a UCLA law professor, about a scenario in which Republican leaders could attempt to block new members on Jan. 3, when they’re supposed to be sworn in.
“It would be profoundly anti-democratic if it happened,” Hasen told the station, but he said it was unlikely.
“If Democrats have won control of the House of Representatives, and somehow on Jan. 3, somebody tries this kind of maneuver, it’s going to provoke such a massive public reaction,” he said. “This just seems very far-fetched.” 
Given what happened on Jan. 6, 2021, the authors of the pledge think it’s better to be safe than sorry, Gottheimer told NPR in an interview earlier this month.“Because we’ve lived through that,” Gottheimer said, “I think it’s really important that we, again, shut down any opportunity for those who want to stop the will of the people.”

name: California
title: Despite lame duck status, Newsom could take a final shot at utilities’ liability for wildfires
text:
When the California Legislature adjourned for the year nearly two months ago, it left a big issue on the table — or maybe not.
During the final weeks of the 2026 session, Gov. Gavin Newsom and legislative leaders engaged in a mostly behind-the-scenes battle over his efforts to reduce the financial impact of wildfires on three investor-owned electric utilities.
Ultimately Newsom dropped his plan, which would have made wildfire victims and their insurers shoulder larger shares of the burden, because he was unable to amass the votes needed. 
Instead he settled for a token measure, Senate Bill 492, which would cap the fees of attorneys who represent insurers, block speculators from trading on insurance claims and speed up insurance payments to fire victims.
Newsom hailed SB 492 as “real progress for future fire victims,” but it fell far short of the massive overhaul of liability he had sought to protect utilities’ bottom lines and — he said — to stabilize utility costs for ratepayers. He urged the Legislature to revisit the issue after his governorship ends next January.
That, it would appear, was that. Newsom would leave it an unsettled conflict involving many billions of dollars and multiple stakeholders for his successor — almost certainly former Attorney General Xavier Becerra — and the next legislative session.
Or maybe not.
Ever since the Legislature left town, there has been an undercurrent of speculation that Newsom might call a special session after the Nov. 3 election to take another swipe at resolving the conflict, or seek a deal after the Legislature convenes a new biennial session in December — when Newsom still has a month left in office.
Patty Poppe, CEO of Pacific Gas and Electric Co., last week told a conference call of investment analysts that she’s optimistic hearings being staged this month by the state Assembly’s Utilities and Energy Committee and a report the state Public Utilities Commission will issue this week will make the case for Newsom’s proposal.
Consumer Watchdog, one of the most vociferous opponents of Newsom’s plan, released a transcript of Poppe’s remarks, saying they suggest there’s movement toward a special legislative session.
Jamie Court, Consumer Watchdog’s president, also criticized PG&E’s announcement that it would stall new power hookups until the issue is settled. He called it “bailout blackmail” that violates the utility’s duty to provide service.
PG&E is the largest of the three major utilities, which include Southern California Edison and San Diego Gas & Electric. It has the greatest financial exposure to damages if its power lines cause fires, as they have in the past.
Newsom’s proposal is grounded in the belief that if utilities remain fully liable, it will drive consumer power bills — already among the nation’s highest — upward, and make it more difficult for utilities to draw investors and borrow money to meet power demands.
The difficulty Newsom has faced in selling his plan to the Legislature reflects the utilities’ poor image, insurers’ political clout and his lame duck status. The stalemate also reflects uncertainty about whether the many legislative measures passed since the danger first arose have been effective. 
As a background paper prepared for one of this month’s hearings put it: “Seven years and tens of billions of dollars into the safety regime, the central question for this committee is whether California is actually safer from utility-ignited catastrophic fire … Utilities add modeled estimates of how much risk their work has removed.”
It added: “Yet, each measure of success has limits. Weather drives yearly totals, catastrophic fires are too rare to show a statistical trend, risk models change from one filing to the next and overlapping mitigations make it hard to credit any single program.”
In other words, politicians like Newsom are shooting in the dark as they attempt to rationalize and respond to something that is inherently unpredictable.

name: Nevada Current
title: Commentary: So how malevolent will Trump get in Nevada this time?
text:
Hopefully, any Nevada-specific election mayhem Trump may attempt to lob Nevada’s way will suffer the same fate as all the other scurrilous lies he’s hurled at Nevada’s elections over the years, and collapse under the weight of their absurdity. (Photo by Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)“Does Trump even care about the midterms?”
I rhetorically asked that question in the Daily Current newsletter nearly eleven months ago, ten days into the new year.
A couple days earlier the New York Times had published a piece in which Trump had been asked if there were any limits on his authority. Trump’s response: “Yeah, there is one thing. My own morality. My own mind. It’s the only thing that can stop me.”
Imagine that.
“So you can see why he gets bored when he hears about people struggling to pay for rent, groceries, insurance, utilities, and other costs,” I wrote at the time.
His callous disregard for those issues has only intensified since then. Your problems, your family, their future — you — seem to bore the hell out of him more and more with each passing day.
Even in early January it was clear he had no 2026 legislative agenda to speak of. 
Little wonder congressional Republican candidates don’t have one now.
Trump doesn’t care.
And he didn’t then.
He’s limited only by, as he put it, “my own morality.” In other words, as countless observers noted after he confided his faith in his magnificent omnipotence, he’s limited by nothing at all. Certainly not any regard for decency or honesty, let alone fairness.
A chronically self-absorbed monomaniacal jerk even before his faculties started deteriorating in real time on rally platforms, it’s hard to imagine Trump caring one way or the other if Nevada’s Democratic U.S. House delegation — Dina Titus, Susie Lee, and Steven Horsford — won or lost their elections this year.
Congress? Trump’s never shown much interest in it.
Indeed, The New Republic’s Michael Tomasky this week outlined why Trump probably has “a perverse desire for Republicans to lose” the midterms.
The reason “that should be most concerning to normal Americans,” Tomasky writes, is that Trump “wants Democrats to win because he wants to be able to accuse them, with of course no factual basis whatsoever, of cheating.”
Unlike most elections since the start of this century, Nevada isn’t getting national “battleground” attention this year. Not only is there no presidential race, there’s no U.S. Senate race in Nevada. 
Apart from the longtime Republican stronghold that is the state’s second congressional district, a Nevada Republican hasn’t won a single race for federal office since 2014. And the ragtag crop of Republican contenders in Democratically held congressional seats this year appear to be no improvement over all the others who’ve ignominiously lost to Democrats over the last decade.
This year there’s a chance that even the Republican running in Nevada’s reliably ruby red second congressional district, a sorry sack by the name of David Flippo, could lose. Trump (or at least whoever has Natalie’s ear), seems unimpressed. Trump literally phoned in a wretchedly low-energy (and yet jammy-packed with skanky lies) audio clip for Flippo, and that’s about it.
So maybe Trump and his deplorable henchmen in the now corrupt, unmoored and, yes, evil U.S. Justice and Homeland Security departments won’t bother with Nevada, and instead will attack and strive to discredit free and fair elections in … Alaska fergawdsake.
Then again, Nevada has committed the unforgivable sin (in Trump’s bitter, twisted mind) of voting for Trump’s opponent in two out of three presidential elections. It is his habit and custom to abuse Nevada by drawing on signature features of the Trump brand: filthy lies, bogus charges, and unconstitutional acts of malice.
Hopefully, any Nevada-specific election mayhem Trump may attempt to lob Nevada’s way in the coming days, and perhaps weeks, will suffer the same fate as all the other fake crimes he’s accused Nevada of over the years, and get laughed out of court, withdrawn by the people who lodged them, or otherwise collapse under the weight of their phoniness.
As Tomasky notes, the activity that brings the most joy to Trump is snarling bitterly at people. So Trump will be doing that somewhere after Election Day. 
Since Nevada’s definitely not going to decide control of the Senate and almost as assuredly will be incidental to control of the House, there’s a chance — or at least a hope — that  Nevada’s free and fair election will be relatively untroubled by Trump’s tantrums.
But even if Trump does treat Nevada’s election as he’s treated Nevada’s economy, i.e., with mere malign neglect, the damage inflicted by his deliberate and vile efforts to undermine faith in democracy and elections in Nevada and the nation will be with us for a long, long time. 
Like the credibility of Nevada Republican politicians from Gov. Joe Lombardo on down who have apologized for and acquiesced to Trump’s sick lies, trust in democracy is also a casualty of Trump’s “own morality.”
Fortunately, there’s a readily available way for Nevadans to fight back against Trump’s vulgar and relentless assault on democracy: Participation in it.
Portions of this column were originally published in the Daily Current newsletter, which is free and which you can subscribe to here.
